 A. Introduction

1, Briefly state the goal/purpose of the project.

‘The goal of the project is to empower rural communities with engagement in planning and
responsibly managing their natural resource base depends largely on building partnership with
local, national and international institutions that shares their interest and objectives. To empower
the community, the project conducts training workshop, ecological awareness, consensus zones
meetings are required to maximise the empowerment of local communities to play a greater role in
sustainably managing their resource base. The program is also designed to develop skills of
community members capable of responding to the needs of environmental defence.

2. Give a brief summary of the development of the project from the stare un
today, stressing the last year.

‘The sustainable development on the Managalas Plateau has been more a string of endless efforts
implemented over the years as integrated under project management support. Under the key
network of individuals with a long history of involvement on the plateau continue to work togel
with 10 community-based organizations in nurturing the projects objectives despite handicaps. T)
kind of participation has had hidden benefits and become more responsive to the social need on the
plateau. Communities on Managalas Plateau are aware that such program exists to help them
manage their natural resource sustainably and for the long-term benefit of future generation.

“The project establishes partnerships with ten existing zones into the project circle. Among all these
zones except one is unable to reach due to isolation. There are number of workshops conducted by
project staif throughout the zones, All these workshops have been hailed as very suecessfil

Early last year (2003) the project had been able to recruit a full-team of staff which includes the
Executive Director, Program Manager, Project officer and office secretary to plan and boost the
overall implementation of the project. Both Eco-enterprise and woman desk officers were also
recruited in the mid year to strengthen the project on the plateau

In mid last year (2003) PWM management set up the Board of Directors for Managalas
Development Foundation (MDF). he Foundation has appointed the chairman to provide directives
to the members of the association. All Board Members were fairly selected representing 10
‘Community-Based Organizations.

‘9. How has the development on the national and local levels influenced the project activities
during the last year?

‘The development in areas of politics and the national economy has not been helpfil for the
implementation of the program. Powerful political and economical interest groups are now speeding
up the exploitation of the country’s natural resources in order to put the country’s economy bi

track. The recent government has declared tax breaks for companies interested in developing
paln industry. Oil palm is now Papua New Guinea's largest agricultural foreign exchange earner,
ahead of coffee. International financial institutions and other finding agencies provide fncls tor the
company. This model offers the companies a better and more profitable alternative from the
‘conventional large-scale plantations owned by the company. Conversely, growers do not own shares
in the companies,

Time has become critical as the logging companies are encroaching in buffer areas just to the
northeast and southwest of the plateau. Clan groups who have involved in the consensus building
 process over the years, to date are vocal about ensuring sustainable development of the plateaus
according to locally defined guideline.

However, the majority of rural communities in PNG are by no means poor. With the exception of
areas degraded or polluted by large mines, logging, agriculture or fishery projects, the customary
Jand tenure system has enabled local communities to have free and easy access to land, clean water
‘and the abundance of natural resources for the decent quality of life.

‘The granting of oil palm, logging and alluvial mining licenses to foreign developers in the province
will have tremendous impact on the rural communities. This is a set back for the program.
Government services such as roads, schools and hospital are lacking in most rural areas and
development such as oil palm, logging and alluvial mining will contribute to environmental and
social impact on the rural communities. Conversely, the local people do not own shares in the
‘companies.

‘The project has some set back because the road was inaccessible and affect programs that depend on
communities generating own funds to sustain their projects cannot move forward, as road condition
deprived rural communities from accessing the urban markets,

B. Implementation of the project

1. Have the project activities been implemented as planned?

“The program has been implemented throughout the Managalas plateau. Our plans and activities are
within the budgeted Considerably more management supervision for the field staff and skill
training was required at all stages of implementation. Field coordinators were tasked to liaise with,
and advise the leadership of zones now operating. The present of the Project Officer on the plateau
proved to be very suecessfill in coordinating, planning and providing feedback to responses of the
project

2, Have there been any changes in the implementation of the project? (details to
be given in the work plan report)

‘There have been some changes done to the implementation of the project. The allocation of funds
which targeted the combine forum activity was diverted to cater for other activities. The
being that in order to host the program the management has to review the whole process of the
consensus building process. Advice from the Managalas Development Foundation office also
supported this idea. Since previous year (2002) this particular program activity was on hold for
various reasons. The management over look this when planning for financial year 2008. There is
short fall of PNGKS1, 000.00 in this year (2003) budget and changes was done to the programs. All
other activities were executed as planned and achieving our project gouls and objectives.

3. Have the changes, if'any, resulted in any reallocations on the budget?

There has been any re-location of funds as mentioned above in point 2, All planned activities were
fully fimded with support from RFN and ODW budgets.

To which extent have the expected results been achieved?

The project was able to achieve some of the expected results. Field staff were undertaking
Programme planning for duration of a week and as in-house training facilitated by Project officer on
the project-site. Stiff monthly meetings were conveyed to discuss staff issues and plan for
improvements for the project activities. During the year four steering committee meetings was held

 which discussed common issues affecting the project and to tind way of addressing the issues.
Combined meeting was conducted between PWM and MDF which aimed at strengthening both
organizations for collaboration and networking partnerships purposes. The establishment of MDF
Board ensures the way for greater participation from the communities

“The establishment of new zones opens the way and actively involving large areas of the plateau to
participate equally and be part of the project circle. The broad aim is to strengthen the work of the
“Managalas Sustainable Development Project.

‘han on-
ss about

World Environment Day (WED) and conservation awareness are significant programs whi
going project component. These programs complement each other and to inform commun}
the biodiversity and the conservation as a priority for the Sustainable Development Option,

Some of the training workshops were conducted during the year to transfer skills and knowledge on
certain areas which are required by the community based organizations. The skills transfer actually
helps most of the community based organization to focus their work in line with the project
activities. In so doing those communities will try to help their own zones and involving the entire
communities to equally participate in the programs. Woman and youth groups are encouraged

participate meaningful in trainings and in other joint project activities.

5. To which extent has the purpose of the project been fulfilled?

‘Phe program had been conducted widely through out the Managalas Plateau all year round, Field
staff were regularly doing field patrol to respective zones to assist management of each community-
based organisation with technical advice. Many of the communities involved have already
demonstrated considerable initiative in organising themselves to develop a sustainable development
plan for their areas. These clan groups have had considerable experience collaborating with one
‘another and with other outside agencies and organisations on other local development initiative.
‘The proceeding of

‘Training workshops to date make it abundantly clear that communities believe in their social and
economic well-being is dependent on sound, long-term management of their resources. In eflect,
communities are learning to build on existing social capital and to expand it for use with new eco-
enterprise activities.

‘Communities are now becoming aware of the importance of managing their environment sustainably
and taking major roies to help themseives as the result of the training and awareness. Every effort is
being made to ensure that an opportunity to participate in eco-enterprise activity follows the initial
to provide greater awareness and participation with the communities. For instance, zone 10 is
currently under negotiation for Forest Management Area (FMA) to tie up deal with landowner for
exploitation of the rich forest resource. The negotiation is still continuing and this will depend on
the landowner to decide between conservation and development.

6. Please explain the deviations, if any, from the purpose and the expected
results according to the work plan.

‘There are no deviations in the purpose and expected results. The project has highlighted a number
of activities conducted over the years and is still in existence with the expected results where
communities should know about the kind of work done in communities as it relates to their needs
and mechanisms for enforcing their rights.

Hand

How has the co-ordination of the project regarding local, nat
international co-operation, including field visits, functioned?

 ‘The program had been well accepted by the local landowner communities. Interest is growing
amongst CBOs, NGOs and other interested parties who have interest in both conumunity
development and environmental work. Local co-operation between MDF, CBOs and communities is
quite good. They have shown keen interest in participating and supporting the project. The project
is working along side other CBOs program because all of these organizations complement each
other. Their position or work on the ground is able to assist in ways of providing logistic support
such as field patrol, planning of workplan or additional materials for the trainings, Such interest
ng others, shown by literacy program officer at the plateau to effectively perform their
is program has made steady progress over the years

C. Other Considerations

1. Are there any specific internal or external conditions that have influenced the
implementation of the annual work plan?

a) ‘There were a number of internal conditions that influenced the implementation of the
annual workplan. These include staff reluctant to implement these program activities on
specific date as planned. Lack of support from the key community members can have
profound impact on the project. Lack of major contribution and equal participation from all
sectors of the communities can have serious and negative impact over the project if focus is
more on the cargo mentality. Though this characteristic is natural and common throughout
rural areas in Papua New Guinea but it can have adverse impact on the project. For the
effective project implementation there must be effective team work among field staff and
understanding the line of communication in term of disposing particular responsibility on
schedule and working toward reaching the goals and objectives of the project.

Last year (2003) the project depends so much on field staff and management to implement
the program and there was no external support or influence from outside the project.

b) The major external condition, which affects the implementation of the project, is
communication and transportation difficulties given the remoteness of the project. The
training workshops have delayed and prolong to the later date for the most target groups.
Road links from fore to Itokama has been covered by bushes and deteriorating road
condition has resulted in less and less produce transported to urban market for sale. Road
and transportation difficulty stops project programs to be implemented on time. It also
reduces a number of equipment and training materials need be used in the area. Also long,
distance of travelling can be very tiring and uncomfortable for the travelling passengers.

2. Isit probable, after the last year’s development, that the project will reach its
goals or is there a considerable chance for changes?

‘There were a lot of lesson learnt from the project over the years. The project has offered so many
good things such as awareness, trainings, exposure of national issues, exchange of ideas, and
collaboration of partners NGOs and government agencies. Last year saw a number of things which
happened and a fall-team of staff were recruited to plan, coordinate and implement the programs
based on the contract. Though the project is moving at slow phase, we are anticipating that
considerable changes will be achieved as the project plan change to accommodate these expected
results of the program activities will be tangible. Trainings have been conducted to develop the
of field stalf to carry out activities with minimum supervision and also to transfer skills to

ity members. It is also the aim to maintain the staff base so that there are no gaps
project staff leaves the organization.

 3. How has the last year’s development affected the probability of the project's
continuation after the professional and economic support from the RFN has
been phased out?

The project will try to seck funds externally to continue. That however, depends on the program's
end results. ‘That is, if the goals and objectives are met then the program will not continue.
However, several international and bilateral organizations would be approached to seek funds from
them after the project term expires.

4. Please evaluate the project’s relevance and foundation according to national
plans and priorities during the last year.

“The program is relevant at this stage during the economic hardships which are faced in rural
‘communities in Papua New Guinea. Current scenario is that investors are harvesting natural
resource at an alarming rate. In so doing, investors do not comply and failure to produce prope
environmental impact and reconstructive planning prior to government granting operational
licenses, In the course of harvesting the natural resources, socio-economic problems have risen to
new heights; hence the only option to prevent such rising issues is to encourage community
evelopment project and actively doing community awareness trainings.

‘The national government and international government donors have recognized the program as
significant. It is likely that after the end of project fisnding period, some of these organizations will
help in the funding of the project. ‘This is because the program is also in Tine with poverty
alleviation. The program is in line with government priorities and public plans which encourage idea
of “bottom-up planning” for the Local Level and Provincial Government Reform System (PGR
and the Education Reform System (ERS) program in Papua New Guinea. The program equips rural
communities with wider thinking capacity and to produce well-framed plans for development.

D. Audit report

PWM's account will be audited and the financial report will be sent to RFN soon.

Respeettilly Submitted

By Cain Lomai
Programme Manager

 1.00verview

The Managalas Plateau in Oro Province is home to 10,000 villagers,
consisting of over 100 sub-clan groups (buy law the sub- clans own all land
and forest resources) who live in small village communities surrounded by
subsistence gardens. The Managalas Plateau is an striking example of Papua
New Guinea's rich biodiversity and one of the areas highlighted in the 1992
Conservation Needs Assessment Report addressing critical issues
concerning conservation and sustainable development in Papua New Guinea.
The area encompasses of 300,000 hectares from alphine heaths at 12,000
feet to multi-altitude forest along with both primary and secondary lowland
rainforests. 10,000 villagers live in small communities surrounded by
subsistence gardens along a snake-like chains winding through a 2500-foot
plateau in the centre of the region. The Managalas Plateau is bounded by
vast forested ranges on all sides, the Owen Stanley's to the South and West,
the Sibium Ranges to the South East and Mount Lamington and the
Hydrographers to the North and East.

Papua New Guinea is fortunate that community-based tenurial systems on
rights to forests, land, water and fisheries are recognised by the national
government and protected under law. In addition the PNG Conservation
‘Areas Act provides a ready legal mechanisms for local groups to develop and
register locally defined resource management guidelines with the national
government.

The main aim of the project is to provide legai and technica! support to the
communities on the Managalas piateau in the preparation and development of
a proposal to the national government to designate the area as a conservation
area. The idea came from the clan groups on the plateau during the pianning
process for the Managalas Conservation Area Project because they want to
protect the area from industrial logging and other large-scale environmentally
destructive operations. The people on the plateau in their group discussion
first agreed the mapping project should be created in the organisation so
should had to do the boundary mapping to have the plateau secured or
protected from being destroyed by any giant companies such as mining or
logging. The group discussion went on from various clan groups in the plateau
for some times and there were disagreements from other clan groups, which
they don’t agree for the project to be created. This sort of disagreement has
also gone on for a while however the group who have been working in the
programme were the one’s who were doing most of the awareness and
educating the people of the plateau the purpose of the boundary mapping that
it will not affect their livelihood. For this reasons the mapping project truly a
local initiative, which the project partners have supported because it is model
that can be replicated in other communities in Papua New Guinea.

The transferring of mapping technology to the Managalas people have enable
them to communicate their perception of land rights and ownership and
 resource management system with the government and outside companies. It
has also contributed to the process on resolving land disputes in the area and
in a way it has empowered them to make discussions on how best they can
manage their resources for their use now and for the benefit of the future
generations.

The main objectives of the project are as follows;

1. To asses the spatial interactions between communities and resources in
the proposed Managalas conservation area.

2, To document customary rights of local communities with regard to land
and natural resources and to gather and guard traditional knowledge.

3. To identify key decision-makers (olan elders) in relation to land and
resource use and management.

4. To identify and resolve boundary disputes between different landowners.

5. To facilitate community participation in the management of the proposed
conservation area.

6. To increase local capacity deals with external threats.
2. Activities complete to date
2.1, Planning and Recruitment of Project Team

The first thing that have done by Partners With Melanesians (PWM) and
CELCOR with regard to the implementation of the project was to liase with the
community based organizations in the project area to appoint the field
mapping team to carry out the project activities. The project is implemented
along participatory lines so it was important to have people on each side of
the plateau represented on the mapping team. It was agreed that Kingsford
Nichoi (East) and Malchus Kajia (West) would continue to be the field
coordinators. There are now two working teams set up in the plateau One on
the Eastern side and the other on the Western side of the plateau. The
Eastern side is made up of a Field mapping coordinator and two assistants
and the Western side is made up of a Field mapping coordinator and four
assistants due to a bigger area. The team of eight members working as
boundary mappers are trying to map an area of 300,000 hectares.

The idea about a Project coordinator based in Moresby and providing support
to the field mapping team was discussed and agreed by both partners. The
position was advertised and Dickson Darebo who is also from the plateau was
appointed to be the Mapping Coordinator. He is now based in the office of
Partners with Melanesians where he coordinates the project. See attached as
Appendix “1” the duty statement of the Mapping Project Coordinator.

Clan Elders Workshop
 The Clan Elders Workshop # one (1) was held in Numba village from the 19"
to the 21 of November 2002 where it was attended by nearly all Clan elders
of the plateau.

The purpose of the workshop was to educate the clan elders that the main
aim of the boundary-mapping project was to provide legal and technical
‘support to the communities of the Managalas Plateau in the preparation and
development of a proposal to the National Government to designate the area
as a Conservation Area.

In the workshop was also scheduled for the signing of the MOU between the
Puija, Benemo and Mararija clan on their customary land boundaries and in
workshop # two (2) will be other clans who are ready will also sign the MOU
and upon completion of the Managalas Boundary Mapping Project a combine
workshop will be held and the clans who have not signed MOU in the first two
workshops will sign the MOU and that will support the proposal to the National
Government to designate the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area
Project.

So in the first workshop at Numba village the three clans have not come to an
agreement to sign the MOU so it was postponed to the second workshop.

The second clan elder workshop was held at Umbuwora village from the 27”
to the 31" of January 2003. All clan elders of the plateau, the external
boundary clan elders, the CBO’s, councillors and the communities of the
nearby villages to witness the signing of the MOU's attended the workshop.
However, we advised them that there was an instruction from Mr. Ase that
there will be no signing of the MOU's in this workshop.

Since Damien instructed us not to allow any signing of MOU at this workshop
but in our own interest we asked the three clans who came from Numba
whether they were ready to sign the MOU but they replied and said that they
haven't come to an agreement yet.

So we asked all the other clans if any one is ready we could find out and seek
advice from Damien and if possible the clans can sign the MOU’s at the
Serefuna Para-legal training. When we asked all the clans they said that they
were not ready but only six (6) clans who share the same customary
boundaries said they are ready and will sign the MOU at Serefuna when
Damien agrees.

Then we advised them that if Damien agrees for the signing of the MOU at the
closing of the Para-legal training workshop at Serefuna we would inform the
both clan elders to attend the workshop and sign the MOU.

When | saw Damien about the six (6) clans agreed to sign the MOU at the
closing of the Para-legal training he agreed on that so | informed the
respective clan elders to attend the workshop and sign the MOU.
 Signing of MOU

At the closing of the Serefuna Para-legal training workshop from the 17" to
the 21" February 2003, the Moeko clan of Kuae village in the Afore District,
Oro Province signed an MOU with the Aubi clan of Wasaero village in the
Kokoda District, Oro Province. The Tuok clan of Anatua village also in the
Afore District signed an MOU with the Imuani clan of ljaro village in the
Kokoda District. The third party was the Uagi clan of Anatua village in the
Afore District singed an MOU with the Misai clan of Tetebedi village in the
Kokoda District, Oro Province. Appendix “II” is the copies of the MOU signed
by the respective clan elders for their respective customary land boundaries.

In the second clan elder workshop and at the Serefuna Para-legal training
workshop we asked the clan elders about what's causing the mapping to
progress slowly. When the question was raised majority of the clan elders
replied and said there was not enough awareness on the external boundaries.
So the internal clan elders all agreed that and said to cooperate with the
mapping team and will go out and do more awareness on the external
boundary and identify where the boundary lies so that the mappers can do the
mapping without any more problems and disputes. Attached, as Appendix
“III” is a copy of the major activity plan for the next eighteen (18) months of
the extension of the contract. This will depend upon producing of the
progressive report for the first contract agreed between CELCOR and the
UNDP/GEF Small Grant.

2.2 Arrangement for Management of the project during the extension
period

The mapping project is one component of the larger Managalas Conservation
‘Area Project, which is implemented by Partners with Melanesians (PwM) a
national development and Conservation NGO. The initial work on the
mapping project was done under a small grant from the MacArthur
Foundation through Education Development Centre; an USA based NGO
working with Partners With Melanesians. When the funding finished there was
aneed for the continuation of the project so CELCOR secured additional
funding from the Rainforest Foundation and the UNDP/GEF Small Grant
because of the shortage of staff in the Partners With Melanesians office.

After all in managing the mapping funds for three (3) years CELCOR had lot
to do and said will not secure any more funds for the project and the issue
was taken to the Boards of the two organizations where it was approved.

The Executive Director of CELCOR then written a letter to the UNDP/GEF
‘Small Grant to transfer the mapping account to PWM so it can now manage
the funds and secure additional funding for the project. The arrangement was
then approved by a form of MOU between the two organizations. Attached, as
Appendix “IV” is the signed copy of the MOU between PWM and CELCOR
‘As part of the arrangement PwM will now manage the funds and continue to
implementation of the project. All the equipment purchased and continues to
 purchase additional needed equipment for the project will be controlled by
PWM, as it is our hope that they can be used for similar activities in other
communities in PNG. There are no problems with this arrangement and the
two organizations plan to maintain such a relationship in replicating the project
mode to other communities in the future.

2.3. Awareness in External Boundary Mapping

After the agreement by the clan elders the western flank mapping team
‘combined with the eastern flank team and with the combination of the eastern
clan elders did awareness on the eastern external boundaries. In the
awareness when the two parties (clan elders) identified where their boundary
lies and if the area is not mapped the mapping team would stop the
awareness and map the identified

boundary and continue again with the awareness.

Aiter the awareness on the eastern flank the western field coordinator was
asked to travel to Sarawak in Malaysia to share the experience with other
friend NGO's in there. During this time the western flank field assistants joined
with the eastern flank team and completed mapping the eastern flank areas,
which were unmapped.

When the western flank field coordinator returned from Sarawak we travelled
together to the project site. It was on the Easter weekend when we went
home so the field coordinator has to spend some time with the family.

On the 28" April the Mapping Coordinator, Western flank Mapping team, the
CBO's zone 1 & 2 and the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) staff
set off for a three week external boundary awareness. The awareness was
done on the external boundaries and over the Owen Stanley Range to the
Central Province.

The out come of the awareness was very good and the both clan elders (the
internal and external) agreed to cooperate with the mapping team and
complete the mapping quickly so an MOU can be signed between the two
parties to support the other document for a proposal to the national
Government to designate the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area
Project.

Itis very hard for the mappers to go into each clan members land and do the
mapping so in order for the clan members clearance and allow them to map
their land they have to educate them first by means of awareness and then
once they agree for the mapping to take place the mappers then map their
land.

2.4 Training of Project Team.
 There were two separate training’s done so far in the month of March 2002.
The training’s were GiS and Landscape training workshop planning in
Madang from the 18" to the 28" of March, 2002 by the Mapping Coordinator
and the two Field Coordinators Mr. Malchus Kajia and Mr. Kingsford Nichoi
have attended the training exercises on how to use GPS and Compass where
they want to be familiar in Alotau by the Technical Adviser Mr. Richard
Brunton from the 21" of March to the 18” of April 2002. Attached, as
Appendix “V” js the training report.

The results of this training’s are okay because they are putting into practise
what they have learnt. One of the results of the training is the way points the
Field Coordinators have recorded on the GPS have been entered into the
‘computer by the Mapping Coordinator and printed out the work been done so
far and there is more points yet to be entered and printed out.

2.5 Recording of Clan Groups and Clan Elders.

There is no register of customary land and landowners in Papua New Guinea
including the Managalas plateau. This does not mean that things are chaotic
and unmanageable. Papua New Guinea has thousands of years of settled
agriculture and traditional land management systems. The people basically
know who owns what land and who belongs to which tribe or clan. This does
not mean that there are no disputes over land ownership. Among the
Managalas, as well as elsewhere in PNG, land was acquired and boundaries
established in different ways including the use of force. The land is owned
and controlled by small social units better known as clans. A landowning
group or clan is that group of people empowered by custom to make
fundamental decisions about their land with reference to any other group.

The mapping project, which is a component of the Managalas Conservation
Area Project, seeks to strengthen plateau wide support for sustainable
developed by the clans and to secure partnership agreement between the
PNG government and the people of the Managalas plateau. For this reason
part of the mapping teams effort was to record each clan group names and
clan elders by consulting the clan groups in each village on the plateau.
Attached as Appendix “VI” are the names of clan groups and the clan elders.

3.0Activities still yet to be completed

3.1 Training Workshop for Mapping Field Assistants.

The training of the field mapping team is to enhance the capacity of the local
mapping team to carry

down to Vuvu lake and finishes at Babarobo where it joins the mapping done.

text:
7 oro CONSERVATION PROJECT

by Harry Aurere of Center for Environmental Law and
Community Rights Inc.

The world's largest butterfly,
Queen Aiexandra’s:
Bir. is found only in the
Managalas Plateau of Oro
Province of Papua New
Guinea. It has a wingspan of
up to 30 centimetres. “The
lifespan of Queen Alexandra's
Birdwing (QABB) is
approximately seven months.
Females lay extremely large
eggs, about 0.16 inches in
diameter, on the leaves of the

pipe vine Aristolochia

‘Order: Lepidoptera schlecteri, which later serve
Family: Papilionidae as the exclusive food source
Genus: Troides for larvae. After about four
species: alexandrae months, the larvae

metamorphose into adults,
which may live for three months. Although this butterfly is a strong flier, it
usually remains within a limited home range. Adults are

rarely eaten by predators; however, eggs are eaten by ants, and larvae are
preyed upon by snakes, lizards, and toads, as well as by such birds as
drongos, cuckoos, and crow pheasants.”

PacScOrean
Oro Conservation Project
10s New Cures
In 1994, a study was conducted for a
conservation project in Afore area of the
Oro Province where the butterfly is
concentrated. And in 1995, the project got
off the ground as was since known as the
Oro Conservation Project (OCP).

Papua New Guinea in Southeast
Asian Region

The project was funded by Australian
Government's International Aid agency,
AusAid. The project, as was reported was a success in many ways. However
many questions are stil unanswered today. One such question was on the

* http://wwnw.butterflies.com/monthlyqueenalexandrasbirdwingbutterfly.htm

©2003 CELCOR INC.
 clarification of how to successfully captivate the rare QABB so that it could be
farmed to generate economic value to the local s of the area?*

The QABB project ceased in 1999. The people were not told of its wined—up.
AusAid hand over the project to Conservation Meianesia without proper
handover takeover arrangement. The locals were not aware of this.

An Australian academic lecturing at the University of Technology of Papua
New Guinea was appointed as the chief research officer of the project. The
academic, at that time was doing his PhD research into insects, and this gave
him the best opportunity to help in his thesis. For him, it was an academic
project that was for his own benefit. He gave less attention to the economic
Potential of the project. This was a real insult to the Australian taxpayers.

The project silently winded up when the officer has gathered enough
information for his thesis. The project lasted five years, an appropriate
timeframe enough to write up a thesis.

At the recent meetings with the locals, people still thought that the project is
still run by AusAid with CM as part of the initial project partners.

In the initial stages, AusAid officers were advising the people that it was a
conservation project and all about sustainable development. People were
happy about the incentive and talked much about sustainable development.
However, when the people ieamt that it was a butterfly project, they were a bit
concern. No proper consultation with the people occurred about the butterfly
project. People were left guessing right from the start. It was really confusing
Mr. Willsion Wahamu of Semehara Village said, “The officers were collecting
vines but did not explain why. This was a concern for us because we thought
it was in the profit motive. They were also taking photos of the butterfly and
vines.”

“People were net clear pf the project.” One villager, Uledi, of Afore said.

Hired workers did most butterfly work, while the villagers were left out. The
villagers were only told to monitor the butterfly's movement, lying of egg and
so fort without pay.

The peopie were proud to see the infrastructure that come with the project,
but were disappointed that it did not benefit all the people of Managalas.

“Awareness on the butterfly was done on brief cases. We were interested but
‘suspected that they were selling the butterflies,” Mr Benjamin of Dariki Village
said.

There was no proper train for the people to catch butterfly or to nurse and
manage them. The conservation part was ok because the people are familiar

* Lester Seri, Executive Director Conservation Melanesia. Letter to the Australian High
‘Commissioner, 7” November 2002

©2003 CELCOR INC.
 with it through their traditional shift cultivation and nomadic traditional lifestyle.
The people lack knowiedge of finance and how to make income with the
project. That part has been lacking since the inception of the project and did
not help much to the people.

Rabbits

After the project has got off the ground, Mr Robinson initiated another project.
This time it was the rabbit project. The people were told to substitute their
protein with rabbit instead of the local meat.

Fritze Robinson told the locals that they were in desperate need of a source of
protein.

To many, people rabbit was a strange animal. They have never seen this
animal before. They do not know of its habits, and feedings. There were no
proper rabbit management workshops and programs done for the people. Yet,
rabbits were imported in cages and given to villagers. Some villages include
Kwainu and Tubone.

Management of rabbit was a new thing to the locals. It was not like pigs and
chickens that they use to fend for themselves. It was labour intensive. Very
demanding work. Feeds were cut in the morning, lunch and dinner to feed the
rabbits. Rabbits love kaukau leaves, thus endangering the early harvest of the
tubercle plant

Women

The project did not over look the role of the women in the community. They
were taught sewing, cooking and nutrition. Many women were happy with this
However, in cooking and nutrition, recipes taught and used lack local
ingredients. There were problems in the sewing as well. There were riot
enough sewing machines to cater for all the women in the training. There
were only two sewing machines for about 10 villages. After the butterfly
project ceased, all these goodies also ceased. Sustaining of sewing did not
occurred. The two sewing machines, worked for a while but lack of
maintenance saw them out of service.

Analysis

The project although highlighted the need to protect this rare butterfly, did
very little to help sustain the project after AusAid funding ceases. The road
leading to the project site has since being neglected.

The Oro Bay-Afore road is a national road, but is now a bush track with only
one vehicle servicing the people. This road, according to the locals, was a
better road during the project period. It provides a vital link between the
interior people and the coastal, to health, education and other services.

©2003 CELCOR INC.
 OCP was a national project and as such was the road. But when the project
ceased, all the infrastructure development in the area collapsed. People of
Afore transport their cash crop, Coffee Beans on this national road but this is
not the case now. Reports from the area noted that for almost 3 years now,
the Itukama-Afore people have not been able to market their coffee beans
due to the condition of the so called Afore national road.

‘One major concern with this project was the accommodation facilities of the
scientists working there. The houses were modest high covenant with solar
water system, satellite phone system, and electricity and other modern
technology in piace. The phone system was such that to call within Papua
New Guinea, one has to call first to Australia and from there, will direct your
call to PNG. This is an example of why people were suspicious of what was
going with in the high ranks of the projects leadership.

Money used in the project was not retained in the area to help the local cash
flow. As in the case of many donor-funded projects, project consultants,
mangers, contractors were all Australian.

There was also now training for localisation after the expatriate mangers and
scientists leave the project after their contract. This was obvious in the QABB.
project. Currently, there is no one in the area that had a proper train in from
the project.

Conclusion

The QABB project was a good project in that it could have helped the local
generate the much needed cash to improve the living standard in the area. It
was also a good project because of the conservation effort in made on the
QABB from unplanned exploitation of forests.

However, much has to be decided on given the following scenario from the
project

1. Lack of consultation with the locais at the initial stages of the project.

2. The contracting of an academic with personal interest n the project to
conduct research for his PhD thesis.

3. Lack of transparency in the way the management of QABB was

conducting the research program.

Lack of localisation training program.

Introduction of an alien animal in the area.

Hiring of consultants not familiar with area at feasibility stages.

Lack of transparency in the projects wind-up program.

Noose

Given this, it can be concluded that the project was never intended to help
develop and conserve the butterfly, rather to exploit the local people in their
ignorance.

© 2003 CELCOR INC.

Pre-test and post-test activity and percentage
A Pre-test was also given to the participants to evaluate, asses and identify individual

a) Pre-test - 70% not clear , 30% understand.

'b) Post-test - 17% not clear, 83% understand

From these percentage it clearly indicates that almost all participants who came for the
training did not have any idea of how to cultivate and farm vanilla, Though the interest
was very high as obvious from the participation list, most participants (70%) came with
the intention to acquire some basic information and knowledge indicating fheir lack of
understanding on vanilla. Towards the end of the training, many came to understand how
to farm vanilla as indicated in the above 83%. As a result the training was very successful
and useful as most people were able to grasp a lot of knowledge in-order to set up their
own vanilla farms in their individual communities.

5.3 Methods /Activities conducted

© Method of Propagation (How to grow vanilla)
To start a vanilla farm, farmers must first clear a land area and establish shades and
support. The spacing of the shades must be a triangular spacing of 2.5m
Planting should be done six months after the shade establishment. To plant vanilla,
cuttings should range from a measurement of $0cm-100em. With two leaves removed
from the nodes, a hole is dug 10cm deep and 30cm long. Place the two nodes in the
hole and cover with soil. Leave the other portion to stick out to allow the wound to
heal up

* Crop Husbandry
i) Weeding:
Weeding is not necessary however controlling of climbing plants must be carried out
to control overgrown of weeds. Spades are recommended to use to clean around the
vanilla garden and the weeds can be used as mulching

ii) Muichii
Mulching is found to be a very important part in vanilla cultivation. There are two
types of mulching; temporary mulching and supplementary mulching.

1. Temporary mulching,
Placing of organic matters around the base of the vanilla plant, such as peelings
from vegetables, weeds from weeding. etc

‘These are mulches that last longer such as coconut husks and betel nut skins that
can be used as sponges to hold the content of water to control the amount of water
that is needed by the vanilla crop to grow.

Researches have proved that mulching gives higher yield in terms of production
quantity.

iii) Pest and Diseases:

 ‘© Pollination of vanilla flower:

Pollination of vanilla is the transfer of the pollen to the stigma. Fertilization occurs
when pollination is successful. In vanilla this done on the same flower by using a splinter
to carry the pollen grain and care fully deposited to the female part or stigma

© Method of pollination.

The vanilla flower is held in between the thumb and the pointer of one hand. Using a
small stick, carefully push back the cover covering the male and the female part of the
flower. Now use the same stick to carefully pick out the pollen grain and place it into the
cavity containing the female part or stigma

Green bean harvesting

Vanilla beans are ready for harvesting 7-Omonths after pollination. When the vanilla
beans changes color from darkgreen to lightgreen, it is s ready for harvesting. The beans
are harvested by hand picking.

© Curing of vanilla beans

After harvesting the beans are placed or spread over a wooden tray and left indoors
for them to wilt and change color from green to brown. This is done for a period of 7-10
days. The beans are then spread on a dark blanket and left in the sunlight for 3hours
(10:00am- 1:00pm) for up to three weeks. When the beans get oily then reduce the time
to Thour per day for Iweek. After this, the beans are sorted out into sound, split and
damage. The beans are then bundled in 200grams and sealed in an airtight container for
conditioning. It takes 5-6months for conditioning. After conditioning the vanilla beans
are now ready for sales

Partners With Melanesians Inc. is one of  
the longest serving Conservation NGO 
still functional amidst the changing and 
challenging political and socio-
economic conditions which caused 
similar organizations to change their 
visions, missions, objectives and 
aspirations or to cease operations.
Background
2002 - 2006
The first strategic plan for PWM was 
developed in 2001, following the first 
external evaluation of PWM’s work on 
the proposed Managalas Conservation 
Area Project. In 2006, PWM ventured 
beyond Managalas to carry out a 
number of scoping activities in other 
local areas upon the interest and request 
of the people. Scoping was conducted 
in areas of Wowonga, Musa and also in 
the Lembena area bothering the East 
Sepik, Enga and Western Highlands 
Provinces. Wowonga and Musa did not 
pass the criteria due to various reasons, 
while PWM began community mobilizing 
in Lembena. However, local political 
differences interfered with work which 
resulted in the early exit. Subsequently, 
PWM in consultation with the donor and 
partners shifted its efforts to 
concentrated on Karimui Conservation 
Area Project, since the local CBO there 
for 4 years consistently requested and 
followed PWM to work with them as its 
partner.
2007 - 2011
The second Strategic Planning 
Document ensured high concentration 
of sustainable livelihood activities to 
support the conservation efforts on the 
Managalas Plateau. The document also 
highlighted systems and procedures to 
be put in place along the systematic and 
strategic lines of the various programs 
that should be accomplished with a 
thorough Organizational Development.
However, Projects like the Managalas 
Organic Coffee Project faced with, high 
establishment, operational and logistics 
costs from the farmers to the markets, 
coupled by natural disaster and miss-
management led to an early closure 
without realizing its full potential. The 
following year, PWM ensured a desk-top 
organizational development review in 
March 2012, of which recommendations 
from the review set the basis for the 
organizational development workshop 
that took place between end of June –
to early July 2013. The organizational 
development workshop ensured PWM 
was characterized through the different 
stages of an organizational development 
cycle, where PWM’s life stage was 
clearly visible as one reaching its final 
stage.
2013 - 2017
The third Strategic Planning document 
made certain the recommendations 
from the second evaluation were 
considered for implementation. PWM 
conducted an organizational retreat in 
February 2016, to revisit its Vision, Mission, 
Goal, Objectives and Values, making 
slight alterations to fit into the changing 
economic and social conditions. 
PWM re-defined its Vision from: “Well 
informed, organized, motivated and self-
reliant societies living in peace and 
harmony with their environment” to 
“Melanesian societies living in peace 
and harmony with nature and the 
environment”. The Mission was also 
redefined to link the objectives. It was 
highlighted during the retreat that 
communities perceived PWM as the one 
responsible for ensuring community 
development, thus the word 
development was changed to correct 
this miss-conception.
From: “PWM is committed to facilitate, 
formulate and strengthen conservation 
and sustainable community 
development efforts through education 
and consensus building process with 
effective networking and partnerships” 
to “PWM is committed to facilitate, 
formulate and strengthen conservation 
and sustainable community initiatives 
through education and consensus 
building process with effective 
networking and partnerships”.
2018- 2022
In this fourth strategic document, PWM is 
aligning its work with the Government’s 
Vision 2050, especially Pillar 5 on 
“Environmental Sustainability and 
Climate Change,” and as embedded in 
the 4th Goal of the Country’s 
Constitution “Papua New Guinea’s 
natural environment to be conserved 
and used for the collective benefit of us 
all and are replenished for the benefit of 
future generations”.
PWM is also guarded by the overarching 
policies including the ‘Environment Act 
2000’ and the Protected Areas Policy’ in 
achieving conservation outcomes in its

Managalas Conservation Area Project
The Managalas Conservation Area Project
(MCAP) is the first and longest of the PWM’s 
conservation projects, spanning more than 30 
years and covering 360,000 hectares of land. The 
Managalas Conservation Area Project is situated 
on the Managalas Plateau in the Ijivitari District 
of Oro Province.
Partnership with the local communities began in 
the 1983 with a literacy program by staff and 
students from the Language and Literacy Dept of 
the University of Papua New Guinea which 
eventually developed into a conservation 
program in 1997 when the people saw the need 
to protect the pristine rainforests of the Plateau 
and in it the richly diverse and unique 
biodiversity.
In 2002 it was decided that a conservation area 
should be established to give more ammunition 
to the protection and conservation effort 
through an official referendum as a National 
Gazette through the Conservation Areas Act of 
1978.
The proposal for conservation area status was 
submitted in 2012. After 30+ years of 
conservation work, the Managalas Plateau area 
was officially declared a conservation area on 
27th of November 2017 by the Minister for CEPA 
& Climate Change, Hon. John Pundari.
Under the conservation area status, the Plateau’s 
forests and biodiversity is protected from 
destructive development practices but the 
challenge now is in the continued management 
and sustainability of the conservation area and 
efforts. The challenge has been taken up by the 
local Managalas community together with its 
local umbrella Community Based Organisation, 
the Managalas Conservation Foundation with the
continued support of PWM. 
Inaina Wildlife Management Area 
(IWMA)
Is the PWM’s smallest conservation project 
located in Inaina Which is in the Kairiku Hiri
District of the Central Province. The IWMA exists 
within the Fagagara Clan land boundary and 
covers an area of 9,712.2 hectares.
PWM entered into partnership with the Fagagara
Clan upon their invitation in 2009 to protect their 
forests and river ways after extensive logging for 
over 10 years so it can be rehabilitated and 
conserved for the future of the people of Inaina.
IWMA was given the Wildlife Management Area 
Status and gazetted on 23rd March, 2017.

Project
The Proposed Karimui Conservation Area Project 
( PKCAP ) is the second of PWM’s proposed 
conservation projects and is located in Karimui/ 
Salt Nomane District situated on the edge of the 
Southern part of the Chimbu Province. 
This conservation project is a partnership 
between PWM and Karimui Conservation and 
Resource Management Programme Inc.                 
(KCRMPI) upon their invitation in 2008 to work 
with them and the local community in protecting 
and conserving the natural biodiversity and 
resources at the same time empowering the 
community to make informed decisions 
regarding their land and resources.
The focus of the conservation area is around the 
Mt Karimui and covers an area of 14,000 
hectares. It is PWM and the local CBO and 
community’s aim to have the target Mt. Karimui 
area protected under the Protected Areas Act 
and have the “Conservation Area Status” in the 
very near future.

Conservation Area Project
The Proposed Collingwood Bay Conservation 
Area Project ( PCWBCAP ) is the most recent 
addition to PWM’s conservation projects and is 
located in the Tufi LLG, Ijivitari District of the Oro 
Province.
Work is only in its initial phase of PWM’s

The CWB communities have had a long history of

now have taken the bold step with the 
partnership of PWM to conserve their forests and 
marine environment, a total of more than

The workshop took three (3) days

PWM Strategic Plan 
 
2013 - 2017

Background and Introduction 
 
Partners With Melanesians Inc. is a National Non-Government Conservation and Development 
Organization registered in 1998.  
 
PNG Trust as it was known then, began as a project by the University of Papua New Guinea Language 
and Literature Department in 1984 with initial work on the Managalas Plateau actively engaged in 
literacy. 
 
PNG Trust ventured into Community Mobilising and Consensus Building in the late 1980s. In the 
1990s when a number of donors became interested in the work on the plateau, the idea of formally 
registering this organization became eminent, thus Partners With Melanesians Inc. (PWM) as it is 
known today, was registered with the Investment Promotion Authority in August 1998. 
 
PWM was actively engaged in Community Mobilizing and Consensus Building, centred around family 
units and clan groups, who were organized in their traditional structures, discussing issues affecting 
them and working on local solutions in enhancing their wellbeing. 
 
In 2001, an external evaluation was called for the Managalas Plateau followed by the development 
of the first strategic plan for PWM. The evaluation took stock of what happened in the past 18 years 
and the next direction in which PWM needed to take. Recommendations from the evaluation 
resulted in the formulation of the 2002 – 2006 PWM Strategic Plan.  
 
It took PWM 18 years (1984 – 2002) in engaging in Community Mobilising and Consensus Building 
with the 20,000 (2000 census) people including men, women and children of the Managalas Plateau, 
of the Oro Province. To date, PWM has taken Community Mobilising and Consensus Building to scale 
by engaging with communities in new project sites, a skill PWM is claiming ownership of as her area 
of expertise and is seeing this process as the corner-stone of community engagement followed by 
conservation and sustainable development options. 
 
In 2003, solid conservation work began on the Managalas Plateau as PWM began preparing the 
application for declaring the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area. Within this period, 
Rainforest Literacy was also introduced which actively engaged community members as the primary 
target audience, engaged in multi-channel learning process on the awareness and importance of 
looking after the environment and its resources without depleting the resource base. This concept 
was ideally complemented by the Community Consensus Building process where clan groups were 
passionately engaged in the discussions and were standing by their decisions in working vigorously 
toward having their area declared a Conservation Area. 
 
In June 2006, PWM developed its 2nd Strategic Plan for 2007 – 2011 with more focus in achieving the 
Conservation Area status for the Managalas Plateau while PWM was looking at scaling down work 
on the Plateau and venturing into possible new sites. 
 

PWM Strategic Plan 
 
2013 - 2017
 
5 
 
Over the years, PWM also realised the need for cash on the Managalas Plateau (sometimes referred 
to as the Managalas Conservation Area Project or MCAP) and, apart from introducing other minor 
alternative income options, between 2006 and 2007, PWM secured funding from the DOEN 
foundation of the Netherlands and began operating an organic coffee venture, registered as the 
Managalas Organic Coffee Project, promising a steady cash income to the farmers as well as good 
premiums. However, high operational costs coupled with miss-management, led to an early closer as 
DOEN withdrew its funding and the project came to a halt early 2008. 
Consequently, toward the end of the 2007 – 2011 Strategic Plan, an independent evaluation of the 
MCAP was conducted by Nancy Sullivan & Associates in 2010, of which specific recommendations 
were made for the way forward for PWM. In 2011, PWM considered the recommendations of the 
evaluation and made efforts in implementing them. 
Recommendations of the 2007 – 2011 Strategic Plan also identified the need for an Organizational 
Development to determine a structure along the strategic lines of the programs.  The Plan also 
pointed out that while the strengths of the organization is visible, the challenges are more visible as 
there need to be staff operational guidelines, development plan, benefit packages revision, contract 
and terms of reference for staff, a personal and organization value systems which deemed to be 
lacking. Furthermore, reporting structure, processes, procedures, community relationship guidelines 
and many other protocols that need to be included in the Human Resource Handbook was a need 
identified which must be addressed by an organizational development workshop. Adding that only 
when these challenges are addressed adequately, the organization will be strengthened to continue 
to grow and do its job well. 
In adhering to this recommendation, and to set the pace for a thorough Organizational Development 
process to take place, PWM engaged an independent desk-top review of the systems and 
procedures in place and the report was released in March 2012. 
Between 2003 and 2012, in a total nine (9) years, PWM concentrated in preparing the application for 
the Managalas Conservation Area Project while exploring opportunities in potentially new sites with 
scoping visits to the Musa and Wawanga areas of Oro Province, Lembena at the boarder of Enga, 
East Sepik and Western Highlands Provinces, and Karimui in Simbu Province. 
The Musa and Wawanga sites were dropped for a number of reasons while PWM moved into 
Lembena and conducted community entry and mobilising at the invitation of the locals. However, 
local political differences developed conflicting ideas on how people perceived the work on the 
ground which resulted in a current law suit at the Enga District Court. Consequently PWM moved 
out of Lembena and concentrated its efforts in potentially new sites including the Ona Keto 
Community Reforestation Project and the Proposed Karimui Conservation Area Project where an 
MOU was signed between PWM, the Local CBO partner, the Karimui Local Level Government, and 
the Chimbu Provincial Government at the end of 2011. PWM is currently conducting scoping into the 
Proposed Inaina Wildlife Management Area Project in Central Province. 
Ideally, 2012 was seen as the end of the second phase of PWM’s efforts in preparing the application 
for the Managalas Conservation Area Project, soon to be declared as the country’s biggest 
Conservation Area while engaging in new sites. Subsequently, PWM also developed its 3rd Strategic 
Plan 2013 – 2017 in April 2012. 

PWM Strategic Plan 
 
2013 - 2017
 
6 
 
PWM now see 2013 and beyond as the beginning of a new era in its effort in continuing to 
strengthen the management of the Managalas Conservation Area Project after its declaration while 
engaging in new sites in community consensus building and mobilising, working and addressing the 
threats of climate change through community forestry, and continues to create awareness in 
educating these rural communities on the importance of looking after their environment while 
utilising its resources through sustainable and appropriate technologies for enhanced livelihoods. 
PWM also acknowledged the recommendations of the desk-top organizational development report 
and realised the need for having in place a proper operating system (standard operating 
procedures), apart from building the staff capacity and that of their key partners on the project sites 
to take on the various tasks in ensuring efficient and effective implementation of strategies 
identified in the 2013 – 2017 Strategic Plan. Hence, the beginning of the third phase of PWM’s 
development as a promising national non-government conservation and development organization.

PWM’s Strategic Direction 2013 - 2017 
 
PWM is guided by its Goal, Vision, Mission and Values to take on the challenge in implementing this 
Strategic Plan for 2013 – 2017. 
 
Goal 
“To mobilise, educate and equip the communities with relevant skills and resources to make 
informed decisions to protect and utilise their natural resources sustainably.” 
 
Vision 
“Well informed, organized, motivated and self-reliant societies living in peace and harmony with 
their environment.” 
 
Mission  
“PWM is committed to facilitate, formalize and strengthen conservation & sustainable community 
development efforts through education and consensus building processes with effective networking 
and partnerships.” 
 
New Core Values 
1. Environmental Stewardship: PWM believes in the protection of the environment and its 
biodiversity. 
2. Indigenous Peoples: PWM promotes and values the cultures of Melanesian societies. 
3. Community Empowerment: PWM believes in facilitating and empowering members of the 
community in taking the lead in their own development. 
4. Partnerships and Networking: PWM promotes strong and effective partnerships and 
networking with relevant stakeholders. 
5. Transparency and Accountability: PWM promotes good governance through transparency 
and accountability. 
 
Supporting Values 
I. 
Trust and Reliability: 
PWM staff must be trusted and relied to accomplish their respective duties with 
minimum supervision. 
II. 
Respect and Equality: 

PWM Strategic Plan 
 
2013 - 2017
 
8 
 
PWM is an equal opportunity organization that provides opportunity for both men and 
women to work side by side to maximise the expected outputs. 
III. 
Participation and Consultation: 
PWM resolved to engage the management and project levels through participation and 
consultation. 
IV. 
Honesty and Integrity: 
PWM staff are expected to maintain an honest profile and good reputation while 
working for the organization. 
V. 
Transparent and Accountable: 
PWM will seek to develop and apply all processes that allow it to be transparent and 
accountable in all its transaction between donors, partners and communities. 
VI. 
Confidentiality: 
PWM staff are required to keep all confidentially all times regarding operations of the 
organization where harm is likely to be attracted to the organization. 
VII. 
Commitment and Dedication: 
PWM staff are required to commit him/herself thoroughly to the goals and objectives of 
the organization at all times. 
VIII. 
Time Management: 
PWM has resolved to apply methods and approaches that promote time management 
for all staff in such ways to improve productivity and output. 
IX. 
Effective and Efficient: 
PWM has recognised that efficiency and effectiveness are required from all staff in every 
endeavour so that sloppiness and time wasters are minimised. 
X. 
Attitude and Conduct: 
PWM staff are required to maintain a cordial attitude and respectable behaviour at the 
office environment and most importantly at the community level. 
XI. 
Stewardship: 
PWM requires all staff to be good stewards of all assets and resources such that 
maximum benefit is accrued to the organization. 
XII. 
Love and Self-esteem: 
PWM staff are expected to maintain a high self-esteem profile that will motivate their 
actions and attitudes to all persons within and outside the organization.
