Requested Dollar Amount: $50,000

Partners with Melanesians

 MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA

2. Executive Summary:

The current situation on the Managalas Plateau in the Oro Province of Papua New Guinea provides an
extraordinary opportunity for establishing an integrated conservation and development program
where the future livelihood of the local clan groups is linked to their present use of renewable
resources. Nearly a third of the plateau's population has already been engaged in preliminary
discussions regarding the establishment of a broad conservation and development program for the
area and has clearly demonstrated both the will and the capacity to implement such a program. After
‘Several months of discussion and deliberation, all 16 of the partcipat-ing clans concluded that they do
‘not want to pursue any path that leads to the destruction of their forests and that they should seek
assistance to develop sustainably harvested altematives to ground logging.

The planning activities outlined here for designing a three-year implementation proposal build on
these earlier discussions and provide a pathway for extending the planning process beyond the Baral
clan groups to encompass all the people of the plateau. The program provides an opportunity to
strengthen the policy framework for such conservation efforts by assisting these clan groups in
utilizing, for the first time, new conservation area legislation whereby local groups draw up their own
forest management guidelines that are then officially endorsed by the government.

Technical support focuses on building national capacity, ensuring that the lead role in developing
systems of support and advise to such community-based projects goes to national PNG institutions
who then can draw on backup support from appropriate intemational organizations as needed.

Community commitment to the guidelines is achieved through a comprehensive consensus-building
process that strengthens eroding pattems of local participation in planning and decision-making. The
process focuses on clan elder participation, taking place on their turf under circumstances that elevate
their status among the various interested stakeholders.

This planning process draws on previous development experience in Papua New Guinea in
addressing the delicate area of establishing means for distributing new benefits to both the extended
family and larger social units.

Local knowledge and capacity is the starting point for developing each of three project components:

participatory biological research, culturally-sensitive socio-economic planning, and community-based

‘8c0-enterprise development. The central role of local knowiedge, local judgment, and local capacity is

kay to local ownership of the emerging implementation proposal, of the conservation area guidelines

that wil be adopted, and uitmately ofthe sustainable use ofthe rch biodvarsy ofthe Managalas
rests.

3. Background:

Papua New Guinea (PNG) is the world’s largest tropical island nation and the richest in flora and fauna
of all the nations on the Pacific Rim. There Is a remarkable range of tropical environments -- from high
alpine meadows to extensive tracts of lowland rainforest. PNG Is biologically rich. More than seven
hundred species of birds inhabit PNG's varied environments. in addition, the forest flora Is one of the
richest on earth with an estimated 9,000 species of higher plants and perhaps as many as 1,500
‘species of forest trees alone.

page?
 MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA BCN PLANNING PROPOSAL

The Managalas Conservation Area is a magnificent sample of this incredible diversity and one of the
areas of significant diversity highlighted in the recent Conservation Needs Assessment (CNA) report
addressing critical issues concerning conservation and sustainable development in Papua New
Guinea. The proposed conservation area encompasses 300,000 hectares from alpine heaths at
12,000 feet to mutti-altitude forest and then both primary and secondary lowland rainforest. 10,000
villagers live in small communities surrounded by subsistence gardens along a snakelike chain
winding through a 2500 foot plateau in the center of the region. The plateau is bounded by vast
forested ranges on all sides, the Owen Stanleys to the South and West, the Sibium Ranges to the
‘Southeast, and Mount Lamington & the Hydrographers to the North and East.

Papua New Guinea is fortunate in that community-based tenurial systems on rights to forests, land,
water and fisheries are recognized by the national government. In addition, housekeeping
amendments to PNG's Conservation Areas Act have recently been passed by Parliament, providing a
ready legal mechanism for local groups to develop and register locally defined resource management
guidelines with the central government.

The communities to be involved in the development of this proposal have already demonstrated
considerable initiative in organizing themselves to develop a conservation plan for the area. Clan
‘groups have been meeting and discussing the long range benefits of such a plan for more than six
months!.

Most of the clan groups of the Managalas Plateau belong to the Kolarian family of languages,
providing important cuttural cohesion for the implementation of a program of this kind. These clan
groups have had considerable experience collaborating with one another and with outside agencies
and organizations on other local development initiatives. These have included the organization of a
coffee cooperative, modeling a coffee rehabilitation program, a ‘walk-about” sawmill program,
‘vernacular preschools, and adult literacy programs.

There is both growing concer about the destruction of their forests through ground logging and a
keen interest in developing economic alternatives for sustainably managing this resource base. One
such potential alternative is the terminalia kaernbachii known locally as the makame or okari nut and
part of the family of nuts sometimes referred to as “tropical almonds". The okari, essential olls,

1 Early preparations for integrating the harvesting of the okari nut with a conservation program for the area,
‘have been supported through the Liz Claibome/Art Ortenberg Foundation and the Biodiversity
‘Support Program, an A.LD.-funded joint venture of World Wildlife Fund, The Nature Conservancy,
World Resources Institute.

page 3
 MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA BCN PLANNING PROPOSAL

artifacts, mushrooms and organic coffee are among the local resources clan groups are considering
for development as part of a comprehensive conservation and resource development program for the
area.

The Barai, located in the heart of the plateau, have taken the lead with this and many of the previous
development initiatives in the area. They carried out a two-year feasibility study on marketing the okari
nut at an earlier stage and hosted the Initial exploratory meeting launching this initiative in June of
19922. They have since organized two participatory forums and extensive clan group meetings
exploring a broad range of conservation and development issues and options with a view to
developing a conservation area program on the plateau. The proceedings of these early forums make
it abundantly clear that the participating clan groups believe their social and economic well-being is
dependent on sound, long-term management of their resources. The challenge now is to develop
planning activities to expand the participation of this lead group to encompass alll the clans of the
plateau.

‘The communities of this area have enjoyed close links to the emerging NGO movement in the country
for some time, participating in various NGO-related literacy and awareness programs over the years.
Information and knowledge of conservation and development issues, while limited, is clearly ahead of
‘many rural communities in Papua New Guinea. To illustrate, the community faced the issue of whether
or not trees of the easily accessible sacred forest plots should be harvested as part of a newly
introduced “walk about” sawmill program. After considerable discussion regarding the ancient and
modem functions of these sacred forest plots, the long-standing ban on harvesting in those areas
was restored, a clear sign of community will for addressing issues of this kind.

4. Objectives:

The goal of the Managalas Plateau Resource Management proposal planning activities will be to
develop an implementation proposal aimed at conserving the valuable biological resources of the
plateau and its mountainous periphery while meeting critical economic and social needs among the
Barai, Aomie, Mountain Koiari, Bariji and Managalas peoples living there.

2 ‘The results of the study are contained in the 1986 report, Barai Okari Estates, Partners with Melanesians,
23 pp.

3 See Issues, Options and Next Steps attached as Appendices I, 11, and III

page 4
 MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA BCN PLANNING PROPOSAL

Planning proposal objectives focus on developing each of three components of the implementation
proposal: a participatory biological research component, a culturally-relevant socio-economic planning
component, and a community-based, eco-enterprise component. Evaluation and monitoring
‘mechanisms will be built into the development of each component. The object of the biological
research component of the planning process is to develop strategies for gathering the biological and
ecological information necessary to ensure sustainable use of the okari and other forest resources, to
conserve the rich biological diversity of the area on and around the Managalas Plateau, and to do it all
in a genuinely participatory way. It aims at developing a composite research team utilizing local,
national, and international capacity to implement the biological research strategies. Planning activities
for developing the implementation proposal will include those local, national and international
researchers who are likely to be involved in the implementation of the proposal.

The object of the culturally-retevant, socio-economic component of the planning process is to
strategize on how best to develop methods and institutional capacity appropriate for carrying out both
the conservation of the biological resources on the plateau and the development of ecologically
sustainable enterprises and to do it in ways that are firmly grounded in locally relevant social,
‘economic, and cultural information. it aims at further refining the Melanesian socio-economic planning
process currently emerging in the area in a way that not only provides for a credible dialogue among all
the stakeholders involved, but raises awareness and provides new information as needed for each
interest group. The planning process aims at incorporating strategies for packaging and
disseminating information relevant to the conservation and eco-enterprise activities in ways that will be
readily accessible and easily understood by the resource owners themselves. It will target the
development of collaborative linkages with national NGO support groups appropriate to the
information packaging and dissemination strategies adopted.

The object of the community-based, eco-enterprise component of the planning process is to develop
strategies for sustainably harvesting okari nuts and initiating the development of other selected forest
products, linking them with markets that will generate benefits for meeting local economic and social
needs. The eco-enterprise planning activity will target strategies that are compatible with local social
organization, recognizing the cultural ‘zones’ on the plateau and the cultural values governing how
such ‘zones’ participate in the amassing and distribution of economic benefits. Further, it will target
the highest level of locally-based value added processing of the forest products as is economically
feasible.

pages
 -MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA

5. Proposed Activities:

‘A Managalas Conservation Area Advisory Board will be established to support and advise the Project
Steering Committee on the design and implementation of each of the three project components; the
biological component, the socio-economic component and the eco-enterprise component. The
Advisory Board will include representation from the Managalas clan group elders and facilitators, the
Managalas Research Team, Nahara Coffee Growers, Okari Eco-enterprises, Partners with
Melanesians, PNG Development Trust, the East Sepik Council of Women, the Business Enterprise
‘Support Team, the National Research Institute, the Biology and Law Departments of the University of
Papua New Guinea, the Forest Research Institute, the Afore District Office, the Department of Oro,
the Department of Environment and Conservation, the World Wildlife Fund, Cultural Survival
Enterprises and Wildlife Conservation Intemational.

Patticipatory Biological Research:

‘A Research Advisory Committee will be established to support and advise on the design and
implementation of the research aspects of the Managalas Conservation Area project. The Research
Advisory Group will include the Managalas Research Team, Okari Eco-enterprises, Partners with
Melanesians, Forest Research Institute, the Medical Research Institute, University of Papua New
Guinea, World Wildlife Fund and Wildlife Conservation International. The Research Advisory
Committee will guide the development of the biological research component of the implementation
Proposal including impact assessments and the recording of species along with a trial biological
research activity.

‘The trial biological research activity will be undertaken as part of the planning process. It will contribute
to establishing local leadership and ownership of the research process, help ensure that it is
genuinely participative, and will provide a base of experience out of which the biological research
activities of the implementation project can be appropriately designed to match the needs,
‘opportunities and constraints of the practical situation on the Managalas Plateau. This trial biological
research activity will focus on 1) an okari tree dispersion sample area, 2) sample okari yield and
monitoring plots, and 3) okari tree reproduction processes.

In a related activity, local knowledge related to the okari tree and how it is sustained in the forest will be
elicited from local paranaturalists using a trial survey format that will later be revised for wider use in the
implementation program. Laboratory examination of the physical and chemical properties of the okari
‘nut will be undertaken to further inform the sustainable harvesting planning process

page 6
 MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA BCN PLANNING PROPOSAL

These initial leam-by-doing biological research activities will use Partners with Melanesians’ field trainer
to support and advise the Baral Research Team (with technical guidance from Wiklife Conservation
international and the Biology Department at the University of Papua New Guinea). These trial
biological research activities will be modified and, where feasible, expanded to other cultural zones on
the plateau during the April collaborative planning forum, which will Involve the full range of project
stakeholders. The biological research activities will continue, as amended, through the April July
activity period. Near the end of July, the experience and results of the biological research trials will be
assessed and evaluated by the Research Advisory Group during which time the group will
collaboratively develop the biological research component of the implementation proposal.

The lead agency of the technical support for the biological research planning activity will be the
Biology Department at the University of Papua New Guinea with backup support and advise from
Wildlife Conservation Intemational.

In an effort to strengthen national institutions through increased involvement in conservation and
development programs of this kind, meetings exploring possible collaboration during the
implementation of the project will held with the Forest Research Institute, the Medical Research
Institute and the Biology Department at the University of Papua New Guinea prior to the proposal
planning meeting of the Research Advisory Group.

Culturally-sensitive Socio-economic Planning:

The Project Steering Committee will advise and support the planning of the socio-economic
component of the three-year proposal. The Project Steering Committee will include representation
from the clan groups, the zone coordinators, Okari Eco-enterprises, Partners with Melanesians, PNG
Development Trust, National Research Institute, and the World Wildlife Fund.

The planning activities of the socio-economic component revolve around a Melanesian-style
‘consensus-building process Involving the participating clans alongside other stakeholders with an
Interest in conservation and development on the Managalas Plateau. A cycle involving an initial 8-
week series of clan group discussions will be followed by a combined structuring forum whose
recommendations will lead into a second 8-week series of clan group discussions, this time involving
an expanded group of participating clans from all around the plateau. The output of that second
series of meetings will culminate in a final combined structuring session that will aggregate opinion
 BCN PLANNING PROPOSAL

from all around the plateau with specific recommendations for each component of the implementation
proposal.

‘The method used will Involve coaching Managalas facilitators through the mechanics of each module
of the process. The facilitator trainer will fade back after demonstrating a technique in a live session,
allowing the facilitator trainee (once he has the idea) to take over and conclude the session with only
backup support from the trainer. During the second forum, the local facilitator trainee will lead the
sessions throughout except for those portions where a new aspect of the overall process is being
introduced.

With this strong, early level of local management of the process, it can easily be adjusted as the
sessions unfold. Frequent dialogue between the trainer and the trainee (and his core staff) in the
planning before, during and after the sessions themselves facilitates situation-specific variations to
the process, as needed.

‘The core principles of the process derive from practices and pattems that are familiar to many
traditional societies. This puts the facilitator trainee in a situation where his own traditional facilitator
skills are not only permitted but encouraged as appropriate for this mix of participants. The most critical
aspects of steering the discussion... ensuring respect for and the solicitation of each clan's
‘contribution, limiting the participation of assertive ‘speech-makers’, honoring dissent through referral it
necessary (until such time as a consensus is reached), etc.... are all familiar to the ‘trainee’ and vary
much a part of the reason for his pervasive influence in the community in the first place. The
innovation here is that such a tradition-based process will now become the preferred style for
resource planning involving local clans and the various external conservation, marketing, and
goverment organizations. The local community has endorsed the participation of the outside
organizations and is pleased to be able to host the dialogue on its own turf,

This proposal planning process will build on an earlier community-based call to action that came at a
June 1991 “town meeting” where the idea of pursuing the marketing of okari nuts in the context of a
broad resource conservation and development program was discussed in considerable detail and

Project Report
Managalas Plateau Mapping and GPS Training

Acknowledgements

It was my great honour and privilege to have participated recently in a project
that took me to the remarkable country of Papua New Guinea (PNG). | am
grateful for having met and worked with, however briefly. a number of people
Id like to mention here.

First, and foremost, I'd like to thank the villagers of the Managalas Plateau.
They welcomed me into their homes, fed me, taught me things about the place
they lived in and displayed incredible patience with a foreigner. One of the
things I learned is how alike we are under the cuiturai and technological
differences. Another thing I fearned is that humour is a universal trait that
unites rather than divides.

Next, I'd like to acknowledge Michael and Sarah at the Education
Development Center (EDC) in Washington, DC: Damien Ase of Partners With
Melanesians (PWM) in Port Moresby: and Vince Manukayasi and the people at
the EDC PNG office, also in Port Moresby. They all played a big part in
arranging things, getting things done, and making sure all the ‘official papers’
got into the proper hands when needed. Very reassuring for a neophyte
waveler.

And last but definitely not least, I'd like to recognize two guys who were
absolutely crucial to the success of the training project - Richard Brunton and
Flint Hobart. These two worked hard at keeping well over a dozen people
coordinated. fed, paid, happy. It was no small task, given the logistical
difficulties one grows to learn to live with in PNG. I admired their facility at
finding just the right ‘Wan Tok’ for any situation. They also worked hard to
help me fit in, to translate back and forth for me, to fill me in with highly
informative current events, history, news, especially the conteyt, and to
welcome me in as a part of their team. My work would have been much
harder without their help and my stay in PNG much lonelier without their
friendship. Thanks, guys. I look forward to a day when we can all raise a glass
of really good Scotch together and toast a new stage of this project with our
new team cheer. Let's try to make it sooner rather than later to get together

again

 © securing funding; and

+ securing a trainer famifiar with tribal boundary mapping.

‘My part in this project begins with the last point above. More specifically, EDC
staff in Washington, DC, USA. required a trainer with acquired skill in teaching
tribal boundary and resource-use mapping, and significant experience
operating within aboriginal legal and political situations within or that paraltei
the PNG experience.

The Work

PWM and EDC staff recently completed a 2-week training exercise with
selected members from several villages on the Managalas Plateau. The training
included several components and events necessary to begin mapping the outer
boundary of the Managalas Sustainable Development Program's proposed
Conservation Area. Given that there was limited time available and different
entry levels of trainees. we (Flint. Richard and myself) decided to concentrate
on doing a few things weil rather than too many things poorly. Accordingly.
we concentrated on those skills necessary to carry out successful mapping of
the outer boundaries. We also sought to reinforce taining exercises with
repetition, repetition, and repetition.

Two trainees, Kingsford and Maichus became central to everything taught over
the length of the sessions, simultaneously learning both course material and
trainer's methodology. They both came into this with good background
experience and a {ot of enthusiasm. I liked them greatly. I am pleased to
recommend them as project leaders for any fieldwork set out over the next
while. They did very well. Briefly described below is the training material
outline, followed by a more detailed report. Topics we concentrated on were
as follows:

* Introduction to May

+ map parts, types, and standards;
* coordinate systems, and map creation.
‘© Introduction to GPS:

= settings and map bases. accuracy. menus. maintenance. care and
feeding of units:

+ reading coordinates. waypoints, transfer to map base.
* Introduction to Compasses:

* reading, declination, accuracy, types of compasses:

* transfer bearings to and from maps, distance and bearing.
‘+ Introduction to Record-keeping:
 * consistency. attention to detail, the buddy system, immediacy of
recording:

« legal importance of "paper trails’, centralization,

© Project Management: planning a field trip, field work on site, post-trip
analysis.

An important factor in gaining acceptance and support for this project was
reporting to and maintaining communication with the Clan Elders of the
participating villages.

An important factor in writing this report was the consideration that the
village team might desire something written they could use as a lesson review.

Introduction to Maps

Although some trainees! already had some familiarity with maps. for purposes
of training, I began with the basics. This gave me a chance to assess everyone's
levels of familiarity, to identify gaps or areas needing more attention, and to
adapt myself to the class’ needs. It also gave Maichus and Kingsford a chance to
Iearn how to teach each concept to their classmates. We began with map parts,
went on to map standards, and worked in terminology throughout.

Materials and supplies
Training materials were kept deliberately small, simple, and easy to transport.
‘An important theme throughout this short course was that making maps and
using GPS to locate features is easy. Anybody can do it, and do it to high
standards without expensive. complicated equipment or university degrees.
We used the following equipment:

© several Garmin 12 & Garmin 12XL hand-held GPS units

‘© several compasses, one professional grade and the others student grade

© several 19" rulers, one 18" ruler, marked in both Imperial and metric
increments

© one 50 metre and one 100 metre tape rule

We use the following supplis

© 1:100 000 scale government issue topographic maps of our study area

"The daily number of parécipants uctuated. This was expected. 2s mest ofthe vilagars were “outin the gardens”
this time of year. There were usualy at least 8, however, and often as many 28 12 at any one tene. Fora istng of
participants and vilages, please see Richara Srunton’s reget
 © aroll of banquet table white paper

* pencils and pens. felt pens

© asupply of ‘AA’ batteries

‘© elementary school student exercise books
Map parts

All trainees worked through every part of the legend first. What each part was
and what they looked fike on the map. How the map parts were organized on
the page. We identified familiar landmarks, such as rivers. contour lines,
villages, cleared areas, plantations. airfields, roads, and footpaths.

We found a valley visible from Sarapuna. We connected chat with its mapped
counterpart, the particular contour fine and river combination that described
the same shape. We connected real-life landmarks with their mapped symbols.
Thus, close contour lines became steep hills, and footpaths whose shapes were
familiar in memory were compared against mapped footpaths.

Map types

We explored map functions, identifying different types of maps such as mining
maps, forestry maps. contour maps. political and electoral maps, road maps,
and the best maps of all, those contained within our own heads and the cian
elders’ heads. We discussed the outer boundary map: what purpose it would
serve and some of thie legal standards this map might require.

Map standards

We are trained from éarly childhood to recognize the authority of paper. And
for the most part, we usuaily accept paper maps from government sources as
being reasonably authoritative, provided they are made within certain
tolerances for error. Therefore, an important part of using maps was learning
to recognize the standards inherent in their creation, and to be able to identify
their limitations as well.

We covered such concepts as:

‘+ scale - the relationship between the mapped size of an area and its actual
size on the ground;

© map grid - the overlay of regular gridded measurements of length, width
and area:

+ datum - the broad set of rules or standards for locating points, lines and
areas on a map. such as Australian Geodetic Datum 1964 (AGD64, for
shor), or World Geodetic Survey 1984 (WGS84);

 * projection - the local set of rules for representing an imperfectly spheroid
globe on a flat piece of paper, such as Albers Equal Area, Lambert Conical,
and Universal Transverse Mercator:

+ map accuracy - the inherent limitations of a map, such as +/- accuracy of
map features, elevational accuracy, change through time, legally
acceptable levels of human error.

Coordinate systems and map creation

In order to match GPS settings to the government-issue map base, the trainees
had first to understand what coordinate systems are, and then to learn how to
use them to locate places on a map. We used the classroom (windhouse
pictured below) itself as an example of a defined area where points could be
located simply and quickly. It had a nice regularity of stud placements and
overall proportions that paralleled map construction. The figure below
illustrates the lesson.

Qs=eavim—>

—
 In this example. four trainees stood up and identified themselves by the
coordinates that corresponded to their seating position within the room.
Starting from the right in figure 1, student #1 was at coordinates 1.1. Student
#2 was at 2.3: #3 was at 3.4: and #4 was at 2.5.

Each student moved to the point of origin, at coordinates (0.0) in the corner,
then paced the number of windhouse units “East” and then “North” needed to
get back to their seats. This method provided the basis for understanding
metric geo-referencing. This was the simple part.

The next logical step was introducing them to the metric coordinate systems
used on their base maps. The maps availabie for the project contain a popular
metric grid overlay called Universal Transverse Mercator, or UTM grid for
short. The kilometre-based grid made it simple to transfer the basic lesson of
counting across, Easting first, then Northing second, to maps. They located pre-
determined places, such as familiar villages. on their maps. Each student then
“filled in the blanks’, identifying coordinate sets for each map location. Then
they worked the lesson in reverse. They took coordinate pairs and worked
back to focate villages, lakes or other map features. This formed an important
part of preparing to use GPS geo-referencing.

Maps creation

Once they understood how easy coordinate systems could be. we transferred
the same steps outlined above to a field exercise. Using a simple measuring
method of pacing off distances on the local soccer field, we began creating our
first map. We located a number of positions relative to “base camp" -a table at
the centre of the field with drawing paper on it. Differences in pace-lengths
created different results and helped emphasize the need for using a
standardized method of measuring distances, such as a tape rule. Students
practised their map-making skills, creating a map that was at a scale of 1:100 in
relation to the field. All students took turns measuring and marking in pairs,
beginning to develop the “buddy system” they would need [ater.

Following the same pattern as in the classroom, we then began gathering GPS.
coordinates for the same positions. The important step here was linking the
very simple hand-created, grid-located locations with sophisticated
technologically-accurate, geo-referenced locations. We substituted GPS
coordinates for the “foot-pace” coordinates, and compared the two coordinate
systems.

Introduction to GPS

Learning to use GPS units to locate points along the proposed outer boundary
was the goal of these exercises. Moving from hand-made maps with highly
variable local coordinate systems. we progressed naturally to the government
issue, standardized maps and global positioning systems (GPS) geo-
referencing.
 Settings and base maps

Base maps come in many different flavours: GPS units have to match the local
base map standards. or the digital readings they collect can be wildly
inaccurate or downright apocryphal with reference to the base map.

‘Our base maps created using Australian Geodetic Datum 1964 (AGD 64) map
standards, By world-wide convention. all GPS units, from the most basic hand-
held units through the most advanced. surveyor-grade units, all units collect
geo-referenced positions in what is known as WGS84, or World Geodetic
Survey 1984. All GPS units capable of displaying coordinates in a local datum.
such as AGD64, contain an internal lookup table that allows the unit to
translate the collected coordinates from WGS8¢ to the focal datum.

Most focal maps also portray features
according to a “best-fit” set of rules called
the “projection”. This is the set of rules
cartographers use when trying to fit an
irregular, objate spheroid (the planet
Earth) to a flat piece of paper (a map).
Latitude/Longitude is a common set of
rules cartographers used for our base
maps. But this projection uses an archaic
set of rules is designed on base 60, and not

“SS base 10. “Base 60" rules require that we

measure map locations in 360 degrees, eacii of which is broken up into 60

minutes per degree, each of which is broken up in to 60 seconds per minute.
There are further subdivisions. This system makes as little sense as the Imperial
system where 12 inches = 1 foot, 3 feet = 1 yard, 5280 feet = 1 mile and 1760
yards also = 1 mile, and 640 acres = 1 mile’.

Sensibly, the map is overlaid with a metric projection grid. based on the
Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) set of rules. For localized maps, this
system is ideal. On our map base, the grid is 1000 metres on a side, allowing
trainees to subdivide 1 kilometre” blocks into 10x10 grids of 100 metre” hectare
biocks. Australian proximity guarantees they are already familiar with the
metric system. The UTM system also made it easy for trainees to measure out
distance or area using a 50 metre or 100-metre tape rule and be confident of
accuracy.

So, trainees were taught to set their units to match their map base's settings in
order to obtain the most accurate readings they can receive. They learned to
detect if their unit was fixed to archaic or apocryphal settings, and to correct
them back to the UTM/AGD64 set of standards.

Accuracy

GPS technology has outstripped its creators. The accuracy of the technology is
far superior to the expectations of its inventors or promoters. It is so accurate

 the American military scrambles the signal with an introduced, randomized
error known as “Selective Availability’, or SA for short. This means sometimes
the coordinates one obtains through the satellite signals is accurate to sub-
metre levels (about 1 decimetre in metric or about 4 inches). And sometimes
the coordinates can be off by as much as 150 metres. We took several single
position fixes at one location and plotted them on our base maps to compare.
Trainees were abie to see what a difference in accuracy a few minutes change
in time makes. Single position fixes to locate a feature is truly only accurate to
about 150 metres.

There are other factors that control a GPS unit's accuracy. Conditions such as
proximity to hilly terrain, dense canopy cover. steep valleys, the angle of hand-
held units while collecting positions, the time of day and battery power all
contribute to a decrease in overall accuracy.

Fortunately. there are reasonably good methods of correcting the errors or
reducing the inaccuracies. The trainees were all brought through the following
methods.

The SA itself cannot be eliminated on site without expensive equipment.
However, the correctness of a fix can be significantly improved by simply
taking a number of positions, say 50 or 60. and averaging them all to get one
location. A good metaphor for explaining this effect is to describe shooting a
single lead pellet and then shooting a shotgun shell full of lead pellets. With a
single pellet, one has no idea how close to or far away from the target centre
the shot will hit. But a shotgun pattern always has a centre where the majority
of pellets always hit. This centre (averaging) Is much smaller than the total
spread of the blast (SA). The Garmins have an averaging feature built in, and
reliably tightens a geo-referencing estimate to about 10-20 metres. Trainees
were taught to use the averaging method exclusively, though they were aware
they could always take a single fix position if they needed one quickly.

Hilly terrain and steep valleys pose a difficult problem to the GPS collector.
Mountains, hills, or even quite small cut banks effectively block the satellite
signals. One solution is to wait for sufficient satellites to gather overhead to
gain a quick fix. A better solution is to move to high ground where a good
signal can be found. Then measure the range and bearing (described more
fully in the Compass section below) back to the desired location in the signal
shadow.

Twice a day the GPS collector can always expect excellent satellite reception
and twice a day he can always expect very poor reception. This is due to the
pattern and timing of satellites overhead. Although there is nothing one can
do to correct the poor reception at this time, there is still a way to get a
position. The solution is easy. Get the position at another time. Move on to
another place where the reception is good and come back later for the missed
place. Another solution is to call a water break. have a snack and wait the
signal trough out. It usually lasts for no fonger than 30 minutes, and can be as
short as 15 minutes. The pattern and timing is designed such that no matter
 where one is on the face of the earth, there will always be good reception
sometime.

Dense canopy presents a special problem for the smaller. fess sensitive hand
held units such as Garmins. The tree trunks and leaves above act like giant
columns of water holding up a lake above our heads. This blocks or dilutes
signals, of course. Generally. however. people are taking a position on a well-
beaten footpath. with a band of sky above. so there is always some signal to
work with. And although one might be

tempted to send the unit up a tree with
a small boy, the practical solution is
very similar to working in hilly terrain.
Move to a spot where reception is good
enough to get a reasonable averaged
location. then take the range and
bearing back to the desired location.

The angle at which a GPS unit is held
while collecting positions affects the
accuracy of a geo-referenced location.

The units are designed to be held flat in
the hand, with the receiver end pointing straight up. Tilting the unit elther
screens out useful satellite signals or catches signals too close to the horizon.

 Executive Summary

“The ranch project of Queen Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly (QABB) was established at Muana in
Tahama village about 300 m from Asiki Eco-lodge and Nature Center. The general ecology of
the Asiki area including the fauna and flora was also conducted. The project was conducted for a
minimum of one week from 8* to 14 January 2007 at Asiki Eco-Lodge. ‘The study included site
inspection, initial assessments for site suitability, identifying number of foodplants and nectar
plants, tagging foodplants (Aristolochia plants), establishment of the study plots, and the
construction of a flight cage.

Further, the study was conducted during the post flowering and fruiting season of most nectar
plants of the QABB (Ornithoptera alexandra) and other fauna species. However, the foodplants
(ristolochia dielsiana) of the QABB were flowering and fruiting when the study was conducted.

‘The flight cage was established as part of the ranch project at a selected site suitable for the
propagation of the Aristolochia dielsiana. A total of 237 Aristolochia vine cuttings were
prepared and planted in black polythene bags. From these 15 healthy and well established vines
will be replanted in marked areas inside the flight cage.

Five monitoring sites were established from which total of 235 Aristolochia vines were tagged.
The local population of QABB was visibly not impossible because of the availability and
abundance of the Aristolochia vines. Two caterpillars of QABB were sighted at Sites 2 and 3
respectively. Two adult female QABB were sighted searching for nectar plants within the project
area. One QABB was observed in the opening of the primary forest cruising at about 25 m high
feeding on the nectar of Syzygium flowers while the other was inflight about 3m high near
Tahama village. It was confirmed that few nectar plants were flowering therefore, the activity of
QABB was low.

‘The ethno-botanical knowledge of the Aristolochia vine differs according to their local use and
how the local communities within Managalas Plateau define their uses. The local people from
‘Tahama and the nearby villages use parts of the vine for various traditional practices which
ies some connections with the plant and the birdwing butterfly. The vine also tends to
posses some medicinal properties and local people in Managalas Plateau use them as traditional
remedy to cure certain skin and gastrointestinal discases.

‘The threats to the local population of QABB is a paramount issue due to various anthropogenic
activities such as fires, and other forest conversions for logging, oil palm plantations, agro-
forestry, and gardening through traditional shifting cultivation practices. Also, natural disasters
such as the landstides contribute to their habitat loss.
 1.0 Introduction

“The ranch project was established as a tourism product of the eco-tourism project of Asiki Eco-
Lodge as well as conserving this endemic and world’s largest birdwing butterfly species
(Ornithoptera alexandrae). ‘This project was designed to complement the conservation of
biodiversity and project implementation towards sustaining people’s livelihood in their rural
settings. Thus, the project would contribute towards the development and attractions of the
NACODA eco-tourism and nature centre in the area. ‘The rearing of Queen Alexandra Birdwing
Butterfly (QABB) was demonstrated in the wild in the natural forest and in flight cages
{artificiaVcontrol environment).

‘The project was conducted for a minimum of one week which included site inspection,
assessments for site suitability, identifying number of foodplants and nectar plants, tagging
foodplants (Aristolochia dielsiana), establishment of the study plots, and construction of flight

cages.

‘The flight cage was established in a suitable site selected for propagating Aristolochia dielsiana,
‘A total of 237 Aristolochia vine cuttings were prepared and planted in black polythene bags.
From these 15 healthy and well established vines will be replanted in marked areas in the flight
cage. The flight cage was initially proposed because it can provide both the shelter for the
propagating vines as the nursery and a rearing area for QABB.

‘The study also covered the ecological and monitoring aspects of the birdwing butterfly and its
host plant. ‘The phenology of the host plants and other associated plant species was significant to
determine the occurrence of the birdwing butterflies and its relatives. However, the study was
conducted during the post flowering and fruiting season of most nectar plants of the Queen
Alexandrae Birdwing Butterfly (QABB) and other fauna species. On the other hand, the
foodplants (Aristolochia dielsiana) of the QABB were flowering and fruiting when the study was
conducted.

Further, the local population of QABB is a fundamental aspect of this study because their
population is threatened and restricted due to profound effects from largely anthropogenic
activities. ‘These activities include fires, and other forest conversions for logging, oil palm
plantations, agro-forestry, and gardening through traditional shifting cultivation. Also, natural
disasters such as the landslides contribute to their habitat loss. However, the local population of
QABB was visibly possible because of the availability and abundance of the Aristolochia vines.
A couple of caicrpillars and female QABB’s were sighted at the study site and the surrounding
forests.

1.1 Scope and Objectives

‘The primary purpose of the project was to establish a QABB ranch project at Asiki Eco-lodge and
Nature centre of Managalas Plateau in Northem Province. Thus, the implementation of the
QABB ranch project also covered the following activities:

+ Establishment of nursery vines

© Construction of a QABB flight cage
 + Determine the availability and abundance of foodplants (Aristolochia dielsiana) and
nectar plants
‘+ Investigate the presence of QABB and determine the occurrence of QABB in the area.

2.0 Taxonomy and Ethno-botany of Aristolochia

The taxonomy of Aristolochia vine is complex and still requires further investigation to determine
the species in the Managalas region. Parsons (1998) and other authors described the food plant as
Pararistolochia dielsiana, It is suspected that there are four different vines of Pararistolochia
dielsiana and one of them is threatening the lives of the wild QABB population because it is
believed to be producing toxic chemicals (Malaisa, 2006). However, in this report Aristolochia
dielsiana is commonly used as the food plant for the Queen Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly.

‘The ethno-botanical knowledge of the Aristolochia vine differs from place to place depending on
how the local communities in Managalas Plateau define their uses. In this case, the people from
‘Tahama village use the large board leaves to wrap white yam, taro, and banana suckers and plant
them in the ground. ‘They also use the fibrous strings of the vine to tie white yam onto the
support sticks in their gardens. ‘The significance of performing this is because the yam, taro and
bananas will grow big and healthy just like the caterpillar of the QABB (pers.com., Ezekiel
Garui, 2007).

However, the people from Kawawoki village extract the seeds and flesh of the Aristolochia fruits
and rub them on their stomach as 2 traditional therapy of curing enlarged spleens (pers.com.,
Solomon Kotumba, 2007).

3.0 Geology & Geomorphology

‘The Asiki Eco-Lodge is located within Managalas Plateau of the Southeastem Papuan Rain
Forests ecoregion. This lowland and montane ecoregion is made up of the Owen Stanley Range
and surrounding lowland and coastal areas in southeastern PNG. ‘The climate of the ecoregion is,
‘wopical wet, which is characteristic of this part of Mclanesia, located in the western Pacific
‘Ocean north of Australia. The surface geology of the Central Cordillera, of which the Owen
Stanleys are an extension, is generally composed of metamorphic and intrusive igneous rocks.
More specifically, this ecoregion is composed of metamorphosed Mesozoic greywacke sandstone,
siltstone, and marine volcanics overlain by Miocene intrusive Pliocene marine and terrestrial fine-
grained sediments, and Quaternary lavas and pyroclasties (Bleeker, 1983).

Most of this ecoregion is composed of tropical wet evergreen forest, with a significant (25
percent) percentage of tropical montane evergreen forest. Smaller percentages of upper montane
and freshwater swamp forest are also found (MacKinnon, 1997).

Paijmans (1976), MacKinnon (1997), Petocz (1989), and Nightingale (1992) confirmed that the
Iowland forest up to 1,400 m on the north side of the Owen Stanleys is made up of Pometia,
Terminalia, Mysristica, Horsfieldia, Celtis, and Ficus. Lowland forest is made up of both alluvial
and hill types. Lowland alluvial forest has a canopy that is multitiered and irregular, with many
emergents. The understory contains a shrub-and-herb layer with a variety of climbers, epiphytes,
and ferns. The dominant canopy trees include species of Pometia, Canarium, Anispoptera,
Cryptocarya, Terminalia, Syzygium, Ficus, Celtis, Dysoxylum, and Buchanania. Koompassia,

 Dillenia, Eucalptopsis, Vatica, and Hopea are locally abundant. Dense stands of Araucaria the
tallest tropical trees in the world, are present in scattered locations.

‘The area has a relatively high annual rainfall with a high variance over the project area. The
weighted average (according to PNGRIS mapping unit averages) annual rainfall is 2,725mm.

Figure 1: Generalised map of Managalas Plateau

4.0 Materials and Methods

4.1 Project Site

The study was conducted at Asiki about 20 km from Afore Government Station, Northern
Province. The area is situated at an elevation of about 660m and within the proposed Managalas
Plateau Conservation Area (MPCA). The mean annual rainfall of the area is approximately
2,000mm (Van Den Ende et al, 2004). The Asiki area predominantly composed of rocks largely
derived from deposits of volcanic origins. The soil is volcanic and fertile with a top-soil depth of
about 20cm. Also, the soil is unstable and vulnerable to weathering and run-offs into nearby
aquatic systems during wet seasons.

‘The QABB ranch project was established at Muana (148° 17.834E, 09° 10.834’S) about 300m
northwest of Asiki Eco-lodge and nature centre.
 Figure 2: Locality of Asiki Guesthouse, Northern Province

sites were selected and plots were set-up according to the availability and evidence of QABB
presence in the area. Within each site the following data were obtained and recorded; number of
tagged vines, GPS location of site, description of leafivine eaten by QABB, height above ground,
and size of instar. Also, the opening in the forest and surrounding vegetation were recorded.

4.4.1 Preparation & Propagation of Aristolochia vines

‘The cuttings of Aristolochia vine were selectively chosen and cut about 1 m above ground from
the forest and the vines tagged. ‘The cuttings of about 30cm long were trimmed off and prepared
for propagation. The base of the growing end of the Aristolochia vine cuttings were dipped in the
rooting powder and put in the poly bags with soil. Rooting powder was applied in order to
stimulate and accelerate the formation of roots of the cuttings.

4,4.2 Maintenance of Nursery

‘The nursery is critical during the early stages therefore the propagation of the cuttings is
monitored to reduce mortality rate. The propagating vines are to be watered about 3
times every week during nil rain periods. A minimum of 15 vines only was prescribed to
be established in the flight cage. Over grown vines should be trimmed well and new
propagating shoots controlled. Other well established and propagating vines will be
transferred to marked sites such as the following; 54 (X1 — X54) marked trees around the
Asiki Guesthouse and 4 (Y1 — Y4) marked trees in the opening of the primary forest east
of the Asiki Guesthouse.

4.4.3 Monitoring of vines in Flight cage

The vin the flight cage will be monitored to determine the growth and survival rate
of each vine. The vines which are not performing well or dead will be removed and
replaced. Treatment of propagating vines should be handled with care and bushy vines
pruned in order to give clearance for their growth to maintain healthy vines. ‘The well
established vines will be transplanted in the marked sites and their performances will be
monitored.

u
 5.0 Conservation Status

‘The local population of QABB is threatened and restricted due to profound effects from largely
anthropogenic activities. ‘These activities include fires, and other forest conversions for logging,

oil palm plantations, agro-forestry, and gardening through traditional shifting cultivation. Also,
natural disasters such as the landslides contribute to their habitat loss.

‘The conservation and management of QABB population is therefore significant. The QABB was
considered rare in 1968 by the government of Papua New Guinea and was listed under CITES
Appendix I meaning that its harvest and trade is restricted. Together with six other Ornithoptera
species all were registered highly endangered (Malaisa, 2006). QABB is also listed as an
‘endangered species on IUCN’s Red List.

6.0 Butterfly Farming

‘The farming of butterflies is a perfect economic means of insect trade rather than large scale
logaing or unsustainable forest conversion. In other words, the butterfly farming is an excellent
‘example of “conservation through development”. The gathering and selling of excess wildlife is
an excellent way for the forest to provide income to the local people, especially considering the
alternative of clearing the land for cash crops or logging (Parsons, 1991). The butterflies provide
aa lightweight, bigh-value cash crop to people who might otherwise be cutting down the rain
forest.

‘The experts agree that in most tropical countries the economic and educational aspects of the
butterfly trade outweigh any small negative impacts (www.sciencebulletins.amnb.org). Because it
is conducted on a small scale, itis not going to save the planet, but in conjunction with its
educational value, butterfly farming will have some real import (Parsons, 1991). For instance, the
Papua New Guinea's Insect Farming and Trading Agency, which started in 1978 was aimed to
handle and expand the growing trade between local butterfly farmers and collectors and overseas
buyers.

7.0 Food-plants and Nectar Plants

The abundance of the foodplants (Aristolochia dielsiana) of QABB was found to be less dense in
some areas and abundant in other areas. There are scattered and found in pockets of opening in
the forests when there is an opening created by fallen trees, gardening, and less forest cover.

Further, the study was conducted during the post flowering and fruiting season of most of the
nectar plants and very little was seen blooming in the forest. Therefore, it was predicted that this
affected the activity of the QABB and other birdwing butterflies. However, it was astonishing to
record a large female QABB feeding on the nectars of a 25 m tall Syzygium tree within the
primary forest about | km from Muana ranch project. Also, another large female QABB was
sighted near Tahama village searching for nectar plants. It was evident that many horticultural
plants such Hibiscus sp., Ixora sp., and Mussenda philippinesis grown by locals at their homes
provide good nectaries for the birdwing butterflies (sce Plate 4 for nectar plants). The QABB also
feed on the fluids of the Ficus fruits (pers.com., Ezekiel Garui, 2007).

> What is Climate Change (CC)?
Climate Change is the changes in the weather patterns that we experience over a long
period, for instance in a year.
In Papua New Guinea we experience rain, sun, hot. cold, windy day. cloudy day and clear
bright day.
With the aid of the changes in the weather, we can tell at what times of the year we will
have the rainy season and the dry season, when to clear the bush and make our gardens,
when the okari, coffee or mango season will start and so on, We grow buai and coconut
only on the coastal areas and not in the highlands. This is normal to us and it has been our
traditional life style.

But, now we are experiencing a change in the weather patterns, It is raining at the time

mangoes are bearing fruit up in the highlands which never happened before. You can see

Mantaining the Dance

SMD CASE STUDY:

THE MANAGALAS PLATEAU
CONSERVATION AREA PROJECT, ORO
PROVINCE, PAPUA NEW GUINE

Partners with Melanisians. Inc. (PwM)

By Rufus Maburu

Program Manager
07th

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

As time passes, people encounter so many lessons and experiences in their own way of Jife. But
one cannot deny that there are challenges and achievements one faces.

Every organization has its own way to deal with their projects especially working in remote areas
where local people have their own way of living. It is not easy to work with rural people and
impart what you believe can benefit them in a short period of time and effort. It takes time and
effort for the process to complete or even more than what you anticipated for the project to
develop.

Asa long term vision to achieve our goal, Partners with Melanesians Inc. (PwM) envisage that
establishing, coordinating and promoting the work of all members of the community and partner
organizations is the way forward for an organization to progress with its project activities. To
achieve this long term vision, PwM encourages equal participation and self-reliance and
practices sustainable alternative development processes.

PwM strongly believes in full participation by people in developments that benefit everyone and
a development process where people are the cause of development rather than recipients and
mere spectators. Hence people be active participants in any development process or program/s
intended to improve their lives or transform the context and conditions within which they live
and upon which their wellbeing depends.
 Therefore, this is a short summary paper for the Managalas Conservation Area Project that
Partners with Melanesians Inc. is working on with the local communities ever since 1984. The
paper will provide an insight of the organizational background which will provide an update of
history, mission and vision and the programmes of the organization.

This paper will also provide the description of the project area in terms of its rationale, the
objectives, goals and implementing mechanisms including the project strategies and activities.

In addition of course there are successes, lessons learnt and impact that the project encounters.
Finally the paper will provide an insight of the future plans and actions of the organization and
its current and proposed project areas in Papua New Guinea.

1.0 BACKGROUND OF THE ORGANIZATION
1.1 Brief History / Mission & Vision

Partners with Melanesians Inc. (PwM) is a national Non-government organization in Papua New
Guinean established in 1984 by the students and staff of the Language and Literature Department
at the University of Papua New Guinea. PwM is registered as a not for profit association with the
Registration No. 5-896 at the Investment Promotion Authority of Papua New Guinea. PwM
began with a primary interest in the Managalas Plateau in Literacy Project and gradually began
its work in Conservation and Sustainable Community Development following together with the
previous work of its founders in Literacy Project.

Initially, it was set up to support groups and communities who were involved in education and
development initiatives in rural communities of Papua New Guinea. As time progressed, PwM
started its work on the Managalas Plateau of the Oro Province in what has come to be known as
one of the best models of community mobilizing and community development work around
conservation in the country.

PwM envisions to have a “self-reliant and communal society” with is mission of having “a
happy, self-reliant and well-educated society that practices sustainable and alternative
development based on communal ownership of the development process” which will be achieved
through: (i) promotion of self-reliance; (ii) improved access to social services; (iii) promotion
and use of alternative and sustainable methods; (iii) strengthening and promotion of community
participation and consensus building processes; (iv) strengthening and promotion of traditional
decision-making processes; and (v) development/promotion of community-based natural
resources management practices.

With initial financial support coming from various sources including MacArthur Foundation, the
World Bank, Biodiversity Conservation Network (BCN), work around Consensus Building was
started in the late 1980s. As the project evolved to include more and more areas, the need for a
long term commitment from donor partnership was realized when the Rainforest Foundation of
‘Norway (RFN) entered into this partnership in 1997.
 Since then, various other partners have joined in this project including the Government of PNG
through the Targeted Community Development Programme (TCDP) and Community Aid
Abroad (CAA) of Australia, IUCN Netherlands, DOEN Foundation Netherlands, World bank,
UNDP GEF funds, Democratic Governance Transition Phase (DGTP) of Australian Aid now
called Strongim Pipol Strogim Neisen (SPSN) and Canada Fund.

1.2 Programmes

Since its inception, PwM has been at the forefront of the implementation of various programmes
in the Managalas Plateau on various aspects: (i) Consensus-Building geared towards gender
participation, increasing information provision and awareness, strengthening and promotion of
cultural identity; (ii) Conservation consisting of efforts protecting & managing the environment
through cultural practices, creating regulations/laws as a guide on sustainable use of resources
and establishment of eco-enterprises; and (iii) Training towards organizational strengthening,
skills enhancement and adult literacy.

From its inception and initial work, other areas or programmes were developed to assist the work
of Literacy and Conservation on the plateau. These areas are;

a) Conservation and Sustainable Forest Management which mainly focus on the entire work
of all conservation and sustainable use of natural resources of the local communities,
landowners.

b) Rainforest Literacy Program (RFL) which aims at educating all local communities on the
work of conservation and sustainable community development especially in family, clan
and tribe levels.

©) Consensus Building, education awareness and training which focuses on building the
capacity of the local people, providing awareness materials and ensuring that all members
of the of the communities reach a consensus using the consensus building processes
which Managalas People have being using since work on the plateau started.

d) Eco-enterprise or Sustainable Livelihood Alternatives (SLA) aims at providing
alternative activities that that the local communities can engage themselves to sustain
their livelihoods so that they are not tempted by industrial logging, mining and palm oil
activities.

e) Culture and Tradition that aims to preserve the cultural identity of Managalas people in
Papua New Guinea and the region as well.

f) Appropriate Technology Support aims to provide technical activities such as mini hydro
and other related activities that the local people can use to help them minimize wlaking
long distances.

2) Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) Capacity Building which aims at building
the capacity of the local NGO who will take over the responsibilities of PwM when it is
time for PwM to exit from Managalas Plateau.

CONSERVATION AREA PROJECT

2.1 Geographical Location 258}

2.0 THE MANAGALAS PLATEAU ES i"

 Papua New Guinea (PNG) is a country in Oceania, occupying the eastern half of the island of
‘New Guinea and numerous offshore islands (the westem portion of the island is a part of the
Indonesian provinces of Papua and West Papua). It is located in the southwestern Pacific Ocean,
in a region defined since the early 19th century as Melanesia. Globally, PNG is located on the far
North of Australia.

PNG is one of the most culturally diverse countries on Earth, with over 850 indigenous
Janguages and at least as many traditional societies, out of a population of just under seven
million. It is also one of the most rural, as only 18% of its people live in the urban centres. The
country is one of the world's least explored, culturally and geographically, and many
undiscovered species of plants and animals are thought to exist in the interior of Papua New
Guinea. It is the home of the beautiful Bird of Paradise and PNG is the third last rainforest
country in the world apart from Amazon in Brazil and Congo basin in Democratic Republic of
Congo.

 Oro Province, formerly (and officially still known as) Northem Province, is a coastal province of
Papua New Guinea. With its, provincial capital, Popondetta, the province covers around

22,800 km?, and has a total population of 133,065 inhabitants (2000 census). Oro Province is
located on the North east of Port Moresby, capital city of Papua New Guinea. It is a three hours
drive from Popondetta to Managlas Plateau in a four wheel drive on an unsealed road.

‘The Managalas Plateau
is a raised valley lying
between 40 to 2500
metres altitude above
the coastal plain of Oro
Province, Papua New
Guinea. It sits between
the Owen Stanley
Ranges to the south and
west, the Sibium
Ranges to the southeast
and Mount Lamington
and the Hydrographers
to the north and east.
‘The 360,000 hectares of
the Plateau encompass
an extraordinary
diversity of
environments including
alpine heath at 3,800
metres, montane and
hill forest, savannah,
anthropogenic
grassland and gardens.

Like many of the mountainous mid-altitude valleys of PNG, the Plateau is an area of high quality
agricultural land and relatively dense populations. The surrounding mountains, by contrast, are
generally infertile and little populated.

2.2 Rationale / Significance / Impetus for the Project

2.2.1, Biodiversity significance

As mentioned earlier, PNG itself is known to be one of the world's least explored territories —
both culturally and geographically ~ with many undiscovered species of plants and animals are
thought to exist in the interiors of the country.

‘The Managalas Plateau is an area of national and international importance warranting the level of
support that has been applied. According to the Conservation Needs Assessment Study in 1993,

s
 the region has been identified as one of the highest priority areas for biodiversity conservation as
it contains a rich diversity of habitats from alpine heath to lowland savanna. It harbours a large
tract of relatively undisturbed rainforest where it is home to a number of rare and endangered
species including the entire range of the world’s largest butterfly, the Queen Alexander Birdwing
(Ornithopera alexandrea).

“These biodiversity resources are important nationally and globally as a storehouse of genetic
material, as an ecotourism attraction and as a source of environmental services such as fresh
water.

‘This high quality environment is also essential to the survival of the human populations of the
area, While gardening provides the vast majority of foodstuffs, the forests are important as
sources of building materials, medicines, water and other services. The maintenance of this rich
subsistence resource base is essential to averting serious poverty in the region.

2.2.2. Socio-economic conditions and cultural context

‘Around 18,000 people from around 150 clan groups live in 40 village communities on the
Managalas Plateau. These are largely subsistence farmers and depend almost exclusively on the
environment for their livelihood especially the mountain forest. Ten dialects are found on the
plateaus that together make up four broad languages (Barai, Namiai, Ese and Omie).

Unfortunately, the Managalas Plateau is relatively isolated and remote from urban Papua New

Guinea. It is linked to the Oro Provincial Capital, Popondetta, by a poor quality four-wheel drive
road and by two airstrips as well as by foot-tracks. This allows a limited sale of coffee and other
produce during dry conditions but high freight costs and poor maintenance prevent regular trade.

Government services are restricted to a number of elementary and primary schools, four top up
schools, four aid posts, a government station (Afore Local Level Government) and three Health
Centers in the plateau. The Summer Institute of Linguistics (SIL) introduced an adult literacy
program to the Plateau in the 1960s and this has provided an important foundation for many of
the development processes now taking place on the Plateau.

2.2.3. Threats

Over the past decade a number of proposals for timber extraction, oil palm and mining

PARTNERS I/ITH \ELANESIANS

 development have been presented to the Managalas Plateau and have been widely met with
concem by the communities. While weleoming the opportunity for development, Managalas
communities are actively opposing many of these projects due to the poor consultation with
resource owners and the failure to guarantee benefits or environmental protection. Community
members felt that these would damage hunting areas, pollute water supply and increase conflict
with neighbours.

In response to these threats, the community motivation to protect Managalas Plateau and more
importantly its surrounding forest environments is uniformly strong. Thus, the relevance to have
a need of a program that is anchored on environmental protection is further underscored by these
immediate threats that have faced and continue to face the Plateau among which include from
forest loss, population pressure, water contamination and introduced species.

2.3. Objectives, Goals & Implementing Mechanisms

‘The over-all objective of the Managalas Plateau Conservation Area Project is to preserve the
biological resources of the Plateau and promote sustainable development at the same time, with
the long term hope of establishing a Conservation Area on the Plateau.

‘The Project is the collaborative effort of the Managalas peoples, PwM, and a handful of other
‘support organizations that have provided both financial resources and technical assistance such
as the MacArthur Foundation, the World Bank, Biodiversity Conservation Network (BCN), and
the Rainforest Foundation of Norway (REN). Other partners have joined in this project including
Audaid and others mentioned earlier above.

2.4, Project Strategies and Activities
2.4.1 Strategy and Approach
a, Consensus Building

The work revolving around the Managalas Plateau is an attempt to answer one of the most
significant challenges of governance in Melanesian society. While the cooperation within clans
isa strongly developed tradition in the Managalas Plateau and wider Melanesia, there seems to
be a shallow tradition of consensus building between other clans and larger groupings.

‘A “consensus building” approach is a significant part of the PwM programme that helps clans
across a zone to identify issues that they are for or against; and at the same time, trying to
develop strategies for collaborative action. This sets up opportunity for cooperation across
boundaries that have traditionally been sources of confli

‘A central aspect of the Managalas Consensus Building strategy is to establish a process of
discussion and agreement at the family, clan, zone, and regional level. The programme is based
on the clan as the basic unit of organization. Zones are self-identified natural groupings of clans
 based on terms of trade (yam exchange), shared heritage, common dialects, and song. They are
confirmed by social mapping.

‘As the consensus building process works at three levels: clan, culture area (or “zone”), and sub-
district -- it seeks to ensure regular informed debate on key issues that start with families, rises to
clans, is then brought to zones, and from there can lead to discussions at combined forums where
are zones are represented. On each level, a consensus must be reached on an issue before it can
progress to the next wherein written information is provided in the vernacular language by the
local literacy associations based on materials prepared by PwM.

The consensus building structure works (o reinforce clan leadership. Elders have an important
position in the process at the clan level and often gain opportunities to represent their clans at a
zone and regional levels in a way that rarely would have happened in the past.

In addition to this consensus building process, the Managalas Plateau is divided into eastern and
westem plateau. Within these two areas there plateau is again divided into 18 wards which are
recognized by the local level government. The plateau is also divided into their cultural areas
which PwM uses and recognize them as zones. The whole area of 360, 000 ha is divided into 10
cultural zones and these cultural zones have their own CBOs who operate with their own
management and board of directors. There are 11 CBOs within these 10 cultural zones and these
11 CBOs are affiliated to their mother umbrella NGO called Managalas Development
Foundation Inc. (MDF) who also has its own management and board of directors.

b. Gender Participation

In the previous years, there was a pervasive gender imbalance in leadership roles at the Plateau.
Asa strategy, gender awareness workshops were conducted, which were very effective in
increasing the recognition of women's roles on the Plateau, and catalyzed a change towards
increasing women's participation in the programme. Gender equality and participation were
among the needs that were identified and addressed during various workshops and meetings.

2.4.1. Key Project Activities and Result Areas

Among the project activities that are being implemented in the area include: boundary mapping,
Participatory 3D model, conservation area management planning, eco-enterprise/sustainable
livelihood alternatives, enhancement and promotion of sustainable land use practice,
strengthening culture, conduct of capacity building workshops, literacy, and gender participation,
school in-service for teachers and final preparation of Conservation Area Application to
Department of Environment and Conservation in PNG, annual successful district wide combine
forums and community reforestation.

 a. Protection of forest habitats

Under the 1996 National Forest Plan, two large areas of forest on the Managalas Plateau were
proposed for forestry operations. The Gora-Itokama Forest Management Area (FMA) in the
centre and north, and the Musa concession in the south were large scale operations that would
have removed a significant arca of the Owen Stanley Range forests.

In part as a result of the growing environmental consciousness among communities through
recognition of the value of okari trees (Terminalia kaernbachii spp.) and a strong opposition to
logging developed to these concession proposals, the communities sought assistance from the
advocacy NGOs to have the concessions removed from their land.

In 1998, a coordinated action (in cooperation with other groups such as MICAD, Greenpeace and
ICRAF) resulted in the cancellation of proposed Gora-Itokama Forest Management Area and
another oil proposed palm operation in the same year. Actions that brought about this result
included letters from lawyers serving as legal representatives in behalf of the communities,
placing of newspaper advertisements, lobbying the government and the Forest Authority Board
and holding press conferences.

A very significant result of this work was the designation of the area for conservation in the PNG
Forest Authority Forest Plans. This was the first time such formal recognition was given to an
area of forest in PNG that was not considered to be a formal conservation area. As a result, there
is greater security for the resources of Managalas and Collingwood Bay. These two large areas
have also allowed the possibility of a protected forest corridor from the Kokoda trail to the Oro
Province border.

The partnership between Partners with Melanesian and Theatre Arts Section

ACTIVITY:_ CA Border Patrol & Zone Boundary Mapping

INTRODUCTION

Zone Boundary Mapping & Conservation Area (CA) Border Patrol were combined activities
undertaken within the given timeframe of two weeks for this 2" field trip. This follows after
informing beforehand the zones concerned (2, 3, 5 & 6) regarding their Boundary Mapping and
informing Kingsford Nichoi on the continuations of the CA Border patrol.

This particular report will encompass these two activities as implemented by the Conservation
Planning Coordinator (CPC) & the Conservation Support Cfficer (CSO) with the assistance from
Zone CBOs concerned, Kingsford and the 3 most cheerful strong young men as carriers. These
activities mostly invelved hiking ridges and steep mountains especially the interior and the exterior
of the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) and also to meet with the concerned
communities which wouldn’t be accomplished if it wasn’t for the assistance. Apart from these
activities, we were also able to monitor the progress of the Pogani reforestation programme and
continue to carry out awareness while there for talks with the Pogani Community
leaders/Chiefs/elders on CA border patrol.

PURPOSE

1. Zone Boundary Mapping
The primary purpose of this activity is to map out the internal Boundaries of the Managalas
Proposed CA (MPCA) that jed into their +1 Cultura! zones. Because of the vastness and the
physical geography of the area, there were only 4 zones selected for a start this year ie. zone 2, 3
(East) 5 & 6 (West)

ll. CABorder Patrol

The Purpose of this activity is to patrol the villages inhabiting the fringes as well as the villages that
directly border with the Proposed CA. This is basically to find out the status of the Proposed
Boundary line of the Conservation Area in terms of having meetings with the Paramount
Landowners/leacers/eldersispoxesperson and coming to a consensus. It is entirely their decision to
either extend the boundary to include them within the CA or vice versa.

METHODS/PROCEDURES:

These 2 activities were planned to be implemented within the timeframe of 2 week. Given the
timeframe to implement the different activities over the vast physical Geography cf the Managalas
Plateau, the strategy undertaken was assigning the Zone CBOs to carry out Zone Boundary
Mapping while the PwM officers with the assistance from Kingsford and his local youths to

 implement the CA Border Patrol. A table in the attachment will show the schedule undertaken to
implement the activities.

Zone Boundary Mapping

1. PwM officers firstly to meet with the CBO Manager's of Zone 2,3 in East and 5,6 in West
Use 3D Model of Managalas to identify the areas to collect coordinate points

CA Border Patrol
The CA Border patrol was more a continuation from where Kingsford Nichoi has started last year
when he was the Conservation Officer on the ground for Managalas Development Foundation
(MDF). He and his team have done the first leg of the Border Patrol from Tetebedi to parts of Musa
and down to Bareji where he finally stopped. Hence, this time, it was from Sigara to Siana and all
the way down to Pogani. This was basically to conduct meetings in those areas as stated above
respectively to find out the status of the CA boundary mark.

Purpose
Revisit background Mapping of MPCA

General conservation awareness

MPCA update & CA processes

Raise their concerns & questions (to be in the discussions)

While at Pogani, we continued to check on the Reforestation progress and at the same time,
