RESULTS
Unfortunately, PwM officers only met up with the Zone CBOs of 5 & 6 while zone 3 & 4 never
showed up due to reasons unknown. With concerns of the time limitation, the team decided to go
ahead with the Zones in the East to implement their Zone Boundary Mapping.

in addition, the 3D Model of the Managalas Plateau display was used to visually point out the zones
concerned whereby the Zone Managers were able to point out their Zone Boundaries. In doing so,
it helped out to identify the areas to collect the coordinate points when using the GPS.

The PwM officers were able to teach the basics on how to collect the Coordinates and note it on
their exercise books for the record. Then we left them to take on the task of getting the GPS.
points.

For the CA Border Patrol, it was a team made up of 2 PwM officers (Patrick & !), Kingsford and 3
local youths that impiemented this particular activity. We patrolied over steep mountain ridges,
crossed rivers, waterfalls to get to Sigara & Siana. Even our last leg to Pogani was quite exhausting
because we had to walk on pebbles & unsteady, rough surface rocks just by tollowing the river
channels downstream until we reached Pogani Wara Buum.

There were only 2 meetings held at Siana village and Pogani village. The elders/chiefs from Siana &
Sigara attencied the meeting while the same was done in Pogani as well.

In the attachment is the 2 separate meeting minutes for Siana & Pogani respectively. However,
here are the outcomes of the meetings respectively;

1) The Siane Chief has expressed their concern now that they have realised the threats they are
facing in terms of ongoing illegal logging and the proposed Oro Bay township extension to include
their land into the proposed CA. In consensus were the Chief and spokesman for the other 2 clans
of Apaora and Marareja from these 2 villages that border with the Siana chief’s Land Boundary as
they are all for Conservation.

2) As for the Pagani People, it is a different story were they are mostly confusing Pw werk with
other NGO who have came before such as Conservation Melanesia that left with a bad record.
Aiter alt, it was alt a misunderstanding so it was all discussed and made clear during the meeting.
Hence, all their chiefs, elders, community leaders decided to make aware PwM’s work and most
importantly with the information that they have obtained from the discussion would help settle
their land issues. it will be discussed further below.

 RECOMMENDATIONS & DISCUSSIONS

For the Zone Boundary mapping, it was implemented as tasked by the zone CBO managers of 5 & 6
of East and the coordinate points were provided to Patrick to produce the internal Boundary
mapping. Gradually overtime, all the zones within the MPCA will be covered.

The meetings that were conducted during the CA border patrol had the common concer for
LAND.

In the case of the Sigara and Siana villages, they share land Boundaries and the fact that all of
Mitataora Clan of Sigara‘s land are within the MPCA while three Clans (Uera, Marareja and Apaora)
of Siana have only part of the land within the MPCA. We did not have to go that far because they
have seen for themselves the damages that are already been done by the ongoing illegal logging
and they face yet another development threat of Oro bay Township and potential prospecting of
mineral resources on their land. With all these that is happening around, the only way is to
safeguard their resources and their environment as a whole.

Action Points

1. It is only considerate that Siana people’ s part of their land on the outer CA boundary be
included as it is a gain to protect as much as possible a bigger landmass of forest area.

2. The Siana and the Sigara people still need Environmental awareness to strengthen &
extend the work of CA. Also to empower the community to mobilise in terms of making
well informed decisions to combat development threats.

3. The Zone CBO responsible (that would be zone 6) must be able to reach out to these
isolated people in terms of information sharing, update on CA work and awareness etc...

For the Pogani people, the misconception of NGO’s work was labelled the same all across whereby
PwM’s work was confused with Conservation Melanesia’s work (CM). CMs reputation left behind
was not all that good when it ceased work on a particular area on the Plateau. It created an
opportunity for someone smart enough to show invalid documents to the ill informed community
to extend logging into parts of Pogani area. The worst part from information gathered so far is that
PwM proposed CA map was used to falsely claim land rights with support from an expired CM
WMA certificate. Hence, it has created a situation where they see our presence as a threat to them.
Through the meeting, everything was being clarified including our Organisation’s profile and our
work, the initial CA Map and the CA process. The response we got was mixed when we touched the
topic of CA boundary. Hence, now that the pogani chiefs, elders and community leaders are better
informed, they are able to disseminate the correct information to the pogani community. Apart
from this activity, reforestation was monitored as well and it seems that it all comes down to the
issue of land.

 Action Points
1. Pogani community to be correctly informed of the outcome of the Meeting
2. Proper consultation with the relevant stakeholders (landowners) in the interest
Y Confirming the CA Boundary if it will remain or readjust

Y Make a available a portion of grassland along the roadside to implement the first
planting of the Kwila species
Forester to give more technical advice on how to do nursery and replanting.
Continuous awareness using various mediums in terms of case studies such as OKPF
reforestation program in posters, brochures and videos. Video show as seen is an effective
medium to educate people on all cross-cutting issues.

ey

CONCLUSION

To conciude, it was an experience that will be cherished as being a female officer out on field and
realising how risky it was to penetrate the hearts of the very remote communities to implement
these activities. it also made me see how isolated the people and being marginalised in terms of
basic services. Seeing all this drives my passion to contribute more in the area of my field for the
benefit of the rurai community. After all, both zone Boundary Mapping and CA Border Patrol were
implemented within the given timeframe of 2 weeks. These activities were implemented by Patrick
& { with assistance from the zone 5 & 6 CBO Managers, Kingsford and the 3 local carriers.
Otherwise, the recommendations are there for your consideration.

MANAGALAS, AFORE DISTRICT, ORO PROVINCE

Compiled by Evengelyn Kove
 INTRODUCTION

The emphasis on Management Plan is very vital for the sustainability of the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area. On that note, Workshops were conducted to train & educate the Managelas
community to prepare to take on the responsibility of the core Management team where it is required
of them as stated in the Conservation Areas Act 1978. As principal stekehoiders in the whole
conservation process, it is compulsory that the targeted groups within the community need to
undergo these workshops to understand what is required of them and in doing so, they are able to
consensually develop the Management Plan & appoint the people that will fully represent the
community based on sound & fair judgment guided by the terms & conditions required under the Act
to implement the Management Pian at the community level. In saying this, apart from other
Workshops, Management Plan Workshop itself was conducted firstly in 2004, followed by 2008 then
in 2011 and now is the 4" time, this workshop has been run.

Now looking at all the 3 past workshops, it has been noticed that, there were no evaluation done after
each workshop so as to keep track of the information transfer to the participants in terms of
enhancing their knowledge as the workshops progressed on. The fact that the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area is yet to be declared and hence, it gave time to run the Management Pian
workshops ahead. However, the issuie identified was not knowing exact'y if they (participants) have
really captured the contents of the workshops. Thus, monitoring & evaltiation on a smaller scale is a
vital component that has been missed out and so it was included in this fourth workshop. It has been
also emphasized strongly at the Partners With Melanesians (PWM) Midterr» planning that in order to
measure the success of your implementation of activities is to monitor & evaluate not only at the end
of the year but at intervals after every individual activity. This is to try & fill in the gaps as much as
possibie to ensure

issues are kept et a minimum.

PURPOSE

With this evaluation, it is more of a summary assessment for all 4 management Pian workshop held.
Simple Questionnaire was designed to evaluate & assess the expected cutcome of the 4 Workshops
and to make improvements where possible.

METHODS

The methods undertaken for this Evaluation was using Questionnaires to get the participants views,
also from observation and side talk as well. Previous Management Plan reports were also used to

text:
“ WARD NO. 4 - KAURA & AWARU VILLAGE
TITLE: WARD PROFILE ~ 2008 - 2013

Introduction
‘The Ward 4 is located at the Northeast direction of Afore District known as Kaura & Awaru community.
It is northwest of the main capital, Popondetta.

It takes about four (4) hours walk and 30 minutes by Transport from Afore Station to reach the ward 4
destination. It takes about 6 hours to travel from Popondetta Town to Afore along east coast road known

as Alex Highway.

‘The ward 4 consists of 458 adults and 408 children adding up to the total population of 866. The
topography is mostly tropical high land rainforest and grassland. The soil is organic which enables an
abundance of garden foods.

‘The main source of income for the local people is coffee and vanilla and other stuffs such as; peanuts
and betel nuts which they sell for basic necessities.

“ESE ESE?” is the unique reception meaning “Welcome” in the local ESE dialect.

Ward Profile
“The ward 4 has a total population of 866 which consists of 8 major clans of various age groups; 18 years
& above, male adults 255, female adults 203 and below 18 years; male children 228 and female children
180; which make up the community of ward 4.

Church Profile

Christian Revival Crusade and Renewal churches are the two (2) main religious groups in ward 4. CRC
has 118 congregation members with 2 pastors, 4 elders, 3 lady leaders, 26 ladies, 4 Sunday school
teachers, 50 Sunday school children, 4 young people leaders and 31 young people. Renewal Church has
150 congregation members, 1 pastor, 2 elders, 2 lady leaders, 2 Sunday school teachers, and 69 Sunday
school children.

Cash Crops

‘The ward’s major sources of income for the local people are Coffee and Vanilla; however, there is no
market for Vanilla at the moment. The people from the ward 4 area alone own a total of 205 coffee
gardens which grows 152,895 Arabica trees and produces 1,265 coffee bags of dried Arabica beans. An
annual earning cash income of K78, 000.00 for ward 4. Recently 54 coffee gardens of Arabica have
been destroyed by the recent disaster.

Vanilla is one of the major sources of cash crop well grown in ward 4 area and the plateau has a whole.
‘The Vanilla farmers have found that there is no market for Vanilla maybe due to lack of proper skill and
support from Government agency. The ward 4 has grown 1,523 vines in 31 Vanilla gardens. ‘Two
Vanilla gardens were destroyed by the recent disaster.
 usiness

Many people are interested in small scale business as we are aware, today we need money to buy goods
and services we need or want. Trade Store is the most common type of retail business people are
engaged. The ward 4 alone has nine trade stores and 14 peddles run privately by local people. Today
money has become important in people’s lives as people need cash for many reasons. They need cash to
pay basic necessities of life such as; food stuff, medicine, clothing and to pay children’s school fees.

El ita

Education plays an important role. The Ward 4 Kaura and Awaru Elementary School consists of 136
students of various grades.

Community Based Constable (CBC)

Concerning with Law and Order.
The Ward 4 Kaura & Awaru consists of four (4) community based Constables and four (4) Ward
Committees. They assist the Police at the village level in settling conflicts and disputes that arises in and
around the community.

‘Youths
‘Youths are mostly made up of a group of young people. Youths are the most concerned people in the
community. The Ward 4 is mostly made of youths. Youths in Ward 4 are keen in Sport activities such
as soccer, and volleyball. These are the two (2) main sports in which most youths in Ward 4 participate
in apart from other social activities. The Ward 4 consists of one (1) Soccer Club and Eight Volleyball
Clubs.

Housing
‘The Ward 4 is made up of 2 main communities Kaura and Awaru. The Ward 4 alone consists of 866
population, 153 houses, one (1) Elementary School and Two (2) Church groups.

Houses are built for people to; (1) _—_—Settle with their family
(2) Keep them warm and safe
 Kaura has 81 family houses, while has Awaru 72 houses adding to a total of 153 houses for Ward 4
alone.

Out off 153 houses, some houses are leaking now, due to no sago leaves to repair and maintain the
broken roof. In the recent disaster over 600 sago palm trees have been swept away by the floods and
landslides. It will take 20 to 30 years for the new plants to grow and replace the palm trees. Sago has
two main uses; one it is eaten as food, however, more importantly its leaves are used for housing roofs.

‘The local people need basic goods and services. We are need dire need of Government aid to assist the
Local people to repair the leaking roof. By assisting the local people with irom sheets to repair the
broken roofs while waiting for the new planted sago palms to be fully grown in the next 20 - 30 years
time.

ent
In the previous years the Ward 4 has been given 15 coffee pulpers (machine), 4 sewing machines and 54
iron sheets by the previous governments as a major need for the local people.
Private Assets
‘The local people have to strive for many years to meet their own needs. In their strive some have been

successful and others are not. The local people own 17 private coffee pulpers (machines) and sadly 26
have been washed away by the recent floods.

For more information refer to the structure of Ward 4, Kaura and Awaru village.

Introduction

‘The Combine Planning meet was the opportunity for each component to present their Work plan activities accordingly. The
Climate Change Component have only two main activities with two others Monitoring and evaluation to check on the
progress of the Activity implementation. It was also the time to discuss the first Activity in April.

Purpose

-imary Purpose of this Pre-planning meeting was to prepare and let the CBOs to be aware of thie activity for the upcoming,
<umate Change Awareness Workshop. The first activity of the Climate change component is the Awareness Workshop for
the 11 CBOs to attend and learn the Basics of Climate Change before carrying out the Awareness in their respective
communities the correct information.

Methods

The Climate Change Work plan is being given out to take note while the Coordinator gave the right information
for the CBOs to. commit their day considering their community Calender with Timeframe. invitation letters for

and filling in the Work plan.

Discussion

‘As this is a new component included for this year, It was the great opportunity to introduce this the Managalas Community
and the fact that this have been one of the cross-cutting issue that has been continuously raised in the Combine forum, the
Managalas Community welcomed this program with anticipation to take in any information to equip them to respond
proactively to the inevitable natural extreme events. So the date is set as 5 April ~ 13° April and will be hosted at
Ugunomo in Zone 5.
  Recommendation

Action Plans

As the date is set the next thing is to check on OCD to release their officer. Their officer and the Climate Change &
community reforestation Coordinator need to sit down and come up with the contents of information needed to develop a

Communicate with the all CBOs for the latest updates and also in terms of logistics (Transport and accommodations) on the
ground.

‘The Awareness materials needs to be sorted out as well as the information needed will have to be designed for production.

Conclusion

‘The New Component was introduced and welcomed by the CBOs as it is long time coming for them. They anticipate the
information needed to develop the action plans that will protect them from further impacts of Climate Change. This year
illbe on data collection and Awareness will be needed for the appropriate measures.

‘Tho Tahama/Kaitama area has a total of about 93 coffee farmers of which 19 plus farmers have a
garden of more than 1 hectares plus gardea, i.c; they have 1 thousand and above coffee trees

The above 15 farmers statistics is collected in 1 week 4 days, i.e; those who cared to spend time with
the enumerator. Otherwise, all do not care due to other reasons and the most common reason was that
it was a Yam planting season and have given priority to it.

Brief Summary on Tahama/Kaitama area.

‘Total No. Of farmers: 93
Farmers with more than 1 hectare area: 19. These are farmers with more than 1000 plus coffee trees.

Total number of parchment bags in one season:
2006 - 158 bags

iz
iS
is

‘The significant drop in the 2006 production was due to farmers neglecting theic coffee gardens
because of failed governments green revolution scheme in air liling and subsidizing freights to
nearest sales depot

General Overview

Harvesting
Mostly, are family member involvement. These are farmers with less than one thousand trees. Those
with one thousand plus or more involve women groups during peak harvest.
 za-ocT-2006 12:40

JAMBORDS 9 STATIONERY 67s 7522788

Pulping
Generally, the ratio of farmers to a pulping machine is about 9:1 depending on the family or clan
ownership.

This, thus often result in deterioration of harvested beans as they await for 2 to 3 days before pulping
and this leads to quality deterioration.

Drying
The method of drying used is of standard drying, i.e; dried above erected beds.

Stormge
Most store their dried parchment indoors unless in larger quantities. Those that store in open are
encouraged to use canvass to avoid exposure to moisture.

‘Transportation -

Previously, transportation was a major problem encountered by farmers. Due to MOCP engagement of
CBO in various point and other buyers the problem has been somewhat alleviated. Incentives of 20t
per kilogram was offered for the labor endured in moving parchment coffee to the buying points as
well.

Pris
Previous price fetched were around 70t to 80t per parchment kilogrammme. In 2006, there has been a
significant increase in price, Lc; K2.00 to K2.$0 per kilogramme. This was due to MOCP involvement
in the area, and other buyers in competition.

‘The price increase has led to rebabilitation of abandoned gardens duc to fail governments green
revolution programme in the area,

Impediments on Survey

Due to poor dissemination of MOCP’s business plan to all farmers in the project area, there isa
doubting approach due to misconception towards officers engaged by MOCP in carrying out
programmes like extension and deta survey.

‘This often results in verbal abuses and on few occasion physical confrontations with MOCP Officers
by il! informed farmers.

The Officers are now stood down til! proper Public Relations and full awareness is established of
MOCP’s business plan and then shall the programme/activities may continue within conducive and
friendly atmosphere. As it is the case the survey programme is ceased, according to the MOCP Project
Manager.

Competition

‘There are few coffee buying agents within the project area with different business plans from MOCP's
and are vigorously campaigning against MOCP’s involvement. This thus results in hindrance towards
MOCP Officers’ programmes,
 z4-0cT-2006 12:49 JAMBORDS 9 STATIONERY ers 1522788

Conclusion

‘There is a great nced for public awareness on the MOCP’s business plan, CBO’s in cach zones must be
pushed to disseminate MOCP’s business plan. MDF Officers must fully cooperate with MOCP
Officers in achieving awareness.

Furthermore, the programme has been temporary suspended until next year 2007 when all matters
resolved amicably. These includes, MOCP Officers specific roles in the project and MDF Officers
roles in the MOCP Project.

From the last MDF meeting on the specific agenda of MOCP operations, the operations plan had been
discontinued. There the Project Coordinator has no option but to suspend programme,

Please note that Derivation of information from datas cannot be made until full enumeration is
conducted in the Project Area

snippet: FINAL TECHNICAL REPORT 2003-2006 2.2 Module A (Forestry and Logging) Under this module, the following are the outcomes achieved (2003-2006) 4 Communication system—2way HF radio 4. Establishment of Managalas organic Coffe Project (MOCP) & Technical assistance from PNG National Agriculture and Livesto
text:
FINAL TECHNICAL REPORT 2003-2006
2.2 Module A (Forestry and Logging)
Under this module, the following are the outcomes achieved (2003-2006)

4 Communication system—2way HF radio

4. Establishment of Managalas organic Coffe Project (MOCP)

& Technical assistance from PNG National Agriculture and Livestock

4 CELCOR and ELC legal assistance on logging and forestry campaign
Impacts achieved (2003-2006)
‘Communication was one of the main problems that hindered the program but since the
purchase of the 2way radios it became easier for the project to flow on Managalas
Plateau. The coffe project is a success activity that NLRPA project, although it was a
big task PWM managed to overcome the task. The project is now in full operation as an
NTEP activity for Managalas people.
Technical and legal assistance from CELCOR, ELC and PNG Agriculture is very helpful
in NLRPA program.
Constrains leading to variations
Although PWM faced difficult problems with communication and coffee establishment,
PWM used its donors funds especially from IUCN and others to cater for the program to
continue as schedule in the workplan.
2.3 Module B (Oil Palm Awareness)
Under this module, the following are the outcomes achieved (2003-2006)

s£ Oil Palm Awareness training with CBOs on Managalas Plateau

4 Soap and Candle Making

= ‘The community producing their own soap and candle using their natural

resources

+ Rice Farming
= Community growing rice for consumption and for market

+ Rice Mill
= PWM purchased a mill for the community to mill their own rice
 4b Honey bee farming
= successfial honey investigation and community willing to farm bees

4 Oil Palm Poster being produced for Awareness and Campaign purpose
4 Technical assistance from PNG National Agriculture and Livestock
4 CELCOR and ELC legal assistance on oil palm campaign
Under this module, the following are the impacts achieved (2003-2006)
Trainers to run trainings and workshops are quite difficult to attach or even expensive to
travel to project site however PWM manage to bring them for the training or workshops.
It took quite a while to engage a specialist to produce an oil palm poster but finally PWM
engaged a cheaper company to produce the poster through negotiation. Although PNG
National Agriculture and Livestock and PWM are yet to sign an MOU, their technical
expertise are continuing to provide assistance to PWM.
Under this module, the following are constrains leading to variations
It is quite expensive to bring specialists from other provinces to the project site. The

calendar or workplans among P' CELCOR and the communities are overlap each
other

2.4 Module C (Dams-Not Appticadle to PWM)
2.5 Module D (Protected Areas)
Under this module, the following are the outcomes achieved (2003-2006)
4. Aircraft Charter
- To transport NTFP to Port Moresby city from Managalas Plateau
sb GIS training by WWF-PNG Specialist
4 Purchases 3 D mode! materials

++ Co-funded a support staff to work on Conservation Management Plan for
Managalas Plateau

Under this module the impacts achieved (2003-2006)

Although the charter fees were increasing, PWM managed to cater for the charters.
Mapping became a problem for GIS activity but PWM managed to collaborate with

WWF to run an internal training.
 Under this module the constrains leading to variations

Charter became very expensive over time between 2003 and 2006. PWM is yet to
complete the mapping and 3 D modeling is still ongoing. The conservation Management
is still in the process with a full time staff.

3. Sustainability of Project/program results and effects

Sustainability of the project results and effects depends mainly with the time frame
finance which seem to be the factors that needs to be addressed.

In terms of the time frame it seems that there is a limited time frame to achieve the goals
of the project. However PWM made an effort to achieve some of the expected results
within the time frame.

The sustainability of the results and effects of the project could have progressed without
further interventions. Taking into account of all results and the effects of the project, the
following follow-up activities could be considered to increase the sustainability of the

project:
> Greater intervention is required to sustain the project

> Increase the capacity of the stafi/human resource
> Anew approach of management and collaborative approach is required

> Lessons leamed should be considered adequately

Within the PWM program on Conservation, there is a major donor (Rainforest Norway)
who has a component of eco-enterprise which assist with the program. Besides that there
are no other follow-up funds but in future PWM will try to seek other alternative
fundraising activities that can sustain the program.

As PWM intends to exit from the current project site, the program and its activities are
essential to be replicated in our new sites. Hence there is a five year exit strategy between
Managalas community (MDF) in place where we would like to build the capacity of the
local NGO (MDF) to be capable of running their own conservation and sustainable

livelihood program on the plateau.
4. Overall program aspects

4.1 What were the main strengths of the program?

* Communities are mobilized in 10 different zones as CBOs and willing to
participate with the program activities
 Established alternative sustainable livelihood opportunities to local communities
on the plateau

‘© Communities are aware of the program as they are also more aware of
conservation activities

© Communities accept the concept of eco-enterprise

4.2 What were the main weaknesses of the program?

‘© Insufficient funding and staff
© Staff tumover
© Lack of government support

4.3 What do you consider as the main lessons learned from the program?

Community aware of the importance of their natural resources

Natural resource management is in the hands of the communities

‘Awareness is very important in the communities

Identifying community's expectations/demands

Relationship between people and their environment

Community's way of life ~ culture & customs

Community's perspective on the work/value of NLRPA project along with the

conservation activities

© The importance of NLRPA project with its impact on people’s lives on Managalas
Plateau

© The value of community participation and consensus building on Managalas

Plateau

cece eae

4.4 What was the added value of the collaboration of natureandpoverty* to the activities
of your own organization in the period 2003 - 2006?

* Communities are willing to be engaged with the alternative sustainable livelihood
activities using their natural resources

© Good coordination between PWM and Managalas Development Foundation
(MDF) to execute actrivities

© Substantial support from main PWM programme budget to assist NURPA
activities

4.5 On which perspective did your organization seek collaboration with other
organizations of the natureandpoverty* partnership?

© The synergy exchange programme
‘© Engagement of partner NGO specializations

4.6 Which were the constraints limiting collaboration?
 ‘© No focal point to collaborate

© Lack of staff to assist

© Communication not effective among partners
5, Communication outputs

* Purchase of 2way radios in 2004

* Purchase of mobile phone in 2005

Production of oil palm posters in 2006

Zone Briefing
17" February 2006
Naukenane Village, Zone 1

Three topics were chosen at the Leaders Summit held on 19 - 22 December 2005, as.
topics that should go through the 2006 zone forums. These issues will form the basis of
the end of the year combine forum. This brief is prepared to present these discussion
topics to the activity coordinators who will be leading and coordinating the clan and
group discussions. The topics are: 1) Council of Chiefs; 2) 2007 Council and National
Elections; 3) Traditional Leaning Centres. Each of the topics has questions that should
stir the discussions in the various groups. Each group will be required to note down
responses to each of the discussion questions and a general consensus reached on each of
the topics. The group’s consensus will be presented at the combine forum.

+ COUNCIL OF CHIEFS (COC)

a) _ Whatis the COC?
‘The idea of having a Council of Chiefs came from discussions during the Leader's
Summit held on 19% —22™ December 2005 at Serefuna Village.

b) Why having a COC?

‘This is an issue within the Managalas and especially in conjunction with MDF and the
issue of leadership between the Traditional and Contemporary Leaders- the Old and the
young educated leaders. It seems that the young educated people have displaced the
‘elders out of the new structure and they have become defunct and of no consequence to
the current developments, After a lot of discussion, the Summit agreed to have in place a
COC. Traditional elders are important members of the community and they need to be
more involved in the new developments that confront the plateau. They need to be
involved because they are important in more than one way.

Traditional leaders are important because:
© Have respect from their own clans.
Have traditional knowledge and wisdom.
Peace brokers
Settle disputes
Control the clan decision-making process,
‘Transfer knowledge and skills to the next generation.
Control over the land.
Control other issues in the village
Body to liaise with Goverment.

te eeceee

b) Who becomes a member of the COC?
 It was decided by the Leader’s Summit that each zone must have a representative at the
Council of Chiefs. The clan representatives from each village come together at the zone
level. The ONE representative representing a particular zone is elected at the zone level
and is represented in the Council of Chiefs.

©) Who does the COC represent?
Each member on the COC represents his zone. The whole COC body represents the
16,000 + people of Managalas.

d) What does the COC represent and what is their major function?
The COC is the highest decision making body on the plateau dealing with Traditional
Laws.

©) How much power does the COC have?
The extent at which COC is to exercise its powers will be vested in their constitution.

1) _Whatare their roles & responsibilities?
Some Specific Roles of Traditional leaders would be:

Deal with tribal conflict

Mediate on land matters

Oversee and provide advice to CBOs on cultural issues

Advice MDF on industrial and economic development and natural resources.
Lead and oversee on cultural, traditional, customary practices in Managalas.
Provide input on political agenda/issues on the plateau.

Liaise with MDF on consensus buil
Others to be included .

ecco eecee

h) Who are the COC answerable to?
They are answerable to the whole of the plateau (16,000 + people) and to each clan
member in their villages and zones of which they represent.

i) Can the community change the COC if they are not doing their job?
Yes. Only at the Zone Forum. Changes made at zone level wil] affect membership to
coc.

i) _Are women eligible to become COC?
Yes. If the woman has the customary right to be the chief of her clan.

k) If NOT, then why not?

Because chieftainship in most communities on Managalas are inherited from father to son
etc.

Dd How long can someone be on the COC?
As long as he/she is not voted out at the zone forum.

m) — Will the COC have a chair?
 Yes. The COC will have a chair elected by the COC to steer and guide the operations of
the COC in agreement and consent of the COC members.

©) _ Will the COC have a constitution?
Yes. The constitution will be written by CELCOR Lawyers with initial baseline data
compilation by the Community Learning Centres.

Pp) Will there be an MOU between MDF Board & COC?
Yes. The MOU will spell out the roles and responsibilities of the COC and how the COC
will complement the roles and responsibilities of the MDF Board.

n Will the COC have an AGM?
Yes. The AGM will be a part of the combine forum held at the end of each year.

8) What happens at the COC AGM?
This is when the COC reports back to the communities about what they have done during
the year including successes and failures. It is during the AGM when members of the
COC could be elected out of the COC. The election of new members of the COC will be
taken back to the zone level.
 ~& 2007 COUNCIL AND NATIONAL ELECTIONS

1. Why is PWM talking about this?

The Kjivitari Electorate is a big electorate that when it comes to choosing a candidate to
represent the people of Ijivitari in the National Parliament, people from the coast are the
ones voted in to Parliament by the people of Managalas and the Kjivitari electorate as a
whole. It has come to being that the Managalas area has long been forgotten. Government
infrastructures have deteriorated and services are worse than ever before.

PWM has been in the plateau for the past 16 years or so and have assisted the people in
small ways using donor support. But his cannot go on forever. PWM is implementing its
exit strategy beginning this year and will end in 2008.

If Managalas people continue to vote into Parliament someone from the coast, the
Managalas will be lost in time. Therefore, it is high time for the Managalas people to
speak with one voice and vote someone from Managalas into Parliament in the 2007
elections so that vital government infrastructure and services will come to Managalas for
the good of our children and their children’s children.

2. Where did this discussion start?
This discussion started from the Leaders Summit last December 2005. The Summit
appointed an election committee who will coordinate this on the Plateau.

3. What is PWM role?
PWM will play an advisory role to the election committee with Kenn Mondiai as the
Advisor.

4, What is the role of the Election Committee?

The main task of the committee was to engage in an awareness campaign to mobilize the
Managalas community to a central place to appoint two candidates for the National
Elections. One from East and one from West. For example, if one from East is appointed
for the Open Electorate then one from West should be appointed for the Regional Seat
The committee comprised of several people.

 Executive Summary

From mere observation of its structure Managalas Development Foundation has
been unintentionally designed to function os a supra system consisting of various
sub-systems and systems of systems hence appropriating it to adapt a training
strategy that will enhance the various sub-systems to function independently yet
collaborate with each other to meet the overall goals of the community based not-
for-profit organization's capacity building needs. [Very similar to the Melanesian
circular system of governance in which service delivery, community mobilizing and
etc. is often led by influential individuals however the emphasis is placed on overall
community wellbeing. It involves active participation and interaction between
individual, groups of individual. and communities. Collaboration and
interdependency hos always been the norm].

The success of its various programs will heavily Gepend on the efficiency of the
individuals involved thus the training strategy is to produce learning individuals who
will tasked themselves to undertake various activities of MDF as personal action
learning projects. It is anticipated that by the end of an individual action leaming
project using “systems learning approach” the participant will have advanced
himself in his personal capacity whilst at the same time appreciating the overall
human resource capacity of MDF.

The ‘systems leaming’ approach is based on Kolbs experiential leaning cycle and
draws also Peter Checkland’s ‘soft systems methodology’. it emphasizes
participation and calls for open and active patterns of communication based on
interdependent relationships’, and necessitates action to develop it. This requires an
appreciation of stages in group development and how to facilitate group
processes. The key is to see things differently, if we are to act differently — and we
need processes that enable this.

Its application has been proven to be a success with MICAD in the Collingwood Bay,
and Dadakol in the Managalasi, where projects based on various activities of
different programs were undertaken by groups of individuals as personal action
learning projects hence meeting some of the overall objectives of their CBOs. The
Airara and Sinafa jetties, the Dadakol Canteen and Resource Center and Coffee
projects have been inspired by this program,

The personal action leaming projects generated through the MOF TNA workshop
basically encompasses the various actions that MDF otherwise would be expected
to deliver using traditional methods which evidently has not been successful thus the
emphasis now is for MDF to shift its activity funding to support this new approach.

This trip to Oro Province commenced on 23" August to 7" September 2018 and the
underlying purpose of undertaking it was to attend the 2019 Annual Planning meeting and

Foundation (MCF) & Partners with Melanesians (PWM). However, travel arrangement

travelled to Afore with Veronica, Patrick & Kovi from PWM, together with MCF Officers,
accompanied by CBOs and Activity Coordinators. We convoyed on 3 hired vehicle through
cost sharing and reached our destination late in the afternoon.

initiated by the communities

After spending a night at Numba village with Joruba’s family, we visited the reforestation
nursery site and other SLA activities in the village on the aforesaid date. There were few
notable SLA activities been initiated by the local and were explicitly continuing. Apart from
coffee, which remains as the major cash crops for income generation, locals have also
involved in small scale rice and vanilla farming.

In the aftemoon, we walked back to Afore but decided to take the bush track at Kavovoki
village towards Ogan village to visit the mysterious Dogarol Lake. While still tracking. we
were soaked by the light aftemoon showers but continued on until we reached Dogarol Look-
out. Locals were there expecting us so we took few shots whilst at the lookout point before
descending down to the lake after getting clearance from the landowners.

Dogarol Lake is formed in a crater created by volcano. Some years back, probably in mid
1700s, there must have been a volcanic cruption and thus, leaving this crater as an evidence.
‘The rain water descending into the crater eventually increase in volume and consequently,
developed into this mysterious lake. I took a ride on a canoe with a local guide trying to
ascertain the water outlet point but unable to do so. Supposedly, there must be an
underground exit as locals said there is no alteration in water level despite heavy rains or long

dry spells.

Dogarol is a potential ecotourism site with a newly constructed access road leading all the
way to the lookout point. There are many disastrous enigmatic folklores surrounding the lake
and hence, locals had never been closer to the lake. However, the breakthrough eventuated in
1960s when the Catholic Priest visited the lake, prayed at the side of the lake and swam.
across thereafter. After secing and heard about this, local were still skeptical until somewhat
recently when legitimate customary landowners decided do away with all bizarre beliefs and
started making gardens beside the lake as part of ecotourism activity due to its astonishing
uniqueness. Consequently, many outsiders have had visited the lake since last year and had
made remarkable comments as one of the devastating tourist attractive site in the plateau

29" August 2018 - AFORE NEW QABB FARM & BIRD WATCH

Visited the newly established QABB and Bird Watch sites at Afore village. This project was
initiated by Christopher- the CBO manager for Zone 7 B. Few QABB vines were
transplanted at the selected location to attract Alexandrea Birdwing Butterflies but many died
out due to long dry season. Nonetheless, some are sprouting out leaves after the recent rain
and it is assumed that all will grow if the rain continues. The potential bird watch spot was
also visited but we couldn’t get a glimpse of a bird as we went there during the midday.
While on this trip, I've also noticed coffees trees covered with flowers and therefore
anticipated that these coffee trees will bear fruits in abundance early 2019.

the vines. The forest floor was covered with vines, fresh drinking water springing out from

inside the farm site and it thus, these features made this site distinctively unique so fa

As per our tentative travel plan, we decided to walk to Yombu village at LLG Ward 1- Zone

massive boisterous Boikiki Waterfall. The blistering roar of 7 meters free-fall of mighty
Pogani River at a narrower passage, sounds like a forthcoming fearsome thunderstorm at
one’s eyesight and was also frightening indeed. Congruently, you can still hear the roar of
massive Boikiki Falls reverberating from the distance when ascending uphill towards Ward 1,

problem.

Coffee
Anticipated quantity in 2019

In terms of coffee, the quantities conjectured for harvesting in 2019 would be 2 or 3 times
more when compared to this year. Every coffee trees in different coffee gardens visited in
East Managalas were covered with flowers. Flower is the first stages of parchment bean
formation in the agro-culture cycle and therefore, those flowers will ultimately transform into
parchment beans in few months’ time. Consequently, the branches covered with flowers will
sooner be seen with parchment beans clinging onto them copiously. Moreover, yielding will
perceptibly increase for the Managalas Organic Coffee.

Parchment Purchasing Strategy
From the discussions I had with the local farmers, they all proposed for CASH BUYING
rather than group marketing strategy. Due to previous issue with MOCP, all farmers disagree
with group marketing and want cash on hand upon delivery

harvesting season starts. These are:

Sakarina Shed
All parchments from East Managalas village: Hugunomo, Dea, Numba, Kavovki,
Sakarina will all be rechecked, repacked and stored here for transportation.

All parchments from Afore villages and other small hamlets that were once part of
large Afore village will all be stored in this shed.

to the buffer zone will be stored in this shed. Pogani is also a strategic location in
terms of transportation due to the current condition of the road between Pogani and

INTRODUCTION

This was a planned activity, for the establishment and swearing in of the CA
committee members. The trip was planned for in collaboration with CEPA to jointly
fund the implementation of the activity. Letters were prepared by MCF Project
Director, Mr Damien Ase for the Representative from the Provincial, [jivitari District,
and Afore LLG.

Damien Ase and PWM Board Member Tom Huasi, went in advance to Afore for the
planning and MCF Board meeting. After the meeting, they travel down to Popondetta
with the four representatives from Managalas whom will represent the LOs in the CA
committee.

There was a delay in the signing of the letters by CEPA MD, Mr Gunther Joku, thus
delaying the release and approval of their funds for the trip. This has also delayed
Rufus’ and myself travelling to Popondetta for the CA meeting.

PURPOSE

The purpose of the trip was to attend the first meeting for the Managalas
Conservation Area Management Committee, and swearing in of the CA management
committee members in Popondetta, Oro Province.

METHODS/PROCEDURES
04" July 2019:

Patrick Vuet got on the morning flight from Port Moresby to Popondetta. Went
straight to Oro Guest House and met with Mr Damien Ase, Tom Huasi, and four (4)
LO representatives appointed by the communities to represent them in the Managalas
Conservation Area Management Committee (MCAMC).

 We had the brief meeting from 10am to 1pm. Patrick and Damien went through
section, Part V. — “Conservation Area Management Committees” of the
Conservation Areas Act 1978, to the four representatives including Managalas
Development Foundation Board Chairman, Mr Malchus Kajia.

‘The representatives ask questions which Damien and Patrick answered accordingly.

They were made aware that this first meeting was the responsibility of CEPA to fund
all logistics and facilitate the committee establishment and swearing in.

,
After the brief meeting, Tom Huasi, Eddison from Orobay, and I went to the
Provincial Forest Office to make appointments to meet the Southern Region Area
Officer the next day to check on the operational maps for the Ifane logging operation
at Girua, which reports from the ground that the operation has encroached into the
Managalas Conservation Area.

Eddison is from the area where possible encroachment has gone into the CA.

05" July 2019:

Tom Huasf, Eddison and I went to the Popondetta Forestry Office as per the

Southern Region Area Manager.
We walked around in town to look for alkaline battery for the GPS but couldn’t find

any.

Budget didn’t allow us to stay longer in Popondetta so we got on the plane back to

All outstanding for the four representatives including for Tom Huasi were settled and
went back to Port Moresby.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

The four representatives from the Managalas are awaie of their roles and
responsibilities as a member in the MCAMC.

 Briefing session with 0 Photo after the meeting

MCF PROJECT DIRECTOR'S 2019 FIRST QUARTER REPORT

1. INTRODUCTION

In 2018 many of the planned activities for the Managalas Conservation Area was not implemented
due to various reasons including the late approval and transfer of funds by the main donor of the
project Rainforest Foundation Norway (RFN) through Partners with Melanesia (PwM), the
holder of the project and implementing partner. The Conservation was gazetted and officially
declared in 2017 so there were a lot of expectation from the local communities/landowners
especially support for sustainable livelihood activities which is the main purpose for the funding
fiom REN apart from the conservation objective. Also there were a lot of issues on this discussed
and decisions taken at the District Wide Combine Forum held in November at Yoivi village in
Zone 8. Therefore, the hope was some of these main planned activities wilt be undertaken in the
early part of the year because of the up-coming Local Level Government Elections in the second
quarter of the year. However, there was delays gain due to late transfer of funds by RFN because
of the delays with audit report. This report is record of activities in the first quarter of the year
which is from January to March 2019.

2. ACTIVITIES UNDERTAKEN IN THE QUARTER.

2,1 Follow-up on Financial Reports/Acquittals

Last year PwM transferred K59,000 to MCF account for its capacity building activities and
becatise the Finance Officer was new I worked with him to ensure that all acquittals of the funds
transferred were done to meet the audit requirements as stringent requirements were put in place
in the contract for this. Also the amount of K#1,000 was not transferred which affected payment
for services and MCF staff and CBO allowances and this remains major concern and issue where
staff wanted to boycott planned activities for the year. I also discussed the reporting requirements
and the financial management guidelines with the Finance Officer to ensure that he was well
versed with the financial reporting requirements

2.1 Foliow-up Work on the Establishment of Managalas Conservation Area
Management Committee.
‘The District Wide Combine Forum held at Yoivi village in zone 8 last November approved the
landowner representatives on the Managalas Conservation Area Management Committee
(MCAMC) as required under the Conservation Areas Act. Therefore, armed with this decision, I
liased and worked with both PwM and Officers from the Sustainable Environment Protection
Division of the Conservation Environment Protection Authority (CEPA) to formally establish the
MCAMC as required under Section 25 of the Conservation Areas Act as the committee plays an
important role in overseen the management of the conservation area including approving the
management plan, making rules/by-laws for the conservation area and supervising the work of

 rangers. These including writing letters, sending emails and holding one on one meetings with
relevant officers about establishment of the commitiee and funding for work of the committee,

2.2 Feilow-up on Ministers Funding Commitment.

A lot of my time in the quarter was spent on following up on the commitment made by the Minister
for Environment & Conservation, Hon. John Pundari during launching of the Conservation Area at
Itokama on 29 November 2017. This was to assist the local communities/landowners with
sustainable livelihood alternatives especially marketing of coffee so I wanted to ensure that the
funding was released to MCF before the season proper starts for the coffee. Our plan was to give
the funds equally to each coffee growing zones accessible to markets to arrange for group
marketing of coffee from their zones organised by the partner Community Based Organisations
(CBOs). These including sending letters, follow-up emails and one on ne meetings with the CEPA
Managing Director and relevant Officers with CEPA’s SEP Division. It was a frustrating effort as
this was continuing from 2019 after the submission of the necessary supporting documentation to
the CEPA Managing Director as requested by him.

2.3 Proposal and Budget to UNDP/CEPA GEF 5 Project for the
Managaias Conservation Area Buffer Zone Support Project.

Upon request by the GEF 5 Project Management Unit (PMU) housed within UNDP I developed a
proposal for the Managalas Conservation Area and Buffer Zone Support Project to cover costs for
establishing the MCAMC, selection and training of Rangers and support equipment and costs,
sustainable livelihood alternatives in line with the Protected Area Policy and education awareness
programme especially targeting schools in the area. They also asked me do develop a budget for the
MCAMC to cover its costs which I did and submitted to them and CEPA. The plan was to have the
proposal considered by the Project Board/Steering Committee at the planned Board meeting in
May. This was to meet some of the funding constraints for implementation of planned activities.

2.4 Meetings with Governor for Gro for Funding Assistance.

A number of meetings were held with the Governor for Oro, Hon. Garry Juffa including follow-up
jetters and emails about the funding commitment by the Governor for activities in the conservation
area including establishment of the Council of Chiefs and the Community Leaders Summit. [also
followed up with the Officers in the Governor's Office for this funding as these were also activities
agreed to at the District Wide Combine Forum in Zone 8 last November. The main issue according
to Governor Juffa is the late release of funds by the Finance Department so he told me to continue
with the follow-ups so that the funding committed can be released for the planned activities.

2.5 MCF Board Matters.

‘There has been problem with having the regular board meetings because of funding constraints and
also the board decisions have to be implemented so I have been in regular contact with the
Chairman who is in Popondetta due to his medical condition to update him on board matters. There
are important matters including funding, implementation of activities , staff matters and networking
with relevant Provincial and District Officers as well as management of the project vehicle that the
Chairman and other board members needed to be up-dated on so it is important for the regular
communication or one on one meetings when I am in the Province.

ig]
 2.6 Arrangement for Management of the Project Vehicie.

The vehicle donated by New Britain Palm Oi! which was parked at the Oro Guest House for a
number of years was eventually serviced by the company mechanics and registered with MVIL last
year. This has assisted with easing some of the transport problems faced for implementation of
planned activities. However, because of the bad road condition it needed to managed and driven by
ateliable driver to serve its purpose. A committee of the board was established to manage the
vehicle including supervision of the driver as per board decision last November. This arrangement
was to be assessed to see if it was working out, if not to make changes to the arrangement.
‘Therefore, I was in constant communication with the Chairman and the MCF staff regarding the
management of the vehicle.

27 ther Administrative Matters

also developed reporting formats for MCF and CBO staff which will be presented at the planning
meeting before they can be finalised. I also ensured at that each MCF staff have proper
identification cards and that the MCE office in Popondetta is properly maintained by the Finance
and Admin. Officer.

3. PROBLEMS, ISSUES/CHALLENGES.

Some of the obvious problems and challenges have been funding constraints to implement planned
activities, communication problems, bad road condition and the main issue with commitment by
MCE staff because of the non-payment of allowances. The late release of funds earmarked for
capacity building activities by PwM has also contributed to some of these difficulties.

A lot of stakeholders including business groups, cooperatives, associations, women and youth
‘groups as well as schools are requesting for funding assistance for their own planned activities but
MCF being a small organisation with no funding base is unable to meet their request thus. creating
frustrations. There is for MCF to carry out awareness on its roles and functions as per its
constitution and the need to have the membership arrangement in place so that there is broad
representation on the board to assist with the work of the organisation.

4, FOLLOW-UP ACTIONS

‘There are number of urgent matters that need to be followed up including the funding commitment
by the Minister, the proposal to the UNDP/CEPA GEE 5 Project, establishment of the MCAMC
and funding commitment by the Oro Governor. The other activities are mainly administrative
matters including contracts for staff, organising the planning and board meetings and supervision of
the Finance and Admin. Officer to improve on the financial reports for MCF.

CONCLUSION

In conclusion, I can say that there are a lot of expectation of local communities/landowners and
stakeholders in the conservation area especially schools for funding and other support since the
declaration of the Conservation Area. MCF is unable to meet these expectations because of funding
constraints and other challenges including lack of support from stakeholders like the Afore LLG,
Oro Provincial and Kjivitari District Administration and line national agencies especially CEPA and
CCDA. Coupled with this is the problem of MCF staff not having the confidence to follow-up with
3
 Provincial Authorities to support the activities in the area. The main issue of MCF having its own
audit report needs to be addressed as this is affecting MCF’s ability to raise its own funding from
donors because the production of an external audit report is one major requirement by donors.

‘The need to have the MCAMC established and in place and properly funded to carry out its
functions provided for by law is a priority. CEPA Officer needs to constantly reminded of their
roles and the work of MCF as a local partner in implementing the Protected Area Policy and
relevant legislations especially the Conservation Areas Act. Also there is need to have MOU’s
signed with Afore LLG, the Ijivitari District Administration and Oro Provincial Administration for
assistance with the implementation of planned activities and especially for aligning the
Conservation Area Management Plans with the plans of each of the various levels of government in

the province.

Respectfully Submitted,

Damien Ase
Project Director

Program and Project Reporting

INTRODUCTION
The Scriptwriting workshop is an on-going activity under the Education Awareness Program. It was

initially the Rainforest Literacy Program that works side by side with the Consensus Building
Program, now the Community Empowerment Program.

‘This Program adds value to PWM’s core program (Biodiversity, Conservation and Community
Mapping) because in order for communities to support and fully engage in this conservation
initiative, they need to be informed and we must ensure that they fully understand what we are
doing and so they can be able to make informed decisions.

So for this year (2019), the Scriptwriting workshop was held at Afore village, just at the edge of the
Afore government station.

‘There were two travel days both for participants, for me as Program Coordinator. i travelled on the
6" of July 2019 to Popondetta, spent a night there and travelled via PMV together with the two field
officers (Crispine Burawa - MCF) and Alking.Fufus - MKTG) to Afore on 7th July, 2019. The two
CBO Officers travelled a day from Afore to Popondetta just to assist me with logistics.

It was a week-long workshop organized jointly by PWM and MCF with Crispine Burava (MCF-
East Field Coordinator) as lead facilitator and co-fa ited by Alking.Fufus (MKTG-Director) and
PWM Program Officer.

‘The workshop started on Monday 8" July, 2019 and ended on 12" July, 2019. I was accompanied
by PWM’s Gender Officer. She was new and as part of her orientation and introduction to the
project area, she took advantage of this workshop to speak to the CBOs and gender reps.
highlighting this new Gender Program and also, picked up vital information during discussions that
are relevant to developing program activities for her program next year.

The workshop started very late the next day (08.07.19) because we had to wait for some
participants to arrive. They were the ones who received late notices for this workshop because they
are living in zones furthest from A fore stati
‘There were a total of 30 participants comprising of MKTG members, CBO reps, MCF Officers,
PWM and observers.

‘A good number of participants are females (see participants list attached). The females are both
mothers and young girls, a number of them are gender representatives from the 10 Zones of
Managalas Plateau.

 At the end of the discussion, it was decided and agreed by participants that this issue be discussed at
the management level and maybe an awareness workshop for a day or two planned out for PWM,
MCE, CBOs and other stakeholder representatives within Managalas to be invited to participate and
have this issues clarified out once and for all.

Gender Equality was the other issue of discussion that saw a lot of interest and because we have
PWM's new program coordinator present as part of her orientation and scoping and research
activity, she was able to grasp vital information/issues of need and contribute where she can.

‘The main issues that came out clearly is for Managalas women and girls to be empowered and be
able to participate in this project with no barriers especially cultural barriers which scem to be the
main cause of hindrance for women/girls to participate in developmental initiatives and in this case
the MCA Project activities.

There are other social issues surround this main issue that was discussed thoroughly and
emphasized like reviving the Afore Council of Women that was foreseen to boost to the women
folk in the Managalas plateau.

They also highlighted a number of necessary skills trainings that they need and further went on to
discuss issues like Violence again women that needs awareness in the community.

‘The gender empowerment coordinator took note of it all and will use them to develop activities for
2020 onwards.

‘The participants were then introduced to the issue on Climate Change and I asked by the
facilitators to define this big term ‘Climate Change’ and gave examples to clarify and further
highlighted that it is a global issue. I also explained that the main cause of CC which is human
activities and briefly highlighted the adaptation/mitigation efforts by governments and NGOs like
PWM. I then, further linked it up to PWM’s Climate Change and Reforestation Program (headed by
Cecil. Senive) as one of PWM's attempt to combating climate change in the plateau.

Trigger questions were asked to generate discussion around their own experiences on the effects of
climate change. In fact, through the discussions it was clear that they have unconsciously adapted to
some of these effects on a day to day basis. They also highlighted that they need awareness
throughout the plateau because some of these effects of climate change like low yield and airbome
discases are blamed on sorcery and other cultural beliefs. These has caused a lot of infighting and
dismantling of communities and within close family units.

A script was done and to be dramatized by the Theatre group.

Mismanagement was a heated issue that brought a lot of discussions all pin pointing PWM
management and MCF management. The discussion went off a little bit with name calling of
certain people in the management level and not so much on how best they would want to see this
issue resolved.

This discussion was not that very constructive and the facilitator did not steer the discussion
towards finding solutions and for participants to be able to do awareness. In the end it was put
forward to be discussed during the Leaders’ Summit.

Finally, it was the issue on Sustainable Livelihood Alternatives. It was an issue that became a
standalone issue and discussed separately because the whole of Managalas Plateau are so excited
about because everyone wanted to benefit from it.

CONCLUSION

‘The 5-day planned workshop ended well with 2 days allocated for travelling to workshop venue and
back.

So we travelled to Afore on the 8" of

text:
Compiled by Jacina Mimigari- Pariers with Melanesians (ly 2008)

Approach and Guide to creating Managalas Conservation Area
Management Plan

For the people of Managalas in their struggle in safe guarding their natural environment

This handbook is basically a guide to assist the Managalas People on how to go about in
creating their own Management Plan Guidelines and rules for the preservation and
enhancement of their Conservation Area. This will be used by the facilitator.

Getting a Conservation Area status is not as easy as you think it is. It is a continuous
commitment, where a Resource Management plan must be in placed to guide and preserve it.
Support must come from the rightful resource owners (Land owners), Local and provincial
level Government and the concern Government Department like the Department of
Environment and Conservation (DEC).

‘Acronyms:

CA- Conservation Area

DEC- Department of Environment and Conservation
NGO- Non- Government Organization

PwM- Partners with Melanesians

MDE- Managalas Development Foundation

What is Conservation NGO?

Conservation Agencies are non-governmental organizations that work in partnership with
government bodies such as DEC to help people improve their sustainable livelihood. They are
not part of the Government. There are many kinds of Non government organizations (NGO's).
The church is one kind of NGO that works to help people improve their spiritual lives. Other
NGO work on improving health (such as save the children fund), and others work on education
such as PNG Trust which works doing literacy training. Conservation NGO's (agencies) work
to help people look after their environment or their renewable natural resources. They provide
education on how to use and manage resources wisely.

Conservation Agencies are not a company or business that works to make money or profit.
They are not the same as trade store or a logging or mining company whose main work is to
make money. They are known as non-profit organizations, that ask other people or
organizations to give them money to do their work. Conservation Agency's main work is to
provide information and training to people on how best they can look after their resources.
Conservation Agency's’ work like schools. People don’t ask schools for money or other forms
of assistance that has nothing to do with education. The same is true for Conservation
‘Agencies. Partners with Melanesians (PWM) and its umbrella organization, the Managalas
Development Foundation (MDF) are such agencies.

 Compiled by Jacinta Mimigart- Partmers with Melanesians (uly 2008)

‘What is 2 Conservation Area?

Comparing all the protected Areas in the country, Conservation Areas (CA) is a very promising
form of protection as customary land ownership can be retained. The general principle function
of the Conservation Areas act is to protect an area having a particular biological, topological,
historical, Scientific or social significance or other special value for the present community or
future generations. No conservation Area has yet to be established in the country (T. Pringel:

2007)

What is a Conservation Area Management Plan?

‘A Resource Management Plan or in our case Managaias Conservation Area Management
Plan is basically a directive plan on how to go about in maintaining the Protected area,
allowing it to still be intact or only littie damaged be done to the environment. Conservation
‘Area Management Plan is the next step after the area is granted the CA status but in light to
achieving the goal of a Conservation Area Status, 2 Management plan has to be drawn up to
ensure the sustainability of the project.

(Brief Reflection of what a Conservation Area is)
Session 1: Why do you create a Conservation Area?
(Why do you want to create a protected area and why other people create Protected Arca?)
(What is special about your Protected Area?)

Purpose: The purpose of this session is to:
1. Find out why people from Managalas think that they want to create a Conservation

Area
2. Explain why Landowners in other areas create Protected Areas; and
3. Clear up confusion about the benefits of creating a Conservation Area

Preparation and Materials: Posters of the “Only benefit you will receive”

Steps:

 Conpted by Jacinta Mimigar- Partners with Melanesians (uly 2008)

Step 1: Ask participants to discuss in small groups the reason that they want to declare their
‘area a Conservation Area and make list and a group member will present it to workshop

participants

Step 2: Do a big group comparison and discussion of all the presentation until a realis
picture is more obvious to all.

Step 3: The facilitator should explain why landowners in other areas of PNG have set up
protected Areas (CA or WMA)

In many places in PNG landowners have seen that some of their wildlife is becoming less
common from too much hunting, gardening or that, plants for building materials and other uses
are becoming scarce. They are worried that there will not be enough left for their children to
use in the future, because they are using too much now. So they set up a Protected Area, and
agree on rules to ensure that their resources are used wisely so that they will still have them in
the future.

In some other areas where landowners have most of their forest still intact, and there have not
been declines in resources landowners have also created protected areas. Why have they done
this? Mostly they do this because they do not want some ‘autsait lain’ coming in to destroy
their resources (animals, plants, etc). Sometimes this ‘autsait lai” might be another clan in the
area, or settlers from other places or big companies such as logging and mining companies
‘These landowners say “why do we want to sell our resources to some ‘autsait Jain’ that will
make plenty of money while we only make a little bit of money from it?” so they want to
tambuim this area to prevent outsiders coming in to destroy it.

Step 4: Explain that the real benefit from setting up a Conservation Area or protected Area is
that their resources will be used and managed wisely and that future generations will still have
these resources to use and sustainable development then can come in place.

Explain that if the community is setting up the protected area for the reasons other than these
that they will be very disappointed. Creating a protected area (CA) does not guarantee that the
landowner will gain some money benefit or that tourist or researchers will come to see the area,
Although it is true that tourists do visit protected areas in some places in PNG, creating a
protected area does not guarantee that they will come.

Note: The most important point to clear up before you get into further Protected Area Planning
is that there are no monetary benefits in setting up a Protected Area (CA). If landowners set up
a protected area for monetary motivations they are almost guaranteed to be disappointed and
the protected area is guaranteed to fail.

(Making Rules)
Session 2: Review of PA Rules created in other parts of PNG

Purpose: To make sure that participants are familiar with rules that have been developed
elsewhere in PNG for protected areas

Preparation and materials:

Stationeries; Papers and pens, handouts- “Examples of rules from other CA or WMA-Pidgin
Version

Steps:

Step 1: Explain that most of the areas in PNG are WMAs. Landowners must make and agree
to the rules because the WMA is on customary Land. In areas that have police they can assist
with enforcement of WMA rules. But in areas without police it is the landowners, through the
Conservation Area committee who must enforce the rules.

Step 2: Give participants the handout of examples of rules created in other protected areas in
PNG. Go through the examples with them. Some examples of rules are:

1) Banning the hunting of Birds of Paradise;

2) Banning the use of Shotguns

3) Completely closing certain areas from any hunting activities;

4) Charging entry fees for tourist

5) Banning Logging and minin

6) Preventing the clearing for

7) Banning littering

8) Restricting the type of Development that can occur in the area

9) Placing a fee or royalty payment for hunting

10) Restricting access by outsiders to culturally significant sites e.g. burial places or fambu
areas;

dens or burning of some or all vegetation;

However, rules can make provision for traditional hunting and collection.

Step 3: Explain that rules should be created to protect wildlife and natural resources that local
people believe that they are very important for their lives and their future. When rules are made
for other reasons, they usually collapse. The purpose of a protected area is not to make money.

 Compiled by Jacinta Mimigari- Partners with Melanesians (July 2008)

People may end up making money out of the protected Area, but that should never be the
reason why the protected area is set and the rules made.

Step 4: Explain that whatever rules are placed over the Conservation Area (PA) depend
entirely upon the iandowners. No Rules can be placed over the area without the landowners’
agreement. Rules will only if all landowners agree on them. The rules that are developed
during this workshop will only be a draft set of rules. They can be changed according to the
community wishes. There is a definite need to talk more about the rules in the community.

Session 3: Resource Use Problems and issue
(What do you want to manage?)

Purpose:
1) To look carefillly at the resources management issues and problems in the proposed

Conservation Area, so that participants can develop effective rules to manage these

issues.
2) To make sure that the rules created at the workshop relate to the purpose for the

Managalas Conservation Area.

Material and preparation:
Stationeries, Hand outs of some examples

Steps:

Step 1: Explain that afier this participants need to start thinking about rules for the
Conservation area, so first they should identify the important resources that they want to
manage, what are the problems, and what are the root causes for the problems. This will help
them to decide what rules they will need to develop.

Step 2: Put the beginning of the following matrix up on the board and ask participants to
break into small groups and discuss what needs to be managed. They can begin by filling up
the first column. To make a start they may wish to look back at the list of resources they use
from the area.

 I. INTRODUCTION

‘The District Wide Combine Forum is the last activity of a cycle of activities under the
Consensus Building and the Rainforest Literacy Program. The two programs complement
each other and therefore their activities form a cycle.

‘The Managalas Plateau has a total of 150 major clan groups and the clans are further
divided into 10 zones.

The Combine Forum serves as an avenue where all 150 clan members come together and
discuss their issues and problems. Representatives from partner NGOs, government
departments and other statutory bodies are also invited and where necessary response to
the people’s issues. In a way, we try to help the people find solutions to the issues in
which they themselves are and will be the cause of development.

For this year’s forum, a representative each from the Media for Development Initiative
and Department of Community Development were able to make it to the forum. Other
partner NGOs and government department, and others send their apologies as they were
caught up with their schedules.

Program starts at 2 pm with welcome speeches by Forum Chairman Douglas Tumais
Community Representative Zone 5; PWM Executive Director; MDI Representative;
Department of Community Development Representative; & MDF Board Chairman.

The MDF chairman Malchus Kajia officially opened the forum and each participant then
did a brief introduction of themselves. (See attached for list of participants)

the participants on what their expectations are after the Combine Forum. Each zone (10
zones) representatives were given the opportunity to say what they think. Unfortunately
there were no representatives for Zone 4 and 10.

the exit strategy
CBOs & MDF work together to reform the Consensus Building Process

= PWM, MDF & CBO should really see where we are heading in terms of the
program activities since 1997

went wrong/failed with regard to the exit strategy and to find the way forward

 = MDF to stand on their own and sign contract with donors directly and not through
PWM

= There should be coordination and cooperation between PWM, MDF & CBO for
the smooth running of the MCAP and that there should be transparency at all
levels

= All communities on the Plateau to come together and start all over again because
currently MDF are the ones running the project and as a result most clan members
did not attend the forum.

* Find out about the cause of lack of people’s interest in the project

* Bottom-up planning approach (Consensus Building process) is slowly dying out,
we have to find out why

4: MOCP Issue

Communities want MOCP to come back into operation but they don’t know the
reason as to why it has not operated since the beginning of this year.

No available report so far resulting in communities/farmers having no trust in

prove how the money was spent

5. Gender Issues

The issue on equal gender participation has brought a lot of constructive arguments. The
whole discussion was started when one of the only three females that attended the forum
asked why only a handful of Managalas women (like her) are involve in the program
activities. The straight response was: it is our culture and no matter what, women will
always take the back stage.

‘A representative from the Media for Development Initiative spoke from a donor's
perspective regarding women involvement in any donor funded project activities. Donors
now have certain criteria that they look at when funding projects and women’s

1.1 Development objectives of the program:
The development objective will be identical with that stated in the long-term plan,

1.1 The long term overall development objective is sustainable rainforest resource
management as well as informed community participation in sustainably developing their
natural resource base. The landowners must be empowered to play an active role in efforts to
protect the local environment, given its rich biodiversity. Additionally, landowners must be
involved in any decision-making related to planned development projects. Most donor funded
projects, whether they be in environmental protection or sustainable natural resource
management, have failed simply because the affected landowners did not have a well-
informed, active role in their design and development.

The government and other donor or development agencies both bilateral and multi-lateral
hhave realized the importance of ensuring well-informed landowner participation in such
projects and are now looking at mechanisms that enable that kind of participation.

1.2 Program objective:
The program objectives are identical with those stated in the long-term plan,
1.2 The program objective is to contain the expansion of food and cofiee gardens amongst

select groups beyond land currently dedicated to the fallow ground cycle and so maintain
existing levels of forested lands,

A related goal is to overcome the limitations of the current system of transferring critical
rainforest management knowledge by a) oral transfers through intermediaries with vested
interests and b) the distribution of ill-prepared print material to local clan groups.

In addition, the Rainforest Literacy Program will improve the low education levels common
among women and the least influential formalities of the targeted populations as a result of
the focused multi-channel learning strategies that will be used in the group learning sessions.
