1.4 Describe briefly and simply the most important results of the cooperation with
ODW keeping in mind that information is to be communicated on to young people
between the ages of 13-19 years of age.

Write approximately half a page.

Papua New Guinea boasts in the diversity of its land and people. There are majestic
mountains, highland valleys, mighty rivers, vast marshes and swamplands, extensive coastal
plains with majestic rainforests, and many legendary islands scatter in abundance in the warm
seas.

Over 75 per cent of the land is covered with rich tropical rain forest. Plants and trees grow
rapidly and luxuriantly because of heavy rainfall and high temperatures. Many trees grow to a
height of 46 metres and more, their branches forming a canopy providing a rich environment
for unique animai and plant species.

The rainforests in which animals, plants and people depend on is becoming increasingly
threatened by commercial mining and logging interest, oil palm expansion and the current
cash crop and gardening practices of expanding local population.

Since 2003, the Rainforest Literacy program have provided critical background and
‘opportunity information to clan members including school children from elementary classes,
youths, women and girls and men who have a vested interest in ensuring their rainforest
resource base is sustainably managed.

 Critical opportunity information include skills related to resource maps and planning the use
of their land in terms of planting food gardens, expanding village space, planting and
expanding cash crop (especially coffee) gardens and other environmentally friendly
developments.

At the same time, Rainforest Literacy program also present modem conservation practices
where locals who are very familiar with local indigenous knowledge on preserving their plant
and animal species try to analyse the information and find a balance with their traditional laws
to conserve the resources on which they depend.

‘The Rainforest Literacy program uses the multi-channel learning system which includes
interactive radio instructions, elementary flyers, posters, newsletters, shell books and
facilitator guides to relate information translated in their local dialects to these various target
audiences in order to overcome the barrier to communication.

Production and circulation of this information are supported by the locally based community
eaming centres (CLC) and the community based organizations (CBO).

1.5 To what degree is the program objective achieved?

A. Since the program began in 2003, managing the use of the land has always been part
of the radio series every year. As part of the bigger conservation component of PWM,
clan members and landowning groups were taught how to manage their land in terms
of expanding community space, food and cash crop gardens, utilising forest resources
etc to cater for the expanding population. Rainforest Literacy provided them with
additional information to assist them in deciding how to use their land,

B. Rainforest Literacy has actually overcome the traditional barrier of limiting the flow
of information amongst local communities. Traditionally, information intended for
specific target population never actual reach their target groups when those
responsible for passing the information tend to limit its spread for various reasons.

‘The designing and presentation of the multi-channel learning systems in using the
audio as well as print in reaching the very under-privileged of society like the
disabled, less influential (women, girls and youths) and silent majority (Less important
members of society) has actually united different classes of people in reaching
‘consensus on issues concerning all members of the society.

‘Complemented by the Consensus Building Process, Rainforest Literacy provided the
different avenues where information is discussed at the various levels (family,
‘women’s groups, literacy classes, elementary classes, clan groups, youth & sports
‘group, church groups etc) and consensus is reached on issues before being presented at
the clan level, the tribal (zone) level and the District Wide Forum where important
stake holders are present to identify actions points and take responsibility in executing
the next course of action.

C. Over the years, number of women and less influential members of the community
participating in the Rainforest Literacy Program have actually increased. Internal
evaluation has shown that this was because the program has actually presented
information relevant to their specific need thus making them feel that they are just as
 important as any other member of the society. Additionally, the program provided the
avenue for them to meet and discuss issues at their own level where they are able to
fully express themselves without fear or favour. This has influenced their thinking
capacity and prompted them to becoming productive members of the community.

D. The multi-channel and interactive radio is fast becoming a model of community based
leaming where it reaches different members of the community at different times
suitable to their information needs. It allows all members of the community, regardless
of their literacy level, whether in school or out of the formal education system, and
even to those illiterate that do not understand the basic English language, to have
access to information that will not only increase their learning gain but to enable them
to become functionally literate with life skills that will enhance their livelihood.

E. Other Non-Government Organizations, Aid Agencies and Government Departments
have recognized PWM as the expert NGO with skills in multi-channel & interactive
learning. We were approached by the Department of Community Development and
the newly established Office of Climate Change to exchange ideas and show case how
we develop the multi-channel learning systems and help them package information to
be distributed to their target audiences on issues relevant to their work.

PWM participated in a media exchange program for the AusAID/PNG Government
Media for Development Initiative in 2007 where PWM produced one series of radio
program (4 programs) and print materials, show casing the on-going program on the
‘Managalas Conservation Area Project where PWM gained popularity amongst civil
society organizations who also participated in the media exchange program.

‘Additionally, the NGO sector in the country has recognized PWM as the expert NGO
in multi-channel and interactive learning and has referred queries relevant to multi-
channel and interactive learning to PWM since.

the cooperation?

 Realising the importance and value of the program, the number of groups participating in the

1.8 To what extent have girls and boys had equal opportunity to participate in the
program?

The program presentation and delivery includes all members of the community. In the radio
program, the drama segment involves characters that portray a typical local Managalas family
where the story line is built around factually events that happen in a family environment. The
segment gauges the attention of the boys and girls who easily identifies themselves with the
young character who by the way speaks in fluent Tok Pisin and uses English jargons and
expressions that excites and trills the audience. The elderly male character speaks in the local
dialect, which is repeated by the women character using simple English and Tok Pisin for the
sake of the shadow audience. Since the radio program is interactive, the audience also
participates in the program which maintains their attention and keeps the dialogue alive.

‘The program also produces elementary flyers that directly feed the schools where girls and
boys are the focal attention. In the classroom environment, they learn first hand the
information being presented.

Girls and boys also lear the same information thru the poster, newsletter and shell book at
different times and different places convenient to busy adults who spend most of their time
tending their gardens.

‘The Melanesian society is clustered together that there are no visible signs of discrimination
between disabled people and other members of the community. In fact, the disabled are given
more care and attention.

‘The Program encourages participation from all members of the community in the various
forms of presentation whereby no one person is left out of the discussions,

“The disabled (young and old) have always been a part of the program.

‘The locals have taken on the challenge in producing print materials locally through the

 in the early 1960’s to translate the Good News Bible to the local dialects as well as teaching,
adult literacy. These materials (news sheets and flyers) are printed in the local dialects.

In light of the exit strategy where locals will be given responsibility in producing the audio

PWM has eamed a reputation as the expert organization in producing and delivering the

TITLE: IMPACTS OF AGRICULTURE IN RELATION TO BIODIVERSITY

1.0 Introduction:
Tetebedi is located 170° North-cast of Popondetta, the provincial capital of Oro
Province. Tetebedi is at an altitude of about 3000 meters above sea level and has an
estimated population of 2,500 people. It has an annual rainfall of approximately
xxxxx milliliters. Tetebedi is only accessible by light aircraft as there are no roads
linking it to other parts of the country. The bulk of the population is Seventh Day

Adventists.

This compilation is an out come of an agriculture survey into the Impacts of
Agriculture In-Relation to Biodiversity. This is the fourth phase of the Biodiversity
Survey in Oro Province and was carried out at Mt. Guguavo, a conservation project
area reserved by the Managalas Development Foundation. The survey was carried out

on the 22/04/08 to the 03/05.08.

2.0 Objective
The primary purpose of this survey is to assess and establish facts on the impacts of

agriculture in relation to biodiversity

3.0 Topography
Tetebedi is on a sloppy and mountainous ridge with very fast flowing rivers at the

base of the ridge. The terrain is rugged and coupled with a few damp and swampy
spots.

The vegetation is mostly grassland at the village and gardening area while further
inland the entire area is covered with moss and pristine montane forest. The forest
floor is covered with thick leaf litter and is mostly damp and wet.

The type of soil found at Tetebedi is silty loam around the village and loamy from the
gardens into the forest.

4.0 Climate
Generally there is rain all year round at Tetebedi. The rainy season starts from late

November through December to January, while the dry season begins around June

and ends at September.
There is an average of XXXXX milliliters of rainfall daily and an average of five (5)
sunshine hours daily. That is the sun is fully visible at around 9:00 am every morning

and is covered by clouds by 2:00 pm everyday.

5.0 Mode of farming

Shifting cultivation is the preferred mode of farming at Tetebedi. Villagers often
cultivate one area at a time. After harvesting of food crops, the villagers leave it to
fallow for a period of fifteen (15) years and move on to the next area suitable for
cultivation.

In the event of making a garden, the women weed shrubs and other small weeds. The
men then cut down trees and other plants left behind by the women. After that
everything is burnt and the men will commence planting immediately thereafter.

“Fourth Phase Biodiversity Survey — Tetebedi, Popondetta, Oro Province, PNG.”
 Practically the gardens are made within easy reach from the vicinity of the village.
‘This has enabled the villagers not to disturb the existing flore and fauna found in the
forest.
In one gardening event a large area of land is cleared and is sub-divided into three
blocks. The first block will have only sweet potato (Jpomea batatas) cultivated while
the second block or plot will have yams (Dioscorea exaltata). The third and final
block of land will cater for assorted crops such as bananas, sugarcanes, pitpits,
cucumbers, pumpkins and a variety of vegetables.
Observations from the survey revealed that the forest is undisturbed from intrusion of
any sort and is intact.
The gardens are often cultivated on siopes and towards the river banks. Because of
the slopes, terraces will have to be made. Currently there are no contour terraces made
and as a result top soil which is fertile are washed off by surface run-offs when it
rains thus leaving the whole garden prone to erosion. Some soil nutrients are also lost
through leeching.
According to viliggers interviewed it is customary not to build contour terraces or
ridges. From an agricultural perspective contour terraces are very important as they
hold back or prevent soil from being washed away by rain and cause soil ero:
Contour terraces will also slow down the flow rate of surface run-off thus minimize
or prevent scil ercsion as well.
In order to prevent soil erosion the villagers have been informed to build contour
ridges on siopes where they are doing gardening. They can build temporary contour
ridges by using dead logs or permanent contour ridges.
Permanent contour ridges can be made with the introduction of the vertiva grass
Wertiva zenzaineades), The vertiva grass has many uses some of which are;

(a) Contour ridges

(b) The feaves can be used to thatch houses

(©) The roots are used as local pesticides (in developed countries the roots are

used in the pharmaceutical and confectionary industries)
(d) Used as a traditional herb in some Asian countries etc

The practice of ouildi
-asi0n, Soi nut

contour ridges will assist immensely in the prevention of soil

ent leeching and most importantly landslides.

6.0 Hunting

The villagers hunt animals to supplement their diets by setting traps to catch wild
pigs, cuscus, tree kangaroos, wallabies, bandicoots, etc. Apart from traps bows and
arrows are also used in hunting. Adult animals are only used for food while smaller
animals and birds are reieased in to the wild. This practice wili aid in the natural
increase of these species of fauna as the animals wil! mature and reproduce thus
keeping their population steady. Over hunting of these animals both mature and
immature and the using of sophisticated weapons such as guns will gradually reduce
their number and eventually lead to extinction.

7.0 Cash crop potential

 Tetebedi has the potential to raise cash crops such as coffee, vanilla, citrus, cabbages,
broccoli, lettuces, tomatoes, potatoes etc. The climate is favorable to cultivate the

above crops.
The dry season is suitable for coffee, citrus and vanilla as it will induce flowering

which leads to fruit formation after successful pollination by insects. Other wise the
other crops can generally be grown all year round.

Bees can also be kept to. generate honey and other by-products of honey such as
candles, soap, wine etc can also be produced.

8.0 Ecosystems health
‘According to practical observations at the biosurveyed area, the river systems, plant
species, animal species and the environment itself is ecologically intact. Animal
species as well as human interactions have shown that they have been living a
symbiotic relationship.

Though trees and other plant species are used for buildings, food and for medicinal
purposes their use is minimal and can not warrant a threat to ecological damages or

loss.

9.0 Vertebrate composition
There is a vast diversity of vertebrates available at the biosurveyed area including
various species of amphibians, birds, mammals and reptiles. The biosurvey team was
able to take a specimen of undocumented specie of the bird of paradise and a rodent
(rat). The team will have to confirm with other literatures available. Otherwise the
specimens will be a new specie found in Papua New Guinea.

A lot of vertebrates would have been caught and documented but bad weather at the
project area hampered the team’s progress and at the same time forced the animals to
hibernate.

For all animals documented, the list can be seen on the appendix.

10.0 Plant composition
‘The composition of plants is such that there are two plants in Im? of land. This is not
dense as the forest is secondary montane forest because most of the plants species
have dried up, fallen and rotten away because of old age.

There are many hard wood trees such as the oak and kwila available as well as
medicinal plants such as salat. From assessments and observations these plants are

well and fairly distributed.

11.0 Threats to biodiversity
1, Human activity
> Gardening and Hunting
> Search for building materials
> Global warming
> Bush fires

2. Natural disasters

“Fourth Phase Biodiversity Survey — Tetebedi, Popondetta, Oro Province, PNG.”
 3. Extinction (Natural Selection)
> lack of breeding partners

4, Diseases
> Introduction of foreign diseases by new species of plants and animals

12.0 Impediments

The main factor impeding cash crop establishment is transportation. Because of the
remoteness and isolation of Tetebedi roads and other infrastructures will be labor
intensive and very expensive to develop. Tetebedi is only accessible via light
chartered aircraft as all regular commercial flights to the area have been cancelled.
These aircrafts are often expensive to charter and even though cash crops can be
raised, the owners can not be able to meet the charter price in order to transport their
crops to markets for sale.

Some crops especially vegetables are perishable and because of transport impediment
mest local farmers have ceased growing vegetables on a larger scale for markets
Instead they have resorted to growing a substantial amount of vegetables enough for
their household needs. Perishability is also a factor hindering vegetable production.

13.0 Agricultural Impacts

(@) clearing of forests areas can destroy rare and endangered flora species

14.0 Recommendations
It can be recommended from facts and findings from the survey that

(a) shifting cultivation must be the only practiced form of gardening. No
mechanical methods of farming must be encouraged

(b) all gardens on slopes must have permanent contour ridges. This can be made
possible via the introduction of vertiva grass (Vertiva zenzaineodes)

(0) all endangered species of flora and fauna identified must be preserved by the
community for future use in the field of medicine or research by the future
generations

(4)all landowners must ensure that the forest and everything it inhabits is
conserved from exploitation by outsiders (companies, individuals,
organizations etc)

(@) all gardens are to be made at certain specific, allocated and recommended
areas only and not anywhere

(®) any new species of flora and fauna found must be recorded, named, properly
identified, documented and be patented

(g) in preserving the biosurvey area all landowners must ensure that there are no
burning of bushes as bush buming is now a common practice and has become
a habit by today’s generation

(h) any young animals caught in traps must be released back into the wild so that
they can mature and reproduce

(i) no guns or firearms of any sort must be encouraged to be used in hunting

G) family planning methods must be introduced to curtail the current trend

(k) building materials obtained from the forests must be replanted with new ones

() when cutting down trees from the forest try to minimize environmental
damage as much as possible

15.0 Conelusion
It can be concluded that the Tetebedi conservation area has an enormous agriculture
potential in terms of cash crop development as well as a conservation reserve. In the
event of population increase, the number of fallow years will decrease with the
increasing need for food and as such will force people to cultivate the forest to grow
food.

The only impeding factor is transportation because of contributing factors such as
remoteness, terrain, local weather, topography and most importantly the cost involved
in building infrastructural developments such as roads and bridges.

‘The status of the biosurvey area is better left untouched as any new development into
the area will eventually lead to exploitation of endangered flora and fauna.

text:
Managalas Proposed Conservation Area, Guguavo Ridge, Tetebedi,
Kokoda District, Oro Province

MAMMALS AND HERPETO FAUNA SURVEY OF THE PROPOSED
MANAGALAS CONSERVATION AREA
PHASE IV REPORT

April- May 2008

Report prepared for Partners With Malenesians, Inc., Port Moresby, Papua New
Guinea

Paulus Kei
Division of Biological Sciences,
University of Papua New Guinea

 Keip@upng.cc.pg

Abstract

From November ~ December 2004, phase one of the mammals and herpeto fauna survey was
‘conducted near Itokama and the surrounding villages of Kuai and Nibaiba. Around the same
period in 2005 saw the second phase and again in 2006, was the third phase, which was the
extension of continuous assessment of the Proposed Managaias Conservation Area. The 4”
(last) phase of the survey was conducted at Tetebedi, which is further to the SW of Itokama
and the highest altitude range. The prime purpose of these surveys were to gather baseline
information on the mammals and herpeto fauna of the Proposed Managalas Conservation
Area. They were also conducted to assess and determine maminal diversity within the
proposed conservation area,

‘The mammals survey was carried out in two selected sites, on Guguavo ridge in a mid
montane primary forest, at an altitude of ~ 1400m asl. Each site had the same number and
types of traps used but different area sizes. Survey site 1 was 100x20m, subdivided into
smaller plots of 10x10m and a total area of 2000m" was surveyed for smaller mammals.

‘Twenty (20) Eilict trap and ten (10) Tamahawk wire cage traps were used in a total of 150
trapping nights, (which means that, a tota! of 30 traps X 5 nights, equals 150). Two (2)
different species of rodents were caught from the 1* site. Unfortunately no bats were caught

caught.

areal hassle with no road rk and no regular flights. Locals rely heavily on walking. it is
found that, the, vertebrate faune of the surveyed site and the vicinity around itis diverse and
intact.

It is recommended that the conservation initiatives by the people of Tetebedi, through
Managales Development Fund in coilaboration witis Partners With Melanesians be
strengthened arid mechanisms put in place to declare that area as Conservation Area.
 1.0 Introduction

‘The Managalas Plateau: Proposed Conservation Area is situated in the southeastern part of
Southern Papuan ecoregion in the Hjivitari District ~ Oro Province. The Proposed
Conservation Area covers an area of approximately 300,000 hectares. The Proposed
Conservation area is located on the Managalas Plateau. In the last three, (3) the Managalas
Plateau Proposed Conservation Azea has been a centre of biodiversity surveys on flora and
fauna conducted by scientists from UPNG and the, Department of Environment and
Conservation. This survey (phase IV) was the last of a series of surveys, which was
conducted on Guguavo Ridge, three and half-hours walk South east of Tetebedi village,
Kokoda District, Oso Province. This survey covered approximately one (1) hectare of area on
the ridge top. The mid montane ecoregion is made up of the Owen Stanley Renges, at
approximately 1400m asl. The composition of mammalian and herpetofauna of Tetebedi area
is relatively unknown with very little or no scientific investigations been conducted in the

past.

Aims and Objectives

‘© ‘The main purpose of this survey was to carry out a preliminary assessment or the status
‘of mammalian and herpetofauna of Tetebedi area, in the Managalas Plateau Proposed
Conservation Area as proposed by Partners With Melanesian.

© Provide hands on site technical scientific advice and experience to participating students
(ribution to manpower and capacity building at

higher education institutions in the coun
© Identify immediate threats to wild animals and other potential threats,
© Provide technical advises to the project coordinators and a preliminary report to

jandowners of the Proposed Conservation Area.

‘This report basically highlights the results and observations of the phase IV mammais and
herpeto fauna survey conducted within a period of 12 days.
 2.0 Methods

‘The investigation was carried using normal field equipment and from a general observation of
the survey site over a period of ten (10) working days

‘The field equipment used were:
1, Aluminium Elliot traps used for smaller ground mammals.
2. Tomahawk wire traps for larger ground mammals

3. Mist nets for bats and birds

Surveys of Frogs, Repliies and arborea! animals such as the marsupizis were done by chance
observations and from local informants.

Species listing of mammats were the results of actual trapping and also from loca! informants
using reference book(s). A total of 30 traps (20 Elliot traps and 10 Tomahawk traps) were set
at two 2) different trapping plots at different intervals.

Site one (1) 2 study plot of 100x2 metres quadrat approximately 150 metres from the camp
site was established at 10 metres intervals from the central baseline for five (5) trapping
nights per plot. Mist nets for bats and birds were erected adjacent to the plot. Traps were
baited with ripe bananas and than rebated with half bumt coconut flesh.

Site two (2) was estabiished approximately 500 metres from the camp site and 350 metres
from the first site along the same mountain ridge where ali the survey was conducted. Again 2
total of 30 traps were used for the same period of time, five trapping nights per plot. Mist nets
were erected paralie! to the trapping plot. The same type of baits were used for the traps in the
second study plot. Traps were observed for five (5) nights, rebaiting was done after every
second night. Mist nets were opened at eround 4.30 om.

Net observations were done every hour and closed at 10.00pm for bats. During this survey ¢
total of nine (9) nets were placed at different locations and observed for ten (10) working
days

3.0 Results

3.1. Mammals

A total of twelve (12) specimen of rats were collected after 300 trapping nights, that is 30
traps x 5 nighis per ploi x 2 plots. The specimens were coitected over ten (10) working days.
Out of the 12 rats trapped, 4 of the same species were released after collecting necessary data
/measurements taken and 8 are kept as specimens. Of those 3 species of rats, two (2) are
identified, while the third is in question mark. Could be e new discovery meaning new species
from that area.

Al specimens collected will be kept at the zoological section of the Natural Science Resource
Centre, division of biological sciences UPNG as reference collections.

(Table 2)

Although not many species of mammals were captured, their presence were evident, such as
the long-beaked echidna, Zaglossus bruijni and short-beaked echidna Tachyglossus
acculeatus. Fresh burrows in the ground were seen within the plot.

‘Though spot lighting in the night did not reveal much nocturnal activities from larger
mammals, especially marsupials, but there were signs of their presence in the area with
remains of claw marks on tree teunks.

Rodents (rats) were the abundant species of the mammals, which resulted in twelve been
caught during the 10 days of survey. (Table 1)

Wild boas (pigs) were no way close to be seen in the vicinity of the survey site. There were
totally no signs of its presence though it was evident closer to the village.

Wild dogs (Canis familiaris) are said to be present, though no signs of their presence. One
was heard calling in the night.

Other bigger mammals or marsupials, such zs the tree kangaroos, cuscus and wallabies were
hardly detected but are believed to be present according to local informants.

Domestic animals were seen in the villege, where they are kept as pets or in the case of a dog,
it is used for hurting. No domestic pigs (Sus scrofa Jere raised in the village because of their
religious status. Main religicus denomination in the area is Seven Day Adventist (SDA).

3.2 Amphibians

's survey was concentrated on mammais, however in just over 7 days, a good number of
frog specimens were collected. 15 frog specimens were collected and of those, 5 different
genus were identified, while the number of species are yet to be identified and confirmed.

It was observed that the frog species composition of the area is very high, Night observations
were also conducted with good results. Unfortunately there was no recording equipment to
record the calls during the night.

‘Of the 15 frog specimens collected, 13 are of the Microhylidae, | Ranidae and the other of the
Hylidae family. (Tabie 3)

3.3. Reptilia

Most efforts were concentrated on the mammals other than reptiles which includes, the frogs,
snakes and tizards

Lizards of the Emoia and Sphenomorphus spp were seen and also a forest gecko,
Hermidactylus sp was sighted within the surveyed sites.

‘A python, (Ziasis amethystinus) of approximately 2.5 metres long was recorded and released.
A water snake was caught at Tetebedi village recorded and was also released.
5
 4.0 Discussions:

The survey was conducted over a period of 10 working days that is from the 22" of April
through to 2™ of May 2008.

4.1 Rats

‘The results for the rats were quite good with 12 rats sampled in the period of ten (10) days of
trapping. Out of the 12 samples, one specie is in doubi, that it could be a new specie and a
new record for the area. This particular specie was common, that seven were captured from

both trapping sites.

‘The other species are commonly found in such vegetation. Non of the species caught is
arborea! Ai! ground dwelling species. frapping in both sites showed good results despite
drawbacks due to climate conditions. Both trap types, Tomahawk and Elliot were doing well,
capable of producing good resuits.

‘Considering the population size compared to the availability of food resources, indications are
that, the population matches the availability of food resources minimising competition rates.
With only few species captured in a particular aree, signifies the abundarice of resources
available and less competition,

This in turn gives a balance in the species composition of the area, As a result species that
cover wider territories can now share the habitat with other species. This could be the likely

case wheve competition for resources is low. The whole area surveyed was of the same

Spot lighting and night observations for nocturnal mammals were unsuccessful during the
survey. Since most of the higher mammals are seasonal species, for zhat reason the timing
wes inappropriate.

ing of bats was quite unexpected, with only 3 bat samples were collected with two
different species. This could have resuited from again time factor. It was not the right season
for the bat species that feeds on fruits { fruitivores) or nectars from flowers. Only 2 species of
bats were sampied over the 1C days period. This is a shocking result especially for
Syconycieris australis species, which is the most common species of bais that car be sampled
almost anywhere. It was shocking to see the decline in bat species in such an undisturbed
forests.

Observations were carried out in the evenings to determine bat activities but there were still
no signs. Time could be the main factor for these poor results.

 4.3 Marsupialia

‘Although there were evidences of their presence, such as claw marks on tree stumps or
trunks, hardly one was detected. Other species of marsupials including tree kangaroos,
bandicoots, cuscus were said to be present in the area by the locals. However non of them
were seen during the investigation. Most marsupials are rather hard to capture as they inhabit
tall trees and forage at night.

4.4 Amphibia (Frogs)

Sampling of frogs was done from chance observations and by searching the forest, under
leave litter and on shrub leaves. Frog species in the area is diverse according to the
assessment on the rate of calis. Generally it can be stressed that there are many more frog
species of interest to be found in the area.

Oftthe 15 frog specimens collected, three (3) different families, with five (5) genus and
couple of species yet to be identified.

4.5 Reptilia (Lizards and Snakes)

Snakes

‘A2.5 metres long python, Liasis amethestinus was caught recorded and released. Also a
water snake caught recorded and released. Although not evident it was pointed out by locals
that there other pythons like the Boelens python, Morelia boeleni (protected by flora and
fauna Act of PNG). Not much snakes were seen during the survey.

Lizerds

Lizards were not frequently encountered during the survey. Skinks of the Emoie ené
Sphenomorhus species wereseen, recorde and released. A forest gecko, Hermidactylus was
also spotted on a tree.

5.0 Previous Draft Repor:

‘The previous Draft Report on High Conservation Vatue Forest (HCVP) on the Managalas
Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) can be accepted on the basis of the value of the
lixerature content. It contains generalised information on the socio-environmental features,

that is; population informetion, location of the Proposed conservation Area, Geology, Climate
and the Physical features of the Managalas area and the types of forest that can accommodate
flora arid fauna of conservation significance within PNG and the Oceania region.

As stated in the report, whilst this survey report is prepared for the MPCA , the list of
mammals provided is based on fiterature information. Also the data presented in this report
does not include ail the mammals of that particular area surveyed, that surely occurs in that
region. Example, the rodents, marsupials, bandicoots, cuscuses, tree kangeroos and the
possibie presence of the echidnas (anteaters)

Many other information on the components such as, the herpeio fauna, insecto fauna (Beetles,
and many other insects) that make up the biodiversity of an area is not included in this report
 6.0 Recent Survey

‘The recent Biodiversity survey that was conducted on Guguavo Ridge near Tetebedi village,
indicates that there is a high rate of species diversity. High sampling rate in in less time, is a
00d indication of the diversity of the area.

6.1 Status of Mammals

At present there is no proper assessment of status of animal species composition for this
particular area. With the species listing and the collection (Appendixs1&2) further
determinations will be required to verify the correct specimens. However, itis a highly
possible that some of the specimens collected might be new species or records.

7.0 General Considerations

Some of the factors that are evident from this survey that supports the conservation initiatives
undertaken by the local people in close working relation with Partners With Melanesians.

‘The forest type and the distribution of animal species are strongly influenced by the
prevailing environmentai conditions. The vertebrate composition of i

and provides an opportunity for further sciemific investigetion/studies of the fauna in the
area.

@ The occurrence of certain species of frogs and mammals that are different will need

proper studies.

@ Due to lack proper infrastructure, the people of Tetebedi and the surrounding villages rely
ineavily on foxest resources for their basic needs. Desinuction of foresis will have very bad
effect on the vertebrate composition of the area.

© Local people should be told clearly on which animal species are on the protected list so
that they should be hunted.

8.0 Recommendations
Given the uniqueness of the vertebrate composition of the proposed conservation area on
Guguavo Ridge, itis highly recommended that the area be conserved. It is also recommended
thai more scientific surveys be conducted and other iong term studies are carried out in the
area, Permanent study plots should be established and consistently monitor the status of
vertebrate species.

Dear Honorable Minister.

SUB: OBJECTION TO GOLDMINEX LTD MINING EXPLORATION LICENSE No. 1547,
MANAGALAS PLATEAU, AFORE SUB DISTRICT, ORO PROVINCE

On behalf of the 18.000 people of Managalas plateau in Afore sub district of Oro province, | am
bringing the above matter to your urgent attention because your Department (Mines) and the
Mineral Resource Authority (MRA) have already given issued or renewed a mineral exploration
license to Goldminex Ltd to do exploration in Afore sub district of Oro Province.

The area identified as ELA 1347 falls directly within the boundary of proposed Managelas
Conservation Area which covers approximately 360.000 hectares of land covered with forests from
altitude as low as 40 m to 2880 m above sea level. This area is the home of the 18,000+ people from
150 clan groups who have been living there for generations.

‘The area that | have described above is on the eastern side of the Owen Stanley ranges, which is
home to some of this country’s unique flora and fauna including the CITES, [UCN Red List and
PNG Protected Species under the Fauna (Protection and Contro!) Act 1966 but not limited to the
follow

The Queen Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly ....the world’s largest butterfly
New Guinea Singing Dogs ...clase relatives of the Australian Dingoes

7 species of the Birds of Paradise .... 2 believed to be new not yet described by science
3 new Species of Frogs ....nol yet described or new to science

The Whistling Snake

Long-beaked Echidna

Numerous parrots and Cockatoos

The Doria’s Tree Kangaroo

Our organization, Partners with Melanesians (PwM). a national conservation and community
development NGO has been wor the local communities since 1985 on a major
conservation and community development programme (see our profile). The Summer Institute of
Linguistic (SIL) has also been doing social and linguistic translation projects over the plateau since
1972. We have come so close to lodging our application to the Environment Council and here we
have this Mining Exploration License issued to Goldminex Limited, an Australian company.

 In the past the PNG Forest Authority demarcated the area as a logging concession called the Gora ~
ltokama FMA. When it came (o the notice of the Managalas community. the entire population
mobilized and lodged notices to refirse PNGFA because they oversighted the local landowners
rights over their forests and customary land. This was rejected outright thus the area was not
declared for forestry and logging and was excluded from the Provincial and National Forest Plans,
as the people opposed all forms of destructive developments, but opted for conservation and
sustainable development projects

Currently. according to the community leaders on Managalas Plateau, only two or three people are
behind this mining activity and these three have signed the agreement by themselves without the
proper consultation and other due diligence processes with ail the indigenous landowners and
community members.

Our Organization has been involved with the Managaias people working on conservation and
community. development activities for more thar 20 years. we are fully aware of the negative
consequences of mining on the environment and the sociai status of the people who depend on the
environment for their livelihoods. We do not have to go far to see for ourselves the impact mi
have on the local people as there are evidence of environmental destruction and socio-economic
impacts such as situations confronted by the people of middie and lower Fly in the Wester
Province. the Hungabungar River in Central and the Guava River in Bougainville, despite the
millions of kina coming from PNGSDP and Ok Tedi Mine Limited, Tolukuma Mine and
Bougainville Copper Limited. respectively. We definitely know that they will never fix the
probiems that were created upstream leaving huge ugly oper cut landscapes that will continue to
have acid rock drainage and splits into the river system for thousands of years. There are scientific
evidences that the freshwater and riverine ecosystems such as those in the Fly River system will be
dead for aimost 300 years after mine closure hence in the next 20-50 generations. the ecosystems
will never be restored quickly to its natural state.

From our predictions of the future of mining in Managalas. the most logical locations for any
mining waste dumping/ailings will be along the Musa or Barige River systems and obviously the
negative consequences will be huge. Therefore. with the concerns of the Managalas people whom
we have been working with for many years. we strongly’ feel it is our responsibility to inform you of
our objection to the issuance of the mining exploration license of Goldminex Ltd over the western
sector of the Managalas plateau (ELA 1547). If mining is to occur we know for certain that the
entire ecosystem of Managaias Plateau including the Upper. Lower and Middle Musa valley will be
destroyed consequently affecting the people. the flora and fauna and the marine and aquatic
ecosystems forever

Managalas plateau is strategically linked to the proposed Kokoda World Heritage Site, which was
recently signed off by the Governments of Australia and PNG. with the Prime Minister Hon. Kevin
Rudd and Grand Chief Sir Michael Somare. The Managalas plateau lies directly east of the Kokoda
trail and so, the same consideration should be given to this areas as well as it has a historical and
biological significance. In World War II, zhe Managatas piateau was the path the American soldiers
followed to assist the Australian soldiers in the batties which were fought in the Kokoda area with
the Japanese. Therefore. it has a historical significance. plus cultural and biological importance for
the country

Mining for gold, nickel and other minerals for revenue and monetary benefits for PNG is a short
term development whereby the vast wealth generated fiom their industrial operations and
development will be transferred overseas by the mining companies and developer leaving behind
pittance for PNG, The entire area hold vast natural treasures worth far more then the gold and
minerals beneath the soil. and its best the minerais are left untouched and the natural treasures

text:
| Partners With Melanesians
a vies

 RFL Analysis of the efficient delivery, effectiveness and impact of RFN
funded literacy activities in Managalas Plateau.

Executive Summary:
The literacy participatory evaluation for rainforest literacy radio programs was conducted

by PWM under the Rainforest Norway funding.

‘The participatory evaluation was conducted in Managalas Plateau, from 04" to 09th
October 2008 to discuss the findings of the Rainforest literacy assessment and needs in
the base communities that are engaged in the literacy activities and foresee the Capacity
Building Training Conduct for CSO literacy facilitators, supervisors and managers.

Partners with Melanesians initially initiated these activities, with the funding support
form Rainforest Norway. In response to the issues of lack of government services
delivery and inequity for women and young girls, Civil Society Organizations (CSO)
have form to influence government policy and bring economic, education and health
services. Fundamental aspect was woman and underserved population has the high
illiteracy rate, which they could not compete with the changing social and economic
development.

In order to compete with the changing development people have to be educated,
rainforest literacy radio program has resulted in greater cooperation between women and
men at all levels, husbands and wives going together with their family and clan members.
The facilitators and adult learners who have gained increased confidence, which in turn
have resulted in increased leadership responsibility at the community level. The project
was aimed at developing small-scale business around conservation in Managalas Plateau
that in-still their capacity into more sustainable approach with the support of the
Managalas Development Foundation.

1. Rainforest literacy radio program in the Managalas Plateau

‘© Awareness raising within 10 zones in the conservation areas

© Hosting adult education forums between zones to enable sharing of
iessons learned and specialist skills through radio progra

© Facilitating the distribution of information on RFL activities and best
practices.
Clan and family group discussion.
Capacity Building training for facilitators and supervisors.
Assisting clans groups in strategic planning for the development of their
adult learning process

‘© Providing technical expertise to zones in implementation of radio program
while concurrently providing technical training to clan facilitator on how
to implement, monitor, and expand the program, including advocacy,

 lobbying, networking and as well mainstreaming of HIV/AIDS
information.

© Providing technical assistance to program coordinators developing in
resource materials.

2. Facilitating links between RFL and Papua New Guinea Government
© Strengthening RFL networking with Literacy providers
© Building relationship and partnership with National Literacy &
Awareness, Dept. of Community Development and Dept. of Environment
and Conservation
© Facilitate the distribution of information on rainforest literacy activities
and best practices to local and national

Rainforest literacy responsible for organizing all the actives in the propose conservation
area, MDF working together with rainforest literacy program have raise concern over the
outcome there is not enough training given to the facilitators for they can execute the
program themselves.

‘The common theme underlying the set of recommendations is the urgency of building
stronger relationships between CSOs and rainforest literacy program and linking
government agencies. The activities outputs were achieving but constant evaluation to
access the impact of the program yearly has lack. Rainforest literacy needs to revisit the
activity plan and re-organize for the boarder approach into community learning. Building
and strengthening Managalas in-heritage through rainforest literacy has retain greater role
of responsibilities.

The RFL ultimately decide the outcome of the project initiate in the communities but
lacks constant follow-up and trainings. Their genuine participation in the processes that
affect them is not only desirable but also essential to the development of rainforest
literacy.

The ideal starting point for integral human development should be through initial literacy
via localized curriculum using myth (technical definition) as the core for theme web
development. This would enforce traditional values’ ideas/ morals through forms that the
CSOs are familiar with and provide a firm foundation from which to draw out critical
expansions in appropriate areas enhancing the development process. Every development
hnas to take course from what people know to what they do not know in this way you can
contain people interest and contribute meaningfilly to the development.

The participatory evaluation was carried out in collaboration with Managalas
Development Foundation (MDF) and PWM in the Managalas plateau.

‘The participants participated were rainforest literacy facilitators, clan groups, women
groups and supervisors. In collaboration with Literacy Specialist, PWM team prepared
REL questionnaires and mapping detail of literacy site for Participatory Evaluation visits.
 Efficient Delivery:
The strategies sets out the general direction for activities in accelerating adult education,
there are some underlying observations that lead to the development of the three pronged
strategy to accelerate rainforest literacy the in Plateau.

Firstly, a general awareness campaign has been carried out for the plateau and more
importantly people at all level recognize that there is a problem that needs attention.
Many people are not aware if they do, they do not see the gender imbalances especially in
regard to young girls’ education as a problem.

This is concer of development and well being of communities. Rainforest literacy and
the education of women population in particular, is not only an issue of formal
knowledge, but has in the long term positive repercussion on HIV/AIDS, Health and
Nutrition, Educating a woman in the long-term benefits families.

Secondly one must recognize the different communities are at levels of progress in terms
of delivery rainforest literacy activities. In REN funded project there are also vary levels
of success in the plateau. In most communities, adult education is still an achievable
target with 50% of clan groups enrolled.

The strategy is to focuses efforts on alleviating poverty and helps people move forward.
By focusing efforts and resources on those worse off are a significant improvement
overall can be attained and tangible benefit realized. In terms of generic outcomes, its
seems that it is the facilitators and adult leamers who have gain increased confidence
which in turn resulted in them taking increased leadership responsibilities at the
community level.

Thirdly, it is recognized that the activities needs to be coordinated and the progress or
albeit the lack of progress needs to measure monitoring the implementation of the
planned activities and evaluate the effects and outcomes. The generic outcomes observed
above derive from the literacy training. The organizational capacity building proved
under this project does not seem to have led to any generic outcomes.

Most of the planning for rainforest literacy is done without consultation and also there is
not constant follow-up on the progress of the project. After the first training there hasn’t
been any follow-up training for literacy workers in the base communities. The literacy
workers acquire management skills for efficient and effectively coordinating the
rainforest literacy in the Managalas plateau.

district level training.

Effectiveness:

Innovative programs/approaches

For the creation of an inform and active citizenry, the promotion of literacy and the
alleviation educational poverty in Papua New Guinea paraliel to the United Nation
literacy decade or acceleration life long learning (Functional Literacy). People has
emerged as a powerful complementary system to the formal sub-sector of education all
over the Managalas Plateau enlisting commitment and endeavors of the Rainforest
Norway and the number of civil society organization, because of the enormous growth in
scope and scale along with very effective and distinct performance in the field of
illiteracy eradication through rainforest literacy system of education for women, young
girls and disadvantage population

Programs related to the United Nations Literacy Decade
United Nation literacy in Papua New Guinea is part of the global strategy to achieve
universal basic education by 2015. It has been from in response to the United Nation
literacy decade initiative. Papua New Guinea with other 25 counties was selected to focus
attention on and improve the status of women and young girls.

Partners With Melanesians has response to the challenge by establishing zones in the
plateau to explore ways to move forward. Rainforest literacy program has come in time
to re-secuted and organized capacity building training for facilitators and supervisors, in
the Managalas plateau. Since the establishment of the program in 2003, the clan elders
and facilitators where gathered through rainforest literacy radio program.

many CSOs and individuals involved in education and related fields came together to

development approach. This attempts to develop appropriate action improving capacity
of literacy leaders and local coordinators on literacy management aspect. Training

‘There are thus three main types of literacy learning programs in existence in the plateau.

- Critical literacy (reading and writing life)

- Technicist literacy (literacy and writing of print text without meaning)

- Functional literacy (listening to rainforest radio program ~ need for income

generation)

On the surface, all of these types of literacy learning programs claim help people to
become useful members of society, to help people to understand changes in their lives
and to participate in those changes. However through seven years of rainforest literacy in
the Managalas plateau, it has become clear that Technicist literacy is not real priority for
the people in the society has taken tremendous change in lifestyle. Critical literacy and
functional literacy are seen as appropriate tools to get back what they have lost and to
maintain what is with them and to build back their confidence in themselves.

In the process of radio series and understanding event that was affecting their daily lives,
people learn to associate and appreciate the nature of the program, making that living text
part of their lives. Critical literacy (in this sense) was already an integral part of peoples’
lives. Critical literacy literally means finding reasons for events and problems that are
occurring in ones life and ones community (critical reading), and then finding ways to
cope with these events and developing solutions to these problems on the basis of an
informed community-based decision-making process (which may be described as critical
writing).

Incentive to community, in contrast, was not critical literacy. Under such influence,
People began to accept cargo unquestioningly. Community participation deteriorate and
in the process repudiating their traditions culture.

snippet: District Wide Combine Forum Naukonane Village, Itokama 11" November 2008 Report: The team of four including the PWM Program Manager, Communications Officer, an Officer on attachment with PWM and a crew from the Nala Times Media left Port Moresby for Itokama on Saturday 08" November 2008. The purpose
text:
District Wide Combine Forum
Naukonane Village, Itokama
11" November 2008

Report:
The team of four including the PWM Program Manager, Communications Officer, an
Officer on attachment with PWM and a crew from the Nala Times Media left Port Moresby
for Itokama on Saturday 08" November 2008. The purpose of the advance party was to
ensure logistics and preparations for the combine forum are in order before the actual
forum began on Monday 10® November.

Upon arrival at Itokama, the team were told that the venue for the forum was moved
from Itokama to Naukonane because the community would not allow disturbances to the
grade eight students who were sitting for their examinations week 10” - 14" November.

Taking into account the time the plane will remain on the ground (45min) awaiting the
Minister for DEC and his delegation, the team was able to convince the community to
move back the venue for the launching of the application for the conservation area back
to Itokama. The Head teacher agreed and allowed deferral of exams until after the plane
takes off from Itokama, That was the alternative arrangement.

Meanwhile, communities in zone one (Itokama, Kwai, Naukonane and Mandokoro) were
exited and geared up to receive the Minister for Environment and Conservation Hon
Benny Allen at the official opening of the District Wide Forum and the launching of the
application for the Conservation Area Status.

‘On Monday 10 November, the feeling of excitement to receive the delegation from Port
Moresby was overwhelming. Singsing groups began dancing as early as 6:00 am in the
morning. A pig was slaughtered and food was roasted in the earth oven purposely for
the delegation.

The arrival time for the place to Itokama was schedule for 9:30 am but the plane was
delayed for about 3 hours and 15 minutes. If finally touched down at Itokama at 1:15
pm to an awaiting crowd of about 300 people singing and dancing excitedly to receive
the delegation:

Much to their dismay, the Minister for Environment and Conservation, Hon Benny Allan
was not on the plane. Nor was there a representative from the DEC Office or his Ministry
except for Mr Paulus Kulmoi, Principle Ecologist with DEC who was invited separately to
present the report of the Biodiversity Survey.

It was also disappointing for us because many of the stakeholders we invited were never
able to make it although they confirm their attendance. Only a handful was able to
attend the gathering at Itokama. This include; PWM Vice Chairman and Secretary
General, Uniting Churches of PNG Rev. Siulangi Kavora; PWM Board Member, Serah
Tsiamalili; MDI Executive Director, Mary Carlua; and George Baure, chairman Forest,
Mines and Lands, Provincial Executive Council, Oro Provincial Government.

Anyway, the community welcomed the small delegation to the grandstand and PWM Vice
Chairman and Secretary General, Uniting Churches of PNG Rev. Siulangi Kavora officially
declare the forum open. A community representative, Brian Kasira from Noukanane
 spoke on-behalf of the community and presented a petition to Mr George Baure,
chairman Forest, Mines and Lands, Provincial Executive Council, Oro Provincial
Government. The petition (a copy is attached to this report) basically called for the PEC
to meet and endorse the application for the Conservation Area Status so the completed
application will be presented to the Minister for DEC early next year. A traditional head
dress was presented to Mr Kulmoi to bring to the Minister for DEC. Pieces of pork meat
(lek pik) were presented to Rev. Siulangi Kavora and George Baure.

Mr Baure, upon receiving the petition, promised to push for the application for the CA to
be endorsed by the PEC at the next sitting.

The delegation left Itokama at 2:15 pm and forum participants were shown to their
sleeping quarters to rest and wait for the forum to begin. However, it was difficult
getting participants together again as they were spread throughout the four villagers so
the forum committee decided to call if off for the day and announced that the forum wi
begin the next day.

The forum committee (MDF/PWM) met in the afternoon and made final preparations for
the forum. There were six topics;

MDF and PWM Operations on the Plateau

MocP

Reconciliation rights

Kinship rights

Biodiversity Survey

Traditional Learning Centre

oy aune

Due to time factor, the committee decided that the forum will only deliberate on two
important topics, MDF/PWM Operations on the Plateau and MOCP. The others
(Reconciliation rights, kinship rights, traditional learning centre) were left to the clan
groups to discuss and come up with action plans as these topics were within their
control to effect changes. While MDF/PWM Operations on the Plateau and MOCP were
topics that concern PWM and MOF and needed to be discussed at the forum. The
committee asked Mr Kulmoi to make a presentation of the Biodiversity Surveys at the
forum as it was not really a topic for discussions as such.

That was the flow of the forum that proceeded the following day, 11° November. The
minutes basically explained who said what and what needs to be done. The forum was
divided into two parts, The issues were discussed, and prioritized; and options were
identified to work on the issue to bring about positive results.

Finally, the forum had a record turnout of 177 participants who represented zones 1, 2,
3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, & 10. Zone 9 could not attend because the river flooded and they could
not cross over. A new inclusion was also present at the forum and attended as
observers. This was the Wawanga community identified as zone 11.

Assessment and Evaluation from the PWM team:

A lot of negative sentiments were said about PWM even from current and former PWM
Board Members and prominent Managalas leaders. That generally explained that the
‘communities no tonger appreciate what PWM is doing despite PWM working in the area
for over two decades and having made impacts in small ways that contributed to the
sustenance of the people's livelihood over time.

 Re

‘An external project evaluation of the Managalas Conservation Area Project has to
be done immediately to determine where the problem(s) is/are and strategi
steps needed to be taken to re-focus PWM's effort in the Exit Strategy and MDF
Capacity Building.
PWM is a national NGO and does not necessarily have to have board members
from the project areas as there is always a risk of project area representatives on
the board to miss-represent the organization because of conflict of interest. The
Board deals with highly confidential information that can either make or break
the organization. These local representatives should be the ones taking leading
roles in correctly informing the community about PWM, her mission, vision, aims,
goals, activities etc. but the opposite was happening with the Managalas
Conservation Area Project.

Aplanning meeting to be convened between PWM and MDF to deliberate on the
‘outcome of this forum as a lot of points raised from the issues were directly to
do with PWM/MDF administrative and program matters. Programs must be
designed to address some of their points and outcome must be presented to
them at the next forum together with points raised at the June forum.

 Introduction

The following document is in two parts. The first is the proceedings of a community development
strategy workshop held at Toma village from the 30" of November to the 4 of December 2009 and
the second part is the strategy for the Berefo Development Association as an output of the
workshop and an action plan to mobilise the Community Development Strategy.

‘The workshop was facilitated by Volunteers from OCEAN with the support from a staff member of
CELCOR with funding support from GGF.

Acknowledgements

We wish to acknowledge the financial support for this project from the Global Green Grants Fund
facilitated by Damien Ase through CELCOR, FoE PNG. Edrick Ninimiro for the submission to GGF,
Marjorie Warisaiho, for taking time out in the field to be part of the facilitating team and Bradley
Dabadaba from MDF for field support and Raymond Hekoroka and Philemon Balasi for local logistics
arrangements.

Back Ground

Berefo Community Development Association (BCDA) draws its membership from 8 villages in the
Afore LLG of the Ijivitari District in the Northern Province of PNG. It is a community based
organization focused on community development originally set up and registered by Partners with
Melanesians (PwM) in 1994 to work with to meet PwM’s Conservation project in the Managalas
Plateau.

Asa part of PWM's local partner MDF which is divided into 10 zones, BCDA is in zone 9 which also is
Census ward 15 in the Afore LLG.

It has an approximate population of 2,050 with just over 400 registered adults in the 2007 National
electoral roll. The bulk of the population are youth between the ages over 12 to 18 any only about
‘5% of them have ever been to a formal school. From physical observation social indicators are very
low. Based on reflection made by participants the mortality rate is very high more especially from
curable diseases and child birth. The strain on the population for just reaching basic services is very
high given the difficulty of the geography especially the Bareji river.

Over the years the people had felt neglected by the Government and their local partner MDF. They
turned to PWM with the hope that they would gain some social and economic benefits that the
government had failed to deliver however these dreams never materialised and the Berefo people
felt that they were an insignificant group of people for whom it was not in any body's be:
{fo risk their lives for. One can not miss the geographically difficult location that these very
humble people have decided to call home as we found out trying to get there.

Raymond Hekoroka and Philemon Balasi, however never gave up the hope that some day some
people crazy enough to risk their lives will come along and with them they will bring hope for a
better future for themselves and their future generation and their persistence finally paid off when
GGF came to their aid through CELCOR to pay costs for a community development strategic plan.
 Geography & Locality

In the hinterlands of the Musa river plains meeting the foothilis of the Owen Stanley range the very
simple, semi- primitive Berefo people go about their daily business of hunting and gardening. It is
made up of 8 villages with Toma, Gewoia and Biriri being the most populated villages. Set ina very
difficult geographic area cut of by fast flowing rivers and ravines these villages are amongst the least
advanced in today’s standards lacking government services as well as other service providers
including NGOs.

‘The expected out puts from this workshop have been met. The out puts being;

1. The Berefo Community Development Strategy. The strategy in its design is
focused on community development objectives which can be achieved through broad based
community participation. It had been identified in the planning workshop that outside
support in terms of skilled manpower lacked in their area, this was largely influenced by the
geography. Therefore the priority area is manpower capacity building and local initiatives
for small scale income generating options.

2. Action Plan. An action plan has also been developed as a catalyst to mobilise the
implementation of the Community Development Strategy. It is anticipated that the action
plan will form the core annual operational budget that can be implemented utilizing the
existing administrative structure. (refer to organizational structure, appendix 2)

fact that land belonging to the Berefo people is also included in the Musa Pongani
special agriculture lease recently.

for 2010

Day1

The workshop initially began with general group discussions. Participants were given the
opportunity to introduce themselves and share with the group what their expectations were.

Expectations;

Having being isolated for so long from outside assistance, the general expectations, were that from
the workshop, participants wanted to clearly identify issues in which the Berefo communities were
facing and the best solutions to overcome these issues and to see change occurring in their
community that would improve their livelihoods.

Community Development;

Within the big group participants discussed in their opinion the definition of community and
development. From the discussion, the participants shared the view of community being defined as
either individuals or 2 group of people living in one place and sharing a common interest.

Their definition of development was planning and seeing changes occurring in the environment
around them. They also viewed development in the form of infrastructure such as aid posts and
schools, roads and bridges that wili enable them to have a better standard of living compared to the
current situations.

Issues facing Berefo communities;

Participants, later had group discussions to brainstorm on the issues, which the communities faced
as welt as envisioning their future. This activity was carried out as a guideline in identifying the main
focus of the communities.

Envisioning Berefo communities

Within the same working groups, participants were tasked to envision what Berefo communities

‘The Combine Forum is an annual activity that is held towards the end of the year every year under

Partners With Melanesians
