snippet: 44) The International Trade of Endangered Species (Fauna and Flora Act (1978) gives effect to the CITES and PNG is bound by its own Laws relating to CITES and we are bound to take positive action to protect the QABB. 14)Despite four (4) biological surveys undertaken in the past by friends of the Man
text:
44) The International Trade of Endangered Species (Fauna and Flora Act (1978)
gives effect to the CITES and PNG is bound by its own Laws relating to
CITES and we are bound to take positive action to protect the QABB.

14)Despite four (4) biological surveys undertaken in the past by friends of the
Managalas plateau including the Department of Environment and
Conservation, the Science Faculty of the University of Papua New Guinea,
and Partners with Melanesia, there is a diverse array of fauna and fiora of the
Managalas plateau that remain to be discovered and documented. Hence
having the area declared as a Conservation Area can allow further research
into the rich diverse ecosystems of the area.

Threats to Conservation & Sustainable Natural Resources use

15) The major threat on the environment and the forest ecosystems is from
agriculture; conversion of primary forests for both subsistence food production
and commercial cash cropping activities like growing coffee- undertaken by
the local communities to enhance human wellbeing.

46) There are potential threats from the private sector; especially companies who
are interested in industrial logging and mining in and around the proposed
conservation areas. Initially there was an intrusion and overlap with mining
Exploration Lease (EL 1547) but the boundary map has been adjusted
amicably between landowners, the Minerals Resources Authority, and the
Conservation Environment Protection Authority (CEPA) to allow mining
exploration activities to be undertaken outside the boundary of the proposed
conservation area.

17) Several industrial logging propositions have been made but landowners in
the conservation area have and are still objecting in preference over
conservation and small scale ecoforestry to meet local requirements including
housing, construction of schools and health centers.

Community Suj

48) The Managalas communities were educated through a literacy program
through the University of Papua New Guinea since 1984 on the issues related
to the destruction of the natural forests and the biodiversity. As a result, all the
Managalas clan elders and chiefs agreed in at a public forum at zone 6
(Numba) in 1997 to have the entire Managalas plateau officially declared as a
conservation area to protect the habitat for the QABB and the forest for the
future generations.

19) The respective government agencies at the Provincial and Local level have
also given their support and endorsement on the declaration of Managalas
Conservation area; Oro Provincial Executive endorsement on 2 December
2008 followed by Afore Local Level Government endorsement on 8" June
2011.

20) At the invitation of the Managalas communities, the Partners with
Melanesians (PwM) a national Non- Governmental Organization (NGO) has
been working in the area since 1997 mainly in raising awareness and building
capacity with funding assistance from the Rainforest Foundation of Norway up

sae
  to present with a total expenditure of some PGK10 million. PWM Focal
Programs in the past had been;

Education, training and awareness

Scientific research, data collection and analysis
‘Support for alternative income earning options
Facilitate conservation area declaration

21) Notable achievements include education and awareness of local
‘communities, conservation commitment of 360,000 hectares; establishment of
base line socioeconomic and biological data; and establishment of a
‘community based organization for the area; the Managalas Conservation

3.0 LITERATURE REVIEW

3.1 General Background of Coffee Production
Coffee production in Papua New Guinea accounts for approximately 1% of the world production

according to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD). After oil palm,
coffee is Papua New Guinea's second largest agricultural export, employing approximately 2.5
million people.

Coffee is the highest foreign exchange eamer for Papua New Guinea, the majority of whi
grown in the Eastern Highlands Province, the Western Highlands Province and Chimbu. With the
Industry not derived on a colonial plantation based system, production Is largely by small farmers
land holdings that grow as little as 20 trees per plot in coffee gardens alongside subsistence
crops. Predominantly in isolated places, the product is mostly certified as “organic coffee”.

Coffee production in the country dates back to 1926 and 1927 when the first Jamaican Blue
Mountain Coffee seeds were planted. However, the Coffee Research Institute claims that coffee
‘was introduced to British Papua in 1890, although it is widely accepted that commercial production

prensa

‘Partners With Melanesians Inc.

 only took off in the country in the late 1920s. in Sengara, Papua New Guinea in the foothills in the
southeast of the country, 18 commercial coffee plantations were established in 1926, paving the
way for commercial production from 1928. Louis Austen, a retired sea-ceptain, once managed 2
government coffee plantation near Sangara.

In 1960s, the infrastructure developed significantly in Papua New Guinea which facilitated a
marked growth in the industry, easing the transportation of coffee beans from the plantations to
the mills to be processed and exported. The coffee industry in Papua New Guinea thrived in the
1970s, benefiting from a slump production in Brazil on the international market because of
problems of frosts. However, in the 1980s, coffee plantation production has declined in Papua New
Guinea and has decentralized towards localized small coffee farmers who are now accountable
over 85% of total national production. The coffee boom in the 1980s profoundly affected many of
the coffee plantation owners and amounted debts they could not pay off with the result that many
were made redundant. From 1986, a number of cases of coffee rust caused by Hemileia vostatrix,
also affected some parts of Papua New Guinea which had previously been free of the disease.

The coffee industry in Papua New Guinea reached a peak in 1998 when it was responsible for some
38% of the country’s non-m'reral exports. Between 1995 and 1998 coffee production con’ributed
to 42 per cent of the revenve of country’s total agricultural exports. Since then the indvstry has
rapidly declined, affected by a world depression in coffee prices with prices falling up to 69%. As a
-esult, production slumped by 23% in 2000 and remained stagnant in 2003. in PNG, coffee is the
major income earner contributing about 41% of the total agricultural export earnings, 12% of the
total exports including minerals and S% of PNGs GDP. Past economic reports indicate that about
85% of coffee exported is produced by the smalihoiders,

3.4 Origin, Distribution and Uses

Coffee may have originated from Africa (Ethiopia esp. Arabica coffee) or South America. All species
are small trees (shrubs) and when left to grow, will reach a height of about 10m. Coffee is widely
cultivated and distributed throughout the humid tropics as a cash crop. Arabica coffee is important
in East Africa and is also cultivated in the highlands of Brazil as it prefers a cooler climate. Robusta
coffee is suited to production on lowland sites in the humid tropics and is extensively grown in
Brazil while Liberica coffee is grown in West Africa and Southeast Asi

In PNG, only arabica coffee and robusta coffee are grown. Arabica is mostly grown in the highlands
and robusta is grown on the-coastal lowlands. Psoduction figures show that 95% of arabica and
only 5% of robusta are produced in PNG.

Like cocoa, coffee is used as a beverage. The relatively modern process is the preparation of
roasted coffee from the coffee seed. Other uses are masticatory (chewed as a stimulant) in Ethiopia
and can be fermented as an alcoholic drink.

3.5 The Coffee Industry in Papua New Guinea

3.5.1 A Brief History of Coffee in Papua New Guinea
It is generally accepted that coffee was first introduce:l into the Pacific area in the late 18" century

by Dutch sailors, The first official record of its introduction to PNG is a note in th2 Annual Reports
of British New Guinea of coffee being planted in “a small botanical garden”. This same source
advised that by 1892 the crop was thriving in the Rigo district and that extensive plantings had
been established in the Sogeri area by 1898. Cartlege makes mention of the first research being
carried out by these pioneers. They were experimenting with direct planting of seed in the field.

Up to 70 hectares of coffee growing in the Papua area in 1908 with an export value of $915 in 1905
and 1906. Cartlege notes that the reports refer to at least three plantations in the Sogeri area and
that implementing of rubber with coffee was practiced. It is also reported that coffee was being
cultivated in Oro Province in the vicinity of Sangara with as much as 73 tons being produced in
1940.

The first plantings on New Guinea side were made by the New Guinea Department of Agriculture
close to Wau in 1928 and 1929. Coffee seed was first introduced into the highlands region by
Lutheran Missionaries in the pre-war years, this seed being taken from planting at the Dregerhafen
and established on their mission station at Asaroka in Eastern Highlands and Ogelbeng in Western
Highlands. It appears certain that coffee was established at Aiyura immediately after the station

INTRODUCTION

‘This report entails activities starting from the preparation works up to the actual declaration
event. The event took place on the 29 of November 2017 at Itokama village. Stakeholder: f y
representatives from NGOs, TV &Print Media, Government and Donor Agencies were flown i) bl { t
on light planes from Port Moresby, some on the actual day while others two or a day earlier. Al

the logistics from Port Moresby to Itokama were arranged by PWM staff while most of ground

logistics were done by the MCF Officer responsible Mr Kingsford Nichoi and the CA Declaration

Committee that was set up purposely to take the lead on all the ground preparation work.

Prominent people and delegates that attended the event include Minister for Environment &
Conservation and Climate Change, Hon John Pundari, Oro Governor, Hon Garry Juffa, Member
for Sohe, Hon Henry Amuri, Deputy Head of Mission Ms Beate Gabrielsen from the Norwegian
Embassy Australia, Delegates from the Rainforest Foundation Norway, and UNDP Country
Director HE Mr Roy Trivedy,

It was a big event for the people of Managalas as the celebration marked $2 years of hard work
and perseverance to have their dream of protecting their land and rainforest from destructive
commercial development come true. The Managalas Plateau is now the second and largest
terrestrial Conservation Area in Papua New Guinea covering $60 000 Ha of forested land,
declared by the Minister for Environment & Conservation and Climate Change on the 29%
November 2017 at 12:51pm at Itokama village.

PURPOSE

This activity is the final step in the process of establishing a conservation area in PNG as per the
Conservation Areas Act 1978. The purpose is to officially declare to the whole country and the
international community that, the Managalas $60 000 Ha of land and forests is now a recognise
Protected Area in Papua New Guinea.

METHODS/PROCEDURES

Seven planes were chartered to airlift invited guests and delegates from Port Moresby and abroad,
as well as food stuff and other goods. The airline companies were, Air Saga, SIL and Air
Catalina/Helifix. The first flight into Itokama was on the 18 November 2017. Promotional
Materials, printed posters, banners, promotional printed shirts and caps and store food for the

Faeplas Cncivatn fova Declaration ~ 29° Uoreaber 2077
 event were airlifted on this charter including two PWM Officers (Patrick Vuet and Cecil Senive),
and PWM Board Member Tom Huasi. The three officers were on the ground in advance to ensure
ground preparations and logistic were going well and to give update on ground situations back to
the team in Port Moresby. The second charter was on the 27° November which airlifted mainly
media personnel’s from EM TV, NBC, FM 100 and Post Courier, accompanied by PWM Program
Manager Rufus Mahuru and PWM Board Member Mr Simon Savaiko. The rest of the delegates
and invited guests flew in on the 20%, Two charters manage to fiy back some guests after the
event while others were flown back to Port Moresby the next day because of bad weather in the
evening. Oro Governor Hon Gary Juffa and Minister for Environment & Conservation and
Climate Change flew in for the declaration event on a Chopper.

Cultural Day

‘The communities from the entire Managalas Plateau gathered at Itokama for the event. Itokama
village took the lead in preparing the venue, cleaning of the airstrip, school ground and oval, built
the stage and prepare accommodations for the people that came in from different parts of the
Managalas plateau and outside guests. A Conservation Area Declaration Committee (CADC) was
set up to oversee and took the lead in organising all ground logistics for the day. On the 28%
November, eve of the declaration Day, a Cultural Day organised by the CADC was held at
Navkonane village. Cultural Dancers from the 11 zones came and perform on this day with
speeches from invited guests Mr Manukayasi, Former PWM Executive Director and one of the
founders of the project, PWM Program Manager and other local leaders.

Prior to the charter trips to the plateau, 14x canvas (large), 2x tuffa toilet pots, assorted nails, and
other materials were sent on SIL plane to Sila airstrip Numba. MCF Conservation Officer
Kingsford Nichoi received them and hired youths to carry them to Itokama, as the road was in a
bad condition. Funds were also sent for airstrip clearance, road and bridge maintenance, and other
activities leading up to the declaration day. MCF staffs were assisting the CADC in the
preparation works toward the cultural day and the declaration day.

Community police officers were engaged to provide security on the day, as important people from
the government and other important people attended the declaration event. A local vehicle was
hired to move food from the zones starting from zone 8 all the way to zone 2 Tahama and shifted
them to Itokama village.

Collection of live animal species was done during the cultural Day show from all the CBOs that
took part in the event. The animals were collected and displayed near the grandstand on the
declaration day.

 RECOMMENDATION

Observation from this event, in future similar events, funds must be controlled by the Officer in
charge at the project site. A committee can be formed to oversee the ground preparations but the
officer in charge must be the chairman or treasurer for the committee. The Officer in charge
knows very well financial situations and will control the use and spending accordingly, thus
minimize expectations.

Managalas Cultural Day Show should be celebrated annually on the 29" November at various
locations on the plateau.

CONCLUSION

Despite hiccups amongst CBOs and the Conservation Area Declaration Committee, the cultural
show and the declaration day went well and ended peacefully. There was no fair representation in
the committee, which cause some arguments and biasness especially on payment of some budgeted
activities. From the beginning of the year until the declaration, there was continuous emphasis for
community contribution toward the day. Some zones like zone + voluntarily contributed some
food and another clan contributed K1, 000.00 to the budget. There were also groups or clans and
individuals that contributed to the event. Cultural singsing groups came from almost all the zones
on the plateau. Minister Hon John Pundari made a commitment of K60, 000.00 for the Managalas
coffee project and capacity building for Managalas Conservation Foundation and the CBOs. The
event was generally a success and ended peacefully.

1. Give a short and to the point description of the project that you are applying for (max
0.5 pages)

A. Proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project
Partners With Melanesians Inc. has been working with the people of the Managalas
Plateau, Ijivitari District, of the Oro Province for over two decades to protect the
360,000 hectares of rainforest, its habitants numbering over 20,000 and its natural
resources. Community mobilization and consensus building formed the cornerstone of
PWM’s mission in strengthening the traditional decision making processes, where the
‘communities voices are collectively echoed as one through the district wide combine
forums. The forums provided the platform to sortout miss-understandings, confusions,
conflicts and differences and to ensure peace, understanding, unity, stability and
cooperation is maintained amongst them as they continue to define their purpose.

‘The idea of protecting the Managalas Plateau was conceived much later, after
‘communities were organized, mobilized and made aware of the importance of several
{important species of flora and fatuna thought to be endemic to the area, one af which is
‘the Queen Alexandria Bird-wing Butterfly.

Additionally, due to the vastness and difficult terrain of the area, the 360,000 hectares of
Jandmass was divided into ten small clusters, made up of several clan groups, known as
 Maltiple yest application form:2018-2022

cultural zones, based on langauge grouping, kinship ane family ties. Originslly, those
clustered groups were convenicatly assembled for the purposes of building consensus
‘among clan groups, however, as it later turned out, these structures made management
of clan lands easily accessible for the participatory land use management planuing in
etermining the various uses of their land, Upon demacating the clan lands, sustainabie
livelihood alternative projects such as honey bee farming, rice cultivation, subsistence
potato ferming, organic coffee farming, amongst others, were encouraged on the
aMloeated plots and proved to be sucessful, eventually providing alternative income for
‘the focal communities.

‘The zones then formed community based-organizations (CBOs) and were formally
registered with te Investment Promotion Authority whose main purpose was to
management affairs of the cultural zones by ralsing income to support clan initiatives,
while sustainably managing the resources in the conservation area in the respective
zones. An umbrella organization, the Managalas Conservation Foundation, previously
called Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) was set-up to coordinate and ensure
efficient performance and management of those CBO, after the arca becomes
nationally declared conservation arca.

On the 8th of November 2012, PWM submitted an application to the Minister for
Environment and Conservation and CEPA for consideration uader the Conservation
‘Areas Act (1978) for processing for the next CA. After waiting for four years for all the
processes, it finally went before the PNG National Execative Council (NEC) in 2026. On
the 15th of December 2016, NEC approved the PWM application by way of NEC
Decision No. 325/2016. The NEC decision will be effected for formality and legal status
through the Nations! Gazettal by the NEC Secretariat and CEPA sfter getting the
insteuments drafted and signed by the Head of State, HE Governor Goneral of PNG.
PWM is now awaiting that process and while waiting for the gazottal, PWM and the
local partners are preparing for the activities after gazettal with the on-site declaration
to be on the Mauagalas pinteau at Kokazns,

For PWM, the clzallenge now is to ensure that the Managalas Conservetion
Foundation’s (MCF) capacity is fully enbanced and MCF made ready to take on the
huge task of managing the 360,000 hectares land, with 11 CBOs and over 20,000 peopte

in PNG’s sccond conservation. Additionally, the task beyong 2018 for PWM is to
consolidate the work with MCF in puttiug in place a Conservation Avea Management
‘Committee to ensure the management and sustainability of the conservation area, and to
come up with a Conservation Area Management Plan and Strategies to guide the
conservation efforts.

PWM will continue to facilitate and link MCF and its CBOs to other partners including
the respective government agencies who aze able to support and ensure sustainable
development options are realised for the focal communities as they continuc to conserve,
‘manage and utilise their natural resources for their livelihood for now and their future
generations.

B. Inaina Wildlife Management Arca Project
It began as an initiative of « visionary Clan Leader in opposing » scam SABL operation
‘or industrial large scale logging in the arca and on their clan land measuring 9,712.20
 Multiple year application form:2018-2022

hectares. The Fagagara clan from Inaina in the Kairuku Hiri District of Central
Province, approached DEC/CEPA and DCD for REDD+ projects and eventually, CEPA
invited PWM to be a partner in 2011 in what was a mere call for support in stopping the
logging operations. After successfully halting the logging operations, the success story
‘was an opportunity for concrete conservation efforts in protecting the area from the
dangers of logging and other industrial developments including Oil Palm. Guided by the
“Flora and Fauna Protection Act’ PWM began the community consultation process,
mobitizing and creating awareness on environment protection and biodiversity
conservation as opposed to industrial, large-scale developments, In exactly five (5) years
of PWM’s involvement, Inaina was declared as a Wildlife Management Area (WMA) on
the 23" March 2017, after having passed all the requirements set by the government's
Conservation Environment Protection Authority (CEPA) in accordance with the ‘Flora
and Fauna Protection Act’,

PWM is now working with the local communities to put in place a WMA Management
Plan and s WMA Management Committee to oversee the management of the WMA,
while at the same time, assisting to set up a focal body to coordinate conservation efforts
and alternative income generation options in the WMA. The capacity of the local focal
body is at this stage is paramount as ongoing plans are in place. Simultaneously, PWM.
is mindful that the WMA status will lapse in 5 years, thas PWM is engaging in dialogue
with CEPA to ensure the WMA or whatever form of conservation status under the New
Protected Area Policy of Government, remains true for the people of Inaina and their
future generations so that PWM’s efforts from 2011 to now is not wasted. In addition,
other clan and nearby communities are expressing interest to extend the WMA
boundaries so they can be Included so this gives the local CBO (Fagagara Development
Foundation Inc.) and PWM to initiate the process with CEPA for these clans and nearby
communities to be included and the current WMA area with their land areas as
extensions to the current WMA boundary and over the next five (5) year, it can be
developed into a bigger conservation area under Protected Area Policy. Itis also in the
plans of PWM that, Inaina WMA with its close proximity to Port Moresby, with pristine
unlogged rainforest and biodiversity with clean fresh water and lots of birdlife, the area
will be converted into » Keotourism hub and Rainforest Education Centre with
conference facilities and other faciities, so that the Centre and Spin-of activities can
financially support the management of the WMA and provide opportunities for local
‘employment and this can further the motivation of the local communities to ensure
protection and conservation of the WMA is maintained.

C. Proposed Mt. Karimui Conservation Aren Project
‘The Propose Mt. Karimut Conservation Area Project was a community initiative,
‘established in 2006 and 2007 with the support from another national NGO called
Conservation Melanesians Inc. (CM), However CM did not continue due to financial
constraints so locals from the area approached PWM with thelr strategic plan and
sought assistance to support the conservation objective. Hence, work in the proposed.
Mt. Karimui Conservation Area Project began with the signing of a tri-partite
memorandum of understanding (MOU) in 2011, between the focal communities, the
local level government, the Simbu Provincia] Government, and Partners With
‘Melanesians Inc,

Ideally located between the borders of Simbu, Eastern Highlands, Southern Highlands,
Gulf, Jiwaka and Western Highlands Provinces, the 160,000 hectares of fertife land is

geographically isolated, yet rich in biodiversity, boasting some exotic species of flora &
fauna,

Amidst the chatienges of a growing population, the locals are determined in addressing
these socia! issues while sustainably managing and utilizing their environment and
natural resources. As the area around them is developing, the need for increased energy
use has compelled the government to explore opportunities in hydropower generation
using the main Waghi river that runs through Tua river, within the conservation ares
‘and passes Karimoi Station on the northern side flowing down to Kikor! through Wabo
‘emptying into the Gulf of Papua, Additionaily, as part of the National Government?s
‘2050 Plans and the Economic Corridor Plans, it is planning to link up Karimuf with
the surrounding provinces through the construction of a national highway to link with
the existing Sir Okuk Highway, and that will expose the conservation azea,

‘Whilst these are unevoidable development plans, PWM and the local communities
through its local Community Based Organization called Karimui Conservation and
Resource Management Programme Inc. (KCRMPD are seriously taking into
contideration these development pians and are considering plans on how to ensure these
developments do not disturb the conservation effort by working closely with the
Government to ensure things are done in the most appropriate and environmentally
friendly manner.

Nevertheless, PWM {s continuing its efforts in ralsing awareness on blodiversity
conservation and cross-cutting issues like population, water and sanitation, gender
‘empowerment etc. while encouraging the consensus building processes in decision
making on the utitization of resources within the conservation area. PWM is also
assisting with building the eapacity of the Karimui Conservation and Resource
Management Programme Inc. (KCRMPM, to enable sound management of the
conservation area, as well as linking the area with exteraal markets especially on
organic coffee and other income generating food crops like peanuts and spices.

2018 and beyond, PWM will be concentrating its conservation efforts in preparing the
area for the conservation area status with the establishment of a conservation area
management plan and committee, and ranger trainings, while at the same time, ensuring
that all externai boundaries are mapped and a rapid biodiversity assessment carried out
to measure against the baseline, with the aim of establishing a research station for
studies on the exotic flora and fauna in the conservation area,

D. Proposed Collinwood Bay Conservation Area Project
Initial community and stakeholder consultation were conducted in 2015, late 2016 and
early 2017 with this coastal and inland community of the Collinwood Bay, Ijivitari
District of the Oro Provinee, with the aim of reviving conservation efforts initially
carried out by a now defunct national NGC conservation organization, Conservation
Melanesia. This community is not new to conservation work. Similar efforts were
carried out over 10 years, however, duc to operational and management challenges
faced by Conservation Melanesia, it affected plans and work programs in CWB,
resulting in the closure of the operations.

Simaltaneously, after 20 plus years of struggling to put an eud to a lengthy court battle
with a logging company, the locals finally won the court case in 2014, ending years of

ci
 ‘Mulple year application form:2018-2022

destructive logging to their forests that also subsequently destroyed the marine life that
supports the coastal communities who are dependent on the marine resources for food
and sustenance.

‘The locals have seen and felt the negative effects of large scale development to their
environment and have opted for conservation and sustainable development options. The
area encompasses a total of 9 customary tribal groups. During the consultation work of
PWM between 2016/2017, the 9 tribes of CWB saw the need and importance of giving
recognition and uphold the status of women in CWB as equal and ereated the Women’s
platform for engagement as the 10" tribe and for the voice of all women. There are 326
clans, and 25 hamlets that spreads over 560,000+ hectares of delta plains, lowland and
mid-montane rainforest and savannah grassland and is geographically challenging in
terms of reaching out to all these communities. Additionally, the entire CWB traditional
and customary practices have no particular definition for gender equality in that women
are not part of any decision making process and are often not considered as important.
While the chief is the ultimate head of the clan and he has the final say, but is done in
consultation and through consensus. The definition of consensus in CWB is absolute;
there is no consensus if one person, one clan or one tribe is mot in agreement to
decision. A number of dialects are spoken throughout the area while English Is
‘commonly spoken and understood amongst the 20,500+ population. Like all other rural
isolated communities in PNG, the Collinwood Bay area receives very little government
services which are limited to basis health and education while they depend heavily on
their environment for food, water, building materials and other environmental goods
and services.

PWM is now gearing up on creating awareness on issues that are affecting the
exvironmeat like climate change and its impact on water and food security. Whilst this
will be an on-going program, PWM will be liaising with the local communities in
identifying 1 focal community based organization to coordinate work ou the ground,
through which a memorandum of understanding will be established in defining a clear
working relationship and partnership between all important stakeholders including the
{ocal communities and thelr community based organization, the local level government
‘and the provincial government, in identifying ways to assist the communities in
‘conserving their environment while managing and utilizing their forest and marine
resources for their livelihoods. This arrangement will ensure all key stakeholders will be
‘meaningfully engaged in ensuring critical enablers like effective leadership and good
governance, environmental legislations and policies, performance and accountability etc.
are in place for achfeving successful conservation outcomes and sustainable livelihoods.

Introduction:

Tne symbolism of their welcome at the gate the splitting of plant was a sign of
harvesting a new garden. In all of Managalas plateau when people are harvesting new
garden this is a sign of showing families and relatives that the garden is now harvested
Therefore it has a very significant symbol shown from the beginning of the retreat as the
community welcomed us by splitting ef plant and second sign was the Bird Wing butter
fly breaking out of the piper during the retreat

The work that we have been doing in the plateau is very significant and simple
illustration of the above stories a reminding us of moving to another level in the work tht
we do for our people in the plateau. A new birth and a new beginning out from the pain
and suffering that we have been going through in the last thirty years. So that boils
down to honesty and total commitment from all levels of leaders in this MCF unique
ministry that we are all called to serve.

The real actions of what we say and write must always been seen in the real
implementation of the work in the community. Transparency in our performance will
bring better transformation in the community where we serve as model for others to
learn.

 Acknowledgement: On behalf of the PWM Board of management | thank the
Managalas Conservation Foundation Director Damien Ase and the MCF staff for the
invitation for Tom Huasi and | (Simon Savaiko) to attend the retreat and the MCF Board
meeting at Dogarol site in Afore, Oro Province on the 28" June ~ 1% July 2019. The
amazing clan group from Dogarol site who played very unique role to host the retreat at
their new site away from Afore main LLG station.

| also thank the clan groups from Dogarol site who offered everything possible for the
four days retreat and to make sure everyone who are there enjoyed their time. That was
an exciting site where we experienced a real model for all the work we have been
fighting for many years in the Managalas plateau. Our going there was just only
beginning of all the many good things that we are going to do in the plateau. The big
lesson is to start with what we have in the plateau to show others what we have | the
plateau. | also want to thank all CBO’s who walked many hours by foot to get there for
this retreat. | believe their walking and time together was great beneficial because they
were able to put together new ideas to move MCF forward with their ideas in the
plateau.

And not forgetting to thank Tom Huasi PWM Board member who was able to come with
me to the retreat and was there for the whole week with the staff and the Board
members. His visit was an expression of his faith and love for the work in the
Managalas plateau. He was a motivator and good encourager to many of the old time
friends who journeyed the work in the plateau together early 1990s

Day one:

On Thursday morning Tom Huasi and Damien Ase, Obert and | (Simon Savaiko)
checked in 5am and travelled to Popondetta on the early morning flight. The MCF
Chairman Mr. Malcus kajia and the driver plus Ezekiel Garui met us at Girua airport
and drove us to town. After banking and shopping we than left met again at the MCF

Office.

 Then we left the town around 5.30pm and travelled the high way to Afore. Damien and |
travelled on MCF vehicle while Obert and Ezekiei travelled on hired vehicle and arrived
Afore at 11.30 pm. dropped off cargo and drove to the camp site at Dogarol at 12.30
midnight. We arrived very late so the clan group in Dogarol lake site did not welcome us
and we all went into our rooms and slept until next morning,

Day Two

clan group performed a traditional weicome by singing composed songs and jad us te
the meeting house. The hosting clan weicomed us into the building at Dogaroi site
where we conducted the retreat for four days.

The official opening began with welcome by the hosting clan leader Jarod and followed
by MCF Chairman Malcus kajia and the Director of MCF Mr. Damien Aseari. Then |

snippet: Enumeration of trees and other vegetation at the Guguavo Ridge in the Owen Stanley Range of Papua New Guinea. Kasbeth Evei Postgraduate Centre, University of Papua New Guinea P O Box 320 Uni PO, N.C.D Introduction This survey was basically done to establish the abundance and species diversity of tre
text:
Enumeration of trees and other vegetation at the Guguavo Ridge in the
Owen Stanley Range of Papua New Guinea.

Kasbeth Evei

Postgraduate Centre, University of Papua New Guinea P O Box 320 Uni PO, N.C.D

Introduction
This survey was basically done to establish the abundance and species diversity of trees
and other plants that occur in the primary forests of Tetebedi area. In Papua New Guinea
(PNG), Montane primary forests are home to many endemic plants and animals.
Likewise, the primary forests at Guguavo ridge is no exception since it contain some of
PNG’s endemic plants and animals.

The Guguavo Ridge upper montane primary rainforest has a sparse distribution of
trees and other forest fiour planis with a 20m visibility. The forest is made up of 80
species of trees ranging ftom 2m to more than 30m, several species of herbs and vines
(lianas), ferns, gingers, orchids, pandans, palms and bamboos which total up to more thar
130 species of plants.

‘This study enabied us to establish tree density (per m2) and species distribution in
the survey area.

Methods

The survey plot is located on Guguavo Ridge some 100km East of Port Moresby and
situated at 1600m above sea level in the Cwen Stanley Range. It is a three hours walk
away from the nearest airstrip of Tetebedi village in Oro province.

A 20m X 200m (0.4 ha) sample plot was randomly selected along the ridge. We
marked trees and saplings with the DBH (Diameter at Breast height) of 7em and above.
We collected leaf voucher specimens for further identification. Cther forest flour plants
were noted as inhabitanis of the forest area.

Tree height data analysis
Height of trees were categorized into six height classes; Om-4m =I, Sm-9m =2, 10m-14m
= 3, 15m-19m = 4, 20m-24m =5, 25m or more = 6.

Results
540 trees were sampled within the 0.4 ha plot. Just over half the trees were between 1m
anid Sra, while nearly 40% were between 10m to 19: andi0% were above 20m. The
highest DBH of the trees was 150cm and the highest tree height was 32m (see
appendix). There are more than 80 species of trees and another 70 to 80 other plant
species that make up the whole of Guguavo Ridge Rainforest area (see appendix 2).
There were about 2 trees/m2. Altogether, there were more than 130 species of plants that
were observed. The dominant species of trees include, Cryptocarya, Litsea, Pouteria,
Evodia and Castenopsis.

Discussions

Tropical rainforests make up 7% of the world’s surface area (Swaine, 1965) and contain
more than half of the known terrestrial organisms but yet, the least understood of all the
major vegetation types (Collinson, 1975). Every effort must be made to protect all
sections of the tropical rainforests of the world, including Papua New Guinea.

‘As such, the Guguavo Ridge montane rainforest is home to some of the Papua
‘New Guineas mest endangered and endemic species of plants (Trees and orchids} as well
as anime!s and fungi. Since occurs at the top of the mountains, it is vulnerable to
tandslides, soil erosion and species loss should there be a slight disturbance in the forest
structure. This would then affect the distribution and dispersion strategies of several tree
species since not al! species of trees have the same dispersal mechanism. For example, in
this survey, the Evodia is randomly dispersed while Pouteria and Castenopsis are
dispersed regularly and the Cryptoceryas and Litseas have e clumped dispersion in the
plot.

‘A good number of timber and non-timber forest products occur within the area
which means that a sustainable forest use practice be encouraged for the region. The
Forest in the long run, will act as a seed bank, sustain all life, retain and recycle nutrients
rapidly and will continue to so for thousands of years (Walter, 1985). Other benefits from
the forests includes poliution indications (esp. SO2) and standing forest biomass will act
as Carbon sinks (absorb carbon dioxide).

Recommendations
‘The people, especially the older men and woman of the Tetebedi area have an invaluable
ethno biological and natural history knowledge of all the natural resources that surrounds
them. it wili be a bonus should there be some sort of documentation of these knowledge

in the future encounters.

i would push for a Wildlife Management Area to be established as soon as possible so as
to instill the concept of “public natural resource ownership” for sustainable resource use.
To continue io show up physically every now and then to oversee how things are being
conducted with the people, by the people with a litile bit of outside intervention will be
rewarding for all stakeholders.
 References
Collinson, A.S. (1977). Introduction to World Vegetation, Lavenham press Ltd, Suffolk,
England.

Piskaut, P. (2005). Vegetation and Plant Survey of the proposed Managalas Plateau
Conservation Area: Phase 2 Report, Submitted to Partners with Melanesia, Port Moresby
PNG.

France.

Van Royen, P. (1963). The Vegetation of the island of New Guinea, Department of
Forests, Lae, PNG.

 L Introduction,

Two facilitators (John Ericho, Abane Haefa) were contracted to carry out the week long
meeting/workshop at Serefuna in the Managalas Plateau from the 19" — 25% December 2006. At the pre-
meetings with the Partners with Melanesians (PwM) the terms of reference was issued and a briefing was
given and questions were raised to ensure everyone was on the same wavelength. The two faciltators
met and presented a tentative outline of the programs to PwM staff to comment and improved the
program outine. The team was transported by hire transport to the ltokama over the Owen Stanley
Range. After about an hour and half walk the team arrived at our destination.

In this report a brief background is presented, followed by a brief description of TOR, a list of the team
members, a brief descriotion of methods used, and the issues to be addressed. Then discussion points
are captured and presented followed by next steps and a summary at the end.

Il, Background.

Partners with Melanesians (PwM) are a national NGO established about 20 years to work closely with the
people of the Managalas Plateau. The Managalas Plateau is described below in the Terms of Reference
background information as follows.

Managales Plateau is a raised valley lying between 600 to 1000 meters of altitude above the coastal
plain of Oro Province and is situated south of Popondetta and North of Port Moresby. It stretches
between the Owen Stanley Ranges to the south and west, the Sibium Ranges and Mt. Lamingion and
the Hydrogrphers fo the north ands east. t encompasses 380 000 ha, comprising areas of alpine heights
of 3 800 meters, montane and hill forest, savanna, anthropogenic grassland and gardens. The
countryside is very mountainous and ridges, rivers, and waterfalls make up the scenery. About 1215000
people of approximately 150 clan groups are living in 40 village communities. Clusters of sub-clan
‘groups, around which most social and economical activity is organized today, effectively fall into ten
cultural zones.

People in Managalas are subsistence farmers and grow their own food of yam, taro, Kaukau and other
garden produce. The Plateau also boasts cash crops which includes; coffee, vanilla and peanuts and
‘kari nut. Most of these have not been sold out due to lack of proper roads and air transport costs being
too high. While the opportunity exist to develop economically. Logging and oil palm development lurks
precariously in the background threatening menacingly to overtake the Plateau in the guise of economic
development. Thus the beginning and inception of the Managalas Program by PwM is to arrest that
threat. The Managalas Program includes three main programs. These include: the Consensus building,
the Capacity Building and the Conservation Program. The Consensus building program embarked on
mobilizing and organizing the Managalas communities into 10 cultural zones each zone incorporating a
‘community based organization (CBO). It was envisaged that the MDF will develop into a well trained and
‘organized organization to work with each of the CBOs to help realize the vision of developing, “A
peaceful and self reliant communal society living in harmony with nature”. This was the Exit Strategy
envisaged years ago. The Consensus building program has nearly completed this task. The Capacity
building project also worked hard to develop the capacity of the MDF and CBO Board and Management.
‘These two projects are ongoing and are nearing the completion stages. The Conservation project is
continuing with mapping and inventory work and this needs more emphasis and focus as it has the
possibilty of being derailed by socioeconomic development requirements.
 ‘A project of this size and magnetite is compiex and dificult to accomplish ia the short term in al its
entirety but a tremendous amount of work, ame and resources have been commited to this aroject over
the last twenty years. Such projects have potential 0; so many provlems of both social. ecenonic,
cultural ssues to develop naturally as a factor of change. Such issues could undo the whole program at
its seams thus the TOR called for the identification of such issues with a view to addressing them, The
leaders of the CBOs andi MDF to come together to identify and resolve any outstanding issues for unity of
purpose and vision can be strengthened fer work to continue to progress and evolve into the future,

Ill The Terms of Reference (TOR).

The TOR specifcaly calls for the deve'opment of an agenda for the leaders Summit by discussing with
various stakeholders and in particular with the Managalas Develooment Foundation(MOF) an Umbrella
NGO estabished by PwM to organize the CBOs taking over from Pw’. Once the agenda is established
major issues could be dentiied. These issues could then be discussed and debated in a workshop
structure and collectively find common grounds and resolutions te be impiemented by all. This report
Contains the outcomes of this process.

V. The Daily Program and Methods

The first day the facilitators spend the evening discussing with MDF staff and other leaders who were
present in coming up with the agenda which is isted below under issues. From these agendas a list of
core issues was identified and a program outine was developed. The following major groups were
‘dented and used throughout tne meeting as discussion groups. these included: ine community
leaders. the CBO leaders, the MDF leaders and staff, and the PwM staff and Board rep. In the main

 these groups were maintained throughout the whole week as the issues raised required the respective
views to be expressed so as too gamer all perspectives from each level. Each moming one issue is raise
and each group is asked to debate it and come up with ideas or recommendations. These are presented
and a combined perspective is gathered. These are summarized pictorially or in bullet points. The above
process is repeated in the aftemoon. The next morning the summary points are presented and time
allowed for discussion, clarification, additions. Then a separate issue is raised and the whole process is
repeated. A general combine discussion attempt nearly proved disastrous so that method was not used
at all drawing remarks that a board meeting type of arrangement has been changed to workshop style
meetings.

ORIGINS OF THEATRE

Theatre existed in the Civilization of the Western world for the last 3000 years.
Little information about the Origin of Theatre has survived. The information we do
have comes from wall paintings, decorations, artifacts, and picture writing system
that show the importance of successful hunts, seasonal changes, life cycles, and
stories of the gods, From these people have seen the necessity of passing along the
experience of the old to the young through art, storytelling and dramatising events.
Even today cultures that do not have written languages have developed some form of
drama to dramatise imagination and the spirituality of people.

Drama is part of most diverse societies’ cultural heritage and it mirrors daily
livelihoods. That is mainly because of its relationship to festivals and religious
practices. In most cultures, communities identify themselves in drama as
dramatization of specific issues reflect the cultures. Drama reflects reality and needs
an interpretation of it to which it has an effect on individuals. Drama provokes
reflection and in a way stimulates the analytic potential of individuals. And it creates
a mirror effect to which individuals look at themselves at a different perspective.

People are bom with body languages which are the early steps of mankind, and
drama was very likely spontaneously embedded in those early steps. Theatre

emerged from myth, ritual, and ceremony. Early societies see connections between
14 ‘Community Theatre Facinator’s Guide 2008
 certain actions performed by the group or the leaders in the group and the desired
results of the society. These actions moved from habit, to wadition, and then to
ceremony and ritual. Rituals have always being a way to communicate with gods and
spirits and are repeated every year, or every season, and relate very much to the
agricultural cycle.

Rituals evolve along two main avenues. Rituals are accompanied by myths and the
myths enter the story telling tradition, gaining a life beyond original rites. This new
life allows the myths to move towards entertainment and admirable and pleasant
appearance. The two main avenues which rituals evolve along include;
© rituals, where myths are central, evolve into full blown religious worship, and
+ Rituals were performance was central, becomes artistic expressions such as
dance and theatre.
Although boundary between these trends sometimes seems narrow, the distinction is
valid for every culture, since the evolution has been similar.

Through these rituals, leaders, or actors of sorts, emerged. These acting or leadership
roles were ofien filled by elders and priests. Jn addition, the beginning of acting
spaces or auditoriums developed as a result of more elaborate rituals. The earliest
example of ceremony and ritual evolving towards theatre come’ from ancient Egypt.
“Pyramid texts" dating from 2800 to 2460 B.C., contain dramas sending the dead
pharaoh off to the underworld. These drames also the continuity of fife and the
pharaoh’s power. There is also the Memphite Drama, recounting the story of the
death and resurrection of the god Osiris, and the coronation of his son Horas. The
most important Egyptian drama, though, was the Abydos passion play. Like the
Memphite drama, the Abydos passion play concerns the story of Ositis. The
paramount Egyptian myth, this drama was enacted at the most sacred place in Egypt,
Abydos the burial site of Osiris. Performed anawally Som 2560 to 550 B.C. and
full of spectacle, t i s the first of its kind ever recorded and is the first
exampic of theatre.

fi is from these jnitial forms of representation that drama became a form of

enable us ic understand what took place among our primitive ancestors. The sense of

In the Developing countries there are two types of Theatre: One is the Theatre which
takes place in a formal context which is very much more European and is aimed at
smal} cultural elite in urban areas, and the other takes place in the open as an
instrument to communicate important messages for the community. There ate many
‘encouraging experiences of popular theatre in some developing countries.

“Popular theatre is gaining increasing attention in the Third World as a tool for popular
education and community organizing. It finds expression in a number of forms including

building confidence and solidarity, stimulating discussion, exploring alternative options for
action, and building a collective commitment to change: starting with people's urgent

text:
Status Report (Desktop Study) on Queen Alexander Bird-wing
Butterfly (QABB) Survival In Response to Natural and Man-made
Threats to Habitat in Managalas Plateau, Popondetta, Papua New
Guinea.

T. MAiA

CURATOR
ENTOMOLOGY
BIOLOGY DEPARTMENT,
UNIVERSITY OF PAPUA NEW GUINEA

For
Partners With Melanesia
25TH - 30TH MAY 2008

 Status Report (Desktop Study) on Queen Alexander Bird-wing Buiterfly (QABB)
Survival In Response to Natural and Man-made Threats to Habitat in Managalas
Plateau, Popondetta, Papua New Guinea Undertaken from 25" - 30th May 2008.

INTRODUCTION

The Queen Alexandra's Birdwing Butterfly (@ABB) (Omithoptera alexandrae) is
the world's largest butterfly with female wingspans up to and over 250 mm
(Parsons 1999). QABB are confined to primary and advanced secondary
rainforest from sea level up to 800 m in the Popondetta Plain, Cape Hunt Ward,
and Afore regions of the Oro Province of Papua New Guinea (PNG} (Fig.1)
(Parsons 1999, Mercer 1999). QABB is monophagous on Pararistolochia dielsiana
in the Aristolochiacea family, a plant family famous for it’s potent toxic
compound aristolochic acid (Mercer 1999, Mebs and Schneider 2002, Jicki
2002). However, several forms or types of P. dielsiana are known to occur with
the range of QABB. These types are largely distinguished by their flower shape
and color (Fig.2). Local conservation biologists have noticed a disparate usage
of these P. dielsiana types by QABB but to date no studies have addressed why
and reportedly one vine form is thought to be harmful to the larvae (pers.
comm. E. Malaisia)..

The tremendous size of QABB, its natural scarcity, and limited range of the
species has made it a species of concem for conservation biologist (Parsons
1984, Gimenze 1996). !n addition, in the 40 years increases in the oil palm and
timber industries in the Popondetta region have fragmented and destroyed
large tracts of suitable habitat for the QABB (Parson 1984, 1990). QABB is
currently protected by domestic, the Fauna and Flora Act, and international
law, the Conservation on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES). At
present it is listed as a CITES | species (highly endangered) and import/export
and collection is prohibited.

A number of research projects on the QABB have been carried out over the
past 40 years. The first was a study by Ray Staatman that helped to illuminate
the life cycle of the QABB and some of its basic habitat needs (Staatman 1971).
Throughout the 1980's and early 1990's a number of surveys and studies of QABB
and its host plant were completed by Michael Parsons (Parsons 1984, 1990,
1991). These surveys helped defined the present range of the QA8B on the
Popondetta Plain and verified the importance of the Managalas Plateau
population in the Afore area (Parsons 1991). However, Parsons work on the Aw
vine led to erroneous classification of host vines by splitting P. dielsiana into

species P. meridonaliana and P. alexandrae (Parsons 1996, Jebb 1993).

1
 However, legitimate recognition of Parson's new Pararistolochia species by the
scientific community has been lacking (Mercer 1999). Until further research
reveals otherwise P. dielsiana is considered by the most as the legitimate host
plont of QABB. In 1992, Larry Orsack carried out surveys on the Popondetta Plain
and with a collaborative group of international and local researchers,
politicians, and wildlife biologists produced a five-year management action
plan (Orsack 1992}. The plan provided an action in order to preserve the
species.

Later extensive surveys and monitoring efforts took place as part of Oro
Conservation Project, largely funded by AusAID, in the Afore region (Mercer
1999). However, surveys were completed in outlying regions to determine the
final extent of the QABB populations, one in the Cape Ward Hunt region and
another in the Musa River region (Mercer 1999). However, the Muse River
population was later extirpated due to devastating drought fuelled fires in the
region in 1997 (Mercer 1999). The Oro Conservation Project was. finally
terminated in 1997. However, low level monitoring continued to take place in
the Afore region and Popondetta Plain region through the 21:' century overseen
by a number of government agencies and NGOs. Recently, a small two-week
study on the host vine and the QABB by a University of Papua New Guinea
honour's student in the Popondetta Plain and Afore regions (Jicki 2007).

In November 2007 Cyclone Guba struck the Oro Province dumping more than
72.cm of rain in less than 24 hours in some regions. The disaster greatly disrupted
the subsistence gardens of the local people and destroyed much of the
infrastructure in the region. Monitoring of QABB largely ceased and has only just
begun again in June/July of 2008.

While a number of research projects on the QABB have taken place they have
not fulfilled the informational needs of local conservation agencies. Furthermore
the scientific rigor with which these studies were carried out is questionable and
what is currently known about QABB seems largely to be based on anecdotal
encounters and casual observation.

Evaluate Conservation and Survival Status of QABB.

Past efforts to conserve QABB have been hampered by a lack of understanding
of the fundamental life history traits of the butterfly and its host plant (Orsack
1992, Mercer 1999). In addition, incentives for landowners to maintain intact
forest are deficient. Proposed solutions to the dilemma have included eco-
tourism and butterfly ranging (Orsack 1992). The ability of PNG, Oro Province
and the butterfly to attract sufficient numbers of tourists to profitably sustain the
tourism industry is unlikely.
 Butterfly ranging is an attractive altemative and many within PNG have
experience in the insect trade. Indeed PNG is the only country in the world with
@ government branch dedicated solely to trade and export of insects, the
Insect Farm and Trade Agency (IFTA) (Mercer and Clark 1989). However, there
are two hurdles that must be overcome for butterfly ranching of QABB to be
successful. First, the status of IFTA as a reliably operating agency must be
ascertained, as recently published literature suggests a breakdown of
functionality within IFTA (Small 2007). Second, the species must be down listing to
occur a formal recommendation must be made after or within the publication
of conservation management plan for the species. Due to the existence of a
number of data gaps the publication of a management plan at this point would
be irresponsible.

The objectives of this study is to fulfill these data gaps and provide those
involved in the conservation of QABB with quality information on the population
structure and life history of the QABB and its host plant, P. dielsiana. In order to
achieve this, the following specific priorities were observed:

Evaluation of Conservation & Survival Status of QABB
Identification of threats of QABB
Appraisal of Economical value of QABB, other bird-wing butterflies
and insects

* Provision of Appropriate Recommendations on QABB Habitat
Rehabilitation
 METHODOLOGY
Study Site:

There are essentially 3 WMAs around Popondetta town and within the study
area that support the QABB and other birdwing species. Numerous patches of
cil palm plots are interspersed between the WMAS, in addition to areas of high
human activity.

Sites visited in the target included Afore government station (S 09° 08.356’ and E
148° 23.369"), Kawowoki (S 09° 06.281’ and £ 148° 23.333), and Vanua (S 09°
08.215’ and E 148° 23.783"). These areas are located at elevations of 751, 756
and 735 meters above sea level, respectively.

Figure 1. Map of Study site (Managalas Wildlife Management Area)

Data collection:

Data was collected using a number of approaches including; site-seeing
observations, insect netting trials for demonstrations on life-stage taxonomic
identification of QABB and other butterfly species, interviews with locals, and the
use of interactive pictorial conservations to draw information on the correct
identification of species of the birdwings buiterflies from QABB.

Pictorial tips of the methods applied in this study to aid in the observations
follows.

from recent flood disaster.

Visits were made to Kowoki and Vanua areas. Sightings and collections of
specimen were done together with surveillance for QABB and other birdwing
species in their different life-stages was cared out by foot patrolling between
the three areas.

Insect Netting & Demonstrations

Figure 4 & 5. Insect netting demonstrations to Kawowoki. Vanua forest
demonstration

These demonstrations were performed to mainly collect delicately species for
corect species identifications of QABB from other birdwing butterflies.
Illustrations were briefly given for the correct identification of adult male and

5
 female QABB and their juvenile stages, making comparisons with those of other
birdwing butterflies.

Interview & Meetings

Figure 6. Afore guest house. Figure 7. Kawoki guest house. Demonstrating the
differences in species of life-stages. Gauging views during a meeting with locals.

Interactive approach was considered here to obtain technical information and
in return providing appropriate technical advice and solution to queries brought
forward.

Observation

Information collection during interviews and meeiings were uiilized io make
direct observation of presence or absence of QABB and other species. A useful
marker for the study to determine presence and survival of QABB was the
availability, abundance and the distribution of host plant species in the study
area. Local information was helpful for independent but often referenced
observations. Although local knowledge can be worth noting, often the lack of
reliability in quantitative precision has always existed.
 RESULTS

Survival Status of QABB

Monitoring activities in the area were up to 1997 by the Oro Conservation
Project under funding from AusAID in the Afore region (Mercer 1999). These
surveys were however completed in the outlying regions to determine the final
‘extent of the QABB populations, one in the Cape Ward Hunt region and another
in the Musa River region. Mercer 1999, reports that the Muse River population
was later extirpated due to devastating drought fuelled fires in the region in
1997, where this project was put to rest in that same year. Monitoring at very
small scale continued to take place in the Afore region and Popondetta Plain
region by a number of government agencies and NGOs. Only recently, a two-
week study on the host vine and the QABB relationship was caried out by a
University of Papua New Guinea honour's student under my supervision, in the
Popondetta Plain and Afore regions (Jicki 2007), looking especially at presence
of food vines (A. fagala, A. dielsiana and A. momandul) and feeding
preferences.

The assessment of current survival status of @ABB cannot quite clearly be stated
due largely fo the limited timing of this study. Ample time is therefore required to
quantify the dynamics of their survival. Ongoing monitoring activities of the
QABB were disrupted by the disaster (Cyclone Guba) of November 2007, which
destroyed greatly much of the infrastructure and food gardens of the local
people.

There were a good number of sightings of GABB adults in the foot pairois iaken.
However, comparably speaking, the frequency of these sightings was quite
lower than observations | made during my many years outings into the study
area (e.g. Parson 1991, Survey carried out for Conservation Intemational) for
such and other entomological trips to Collinwood Bay, where O.meridionalis was
first ever found and collected by me. Locals interviewed and asked for sightings,
however indicated that the QABB population is sustaining but highlighted the
eminent threats from logging and human activities.

Threats (Natural & Man-made):

Obvious eminent threats were noted to exist that might have already affected
the QABB population. These among a host of other faciors included human
activities such as extension of oil palm fields, logging activities, and other
intensified human activities in response to population growth, and natural
disasters, all have a potential of destroying the QABB habitat.
 Extension of Oil Paim Fields

The recent extensions of oil palm field, both of private block-holder plots and the
Higaturu Oil palm have involved clearing of forest areas. A similar study such as
this was carried out in 1991 where | was part of, where we interviewed several
villagers from villages that are now gone. | have noticed that the expansions
have displaced several villages that were there in 1991. Such displacement
obviously increases social pressure to scavenge the surrounding forests thereby
increasing pressure on the forests habitat and QABB survival.

Population Growth

Pressure exerted on the local natural environment as a result of population
increase was apparent and observable and is deemed to be another important
factor that will influence the successful QABB population. Within the WMAs and
the study sites, increased human activities were noted that include extensive
subsistence gardening, regular combing of the woodlands for firewood, and the
general use of the forest products.

Logging

Logging activities are very common in the nearby regions of WMAs and has a
potential of expanding into the area. From the discussions and meetings held
with the locals, this was one other major potential QABB survival threats.

Reforestation

There are no plans curently in place to undertake rehabilitation of the
destroyed part of the habitat by reforestation. If this trend continues without
forward planning to reclaim wasted forest areas, then the ability to maintain
QABB population and other important species in the area over the next few
decades is dubious.

Natural Disaster/Floods

Disasters such as those of 1997 drought fuelled fires in parts of the area
especially Musa river (Mercer, 1999) that was affected, could occur at sites
where savannah or manmade grassland patches adjoin forest vegetation with
important food host species. Irresponsible clearing of forests (that is occurring)
and promotion of grassy and herbaceous vegetation will certainly encourage
bushfires in times of drought and dry season.

Experiences also from the 2007 Cyclone Guba disaster that devastated many
local communities in terms of infrastructure and food gardens can be seen as a

8
 potential risk for the survival of QABB. This can come about when feeding and
host plan species in the local area becomes destroyed by the disaster.

Butterflies & their host plants:
The essential component of the critical survival of QABB and other birdwing
species is and feeding ecology associated with their life-cycle, which include
how each individual species interact with host plant species at particularly
caterpillar and adult stages. This bulk of information is very important for the
local people, as they are the direct custodians and caretakers of the butterflies.
In order to ensure a sustained monitoring of the survival of the @ABB population
in the WMA, locals need to correctly identify QABB at each life-stage and
equally identify the corresponding life-stage, from other birdwing butterflies.

This sort of information and the practical field training works may be required to
impart this very important piece of information. This is important because
interviews and communication with locals regarding taxonomical identifications,
often did misidentify, which indicated a need for practical training and
awareness in future.

Economical Value of QABB:

QABB is a protected species and cannot be harvested for any commercial
exploitation, whilst the other birdwing butterflies can be farmed, harvested and
sold commercially. Although QABB is not exploitable, the non-market value for a
pair (male and female) is at $US 10, 000 approxmately and is listed as a CITES 1
species.

Other birdwings butterfly species are on CITES 2 which can be harvested for
export at market-value. It is noteworthy that direct harvesting from the wild is not
allowed and is not encouraged. It however can be farmed in order to maintain
a sustainable supply population from which harvesting can be made. The price
list of birdwing butterfly species is appended as Economical Group of Insect —
Lepidoptera (Butterflies & Moths) & Coleoptera (Beetles & Weevils) Please ref. to
Attached lists.

Outcomes of Meetings:

Meetings were held at different sites with locals in a bid to obtain information
related to the objectives of this study. Information related to the importance of
species to plant host relationships of @ABB and other birdwing butterflies was
imparied as the need for it was apparent since the locals are the rightful
custodians of this rare creatures and their survival is in many ways connected to
their livelihood.
 During these meetings general impression was made by the locals for the need
to foster the concept of conservation from a rejuvenated paradigm. In this case
conservation which transpired mutual benefits was largely expressed. One
‘apparent examples of such mutuality in benefits was the need to venture into a
tangible insect farming project. It was also expressed that for over 20 years of
involvement with the Wild Life Management Area (WLMA), there was a general
lack of tangible benefits. Venturing into Insect Farming would bring sustainable
monetary benefits to the locals, at the same time the maintaining of QABB and
other species diversity within the area.

An Insect Ranch and a guest house in the area have been constructed at their
own initiative. The establishment now requires Department of Environment &
Conservation (DEC) to give approval and also grant export license for their
insect specimens to be exporied to overseas markets. This group of people from
what is known as DataCol WMA would like the establishment fo serve equally as
WEI and IFTA. The reason being that, harvested and fixed marketable insect and
butterfly specimen often lose market value due to damages sustained while
transported to Wau for inspection. They also suggested that DEC would approve
of this proposal to help aspiring insect farmers in Oro and the Southern region as
awhole.

Figure 8 & 9. Ranch establishment and Guesthouse

10
 Figure 10. Greenhouse nursery for host plant species

DISCUSSION

Potential threats to the survival of QABB and related species were identified and
highlighted providing specific details. Among these factors of influence
presented, logging activity in the area and oil palm has been seen as potential
isk factors. The monetary benefits associated with logging and oil palm were
seen to be more attractive to the local people who are the custodians of the
WMaAs who claim previously have not had adequately and tangibly benefited
since the establishment of the conservation areas. Influence of logging activities
and also the lucrative oil palm industry can however be suppressed by
encouraging incentive-based conservation practice in these areas.

Whilst observations made during this rather short visit has provided some basic
insights into the questions posed an extended time period in future can allow for
a fulkscale species inventory. Anecdotal entry of such data is misleading
especially when information is required for management purposes.

Due to the general inadequacies in the monitoring and QABB management
skills of the local people, further workshops and practical field demonstrations
are encouraged. This is a way forward for responsible management of QABB
and other species by locals. This brings us to the idea brought forward by the
locals for an incentive-based conservation as has previously being discussed
extensively by Orsak (1999). This in fact is ‘gap’ identified. DECs approval for
Insect Ranching and issuance of a license would be a step in the right direction

 Background

Environment and Conservation is a huge problem faced by our
community throughout the country in the global changes rapidly
happening; PWM is taking the lead in addressing the Conservation and
Land Use issues in the project site Managalas in the Afore District, with its
different partners. Each year, new concepts and strategies are spent on
community and institutional project to help people to understand the
basic function, roles and responsibilities of conservation and Land Use, to,
MAKE OUR ENVIRONMENT JUST, SAFE AND SECURE PLACE TO LIVE FOR
NOW AND FUTURE GENERATION.

There are several ways to devise different activities that could enhance
and create conservation issues to be easily understood by the community
members, by using Melanesian Institute of Arts & Communication (
Theatre Arts Section). The most obvious one was in the area of Creative
Arts; however, to achieve solid results the workshop was conducted in
Poponedtta Town, Anglicare Training centre.

This workshop recognizes that one of the strategic way to create
awareness in the conservation Land Use issues is to involve the
community, particularly the youths and the senior members of the
community and expose their skills and abilities in different dimensions of
Art of Drama. This workshop illustrated the medium drama, exposed the
inner feeling of a person how they perceive Conservation and Land Use
issues in their community as evident in their drama session , the other
aspects of the arts will be addressed in due course time if similar
opportunity is given and please see the interview by the participants
after the closing ceremony DVD attached.

When we know why our community is not conserving and proper planning
for the usage of the land, then we can mitigate or hopefully stop
completely or strategize for a better community. The solution lies within
the community, the participants told us how they want to solve their own
problems by using the medium of Drama to create constructive and
creative environment for community discussion.

Artistic Product

The primary target for Melanesian Institute of Arts & Communication
through the application of Community Sustainable Arts Education, in
using Drama helped different members of the communities in the target
locations within Managalas Development Foundation broaden the scope of
understanding. Towards the end of the workshop we achieved the
following results,

1, Basic Drama Skills
2. Different Techniques of Drama
 Written three scripts related to conservation and Land Use and
finally performed for public at the Anglicare Training Centre

3. Produce the Photographs of the workshop from Day 1- day 5

4. Video shoots of the workshop end its various sessions and
activities

5. Finally, the participants admitted that they are now very confident
to conduct awareness by using Drama

This project was coordinated and executed by the MIAC in partnership
with PWM under artistic coordination and direction of Mr. Motsy David,
Theater Arts Staff at the University of PNG as part of PWM Effective
Communication and Awareness Training. The Community Sustainable
Arts Education Strategy acted as the mirror of the society, because it is
one of the most effective medium of communication and also empowering
the Members of the Managalas Development Foundation. The project
certainly make aware the peopie in the project area and other target
areas the consequences tc realize their abilities and creative skills so they
can meaningfully contribute to their own community and the country. The
Conservation and Land Use issues are of great concern for everyone,
drastic effects it has on our country both economically and sociatiy. The
Melanesian Institute of Arts & Communication through the workshop
contributed artistically to minimize the environmental calamities and most
importantly through thi g we will change the attitudes and the
behaviors of the people.

My cori fon in this gare! was to build a solid
foundation for sustainable and continuous promotion and preservation of
Conservation and Land Use by suing Drama. There are huge amount of
people in the target areas which are illiterate and ignorant of the
importance of PWM and MDF roles end it primary responsibilities must
consistently informed the community to various mediums of information
dissemination such as 2.

1. Advocacy, Communication ocial Mosilization activities for the
people in the target areas through the Community Sustainable Arts
Education program under Drama. It stimulated and created avenue for
community discussion on how best they can solve the issue of
Conservation and Land Use. This medium is very powerful tool to identify
some possible solution to the community problems. It is our firm believe
that through this exercise we have identified and advice MDF and PWM.
how best they can devise some possible strategies to overcome this
pressing issue of Conservation and Land Use issues.

The Community Theatre members are willing to work with Host
Institution MZAC ( Theatre Arts Section)and other stakeholders such as
Poiice Department, Community Policing, Establish Youth Association in
various areas, Churches, Informal Sector Association and National
Cultural Commission for advice and possibie assistance for manpower
 and other relevant organization that we will be closely working with them
to improve their artistic skills.

2. To increase the awareness on the importance of Roles, Responsibilities
and its functions so the people must appreciate and respect the
significance of conservation and Land Use.

3. Development of a better understanding of the school children for the
future generation. Making use of all organization’s experiences in control,
share experiences, best practices and lessons learned for the benefit of
the children and the youths and communities in Afore.

Conservation and Land Use and other social related issues, and
improve knowledge, attitudes and practices through the Workshop.

* Increase engagement and involvement of communities and
households at the Managalas and other relevant stakeholders in
analysis, planning and implementation of activities to protect and
respect , use it properly for the collective benefits in the

community

Increased quality assured, client oriented approach among service
providers to market the community must establish mutual respect for
others and themselves.

Goal:

Increase their knowledge and seeking behavior among communities, in
order to increase awareness about their own attitude and the
environment. Through Community Sustainable Arts Education, Drama
production and Exhibitions about the importance of the role of PWM and

MDF.
Objective:

To prevent the Community members and also to minimize its adverse
impact on Conservation and Land Use, among individuals, families and
communities and other social influences through the application of
Theatre Training

Inadequate political and societal commitment and poor levels of public
awareness on the importance of Role of Conservation and Land Use and

 Mobilization through the workshop using Creative Skills built stronger

This workshop mobilize communities and individuals through 3
participatory approach towards appreciating the vaiue of the PWM & it’s
