 1 Background

In May 2011, Paul and | were invited by Partners with Melanesians Inc (PWM) to talk to farmers and
inhabitants on the Managalas Plateau in Oro Province on the impact and coping strategies of extreme
weather pattems such as Drought. As project staff on the National Agricultural Research institute's PIP
project titled; ‘drought preparedness’, providing such information was a major project objective.
Confirmation of our participation eventuated in a visit being proposed and confirmed for August 2011. This
report outlines the activities and outcomes of our two day visit to the Managalas Plateau in the Afore
District of the Oro Province in Papua New Guinea in August 2011. L Kurika

‘My previous visit to Afore was to assess the after-effects of the 1997-98 drought with colleagues from the
Department of Agriculture and Livestock. | was eager to return to the Managalas Plateau to educate people
in how they can prepare themselves and their communities if there is @ drought. P Osilis

1.1 Partners With Melanesians Inc.

Partners with Melanesians Inc (PWM) is a national, “not for profit”, non-government organization (NGO)
currently focused on conserving natural eco-systems and promoting community development in certain
locations in Papua New Guinea (PNG). The organization has worked with the Managalas Plateau
inhabitants for over 23 years and continually support and provide helpful information to assist the people in
conservation initiatives such as the recently started Managalas Conservation Area Project (MCAP).

1.2. The Managalas Plateau

‘The Managalas plateau is situated between 600-1,000m in the midst of the Owen Stanley Range (to the
south and west), with the Sibium Ranges to the south-east, Mount Lamington to the north and the
Hydrographers to the east. The plateau covers about 300,000 hectares of area and has an extremely
diverse environment; moorlands, mountains, hills, savannah, anthropogenic grassland and gardens.
 ‘Awareness Trip Report L Kurika & P Osils

The plateau is inhabited by about 15,000 people from about 150 clan groups who live in 70 village
communities. The people are mostly subsistence farmers who depend almost entirely on the environment
for their livelihood. Basic government services is restricted to a number of community schools, a top up
school, two aid posts, and a station and health centre at Afore. The Summer Institute of Linguistics
introduced an adult literacy programme to the plateau in the 1960's which since then has helped paved the
way for more recent development initiatives on the Plateau. This relatively isolated and remote area is
linked to the provincial capital, Popondetta, by a poor quality four-wheel drive road and foot tracks. There is
an airstrip at Afore station but it was overgrown with weeds and was not in use at the time of this visit.

‘The remoteness of the area, poor state of infrastructure like roads and airstrips and lack of markets pose
great challenges to cash income generating initiatives such as the production and sale of coffee. The
abundance of natural resources in the area and the high quality agricultural land has attracted in the past
decade a lot of interest from potential investors in timber extraction, oil palm plantations and mineral
ining. However the communities have actively opposed these interests due to the lack of consultations
with resource owners and the failure by interested developers to guarantee benefits and/or environmental
protection.

1.3. The Managalas Conservation Area Project

‘The Managalas Conservation Area Project (MCAP) is managed by PWM with support from various Donor
agencies; the main one being Rainforest Foundation Norway. The ultimate plan is for the Managalas area
to be declared a conservation area under the relevant conservation laws of PNG to enable the people of
Managalas to retain and transfer their inherited natural resources to future generations. The core
programmes under MCAP are: (i) consensus building, (ji) conservation and (ii) training and capacity
building. The overall objectives of the programmes are to promote conservation of natural eco-systems,
prevent unsustainable ways of resource exploitation and encourage small-scale eco-enterprises to
generate revenue for the communities to meet their modest needs. The programmes are implemented
through a network of players that include: the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF), also an NGO,
and eleven small community based organizations (CBO). For eco-enterprises and income generation,
PWM has been working closely with the local CBOs and community groups to promote the production and
marketing of organic coffee, village artifacts and handicrafts, okari nuts, peanuts, forest products,
vegetables and garden produce.

2 Workshop on Drought at Afore Station

The Managalas area like many rural locations in PNG received the full brunt of the negative impacts
caused by the 1997-98 drought. Both NARI staff, Louis Kurika and Paul Osilis visited Afore station on two
separate occasions in 1998. Kurika visited on an RAF flight that delivered relief food to the station while
Osilis was a member of the team that visited the area by road and conducted an appraisal of the food
security and water situation in Oro Bay and the Managalas area.

In the 1997-98 drought, the forest and grassland areas within the vicinity of Afore station were totally
ravaged by bush fires. There was a bad shortage of water and as a result people either left their villages to
resettle in places where they could access water or had to walk long distances to fetch water. Many food
gardens were destroyed and hence relief food was air-lifted to Afore station.

With the experiences of the 1997-98 drought still vividly fresh in people’s memories one can imagine the
sense of apprehension that can arise as a result of the recent news flashes in the media about a severe
drought looming to occur next year, 2012. To dispel any sense of apprehension amongst communities and
create awareness on drought, an awareness workshop on drought was conducted at Afore station.
 2.1 Workshop Purpose

‘The purpose of the workshop was to equip the CBO Managers and trainers with information on drought
and recommended drought coping strategies for them to disseminate to their respective communities to
prepare the communities to cope with the negative impacts of a severe and/or prolonged dry weather
period.

2.2 Sponsorship, Facilitators and Participants

The workshop was organized and sponsored by PWM and facilitated by Patrick Vuet, Conservation Officer
with PWM. The awareness on drought was conducted by Louis Kurika and Paul Osils, staff from the
Drought Project with the National Agricultural Research Institute (NARI), based at NARI's Souther
Regional Center at Laloki in the Central Province. There were a total of 38 participants who attended the
‘one day workshop. They included MDF Board Members, CBO Managers, Activity Coordinators, Gender
Officers and various community representatives from Afore District Zones 1-9 (Appendix 1. List of
Workshop Participants).

2.3 Workshop Terms of Reference

A Terms of Reference (ToR) was prepared for the workshop. The NARI Drought Project staff were
assigned the following workshop duties and responsibilities:

‘* _ Impart the basic ideas on the causes of drought and its impact on the lively hood of the
‘communities/people
Use case studies of other areas around the world that have been affected by droughts
Basic ideas on the type of food that can withstand drought conditions

* Deliver posters or pamphlets containing information on drought. There are ten CBOs within the
Managalas Project areas.

‘* Deliver basic information on the concept of food security.

24 Workshop Programme

The workshop on drought awareness was conducted on Thursday 11 August 2011 at the MDF guest
house at Afore station. The workshop commenced with opening statements from Patrick Vuet and Luke
Mambe, Project Director for MDF on the purpose and the expected outcomes from the workshop. This was
followed by the core activity of the workshop which was the awareness on drought. The information
presented was put together in accordance with the five duties and responsibilities outlined in the agreed
ToR of the workshop between PWM and the two NARI staff, Louis Kurika and Paul Osilis. The awareness
campaign included the following:

© Poster Display
* Power Point presentation on climate change, 1997-78 Drought and its impacts on PNG and NARI
recommended drought coping strategies
‘Session on preparing a Cropping Calendar
Distribution of A4 portfolio posters and information leaflets on climate change and drought to
representatives of the ten Community based organizations,
* Distribution of seeds: open-pollinated corn variety - Suwan and High Protein White corn varieties:
to workshop participants.
‘© Aninteractive session during which some important community perceived issues on climate
change, drought and food security were noted and discussed.
The workshop ended on the afternoon of Thursday 11" August 2011. On Friday 12” August 2011, all
facilitators retumed to Popondetta and then returned via air travel to Port Moresby the next day; Saturday
13” August 2011.
 Awareness Trip Report L Kurka & P Osis

3 Workshop Outcomes

The workshop was a success. It attracted a large number of participants despite its location; many of
whom had walked long distances to attend. Workshop facilitators were able to cover all workshop
requirements (as outlined in the workshop ToR). An overwhelming amount of information was provided and
‘open-pollinated com seeds were distributed so that farmers can use the seeds to replant, unlike hybrid
com seeds. Participants were not only able to learn about drought impact and coping strategies but
understood the presentations and exercises well enough to raise questions and issues on related topics
‘such as insect pest management and the recording of traditional knowledge on famine and bush foods.

During the workshop we felt, first and foremost, that it was essential to clarify and dispel any sense of panic
or apprehension over the prediction that a drought with a severity equal to the 1997-98 PNG drought would
‘occur in 2012. We explained that the forecasting of an El Nino event that would cause a drought(s) was
quite complex and dependent on calculations from experts who are monitoring climatic developments at a
regional and global scale. We stressed that the primary importance at present is for communities to be
made aware of droughts and how to cope with their negative impacts.

3.1 Some Community Perceived Issues on Drought and Food Security from
the Workshop

3.1.1 Taro beetle, a problem in taro gardens
‘Taro beetle damage on taro cultivars was reported to be a problem in all nine Afore Sub-district zones.

Resolution(s): Taro beetle damage is a problem that NARI can immediately address through the
‘use of the two chemicals Bifenthrin and Mustang. The technology is available and NARI staff do
conduct training on taro beetle control upon request from various clients. A demonstration plot for
taro beetle control work can be established in collaboration with farmers at Afore station to
demonstrate how and when to apply the treatments and the effectiveness of the control method. It
may also be worth the effort to conduct some studies on taro beetle population in the gardens and
their breeding sites to see if the pest can be controlled using some form of cultural method. Other
reported insect pests e.g. cut worms and caterpillars can be controlled using Plant Derived
Pesticides (PDP) like chili, derris plant and extract from the neem tree. This technology is
available with NARI whose Crop Protection Staff do conduct training on how to prepare and use
PDP to control insect pests.

3.1.2 Training on food processing and preservation e.g. how to make cassava flour
The need for practical demonstrations on the methods involved in making flour and jam was raised.

Resolution(s): The Ad portfolio posters supplied to each CBO Manager at Afore station contains a
number of recipes on how to process and preserve certain staple crops like cassava and bananas
in storable products like flour and chips. Food processing involving the processing of the
perishable staple crops to storable products is one of the important coping strategies for drought.
NARI does have experts in post harvest, processing and storage who can conduct training on food
processing and storage technologies; based at NARI's Momase Regional Research Center at
Bubia, in the Morobe Province.
 3.1.3. Documentation of traditional knowledge on the utilization of bush and famine foods

The recording of traditional knowledge on bush and famine foods for future utilization was realized and
understood to be a very important issue.

Resolution(s): Reports on experiences from the 1997-98 drought reveal that many rural
‘communities survived by eating bush and famine foods. There are quite a number of bush and
famine food plants that people have resorted to during times of food shortage. These include
banana corms (Musa sp.), Pueraria lobata, wild yam (Dioscorea sp.) and tulip (Gnetum gnemon).
The use of some is widespread while others are utilized only in certain places. However, the
knowledge on traditional recipes on how to prepare and utilize many of these bush and famine
foods often remains with the older generation and is in danger of being lost. NARI has documented
‘a number of these used by coastal and highland area communities in PNG. Each of the 30 A4 size
portfolio posters that were distributed to the CBO Managers at the workshop contains details on
foods and practices suitable for extreme weather patterns such as drought. There are however,
many more still out there that need to be documented and the knowledge passed on to the
younger generation. This has to be done on the Managalas Plateau as part of a strategy to

strengthen the community's ability to cope with droughts.

3.1.4 NARI Drought Project to utilize MDF base at Afore station as a Resource Centre

A query was raised for further NARI collaboration and participation by the PIP Drought Project at Afore;
continue drought awareness.

Resolution(s): The NARI Drought Project does not have the resources to separately undertake any
long-term programme activity at Managalas but it could collaborate with PWM and MDF to be
involved in certain specific activities that require NARI expertise and involving NARI released
technologies, especially in the area of food security. Some of the possible activities that NARI

‘could be involved in at Managalas are:

‘+ Introduce drought tolerant and other useful crops and to encourage farmers to
maintain diversity of their food crops in gardens.

‘+ Introduce the rope and washer pump technology for accessing underground water
sources,

Conduct training on food processing and storage.

Conduct training on taro beetle control and use of plant derived pesticides.

Conduct training on seed and vegetable production.

Introduce small livestock like goats, ducks and chicken.

Establish fruit and nut orchards of both exotic and native species.

Conduct training on vegetative propagation method on certain fruit and nut species.

Rapid propagation of African yam and taro using mini-setts,

Rapid propagation of bananas using banana bits.
 ‘Awareness Trip Report L Kurika & P Osilis

4 Acknowledgement

On behalf of NARI, sincere gratitude is expressed to Partners With Melanesians Inc. for the invitation to
participate in conservation efforts at Afore, Managalas Plateau in the Oro Province. To PWM and MDF for
organizing the workshop, our travel and the warm welcome and stay at Afore. Thank you especially to
Patrick Vuet and Luke Mambe and the workshop organizing team at Afore.

‘Thank you also to senior colleagues at NARI SRC — Laloki; Dr. Amanda Mararuai for editing and Mrs.
Rosa Kambuou for commenting on the report.

There are a lot of conflicts, misunderstandings, and rumours circulating across the Plateau. Our

SUBJECT: SUBMISSION TO MINISTER FOR ENVIRONMENT AND
CONSERVATION FOR THE DECLARATION OF TE
MANAGALAS PLATEAU AS A CONSERVATION AREA
CONSERVATION AREAS ACT ~ (1978)

1. Purpose:
The purpose of this submission is to inform the National Executive Council (NEC) on

the plans that the two NGOs (Managalas Development Foundation Inc (MDF) and
Partners With Melanesian Inc (PwM) have in place, and that is to apply for NEC
approval to declare the Managalas plateau as a Conservation Area in the, Afore Local
Level Government, Injivitary Electorate of Oro Province, under the Conservation
Areas Act 1978.

2. Background
Papua New Guinea (PNG), being a signatory to a number of International
Agreements, Instruments and Conventions such as the Conventions on Biological
Diversity (CBD) 1992 calls for:

i. The development of National strategically planned programs for

conservation, the sustainable use of biological diversity and the integration

to move this into sectoral plans, policies and programs (article 6) of the

National Government.

The identification of components of biological diversity important for its

conservation and sustainable use and monitor the components and identify

the activities which have the adverse impacts on conservation and

sustainable use of biological diversity and monitor their effects (article 7).

iii, The establishment of a network of protected areas and the development of
guidelines for selection, establishment and management of protected areas
where measures are

iv. needed to conserve biological diversity (article 8b and ¢).

v. The development of necessary legislation and other regulatory provisions
for protection of threatened species and populations and the promotion of
public education and awareness (article 8 (k) and article 13).

Page 1 of 66
 Other conventions include the Conservation of Nature in the South Pacific, Apia,
1976; the protection of Natural Resources and Environment of the South Pacific
Regions, Noumea, 1986; and the International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild
Fauna and Flora, Washington, 1973.

Furthermore, Papua New Guinea has undertaken its international obligations
approved in the CBD in 1992 by developing and adopting the National Biodiversity
Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) 2007. The NBSAP will be implemented to fulfil
not only its obligations under the CBD, but other international instruments such as the
Rio, and MDG (specifically goal 7), and other international environmental agreements
which PNG has obligations to perform. In addition, the Department of Environment
and Conservation has a new strategic direction which base around the Millenium
Development Goal # 7 (Promote Environmental Sustainability). Stipulated in this
strategy and action plan are its six (6) main goals;

Goal 1 To conserve, sustainably use, and manage the country’s biological
diversity

© Goal 2 To strengthen and promote institutional and human capacity building for
biodiversity conservation, management and sustainable use

© Goal 3 To strengthen partnership and promote coordination for conserving
biodiversity

© Goal 4 To strengthen existing protected areas and ensure that protected areas for
terrestrial species and marine species are increased to 10% by 2010 and 2012
respectively

© Goal 5 Ensure a fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of genetic and
ecosystem resources

© Goal 6 Promote and strengthen research of the country’s biological diversity and
the sustainable development of the country’s biological resources

The proposed Managalas Conservation Area is certain to have a range of measures
that act in accordance with the objectives and goals of the NBSAP and other
international conventions for Papua New Guinea. It promotes millennium
development goals (MDG); Goal 7: Promotes Environmental Sustainability, where
government seeks to and reverse the law of Environmental Resource, and address
pillar 5 of PNG’s Vission 2050 which focus on Environmental Sustainability and
Climate Change. Managalas Proposed Conservation Area if declared will increase
the percentage of protected areas in PNG by 0.9%, obviously contributing to achieve
Goal 4 of the PNGNBSAP (To strengthen existing protected areas and ensure that
protected areas for terrestrial species and marine species are increased to 10% by
2010 and 2012 respectively).

3. Facts and Considerations

Managalas Development Foundation Inc (MDF) and its facilitating partner, Partners
with Melanesians Inc. (PWM) are two “not for profit” organizations working as

Page 2 of 66

 partners with the people of Managalas Plateau since 1995 towards the goal of
establishing the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area, covering a land area of
360 000 hectares in the Afore LLG. The entire core program that is carried out in the
plateau is community based and the focus is on Conservation and Sustainable
development in the target community. The Afore LLG has 18 ward councils with a
population of over 18 000 people (2000 census), 152 clans and over a 100 villages.
Attachment - Appendix 2, details sociological information of the area and in
Appendix 4, is the Conservation Area Boundary Description and Map.

As detailed in this submission, the area under consideration has significant biological,
geographical, and cultural values to the local people of Managalas and the
International scientific community as a whole. The area is still in its proposed stage,
and foreigners are already enquiring to know more about the biodiversity of the area,
while some have visited the project site. One of the main animal species that is and
will be attracting the international community is the World’s largest butterfly (the
Queen Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly) which is endemic to PNG particularly to the
Oro Province. This species have migrated from the Oro plains after it was deforested
for oil palm development. Managlas plateau provide the habitat for this endangered
and threatened species and if loss to improper management of commercial
developments, will result in the extinction of this unique butterfly species. Four (4)
biosurveys have been conducted in the area at various altitudes and locations and are
summarised in a separate document title; “The Biodiversity of Managalas Plateau”.
Specific advantages and facts of establishing the Managalas Conservation Area under
the Papua New Guinea Conservation Areas Act 1978 are as follows:

i. It would be the largest second recognized Conservation Area in Papua New
Guinea and would serve as a model for setting up conservation areas in other
provinces throughout the country.

2. 360 000 hectares of land area in the Managalas Plateau, Afore Sub district
would be inciuded to protect the endangered Queen Aiexandrea bird wing
butterfly, Doria’s Tree Kangaroo and other endangered and endemic wildlife
species.

3. It would extend from sea level to 2900+meters mountain rangers, spanning an
altitude and habitat range un-parallel among protected areas in PNG.

4. A Conservation Area Management Committee will be established to manage
this Conservation Area for the long term.

5. Given the uniqueness of the forests and the resources contained therein,
outside institutions, researchers and tourists would certainly want to visit the
area.

6. The Managalas Plateau presents good prospects to study past climatic changes
and their influences on the vegetation.

7. Through the Exit Strategy PwM developed between PwM and MDF, all
management responsibilities will be handed over to MDF to maintain and
manage the proposed Conservation Area once declared.

8. The Afore LLG as an important stakeholder and local authority will jointly
oversee the management of the Conservation Area along with other
stakeholders from the Managalas Plateau.

9. If declared will increase the percentage of protected areas in PNG by 0.9% to
4.1% from the current 3.2%. PNG is required to set aside 10% of its landmass

Page 3 of 66
 for bio-diversity conservation, as per its commitment to the Convention of
Biological Diversity (CBD).

10. Address pillar 5 in the Papua New Guinea Vission 2050, which focus on
Environmental! Sustainabillity and Climate Change.

‘The Conservation and Sustainable Forest Management Program carried out on the
Managalas Plateau has a community based approach and it is jointly implemented
with several other components which include: Consensus Building Programme, CBO
Capacity Building Program, Rainforest Literacy Program and Sustainable Livelihood
Alternative activities for the local population. The Managalas Proposed Conservation
‘Area Project (MPCAP) has developed its conservation approach in recognition of
PNG's unique land tenure ship laws and local needs. Because long term conservation
depends on the actions of the local people, the MPCAP is helping to provide the tools
and training necessary for making informed decisions and supporting the local
community. Partners with Melanesians have already established a locally owned NGO
= Managalas Development Foundation which will manage the Managalas
Conservation Area for the long term as stipulated in the Conservation Areas Act
(1978).

4. Views of the Provincial Governor:
Sought through the PEC endorsement

5. Views of other Ministers affected:
After the 90 days public viewing and negotiation with the NEC Secrateriat,
Department of Environment and Conservation will seck views of other vital
departments particularly, the Department of Mining and Petroleum, National Forest
Authority, Department of Agriculture and Livestock, Department of Community
Development and the Provincial and Local Level Government Affairs.

Five other major agencies nave given in their support through writing and these
include the Department of Community Development, Conservation Forum of PN
Bishop Museum, Oro Provincial Government, Afore Local Level Governement and
the Managalas Development Foundation (Refer Appendix $ for support letters).
Adversely views of other vital line agencies are yet to be sought; PNG National Forest
Auhtority, Department of Agriculture and Livestock, and Department of Mining and
Petroleum. Views of the three later Government Departments will be sought by DEC
during the 90 days public viewing.

6. Financial Imptications:

At this point in time no financial assistance is requested from the Provincial or
National Governments, but a longterm agreement with the Provincial Government is
to be arranged at a later date when the full submission is made for the endorsement of
the CA is an all stakeholder’s tasks. All funding required to facilitate the Managalas
Conservation Area Support Program is supporied by Norwegian Rainforest
Foundation (RFN), International Union of Conservation Networking (IUCN), the
World Bank, and other donors.

Page 4 of 66
 7. Staffing Impl

tions

‘The future management of the Managalas Conservation Area will be controlled by the
Managalas landowners themselves through the Managalas Development Foundation
and the Afore LLG and with assistance and technical support from the Partners with
Melanesians and eventually hand it over to the Managalas Development Foundation,
where a Management Committee will be appointed by all stakcholders in consultation
with the Department of Environment and Conservation.

8, Employment Implications:

Future employment opportunities will depend on the Conservation Area Management
Plan (CAMP) to be developed by the landowners with Afore LLG and with technical
support from PwM and its partners/donors. If the decision is made to develop some
areas of the land, itis assumed that these developments will be self sustaining.

For example, there is an initial plan to develop an eco-tourism industry on the plateau
under the Conservation Area and besides that tracking along the famous Black
Cat/Ghost Trail from Abau up into the Owen Stanley Ranges to upper Musa round
Dorobosoro and into Aiari, Suari and into the Managatas plateau the path used by the
‘American soldier in aid of the Australian at Kokoda, is now in the pipe line and it is
predicted that it will be relieving visitors. So employment opportunity along this track
will be a big income earner for the local people plus the Afore LLG through taxes and
this will create employment opportunities for the local people. The scale will be
similar to be near or bigger than the Kokoda Trail.

In light of the Conservation Area Plans, there is huge potential for the development of
a scientific research station within the area that will see the development of other
employment opportunities.

9. Legislative Implications

The Proposed Managalas Conservation Area submission proposal has been developed
ine with the Conservation Areas Act (1978). There are several steps followed as
stipulated in the Conservation Areas Act which culminates to two major phases 1)
declaration and gazettal of the Proposed Conservation Area by NEC and 2) approval
of the Conservation Area Management Plan and swearing in of the Conservation Area
Management Committee Members by the DEC Minister. The Managalas
communities, Managalas Development Foundation and Partners with Melanesia will
have completed phase | after this submission as the first requirement by the Act and
have began the preparatory work on the second phase which will also be submitted to
DEC for approval by NEC.

10. Constitution Implications

Papua New Guinea’s Fourth National Goal of its 1975 Constitution calls for the
conservation of PNG’s natural resources and environment for the collective benefit of
the current generation and should be replenished for future generations. The creation
and formal gazettal of the Propose Managalas Conservation Area directly
accomplishes this Constitutional goal. This is clearly stipulated in the Conservation
Areas Act, Subdivision IIL3.C (qualified rights) of the Constitution, namely—

Page 5 of 66
 (@ the freedom from arbitrary search and entry conferred by Section 44 of the
Constitution; and

(b) the right to privacy conferred by Section 49 of the Constitution,
is a law made for that purpose, taking into account the National Goals and the
Basic Social Obligations, particularly the fourth goal of the National Goals
and Directive Principles entitled "natural resources and environment”.

In addition, once declared and gazzetted will fulfil pillar 5 of Papua New Guinea

Vission 2050 which focuses on Environmetal Sustainability and Climate Change.

11. Political Implications:

‘The Oro Provincial Government and Afore Local Level Government support the cry
of the indigenous Managalas landowners’ to have their 360 000 ha of land and
pristine rainforests (Managalas Proposed Conservation Area) be declared the second
Conservation Area in PNG under the Conservation Areas Act (1978). The process has
followed a bottom-up approach and up to this level any unforeseen implications will
be of little significance. The Oro Provincial Executive Council formal endorsement on
the Propose Managalas Conservation Area was granted on the 02™ December 2008;
whilst Afore Local Level Government Ward Members endorsement was obtained on
the 08" of June 2011. These endorsements can be found in the Appendix 4.

12. Planning Implications:

All planning and development of the Managaias Conservation Area will be decided
upon by the entire Managalas community through their clan elders through the
Managalas Consensus Building Process which is a very unique process of
consultation and decision making where all the 152 landowning clans come together
to decide on the development priorities and options that are available to them, and
based on resource availability and by discussion and talking, consensus is reached.
The Afore LLG through the Ward Councillors will be fully involved so that the Afore
LLG has a major role in development planning which will also include the Oro
Provincial Government, the Department of Environment and Conservation (DEC) and
other major stakeholders.

13. Implementatio

Conservation Area Support Project (MCASP) with support from the Norwegian

41. Introduction

This manual is designed to assist the Board in the organizational management of the
Managalas Development Foundation (MDF). This initiative is supported by the Inter-church
Organization.

Since the formation of MDF there has been lack of direction and guidance in particular the
decision making on the Board’s front in governance, accountability and transparency relating to
decisions of MDF.

This manual includes the Board's general responsibilities, terms of reference for Board's
committees, general rules of procedure guiding the conduct of the Board's activities and other

Board's policies.
14. Ensure Mission, Purpose, vision and values Identified

The mission and vision of the organization should always be captured in striving to achieve the
vision of MDF in all its planned activities.

The Vision of a peaceful communal society living in Harmony with nature and a mission to
strengthen community participation & ownership through coordination of activity that promotes
self reliance, education & sustainable livelihood, while maintain cultural heritage & conserving
the natural resources.

The Board should at all times conduct activities in such a way as to uphold the mission and
vision of the Foundation.

1.2. Rational for a governing Body

Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) as an umbrella local NGO for the 10 CBOs
Managalas plateau that is expanding in terms of affiliations has seen that the board manual
should capture certain guidelines within which the Board should govern the affairs of MDF. The
mission and vision as enshrined in the Constitution of MDF.

a) To assist the Managalas plateau people in providing the medium through which they can
resolve issues of concern and conflicts amongst themselves and with groups or people.

b) To undertake education, training and awareness campaigns, and programs on
environmental issues, development, human rights, land and resource rights of the
Managalas Piateau peopie.

c) To assist the Managalas plateau people acquire resources and skills including

specialized training which could be used to advance their individual as well as collective
interests.

4) To promote the efficient management of customarily owned lands and sound economic
principles and to assist the Managalas Plateau people in establishing income generating
projects.
 © Managalas Development Foundation 2010

e) To regulate and monitor on behalf of the Managalas plateau people the sustainable
utilization of natural resources both on the land, in the land and rivers so as to ensure
that they receive maximum benefit from the development of these resources,

f) To receive, organize and administer funds, compensation payments, grants and gifts
from the nationals, Provincials and local-level government and other donor agencies in
Papua new Guinea or overseas in pursuance of its objectives

g) To plan and implement community based sustainable response management and other
community based projects in collaboration with other such Associations, Groups,
Cooperatives, Government agencies, Institutions and Non-Government Organizations
within Papua New Guinea or overseas whose aims and objectives are similar and lend
assistance and support to such other groups and organizations.

h) To collaborate and arrange for exchange programs with other like minded NGOs, CBOs
and institutions at the national and International level on issues relating to environment,
sustainable development and customary Landowners

Date: 08 September 2010

PROGRAM: Conservation

ACTIVITY: Community Reforestation /Mock Combine Forum/HCVF Dissemination

INTRODUCTION

This paper reports on our visit to the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area to attend to the
above activities. We spent almost a week at the project site and returned on the 6"” of September
2010.

PURPOSE

The purpose of the trip was to do a follow up on the progress of the community reforestation
project, deliver the summarised HCVF report to the Field Conservation Coordinator Mr Bradley
Dabadaba, and attend the mock combine forum which was held at Numba zone 6,

METHODS/PROCEDURES

Upon arrival at Girua airport Popondetta, we got on the hired vehicle and went back to town to
purchase parts for the damaged vehicie at the project site. There was a hold up at the Pogani
River. We could not cross as the river was tide due to heavy rain the previous night. We overnight
at the pastor’s house and cross over the next morning.

We dropped off the vehicle parts and the mechanic at Afore station and drove all the way to Sila
junction. We walked from there to Numba where the mock combine forum was held.

We were welcomed by the communities and the elders. i met with zone 7 manager (Ezekiel) and
Bevan Evare (the person heading the reforestation project in zone 6). Ezekiel updated me on the
progress of the reforestation work in zone 7 particularly the one in road 2; and Bevan showed me
his necessary shed where he is still filling his poly bags. There was a deceased in his family that
caused the delay of his work.

‘At the mock combine forum | played more of an observatory role. it was an eye opener for me so!
just observed and take note of the procedures that should be followed in a forum, but were not
followed in the past forums.

After the mock forum we walked back to Afore station. | met with the conservation coordinator at
the guest house and we briefly went through the simple version of the draft HCVF report. | was
told that the dissemination of this hcvf report will be done during the zone forums. This will also
 help prepare them for the actual combine forum asone if the issue to be discussed in the combine
forum is on land use planning

| personally visited the other nursery shed for the Sugokol Baru clan in zone 7. The nursery shed
has been built but the filling of the poly bags are yet to be completed. | was unfortunate to meet
Christopher (the person heading the reforestation work for the clan) as he was busy with the
theater arts performing groups doing the awareness on the western side of the plateau.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

Reforestation Project

The progress of the reforestation project is progressing well but not at a fast rate because the clan
members who are taking the lead in these work are also playing major parts in other programmes
such as the literacy and consensus building programs while others have personal problems. The
Narija clan in zone six and the Sugokol Baru clan in zone seven are currently still filling the poly
bags and collecting native tree species for their nurseries. The other group in zone ? (in road 2);
their nursery is ready for transplanting but the clan leader is continuously being sick thus the work
is delayed. From conversation with zone 7 CBO manager, | was told that, if the clan leader had
allowed him to take the lead in the reforestation work, the planting process would have been
done. However the conservation coordinator said that he will start off the transplanting in the
area now that he has free time as he was busy with preparations for the mock combine forum and
other activities under the RFL and CB programs.

Mock Combine Forum

One of the purposes of the trip was to attend the mock combine forum to see how it is conducted,
the procedures, and who the main participants in such gathering are. A full report of this mock
forum is compiled by the officer in charged Mr. Nickson Piakal (Education and Awareness Officer}
Delivery of the HCVF Report

Copies of a simple and summarised version of the draft HCVF report for the Managalas Proposed
Conservation Area was delivered to the field conservation coordinator for dissemination to the ten
zones on the plateau, This will be done during the zone forums that will be conducted before the
combine forum in November. The report is useful to provide information on various geographical
features such as; rainfall distribution, wind patterns, population distribution, threats, agricultural
activities, forest types, and the geology of the Managalas plateau. Being equipped with
information on these features will help the communities or clans to properly develop their land
use plans.

RECOMMENDATIONS

A contributing factor to some of these delays might be because there is no specialised
conservation officer that would concentrate on the conservation works and its other minor
programs. However, as we were about to depart the project site, | was advised by MDF Project
Director that he will employ a new conservation officer who will concentrate on the conservation
works.

It is important that the field conservation officer should have a digital camera to take pictures of
the work being done. Pictures are vital for reporting purposes. | am not sure whether this is the’
responsibility for MDF or PWM.

CONCLUSION

| found the trip to be fulfilling as it was the first time that | was involved in three activities at the
same time. | also learn new things from the mock combine forum that was conducted and to meet
new faces on that part of the plateau. Generally, the reforestation work is progressing well but it

/2
 will be better for a specialised officer that will work closely with the three participated clans so

that work will run smoothly and up to date.

“ilaintaining the Lance”

Date: 28/6/2010
PROGRAM: Consensus Building ++
ACTIVITY: Education and Awareness

INTRODUCTION

This report details the awareness expedition | undertook under the banner of Hope Trek. Leaving on the
19th of May 2010, it took me and 9 youths from NCD one month through five (5) provinces to conclude this
awareness run in the Western Highlands Province.

Taking off from Ower’s Corner in Central Province, we took on the arduous Kokoda Trail and conducted
awareness and distributed posters every step of the way to Oro Province and onwards to Morobe, Eastern
and Western Highlands Provinces.

As put forward to you and PWM as an organization, this project is an initiative that takes a whole new
innovative approach into the idea of education and awareness on environment and conservation to include
people and places outside of PWM’s project sites without placing any extra financial burden on PWM’s
working budget. Furthermore, it was included in my initial work plan and was scheduled to coincide with
both my annual leave and the World Environment Day 2010, thus creating as little a dent in the overall
work plan of PWM and MDF and other stake hoiders.

But in so doing, | am of the strong belief that it has raised the profile of this organisation and helped shed
‘more light on our work and the whole idea of environmental and conservation awareness, notwithstanding
‘our commitment to the Managalas Plateau and our joint bid with the people there to attain its
Conservation Area status.

My push to engage the support of all media formats without any reservation has also seen more publicity
and increased support from interested people and organisations both within PNG and abroad.

PURPOSE

The purpose of this exercise was to reach not only PWM'’s project sites but beyond and outside their
confines to enlighten as many people as possible about the importance of the environment and what we as
Papua New Guineans and citizens of this world stand to gain or lose, in either the practise or non-practise
of conservation in our day to day living.

In topping of our run, we went and delivered donated library books to schools in Western Highlands
Province and Enga Province. This gesture was hoped to drive home into children and adults alike the
importance of books, as the most sure-fire way to help enlighten them and broaden their horizon. This in
time will help in addressing the challenges we face in educating our people and the future generation
about the importance of our natural environment because | believe that a literate society will be better
equipped to address not only conservation issues but the entire development of this country.

 METHODS/PROCEDURES

Awareness points

‘The key awareness points include the following:

1. Books and the importance of reading

2. Environment and conservation awareness

3. Climate Change

Looking into sustainable income generating ventures
Being responsible and self-reliant

Basic Hygiene & Cholera Awareness

oe

As appended to our list of awareness points above, the cholera outbreak was a hot issue (and still is) at the
time of our departure, so we made it as a last minute inclusion into our awareness points. Thus we also
made mention of this health crisis facing the country and explained its basic symptoms (information
gleaned from general knowledge) and pointed out its impact in the livelihood of their community in the
likelihood of a cholera case within their community. In closing, preventative measures by practising basic
hygiene in our day-to-day living was stressed and highlighted as the best possible way to keep our guard
against such a disease from reaching our door steps.

Methods of Awareness — Walking the Talk

‘As a demonstrative awareness exercise, we embarked with the silent motto of “walking the talk”. Hence a
total of six plastic shopping bags of litter ranging from empty containers and tin cans to candy wrappers
were collected, starting from Ower’s Corner all the way to Kokoda Station. The same was practised the
entire length of our travel up the Okuk Highway to WHP and back. Furthermore, we made certain to guard

against our litter as well.

Methods of Awareness — Outreach & Posters

‘On most occasions, all these points of order seemed new and foreign to them. As such, we used familiar
grounds to start with so we went back to relating the idea of conservation to traditional practises as well as
the Bible story of creation to drive home the message of conservation and environmental awareness.

In addition, our outreaches were structured to engage our audience in discussions through the idea of
having a Question & Answer session after every talk. Even in some instances ~ especially along the Track
route — some of the Hope Trek youths familiar with Motu stepped in to carry the discussion forward and
further helped to pave the way for the locals to step forward with queries and questions. This enabled us to

SD
 elaborate further on the discussed topics and to further gauge their views and get an overall understanding
of how they digested the underlying ideas of our talk.

The dissemination of information materials in the manner of posters also enabled them to better
understand concepts and the mechanics of what we were trying to get across to them. Furthermore, this
provided a way for them to be constantly reminded about our campaign, long after we were gone.

VIVE Nt
a \\

SS
 Leading up to and eventually coinciding with the World Environment Day, our awareness was aimed at
enlightening people to be more aware about the natural environment and to understand its significance in
‘our day to day living with an insight into the future as well. This was followed by the challenge put forward
to them to be more proactive in practising conservation in their day to day living by the mere act of
minding our litter, starting with the very mundane of actions of minding their cigarette stub, match stick
and bubble gum wrappers.

Target Audience
‘With our hope that these messages and ideas should be carried o1 (0 the future, our preferred target

audience were mainly school-aged children but not necessarily restricted to that. To further drive home
this message, our trekking awareness campaign was topped off with the delivery of library books which had
been sourced from Hope Worldwide (PNG) to schools in Western Highlands Province (Bukapena Primary
School) and Enga Province (Yambaitok Community School, formerly known as Saluk Community School as it
was earlier located in Saluk Village).

This awareness venture was void of any form of discrimination. In fact, whenever we came into contact
with any people, whether individuals or groups, we kept on with our outreach. And it did not stop there. |
carried on in the buses, on boats, on trucks, in schools, in villages, in urban settlements, in market places, at
bus stops, on local radio stations and even around the age-old fireplace. In short, | was simply on fire and
everybody else around me could fee! the heat and they were all burning and lapping up every single word
from this silver tongue. Whow!

Presentation of Facts & Figures
But it was not all verbal foreplay. We talked facts and figures while being mindful about the varied
background of our audience and made it as palatable as possible in their comprehension of key issues like
Global Warming and Climate Change — among others; by laying it down in the most laymen of terms as
possible, using local examples as illustrations whenever required.

‘As further illustrations of positive steps being taken by existing conservation organisations, we detailed the
work of PWM, especially with regard to our work on the Managalas Plateau and our bid to attain
Conservation Area status for Managalas. In addition, the work of the Eco-Forestry Forum and our partner
NGO's all over the country were highlighted to them.

We encouraged and promoted the idea of taking a more proactive approach by demonstrating that we can
start small by minding our litter, starting with the smallest of them like the match stick and bubble-gum
wrappers. Starting with this fundamental of idea, we appealed to our audience at the end of every such talk

/*
 sessions that there is the possibility of making a difference in looking after our natural ecosystem and in
being more mindful about our actions in relation to the bigger picture as to how our actions will impact our
natural environment. We further appealed to them to go on and pass on this message to their wantoks,
relatives, friends and neighbours about these issues.

PWM Project Site Visits

Managalas

In our itinerary, we made sure to include all the project sites of PWM. However, upon arriving
Popondetta, we bumped into Luke Mambe and Douglas Tumai who advised us that it would take us longer
than we were expecting. With our ship scheduled to leave in 2 days, | only followed up with the posters and
awareness materials that Bradley Dabadaba had taken with him the previous week.

Ona-Keta

After dropping off the rest of the Hope Trek team in Hagen, | came back to Goroka and caught up with
Patrick Jack, Richard Wapo and Nelson Duabane. The next morning | went over to Konningi Primary School
where we celebrated World Environment Day with the children and teachers there. It was interesting and
fulfilling to reach out to these eager children.

Lembena

Due to the situation on the ground at Lembena, | could not get into that area. Even if there were no
problems on the ground, | would have still had problems getting there due to financial constraints. But
because | initially got the library books for the school children of Lembena, | instead went and dropped off
a couple of boxes of books at the Baptist Union headquarters in Kimininga at Mt Hagen and advised people
responsible for the Lemebena area to take the books with them the next time they charter a plane to
Yamabitok.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

It was apparent that all the information presented was lacking in the communities we entered and passed
through. It was evident from their reception and feedback that they very much needed to hear about the
things we had to say. According to most people including village leaders, church leaders, women in the
‘community, and local youths alike, such vital information was lacking in their community and our messages
were an eye-opener for them.

As such they asked us to stop by again in future and ensured our safe passage as well as catering for our
refreshments.

Such gestures were very much encouraging and it further spurred us on with renewed energy in our
trekking campaign. it further gave us the reassurance that the spirit of giving in the traditional Melanesian
way was pretty much alive within most, if not all members of the community.

RECOMMENDATIONS.

It is therefore of my strong belief that the idea of environmental awareness and conservation is something
that needs to be shared with everybody in our country. From urban centres to rural isolated communities
alike. This is of vital importance because this notion has to be reiterated and ingrained into the psyche of all
members of our communities so that it can be transpired into ACTION at the individual level up to the
bigger community level. Only then can we make inroads into the communities in seeing the message of
conservation being spread and practised in our day to day lives.

Take for example the hot topic of Climate Change. We talk about trying to reverse this global crisis but the
fact remains that we cannot make even a dent in the outcome if this message is confined to only our
project sites. It has to reach out into all corners of this country if we want to truly drive home this message.
‘And we have seen time and time again that we cannot rely on the government and their various designated
 offices to further this cause. As such the onus is now on us as conservation organisations and individuals
within these organisations to spread the word.

In saying that | do not expect us to reallocate funds and realign our budget into such awareness exercises.
We can instead start small at the level of practising what we preach and look into supporting similar
initiative wholeheartedly instead of seeing it as a one man show.

Furthermore, programme activities aside, it is of my view that many a times those of us within the
conservation NGO network at often times only preach about such issues and that is about as far as we go.
Our actions often veer away from the path of our mouths. It is high time we reanalyse our very mundane of
actions. That brings me back to the point of littering. In saying that it takes me back to the very minute of
litter like cigarette stubs, match stick and bubble gum wrappers, buai spittle notwithstanding. In short, we
have to practise what we preach. Only by doing that will we be able to demonstrate to people that there is
a starting point where conservation can be practised.

CONCLUSION

All in all the Hope Trek expedition, as a demonstrative awareness exercise proved to be an eye opener
not only for me but for all who participated in this exercise, including the people who were the recipients of
the information (in our awareness outreach) and the donated books as well as the youths who trekked with
me.

We were all very well received in most areas we went to because the ideas being broached were all new to

the people and the children in the schools | attended. This is evident of the need for more similar initiatives
to be undertaken to promote our cause to garner more support from the wider PNG community at large.

PROGRAM: Conservation

ACTIVITY: Finalise Conservation Work Programs with Field Officer/ Combine Forum.

INTRODUCTION

This report details my final visit to the project site for the year 2010. This trip was tied up together
with the trip for the District Wide Combine Forum which was held in Jorura in zone three (3). 1
took off on Wednesday 10" November to finalise conservation works with the field officer, and
then went on to join the participants from Port Moresby who went up for the Combine Forum
which began from the 16" to the 18” of November. We all return to Port Moresby on the 19" of
November 2010.

PURPOSE

‘The purpose of the trip was mainly to finalise with the field coordinator the remaining conservation
activities that were still pending. In addition, the trip was also meant to attend the District Wide
Combine Forum.

METHODS/PROCEDURES

On Wednesday 10" November, I flew over to Popondetta and got on a PMV to Afore.

I met Edrick Ninimiro, PWM Admin Officer and he updated that preparation work for the Combine
Forum on the ground need polishing up. Since Nickson was late for his flight and has to fly over the
following day, I took his place and together with Edrick, we went to Jorura to check for Brian
Kasira, the Consensus Building Officer on the ground, to polish up the preparation work.

In the afternoon of the same day we went back to Afore to meet with Nickson. The following day
(Friday), I met with Bradley and we finalised the remaining conservation works. On the same day, I
had the chance to meet with the Chairman for Afore Primary School where we had a walk down to
their school to see their nursery seedlings.

RESULTS/FINDINGS
From our discussion, Bradley is yet to carry out the CA Border Patrol in Zone 8 where the threat
from logging is slowly creeping into the CA Boundary. There are two clan groups that are pushing
for logging activities. What we have come up with from our discussion was to get CELCOR
officers, the field officer and myself to visit the zone and get their opinion whether we have to curve
them out from the CA Boundary or let their area remain as part of the CA. However, since we ate
winding up program activities for this year, this can be brought forward to next year’s work plan.
One of the primary reasons for the logging threat according to Bradley is that the deal between the
WMA and Dadakul has expired. The two clans here are Dokapol and Sarila.

 The reforestation work by Bewen in zone 6 is progressing well. Out of the 500 nursery bags given
to him for seedlings, he has transplanted 300 seedlings during the last rainy season. Now he’s
waiting for the next wet season to transplant the last 200 seedlings. The status of Christopher's
group in zone 7 is that they are still working on their nursery seedlings. According to the
conservation field officer, they are to relocate their nursery shed close to the area to be reforested
which is at Afore. Jerome and his clan has not settled the land disputes amongst them, so I have
advised Ezekiel who has prepared the seedlings for the grassland on Jerome’s land to transplant the
seedlings on the grassland areas around the Afore Primary School. Ezekiel is leading the students at
Afore Primary School to set up their nursery seedlings. The school is making use of the K200
which we have given to all the schools on the plateau during the World Environment Day this year,
to start up small reforestation projects for their schools.

A detail report for the entire District Wide Combine Forum is prepared by the officer in charged,
Mr Nickson Piakal. I'll just give a brief report as this was an eye opener for me. The participants
that flew over from Port Moresby are tabled below.

 Introduction
‘This year’s scriptwriting workshop saw an increase in the number of women participants
and also an increase in the number of young participants compared to the previous
Scriptwriting workshops. This resulted in a better and more constructive discussion in the
course of the workshop.

By this, I don’t mean to say that the other participants are not contributing and sharing
ideas, they were very helpful because the new participants have learnt a lot from them
and vise-versa. This is where the heart of leaming is because each participant brings in
their ideas and views on what they know about each topics/issues. During the discussion
and sharing of ideas everybody learns in the process and at the same time learning
materials are developed.

In terms of producing learning materials, for this year we are going to include
Theatre/Drama instead of the usual radio programs that Rainforest Literacy produces.
‘The reasons are simple;
1. radio programs are too costly to produce
2. itis also (oo technical for MDF to take it on when PWM leaves full responsibility
to them to take it on.
3. the impact of RFL was at a very slow rate since the program began, so we decided
to try theatre instead

Review of 2009 Issues

The first part of the workshop was spent on reviewing last year’s topics and the topic that
‘most time was spent on was Land Use Plan. Through the discussion it showed that most
clan members in the plateau are realizing the importance of having a land use plan which
‘means that the program has had an impact by at a slower rate.

‘The participants identified main problem areas and discussed how they will solve these
problems. For example, members of Zone 8 have used their clan elders and chiefs to
solve any land related matters because the elders/chiefs have the upper hand in decision-
making. As for zone 10 they suggested that there is a need for awareness especially on
issues such as family planning as it leads to population increase and further to land
related problems. When people start to have more children, the population increased,
villages and gardens expand. This leads to all sorts of land related problems and disputes.
So they suggested that if they are better informed on the issue of family planning, this
would solve land related problems. Similar solutions were identified by the other Zones
while two zones (5 & 7) mentioned that there is no sign/indication at all on whether they
understand Land use plan or not.

As mentioned above, this was one of the reasons why we had to do a trial theater/drama
program instead of the usual radio program. We had to try something else because
different people have different learning styles e.g.; some learn better by seeing pictures
and illustrations while some learn better by listening and watching CD/DVDs.

‘The responses from the other issues/topics vary from zone to zone but the impact is
happening very slowly. We can’t really measure a person’s learning ability but in terms
of the impacts, there are visible impacts but then again it will take a while for the people
to really grasp the message and put it into action. This was one of the reasons why we

 had to take a different approach by trialing out Drama/Taeatre instead of the radio
programs.

The 2010 Issues & discussions

The second part of the workshop was spent on identifying and discussing the new
topics/issues for the year as per the 2009 clan group discussions and the Combine Forum
in November 2009.

Disaster Risk Management

Climate Change

Land Use Plan cross-cut with family planning

Conservation cross-cut with Social Problems

SeNE

These topics (above) are discussed by the participants and the discussion was based at
answering these 3 main questions;

1. what comes to your mind when you see or hear about these topics

2. how has it become an issue in your community (good/bad)

3. who are the main actors.

4. how do you solve them if they are a problem in your community

In the course of the discussion, it showed that participants have understood the topics on
land use plan and conservation better that Disaster Risk Management and Climate
Change.

They were able to comprehend and come up with good discussion points, views and ideas
for topics 1 & 2 than topics 3 & 4. They also needed more information and clarification
on the cross-cutting issues but they were able to connect them well with the two main
topics.

The interesting part is when participants get to develop trigger questions for each
topics/issues. The participants come up with very simple question (i.e. who, what, where,
when, why & how) for each of the topics.

Learning objectives are then formed out of the trigger questions while at the same time
they will be used (o stir up discussion during the clan group discussion sessions.

The learning objectives are then distributed to each of the learning materials (print &
theatre/drama). Using the learning objectives print materials will be developed and
produced soon while the story lines and scripts for the theatre/drama programs have
already been developed by the participants

There will be a basic theater/drama skills training which will be facilitated by the UPNG
‘Theater Arts Strand in a few weeks time. So the story lines and scripts that the
participants developed will be used during the training. It is only a trial program and we
don’t know yet what the training will be like but we are hoping that the training will be
made simple and the methods/skills will be user friendly to the participants and will suit
the Managalas setting.

Acknowledgement

The team members would like to thank the following zones; Zones 4, 6, 8, 9, and 10 for
their hospitality and making sure the Patrol was a success. Acknowledgement is also
extended to the management of both Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) and
Partners with Melanesians (PWM) for the logistical arrangement and approval. Special
thank you to all the patrol team members especially the Desert Storm and its Commander;
your jokes, encouragement and support all throughout the patrol was great.

May the spirit of oneness reign on Managalas Plateau, and let us continue the fight to
safeguard and protect our home which is also home to the endangered and unique species of
plants and animals.

Executive Summary

‘This is the combined report of the Conservation Area border Patrol (1) for targeted zones as
per the 2010 MDF/PWM Combine Conservation work plan. In light to the Conservation
area Application procedure, a complete Boundary map of Managalas Conservation Arca
(MCA) is required by the concerned Government Departments. Therefore the need for a
patrol to the disputed and threatened areas was planned. The targeted or affected zones are
zones 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10.

Two Patrols will be done as agreed upon by both PWM and MDF Staff during their
combine planning workshop that was done in January 2010. As MDF, PWM and the people
cof Managalas are gearing up and preparing to submit their Application to the Government in
June this year 2010, these patrols are vital to see that all requirements are in place. This first
patrol is to confirm boundary gaps in the disputed areas and find ways to solve that and also
to find out about the status of the threatened areas. The second Patrol will be done following
the recommendations from this report.

Introduction

‘The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) is found in the Afore Local level
Government in Oro Province and covers a land area of about 360, 000 hectares. A Boundary
Map of any proposed Conservation Area is one of the main requirements of the Department
of Environment and Conservation. There are 18 ward councils found within the MPCA area
and over 150 clan groups which are then divided into 10 zones. From these 10 zones, there
are 5 Zones (Zone, 4, 6, 8, 9, and 10) with Boundary Dispute/ issues that had prevented the
mapping team to complete the Boundary of the Managalas Conservation Area, in 2005. To
tackle this, members of the patrol team were divided into two (Team | and team 2) and
visited the targeted zones.

Team I members are: Chrispine Burawa (Team leader), Edwin Noaka, Brian Kasira, and
Peter Sawari

Team 2 members are: Bradley Dabadaba (Team Leader), Jacinta Mimigari, Douglas Tumai,
and Malkus Kajia

Team 1 were assigned to Patrol areas on the Western flank of the Plateau, which are zones
(4, 10) while team 2 were assigned to the Eastern flanks of the plateau & 8 and 9)
excluding Gewoia, due to threats from that area. The teams departed on the 15" of February
2010 and returned back safely on the 25" of February at MDF base at Afore.

As PWM, MDF and the people of Managlas are in the process of submitting their
Conservation Area Application, such Boundary Patrols have to be done to see that all
requirements are met and that the communities are kept informed.

Found in this report also are recommendations, Action Plans and details of the Patrol.

Results and Patrol Brief

‘A briefing was held on the 14" of February 2010, before both teams set off for the Patrol.
During the briefing, patrol teams were reminded and each encouraged themselves on how to
constructively attend to possible sensitive issues that could be raised during the Patrol. Each
teams’ schedules were drawn up, food rations, logistics and patrol equipments were
distributed during the briefing. (See full briefing minutes in Appendix 3).

At the end of the patrol a combined debrief was organized again by the Conservation Patrol
Coordinator, Mr. Dabadaba for 1 whole day to allow both teams to highlight issues/
challenges identified during the border patrol. The briefing found out that most issues or
challenges identified by both teams were similar but few new issues were discovered. These

were the findings;

a) Land disputes and Boundary mapping of the gaps
Clan leaders and elders explained about the nature of the disputes, and discuss
amongst themselves how they can tackle this so as to complete the CA Boundary. It
was also realized that communities themselves have their own internal issues, but the
Patrol members made it clear to them that this is their own problems/issues to
handle.

In zone 6, Kingsford. N, who once worked on the mapping project, gave a brief
background history of the mapping work and the problems faced that hindered the
completion of the project. From that Recommendations were down.

b) Awareness on Reforestation, Reorganize clan groups, Land use plan and attend to
CBO’s issues.
During the meetings communities were informed about the selection criteria for
potential reforestation project sites. And if communities/clans are interested then
they should inform their CBO’s about that. The importance of land use plans were
explained also. MDF also took notes of the CBO’s issues raised by the communities
and advised the communities to organize and re-elect new board members and CBO
Staffs to make the CBO function effectively. The power to create an effective CBO
lies in each community. CBOs were also told to reorganize clan groups and all the
sub clans must remain under the main clans. Communities were encouraged to work
closely with their CBOs. It was encouraging to see Ward 5 council member present
at the meeting in Numba and communities present saw the importance of both
Government and NGO’s working together.
‘The communities were also advised that the above mentioned activi are all in the
work plan for 2010, and these activities will mostly be carried out by the CBO’s
therefore the CBO staff, board and community members need to reorganize
themselves in order to execute these activities.

Partners With Melanesians

“Uinta

PROGRAM: Conservation Component

ACTIVITY: Afore LLG Resolution: Workshop conducted by PWM & CELCOR to explain to
the councillors the CA processes and the procedures, Conservation Areas Act and the
advantages and disadvantages of a Conservation Area.

During the 2010 Christmas Holiday a team consisting of officers from PWM and CELCOR, went
up to the Managalas platcau to meet with the Afore LLG President and his 18 ward councillors. The
purpose of the mecting was to get clarification from them as to why the assembly had adjourned the
signing of the Conservation Area (CA) resolution to the end of 2011. Unfortunately, only three (3)
councillors and the President attended. During our meeting with them, the President advice the team
that they (Afore LLG) have prepared a resolution and issues that they want PWM to address. One
main issue is for PWM and its Partners to conduct more awareness to the councillors as majority do
not understand /) the CA procedures, 2) the advantages and disadvantages of a CA, and explain the
3) Conservation Area Act. Therefore, this workshop was an action taken to address the main issue
that the President pointed out above.

The purpose of this trip or workshop was to make awareness to the councillors on the above
mentioned areas so that they can be in a better position to make decision. In fact a similar workshop
‘was also conducted in April 2010.

Officers that went up for the workshop were
Kenn Mondiai, Damien Ase and Patrick Vuet.
Damien was late for the flight so he flew over the
following day. Kenn and 1 flew on the 11" of
May 2011 and were supposed to go straight up to
the project site (Afore), however, a block road
occurred at Eroro Village where the villagers cut
down two coconut trees to block the road. We
couldn't passed through so we over night at Oro
Guest House with two councillors (Remingius
Juharo & Abraham Tarabu) and Edrick Ninimiro
(PWM SLA Officer).

 ‘We travelled up to Managalas on the 12" of May.

We arrived at around 11 am at Afore. We started the program for that first day after lunch and
ended at Spm. As per the two days program, Patrick went through the CA processes and
procedures, update on the current status of the Conservation Area, and the activities that PWM,
MDP, the LLG and the communities will do after the Managaias Proposed Conservation Arca is
declared a Conservation Area.

Kenn Mondiai explained the terms used in the legend of the Forestry and mining overlay maps
that cover the Managalas area. He clarify to them the exploration licences within the proposed CA
and the logging activities that are slowly moving in passed the CA Boundary line.

After the day's sessions the floor was open for discussions. They raised some questions where both
PWM and MDF Staffs made clarification on.

The second day was the session for CELCOR & DEC Officers to go through the legal
Conservation Areas Act, the advantages and disadvantages of CA and the LLG's and other
stakeholder’s roles in the CA Act (CAA) and the MPCA Project. In day one Kenn also went
through some parts that DEC officers were assigned to stress on, because they were fully
committed and could not make it to this workshop.

Damien from CELCOR, explain to them the CAA, the roles of the LLG in the project, the threats
that will occur if not Managalas is declared a conservation Area, and the opportunities
forthcoming when Managalas is declared a conservation Area.

Nine ward councillors and two women

representatives, a few village chiefs,

MDF Board ‘members, a few CA

committees and CBO managers

attended the workshop; «wo other

councillors. who were also in full

support for the endorsement of the

B LLG resolution could not make it due

to bad weather condition. George King

(Ward 5 Councillor), asked Damien if

the Vice President can sign the LLG

support letter on behalf of the

President, Damien explained to. them

that there are legal processes that they

~~ need to follow if the President is being

stubborn to sign. After everything was explained to them, some of them commented that they are

in support for the signing of the ALLG support ietter, but it is the president that is prolonging
the process for reasons unknown.

Damien asked them to hold a special meeting now that the dead line for DEC is approaching to
sideline the project. The Vice President has to take the lead to draft a letter to the President
inviting him for the special meeting. If the President does not attend the special meeting, the Vice
President can chair the meeting. Minutes must be taken, the time, venue, and location must be
noted. PWM, CELCOR and MDF assisted the vice president to the draft the letter and signed by

 all the councillors that attended the workshop. Copies of the letter were distributed to the
councillors absent during the work shop, the Afore District Administrator, and the Afore LLG
Manager. Copy of the letter to the President is attached to this report.

The councillors set a date for the special meeting to be held on the 26" of May 2011. There will
only two agendas to be discussed in this meeting they are;

1, The endorsement of the Managalas Conservation Area Submission by Afore LLG.
2. The MOU between MDF, PwM and Afore LLG with the Oro Provincial Government
over the Conservation Area and activities thereafter.

‘The Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) Project Director is an obstacle to a smooth
progress of the project. Some councillors and the communities are not satisfying with the way the
MDF management is running the organization. There are counts of misappropriation of project
funds which have fragmented the working relationship between MDF and the community based
organizations (CBOs). Therefore; he needs to be terminated or suspended. This could be one of
the issues that are delaying the signing of the LLG Resolution.

Funding allocated for the Afore Local Level Government is not reaching the ward councillors.
‘Therefore, they want the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area to be declared and with
assistance from the NGOs would seek funding from donors to implement projects at their LLG
wards.

Some participants were commenting that the President be taken to court. Damien advised them to
take all necessary procedures at the local level to try and get the President sign. After exhausting
all necessary procedures then the President can be taken to court,

The team successfully carry out the activities as per the program. A few councillors who were
often against the NGO work were convinced and willing to support the Vice President to sign the
LLG endorsement letter.
