Dear Mr Thomas, SUB: BRIEF MEETING WITH PWM AND MDF ON THE PROPOSED MEETING WITH AFORE LGG PRESIDENT ON 12™ SEPTEMBER, 2014. A meeting wa
text:
6" September, 2014

Benside Thomas

Manager ~ Terrestrial Protected Areas,
Department of Environment and Conservation,
P.O. Box 6601,

Boroko, NCD,

Papua New Guinea.

Dear Mr Thomas,

SUB: BRIEF MEETING WITH PWM AND MDF ON THE PROPOSED MEETING
WITH AFORE LGG PRESIDENT ON 12™ SEPTEMBER, 2014.

A meeting was conducted on the 6" of September, 2014 at the Oro Guest House Conference
room. The meeting was attended by representative of PWM, MDF and myself (DEC).

Major concerns were raised by PWM and MDF that immediate actions need to be undertaken
with regard to the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project. This is because there is a
continuous and overwhelming support by the Managalas people to have their area conserved
afier the two east and west field coordinators conducted a one week zone to zone awareness from
27" of August to 2 of September, 2014.

PWM and | were briefed on the outcomes of the zone to zone awareness conducted which were
summarized as follows:

© All clans and community elders want to know why Afore LLG President is still against
Proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project and not allowing project activities to
proceed.

© The remap area is good and allow it to be declared as a CA

«The remap area to be mapped out clearly as some areas in zone 2, 5 and 6 will lose their
Jand when declared so remapping must include those that are not in the original remap
(Desktop).

© Clan and community elders asking Oro Governor, PWM and DEC why it has taken too
ong to declare Managalas as a CA since 2012.

© Those whose signatures forged want DEC, Damien and PWM to sue those who did that
and allow the court to deal with them.

«Clan and community elders want to know why they were not given the chance to speak in
the first consultation by DEC with Afore LLG President during their visit with Mr
 Damien Ase on 18" April, 2014 which was seen as an hijack process by the Afore LLG
president who also intimidated all his councilors to support him rather than CA.

Clan and community elders want to know why is Afore LLG President telling his ward
councilors to support him to go against CA and if those that does not support him will not
receive their ward funds.

Clan and community elders want DEC to be part of the team lead by MDF Board to
revisit Afore LLG president and get his views again on the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area Project and all its activities in the Managalas Plateau.

‘© Clan and community elders want DEC to present the remap areas to Afore LLG president
and let him decide and ask him that those majority who have agreed their areas to be
declared as CA in the remapped map wants their arcas declared as CA while he can do
whatever he wants with those that are carved out from the original Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area.

‘Clan and community elders expressed their views that they all respect him as a mandated
leader of the plateau and he must respect the wishes of having their areas declared in the

remapped map

We have concluded in the Popondetta meeting that there will be another combine visit to Afore
LLG President made up of MDF Board members, selected community reps and DEC to discuss
the following agendas:

President's current views on the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project
Remap of the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project
Results of a current zone to zone awareness patrol on both sides of the plateau (East and

West)
‘© Community Elder’s views on Proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project and the
results of the zone to zone awareness results
DEC views on the zone to zone awareness results
Way forward for Proposed Managalas Conservation Area Project

Finally the MDF Board members and Clan and their community elders have decided to make the
visit on Friday 12 September, 2014. Therefore I strongly recommend that as the Government
agency we should support them and be part of the team to revisit the President and address all the
issues above. Let us not fail them especially PWM and its donors have spent a lot of time and

This is praise item and on behalf of the PWM Board I take this
opportunity to thank PWM Admin and the MDF interim Board for
arranging this forum at Kokoro village. This is another opportunity to
bring people together around the plateau and also bring people from the
media to come out to the village and see For themselves and get report
to present to the print media for the leaders in the country to see and
help the concerns for the people in the Managalasi plateau.

Thank you Crispin Burava and Bradley for job well done to accommodate
people and toorganize people to Feed them during the forum. Thank you
all members of the Kokoro and Serefuna community who worked
together to look after people who came to the Forum.

A big thank you to the media team who took time out From their busy
schedule and willing to come to the remote villages in Barai. Especially
the representative from DEC Mr David Kau who was happy to be with us
out there in the village to respond to peoples questions.

Then Finally the MDF Chairman Mr Malcus Kajia who lead the staff of MDF
and the community From Namiai dialect to host this forum for Four
days. Once again thank you for every bit of work done to make this
forum a successful forum.
 Logistics work

The people began arriving at Kokoro village on the 2" November 2014 where
they were accommodated by the community members from Kokoro and Serefuna
villages. Arrangement was for people to eat in their houses and eat together only
for lunch and dinner in the central place in the community.

The facilitators Crispin Burava from the West and Bradley from the East worked
together with the community members to get people there in time for the forum.
There were would have been a big traditional welcome in Kokoro community how
ever there were two deaths in Kokoro village just few weeks before the forum. So
the welcome was only arranged by Elementary school children to bring people
into the community. Thank you Kokoro Elementary school teachers and the
children for participating in this forum.

There were groups set aside that helped and did all the logistics work in the
community. The officers from Port Moresby were placed in homes where people
cared for them. We ate our breakfast in homes where we stayed but ate lunch
and dinner together in the one place. The clan groups and participants for the
forum did the same and ate lunch and dinner together separately from the officers
from PWM and the DEC and media from Port Moresby.

Thank you facilitators for involving the church leaders to share Word to encourage
people about the importance of conservation. The challenge was to manage
Gods creation and know him better and seek his wisdom to manage his creation.
 Day 1

The forum on the first day began at 9.30 am with a word of prayer and devotion
was led by George Isurufa from Kokoro village.

Devotion

The reading was taken from Prov: 3:1-6 to encourage the people of the plateau to
be good managers of the God’s resources in the world as well as the blessings in
the Managalasi plateau.

He also quoted from the Gospel John:10:10 to challenged the members of all
clan leaders and the people of Managalsi plateau that thieves comes to steal and
Destroy but Jesus came to give life in full.

We are to have him in our lives to give us the wisdom and guidance through his
Spirit to manage his resources.

The facilitator Crispin Burava continued and welcomed every one for coming to
the forum. He then explained to the clan leaders and the participants the purpose
of the forum.

1. This forum is a follow up of the last forum hosted by the Ugunomo
community last year November 2013.
a. Managalasi plateau to be conserved as a conservational area in the
Afore district Oro province.
b. Then discussion of the new remapped area for Managalasi Plateau

This was the first kind of forum that the facilitators allowed leaders from the church
to share the Word that was related to conservation. The passages shared were
all about the creation and the work delegated to us to manage them.
 Apologies

Then Remenge’s the clan leader and the councillor from Kawowoki apologised
the forum on behalf of that the people in the west near Sakarina. The people may
not attend the forum because they are attending another meeting for the newly
opened high school at Sakarina. They all knew that the topics for this forum are
the same discussed in the last forum at Ugonomo in November last year 2013.

The ward councillor from Kavovoki said the people in Sakarina area sent their
apology that they will not attend the forum at Kokoro because they are attending
the a High School meeting in Sakarina. They sent their apology but they are all in
favour for the whote Managalasi area to be conserved. He aiso said, what ever
decision the forum make to set date and venue for declaration, they will agreed
and work forward to the date for declaration.

He also said the High School for the district is one of the big needs so they are
attending the meeting to discuss and distribute work load for churches and people
in the communities to participant and complete work in the short time frame give.
This is one of the development in the district and so conservation for the
Managalasi plateau is a urgent need in plateau.

Alban Varure and Emmanuel Garava were there from Popondetta representing
the LLG President to observe in the forum. So Alban apologise the forum that the
LLG President Hon: Douglas Garava will not be in the forum because of the issue
related to the Oro Governor Hon: Mr. Garry Juffa in Popondetta.
 First topic For the forum.
Crispin Burava then introduced the first topic for the forum:
Agenda 1: CA for Managalasi plateau for more discussion again.

The five councillors who attended the forum spoke strongly that and supported by
the clan leaders that we do not want to our area or district be divided again
because of the conservation. We want to call ourselves Afuruve people meaning
that we are people who live and work together as one people and so conservation
the Managalasi area will hold us together as one people.

Hon: Mr Brian Kasira who is the ward councillor for ward 14 and the founder of the
MDF project in the Managalasi plateau spoke strongly that, We the Managalasi
people do agreed that the Managalasi area be conserved. There should not be
any more forum on conservation because we all agreed in our first forum in Tama
that our 360 hectors of our Managalasi area must be conserved. We do not want
any outsiders to influence us and take our land for their own benefit by logging or
mining in the plateau.

He said that the work that he started must bring benefit to the people of
Managalasi. But why is one person making it difficult for us to make our 360
hectors of our land to be conserved. This is unfair for one person to stop the
change that the majority want it to take place in the plateau.
 The people were sent out again to their clan groups discussion on the same topic
reported back to the forum that they all were happy to see their area be
conserved. The discussion on the CA took us to the end of the day

The facilitator told the forum to go and talk more and come back with fresh mind
next morning and give their last comments before moving into other agendas.
Then he dismissed and closed the forum for the day at 3.30 pm.

Day 2 continues the First days topic on CA.

On the second day the question was raised about the ILG because the council
president Mr .Garava wants to see ILG done first before going into the CA.

iin

After few comments of ILG and the CA Mr. George Tumai one of the founder of
MDF told that forum that we have come iong way seeking CA deciaration so in
this forum date should be set for us coming together for celebration. Then he
strongly supported Hon: Brian that there should not be any more forum for this
same agenda CA. Then he referred question to PWM and DEC to explain where
is the hold up in the process.

Alban Varure and Emmanuel Garava were sent by the LLG President to observe
the forum. So they travelled by road on his vehicle and arrived there on Tuesday
morning and attended the discussions for Tuesday. Alpban mentioned that this is
‘one of his priority for the people in the Managalasi plateau before CA.
 Tom from the PWM Board was very helpful to explain the different between ILG
and the CA. Tom explained that the ILG is not yet because we need to get the
whole area conserved first and come down to the clan and family groups to talk
about ILG. That is the next lot of work that we need to do and we are not to jump
over the first step. The Afore LLG President needs to know that CA must take
place first. If we give the priority to the ILG then the whole area will not be
conserved and that is not safe. ILG is all about small clan groups and family trees
to really see where you belong and do the ILG. So that will come about later when
the CA is done.

Then David from DEC explained the steps that people go through to get their
areas ready before conserved. All the decisions are made from the community
and clan groups level and not from the National Government of Department of
Environment and conservation. People are the owners of land and the
Government will not make any decision with the land owners.

There are several areas that we will need to go through to get our area conserved.
The Department of Environment and Conservation can not give okay for
declaration. But he can work with the people concern like the LLG president and
the provincial level Government to Government to get this area conserved.

After the long talk he said he heard their concern and he will take it from there to
the Government level to see that the people cry can be heard by the leaders at
different level in the LLG level and in the provincial level.

In this forum the main people who spoke strongly and wanted to see the area
conserved were the councillors and the Former Regional member for National
Parliament Mr .Benson Garui.

Agenda 2: Topic was on Remapping.

After the morning break the second agenda was introduced in the forum. Crispin
Burava the facilitator from the west showed the copied of the remapped area and
told the forum to their clan groups and discuss the on this agenda and report to

Not much was discussed on this agenda because many of the clan leaders

We are people working and deciding and listening together and that is what Afore
really means in the language . If one man is making a decision to divide our

The five Ward Councillors who were there in the forum totally agreed and spoke

us as one district and people of Afore.
 Benson added that this forum is not about the remapping but it is about deciding
date to declare the Managalasi area as a conserved area. We are not here to talk
about division but to decide for unity and CA is a good fence for the Managalasi
people. If there is one leader like our LLG President tries to divide our people then
he needs to attend this kinds of forum and explain to the people his reasons.
Good leaders are for people to work together and see there is unity and peace in
the communities.

The women representatives also gave their views to support the discussion for CA
for Managalasi plateau. The ladies who were cooking and did not have time to
attend the forum gave their input for CA for Managalasi plateau. Already different
individuals are flooding into the Afore district and influencing young people
especially girls and so to protect our people CA is one of the ways to start ina
smaller way to protect our people.

| (Simon Savaiko) added that CA is not just for the land but the people and

languages for each tribes for better communication. Languages are where the
culture is and we need to reserve the languages for better communication to
understand why we are doing conservation in the Managalasi plateau.

 Naming of all plants and animals and reptiles and birds etc are very important.
Next year there will be a huge amount of literacy work in the plateau to do more

These topics came from the discussion that people had in forum so they were
parked away and later brought it out for discussion at AOB.

I, Simon Savaiko took this as a big issue for the churches and the

the forum to own this issue and put in the first list to see that the

this reconciliation event. This is part of the healing process for healing

churches must take the lead in working with our political leaders

 Reactivation of MDF work in the Managalasi plateau.

After listening to different views from clan leaders and ward councillors the forum

The MDF interim Chairman Malcus explain that one of the reasons for this

George Tumai the clan leader for Uva and the former Board member to PWM also

text:
DRAFT

The District Wide Forum Report 12" November 2014

Managalas plateau in the Afore district is the last sanctuary for the largest butterfly in the
world, the Queen Alexandra Birdwing butterfly. Along the foot of the ower Stanley range so
called developments in the form oil palm plantations clear large amount of virgin rainforest
to plant small amount of trees. A seedling needs a space of 10cubic square meter so in a 100
hectare plot a mere 100 trees are planted which is too much space for less production
unlike the cocoa and coffee trees. And so as the plantation slowly eats up the jungle slope
50 too did these unique species endemic to this region eventually head up high to settle in
the cooler plains of this beautiful valley.

Unlike the people living along the main highway, here the people of the Afore LLG have a
different mindset. They want their rugged vegetation only to be used by them and their
generation. But in a corporate world where global economy fights to take over everything,
the simple people wage a losing battle. There only hope of salvation is through
internationally recognized nationally declared conservation area projects. Only then can
their efforts be protected from outside manipulation.

Over twenty years ago PwM an NGO who with the support and financial assistance of
international donors such as from the Rainforest Foundation of Norway (RFN) have pushed
and prodded, slaved and paved their way through sometimes hostile environment to
promote conservation and sustainable development awareness to the Afore people
including facilitating the eight CA steps in the process. Until now the Managalas
Conservation Area Project (MCAP) application is in the gazettal stage to be validated by the
Department of environment and Conservation (DEC).

Introduction

My name is Talitha Kove and | am a freelance writer. | was engaged by PWM to cover the
annual District wide forum of the people of the Managalas plateau in the Afore LLG of oro
province. The event was held from the 3 to the 7" of November 2014 in Kokoro village of
the ijvitari electorate. The forum is that time of the year where community leaders of the
different zones along with their ward councilors gather to appraise and evaluate the years
end progress of their respective areas. Addressing issues and discussing ways to best go
about in help solving them. The two main issues this year were;

1. Department of environment and conservation (DEC) and Afore Local Level
Government (ALLG) to respond to the status of the Conservation Area (CA)
 2. Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) and Community Based Organizations
(C80) work programs to resume.

‘The forum was a success; the most important agenda on top of the list was the people's
vehement demand for the declaration of the CA. The three days of open discussion saw
some women and youth reps present who also contributed to the group talk times. On the
last day of session everyone was happy and there was a general concession on the
outcomes and the recommendations presented.

PURPOSE

When an application for a proposed CA is in its gazettal stage awaiting validation, a 90 day
window period is allowed for any matter pertaining to the project site can be raised within
this timeframe. Any concerns, any loopholes and any grievances this is the time they will be
considered. In November 2012 the governor of Oro Province Garry Juffa on behalf of the
majority of the Managalas people presented the CA application to the DEC Minister.
Unbeknownst to them, a small faction of the east side community was also compiling their
objection letter to stay the project. This group of clan elders along with the LLG president
claim that the purported CA application may have the majority’s support but does not
represent the whole community's view on the proposed 360 000 hectares. Thus the CA has
come to a halt. The last remaining years has been dedicated to consultation processes.
Trying to find loopholes and how best to address this issue of the objection letter. My task in
this forum was to

DAY ONE SESSION ~ DEC & LLG RESPONDS TO CA STATUS.

Day one session saw the DEC and Afore LLGs respond to the status of the CA. The forum
asked the DEC and Afore LLG to update on the delay of the process. DEC representative
David Kau explained that the objection letter has delayed the process. DEC has no power to
endorse when the LLG president has said no because is a mandated protocol that cannot be
bypassed. Therefore DEC's presence here was only through an observation and advisory
role.

‘The forum then asked an LLG rep for the president to tell the people of his view. The
representative- Alban said he is only here to observe and deliver the president's message via
a phone text stating that CA is non-negotiable and only the ILG can be discussed within Clan
elders. When pressed to elaborate on the message Alban digressed stating that he’s sole
purpose was to deliver the message and nothing more.

This caused confusion among the participants as ILG or incorporated Land Group was a new
concept to them and others were not yet ready to listen. The main priority right now was
the CA. All participants who spoke strongly demanded that twenty eight years is a very long
time to be waiting for the project. They want it declared so that they can move on to doing
 other little projects to sustain their livelihoods. The CA would act as a “banis” to protect
them from outside manipulation. One local leader Newton Kasiri gave a classic example of
the African people who drink from the same waterhole as the wild animals. He urged the

 MANAGALAS people demand for Conservation. by Talitha Kove

Papua New Guinea is one of the last remaining countries in the twenty first
century whose people still own and live off the land. Its landmass is covered
with thick impenetrable rainforest and wild rugged terrains, its biodiversity
flourishing right to the treetops with a wide variety of fauna and flora. It is a
scientist wonderland where the discovery of new species are inevitable and
most often its endemic uniqueness a certainty.

One such place is the Managalas plateau situated high up between the dividing
ranges of the central and oro provinces. The Plateau is home to about 20000
people under the Afore Local Level Government (LLG) in the ijivitari electorate.
This high plain has become the last sanctuary for the largest butterfly in the
World, the Queen Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly (QABB), which is also the

provincial emblem endemic only to Oro.

However, along the foot of the Owen Stanley Range developments such as oil
palm plantations have slowly eaten up the jungle slope destroying their homes
causing this beautiful insects to flee upwards into the plateau. Unlike those
living along the highway people the Managalas people have a different
mindset. They want their virgin vegetation only to be used by them and their
generation. But in a corporate world where global economy fights to take over
everything, the simple people wage a losing battle. Their only hope of salvation
is through internationally recognized nationally declared conservation area
projects. Only then can their efforts be protected from outside manipulation.

Over twenty years ago Partners with Melanesians Inc. (PwM) an NGO who with
support and financial assistance of international donors such as the Rainforest
Foundation of Norway (RFN) have pushed and prodded, slaved and paved their
way through sometimes hostile environment to promote conservation and
sustainable development awareness to the Afore people including facilitating
the eight Conservation Area (CA) steps in the process. In 2012 their efforts for
the Managalas plateau to be conserved paid off when the Governor of Oro on
behalf of his people presented the CA application to the Minister of the
Department of Environment and Conservation.
 Unbeknownst to them a small faction of the east side community led by the
president of the Afore LLG raised an objection letter staying the project. They
claim that the purported CA application may have the majority's support but it
did not represent the whole community’s view on the 360 000 hectares
proposed. A week long district wide forum held at Kokoro village on the 3° to
the 7" of November 2014 saw the people discuss ways on how to best address
this issue.

Everyone who attended the forum vehemently demanded the Managalas
Conservation Area Project (MCAP) to be declared. They stressed that twenty
eight years is a long time to be waiting for the declaration. There are other
projects that they would like to pursue but wanted to be assured that the
conserved area can be protected from outside manipulation.

Tom Huasi a member of PWM board of directors and one of the surviving
project initiators paid tribute to those who had passed on and hopes that
before the rest go they would love to see their project (MCAP) fulfilled. “You
must take ownership. It is for your future generation.” He said.

Newton kasiri a local leader supported Mr.Huasi, by giving an example where
some parts of Africa humans share the same waterhole with the animals.
“Don’t let others take away your rights. You must fight for your rights now
otherwise we will lose our land and become like these Africans.” He said.

The Afore LLG president has refused to comment. He has not responded to the
two letters of invitation sent to him by the forum requesting his presence. The
forum has asked if Department of environment and Conservation can help
liaise with the Afore LLG on their behalf and set aside a date.

 Barai women in Literacy workshop report
27" -29" Dec 2017.
Summary.

This is the kind of workshop that the Barai ladies have been struggling to attend to get
help for their fluency classes. It came to the right time where this workshop was conducted
in Itokama village in the Barai tribe to encourage the women in literacy in the Barai
language. That is where all thirty three (33) Barai ladies representing two tribes in the
Barai speaking area who attended the workshop. For them this is just the beginning of
many workshops yet to happen in the Managalasi plateau to encourage women in the
area of Life Long Learning for women in that has been neglected for years.

This workshop brought vibration in the lives of ladies in the two tribes to see beyond
women’s future. Women in the plateau are always seen as house wives and cargo
carriers and this workshop highlighted their minds and hearts to see beyond opportunity
ahead of them. The workshop opened their minds to have vision beyond grade six (6) or
grade eight (8) in the Primary schools. There is great opportunity for women in the Life
Long Learning in the village level They need to start from their own language to be fluent
before learning outside ideas and ways to make right decisions for their communities in
the plateau. The name literacy now called as Life Long Learning will help them to accept
what is good for better transformed communities in the tribe.

| take this opportunity to thank Managalasi Conservation Foundation (MCF) who
authorized PWM to release Literacy Fund for us to conduct this four days workshop for the
women in literacy in BNEA training centre at Itokama village. This is just the beginning of
many more good materials production workshop for the Barai adult fluency classes to
have more books to read about conservation and other helpful information from outside.

In this workshop the production of materials began with a book on conservation of land
and the garden food that the women plant. Then the book also quoted related scriptures
from Genesis where the students learned about what the Scripture says about
management of ail that God created. These stories brought excitement for more of this
workshop to produce more books to encourage women to study about creation. They also
were encouraged to do more to see some can be good writers of stories of the forest in
their plateau in their own languages.

Managalsi ladies are hard working ladies but they are always neglected and do not get
them involve in workshops and leadership like Life Long Learning. This kind of workshops
motivated women to have voice and to play leadership role in the village starting from
literacy classes. It was amazing to see the number of women who turned out for this
workshop and how they show their interest in the workshop.

In their the officials closing, Mrs, Ritha Bania expressed her concern on behalf of the
jadies and urged the fathers and husbands to help their wives and mothers to be involve
in Life Long learning to qualify them to play leadership role in the tribe. Women have
 supported men for many years and men has dropped some of these opportunities. So this
‘is an opportunity for men to give the women chance to start with Life Long learning. Thank
you for the support to send women to the course and may you continue to encourage
__ them to apply what they have learnt in the workshop. That will help them to start playing
their leadership role in a small way in the village level.

~ The workshop
The women met next day, on Tuesday after our arrival on Monday to have closing
ceremony for the Women in literacy for the year 2016. Then before they went home they
agreed to meet again for the workshop straight after Christmas Day 27" Dec 2017 at
Itokama in BNEA classroom. Then they all went home on after the closing of the work for
> the year.
Then on Tuesday 27" after Christmas all women met for the literacy workshop at BNEA.
The workshop was officially declared opened with few remarks by the MCF Manager
Dickson Darebo. The literacy workshop lusted for only four days at BNEA classroom.

~The workshop started with thirty three women all Barai the two different dialect the Birare
and Namiai tribes. The four day teachers in service workshop was conduct in BNEA
centre. Most women from outside of Itokama village stayed with families in Itokama village
for the workshop. It was a busy time but the women really made commitment to stay away
from families for four days to attend the workshop. Many of them were all women leaders

eo

from all villages in Barai speaking area.

a ee
The workshop was planned for only fifteen women leaders to do teachers in service
however there were many other women who were interested to take teachers training
course. So | extended the schedule to fit the request made by all participants by adding
materials production with teachers training. That is why we started with materials
production and finished with teachers training with materials related to conservation.

 Each one of those women trainers from seven villages were already conducting Adult
fluency classes at home. Five of the villages who were conducting classes came to stop

during the planting season while Tama and Itokama continued to the end of the year. In

the workshop they reported their concern and needs of materials and support from the

men.

Material production:

In the workshop women listed all their issues in the communities and put them into
priorities. Amongst the many very high priority (25) issues they decided to take
conservation. The women were divided into five different groups to develop stories on kind
of food they grow in their gardens. That is to help them with easy stories where they knew
the best and can handle well before going into harder stories. The women developed thirty
three short stories in their own Barai language about food they grow. Many of them plant
all these vegetables in gardens but when it came to writing stories it was amazing to see
how they struggled to put into words. Many of them struggled to write in the same way as

_ they speak about kinds of food they grow in their gardens in Barai area. The translators
George and Dunston Unini helped them to edit their stories. Time could not allow us for
printing all three books so taken to Moresby for printing.

Practice teaching:

Then we printed 120 copies of book prepare in Port Moresby for the workshop on what
Bible says about conservation in Genesis the teachers guide. Then we used the book for
practice teaching adult fluency classes in Barai. On the third day after the demonstration
in the afternoon all women got into their groups again and started practice teaching using
the book on conservation.

There were three levels of needs that the women brought to the workshop. The beginner's
need that related to children and even adults while others have needs for adult fluency.
~The fluency was a big priority because they need fluency in understanding and reading
and writing. Amazing to see how women can read fast and if were were giving 100% for
students in the class, almost 75% of women in the class can read well and fast. But for
fluency in understanding is almost 35% of women in the class could understand well what
they read. But the great needy part was the fluency in writing could almost be 10-15% of
participants in the class would creatively write well. So there is a great need for literacy or
 long life learning in the Managalasi plateau. We need a good literacy survey to see the
real literacy need in the Managalasi plateau to help RFN to see why their support is

) All women showed great interest and took seriously to learn the best ways to teach
classes in their own villages to encourage women. This training has encouraged many
women to see beyond 2017 to see that many of those ministries in the Barai area are to

many of the projects in the Barai area come to stop. Women in literacy is the way to raise
women up to another level because people see them as house wives and also men’s

DISCUSSION

RECOMMENDATIONS

 1.0 Introduction

Awareness is one phase of education that introduce the conservation project and the activity carried
out by Partners with Melanesians and Karimui Conservation and Resource Management
Programme Inc. People who are aware won't be able to do anything until they understand from the
project activity that carried out by PWM and KCRMPI because not much information had given at
that time. The local are highly encouraging video show to be carried out for the people to see and
Jeam by themselves. However the current situation on the ground will be also assess during the
awareness activity. The awareness activity have presented in the form of video show as it had
recommended in 2016 awareness activity report and the Rainforest Literacy programme on identify
and strengthening of medium of communication in Karimui area

2.0 Purpose

The aim of the video show is to motivate people on the conservation project through invoking
emotion like; happiness; joy; worry; fear/fright; anger; and outrage. Also to inform them on the
work PWM and KCRMPI are doing with their roles and responsibilities.

Apart from that, the current situation on the ground related to 2017 general election will be also
assess basing on the cooperation and interest of people on the conservation activity.

 1.0 Introduction

‘The vegetation of the Managalas Platcau is largely pristine forests comprising of lowland,
upland and montane forests. These forests are intersected by many creeks and rivers that
form the main catchment for the Bariji and Musu Rivers. Coarse scale analysis of land-
use threats, species concentration and endemism, catchment pollution, forest
defragmentation and habitat lost places whole plateau ecosystem as High Conservation
Value Forest (Partners with Melanesia (PwM), 2004). Through conservation awareness
programs initiated and run by PwM within the plateau, the villagers have decided to
conserve their forests. The villagers have formed a core group; the Managalas
Development Foundation (MDF), that will work in partnership with PwM to develop
conservation strategies for the area.

In November 2004, a preliminary biodiversity survey on the plants, birds, mammals and
herpetofauna were conducted by a team of scientists from the University of Papua New
Guinea and the Department of Environment and Conservation. Samplings (plants and
animals) were conducted over 14 days (II effective sampling days) in forests around
Itokama Government Station. General observations on biodiversity were conducted
around villages of Iiokama, Kuai and Nibaiba.

The Managalas Plateau is predorminantly composed of four major forest types: low
altitude forest on uplands, lower montane forest, iow altitude forest on plains and fans,
and savanna. ‘The MPCA is largely covered by low altitude forest on uplands below

 1000m, and lower montane forest on high lands above 1000 m. Also, small scattered
forests of low altitude forest on plains and fans which were found to be predominant

below 1000 m.

‘The vegetation types of the proposed Managalas CA are fragile forests and of biodiversity
importance comprised the low altitude forest on plains and fans, the lower montane
forest, and savanna. The dominant forest types are the forest on plains and fans, and the
lower montane forest which cover more than 75 percent of the MPCA. The lowland
forest and Jower montane forests are predominant and extend to areas where rainfall
exceed 1800 mm per annum, and at higher altitudes with decreasing temperature
respectively (Bleeker, 1983). The lowland forest is structurally and floristically the richest
and typically contains numerous palms, vines and climbers on well drained alluvial
plains. However, in very poorly drained to swampy conditions, sago and pandanus are
found in the understorey.

 6.0 Discussion
6.1 Vegetation

Forest formations in the proposed Managalas largely reflect the geology, topographic.
edaphic and climatic conditions in the area. Within the Itokama area the forest types
display very unique sets.of features. In a broad sense, the general forest zonation appears
irregular. Although the forest type resembles tropical lowland forest observation on
surrounding hills shows that undifferentiated stands occur and are influenced by

topography.

Certain features, characteristic to lower montane formation become obvious at around
700m asl. The presence of Castanopsis accuminatissima and even Lithocarpus and
Dacrydium in the forests at Jarefa and towards the villages of Nibaiba und Kuai indicate
low montane elements. Large woody lianas. plants with compound leaves, cauliflorous
plants, and species of Myristica which are typical features of lowland and lowland hill
forests (Whitmore 1975) become scarce at Jarefa.

By comparison, forest adjacent to Barije River zepresents typical lowland forest with
abundant plants possessing compound leaves. cauliflory and large lianas. Coramon
lowland species of Elmerrillia, Aglaia. Dysoxvlum. Elaeocarpus, Sterculia. Cryptocarya,
and Terminalia abundant.

6.1.2 Status of Plants.

Currently there are no proper assessmenis on the status of plant species in Papua New
Guinea. The only plants that have received much attention and included in the CITES list
are members of the Orchid family. Although only few orchid specimens were collected,
both epiphytic and ground orchids were abundant especially at the Jarefu forest.

With the collection (Appendix 2) further determination is needed to verify the correct
specimens. However. there is a high probably some of the specimens collected might be

 7.0 FOREST USE

The local people depend heavily on plants and forest resources for their livelitioog. Plants
provide them with basic necessities like medicines, food, poisons, raw materials for house
constiuction, shelters, canoes, crafts and tools and numerous other minor forest products.
Furthermore, forests collectively act as a reservoir for plants. germplasm base and a gene
pool and, provide refuge for game and other animals. With limited access to essential
services plant resources thus become a life support base for the local people. It is
worthwhile therefore to record the different plant and their uses of the area. Some plants
and animals used by the locals were recorded during the survey and the list will be
provided in the full report.

Trees and poles are readily available as raw materials for general construction purposes,
but the locals traditionally use few selected species. The heartwood of Fagrea sp. for
instance, provide good posts for houses while secondary species such as Macaranga
aleuritioides, and Homalanthus sp., provide materials for knobs and raflers of houses.
Stems of palm trees and bamboos are conveniently split and spread for purposes of walls
or floors in house construction.

1.0 Introduction

The vegetation of the Managalas Plateau is largely pristine forests comprising of lowland,
hill and montane foresis. The forests are intersected by many creeks and rivers that form
the main catchment for the Bariji and Musu Rivers. A rich diversity of fauna and flora are
supported by these forest types. Oil Palm development, and subsistence agriculture are
posing great threats to these pristine forests. The villagers within the plateau have decided
to conserve their forests and are seeking assistance from Partners with Melanesia (PwM)
to develop their conservation initiatives. The villagers have formed a core group; the
Managalas Development Foundation (MDE). that wil work in partnership with Pw
develop the conservation strategies for the area.

In November 2004, preliminary biodiversity survey on the plants, birds, maitnals and
herpetofiuna were conducted by a team of scientists. Samplings (piants and animals)
were conducted over i4 days (11 days effective sampling periods) in uphill forests of
Jarifa near Kam creek. General observations on biodiversity were conducted around
villages of Itokama, Kuai and Nibaiba.

This report highlights the summary of the survey. A more detailed report of the survey
will be provided after thorough synthesis of the data. Note samplings were concentrated
in one area representing only a small fraction of the whole proposed Managalas Plateaz
Conservation Area.

Crxptocarva, Sioanea, Castanopsis, Spxygiun, Weinmania and Elasocarpus. On ridges
mixed Castanopsis forest predominates with canopy reaching up to 35m tal. Casanopsis

accuminatissima is the dorainant tree species in this forest type. Disturbed forests also
form minor formations within the area and are represented by early regrowth, secondary

and advanced secondary forests. The frequently disturbed riverine forest forms a narrow
strip along the rivers.

4.0 Mammals and Herpetofauna

Fifty five specimens of rats and bats were collected after 440 net and trapping nights over
11 working nights. In total twenty-three (23) specimens of rodents were captured and
thirty two (32) specimens of bats were collected. After measurements were taken
seventeen (17) bats, all Syconycteris australis were released. Of those, eight (8) species of
rodents were trapped and 3 species of bats were netted. A colony of 5 of the large Forbes
tree mouse were captured when the villagers chopped down the tree they were living in.
The colony of 5 rodents are now kept alive at the Museum of the University of Papua
New Guinea. Details are all given in Table 2.

Although, our netting and trapping nights did not produce any marsupials we observed
three (3) species of marsupials at different times of the survey. That included a juvenile
southern brown cuscus that was kept as a pet after the mother was killed for consumption,
Dorias tree Kangaroo was also kept as a pet by a family after the mother was also
captured and consumed. During the period of the survey, villagers captured three (3)
forest wallabies, which were later consumed (refer to Table 2).

4.1 Wild dog (Canis Familiaris dingo):
The presence of the wild dog was confirmed when a half-crunched bird was left hanging
in the lower shelve of the mistnet in the undercroft of Pandanus trees. Villagers insisted
that this could not have been left behind by domestic dogs but wild dogs

4.2 Reptilia:
Most of our efforts were concentrated on mammals and not on reptiles and frogs.
However, over the 11 working days our chance - collection and observations resulted in
thirteen (11) specimens of reptiles and frogs. Of those thirteen specimens, three (3)
species of reptiles (2 pythons and a keelbacked snake) were seen. The two species of
pythons were captured by villagers and eaten, while the Keel-backed snake was seen at
the Camp site, The other eleven (11) species (4 frogs & 8 reptiles) were collected with the
help of the villagers and taken as specimens. The frogs comprise of two ground frogs of
the same species, one hylid and one ranid (refer to Table 2).

4.3 Domesticated animals:
Domestic animals were seen in the villages. Of the three, domestic dog, pussy cat and
chicken, dogs and cats can have an influence on the presence of wildlife. Both dogs and
cats are kept as pets but villagers seemed to keep dogs especially for hunting. From our
investigation, it seemed that dogs were kept for hunting more than as pets.

Wild animals were also captured and kept as pets to be sold later of for consumption. A
Doria's Tree kangaroo was kept as a pet after the mother was killed several years ago. In
another house, a juvenile southern brown cuscus was also kept as a pet but later escaped.

5.0 FOREST USE

‘The local people depend heavily on plants and forest resources for their livelihood. Plants
provide them with basic necessities like medicines, food, poisons, raw materials for house
construction, shelters, canoes, crafts and tools and numerous other minor forest products.
Furthermore, forests collectively act as a reservoir for plants, germplasm base and a gene
pool and, provide refuge for game and other animals. With limited access to essential
services plant resources thus become a life support base for the local people. It is
worthwhile therefore to record the different plant and their uses of the area. Some plants
and animals used by the locals were recorded during the survey and the list will be
provided in the full report.

‘Trees and poles are readily available as raw materials for general construction purposes,
but the locals traditionally use few selected species. The heartwood of Fagrea sp. for
instance, provide good posts for houses while secondary species such as Macaranga
aleuritioides, and Homalanthus sp., provide materials for knobs and rafters of houses.
Stems of palm trees and bamboos are conveniently split and spread for purposes of walls
or floors in house construction.

6. GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS

Several factors were evident from the survey that support the conservation initiatives
undertaken by the local people.

‘© The forest types, and the distribution of plant species are strongly influenced by the
prevailing environmental conditions. In effect this means that the vegetation is quite
unique and presents windows of opportunities for long term scientific studies on this
forest ecosystems.

The apparent lack of regeneration or recruitment of trees to larger size classes requires
proper studies.

plication of past geological events on the present vegetation formations is an
factor and further research would help to explain its effect and impact on
biodiversity.

© Due to the lack of proper infrastructure, the people of Managalas rely heavily on
plants and other forest resources for their basic needs. Destruction of these forests
would reduce the resource base of these plants and their products and may affect the
local inhabitants.

© The Araucaria hunsteinii trees represent a historical time scale. Dendroclimatology
studies in New Zealand have established time periods of similar soft wood species
dating several thousand years back into the past. The remnant trees within the
 Managalas Plateau present good prospects to study past cli
influences on vegetation

tic changes and thei

Standing forests act as carbon sinks. With respect to global warming, it would de
interesting to know the carbon sequestration potential of these forests by carrying out
appropriate studies.

Given the uniqueness of the forests and the resources contained therein, outside
institutions, researchers, and tourists would certainly want to visit the area. To prepare
for such influx, the landowners through PwM can draw up sets of conditions and
guidelines that would protect the pristine forest and at the same time generate income
for the forest owners.

10
 7, RECOMMENDATIONS

Given the uniqueness of the forests within the conservation area, we highly recommend
that the forest be conserved. The followings are offered for guidance.

Proper tramping tracks into the forest or important sites such as camping or resting
sites be identified then design to allow minimal disturbance.

The pine is a tree of scientific and historical significance. Scattered stands of these
species should be identified and mapped out, both, within and outside the proposed
conservation area and these areas be protected.

The mixed Castanopsis forest is very sensitive to human disturbances. Conversion of
this forest type to grassland is already a common feature in the Highlands of Papua
New Guinea. It is strongly recommended that these stands be conserved.

Proper records of plant animal uses be established. This requires someone with good
knowledge of traditional beliefs and rituals to be able to readily access traditional
knowledge.

Proper methodology or experiment must be designed to optimally assess the ecology
of the area. This should also encompass a full botanical reconnaissance survey of the
area, Permanent study plots be established and consistently monitored.

Establish research collaboration with known research organizations like FRI, CRI,

Wau Ecological Institute, and UPNG, so that research can be conducted in the area to
generate more knowledge on the ecology of the forest communities.

  Facilitator Trainings

Facilitator training alongside materials development are the comerstones of all the
Rainforest Literacy activities.

Facilitator trainings enables the workshop participants, themselves, to identify the
skills and abilities of a good group facilitator. The objective was to develop local
ownership for what facilitator training is all about

A good community group facilitator:
is motivated to try and capture the collective wisdom of the group

© isnot a bossy, know-it-all type of person

+ is able to sense different kinds of personalities and is able to draw out opinions
from everyone in the groups

© does not feel the need to present his or her own opinions from everyone in the
groups

«is able, at the conclusion of the group’s discussion, to put together a summary
statement expressing that opinion that was widely held across the group

‘should be able to read and write but does not necessarily need any high
educational qualifications

* avoids setting himself up in a position of importance at the front of the group, i.e.
Joins the other s in a circle, situation himself at the same level as the others.
‘Avoids using tables or a podium that separates himself from the others.

‘+ is responsible and demonstrates his or her commitment to the group

Is able to restrain outspoken members of the group who tend to dominate the
discussion

is mature and respected by the group and the larger community
+ is creative in using strategles to elicit group participation

© is creative in thinking of ways to get the group actively involved in the learning
process

+ is clever in integrating the use of the radio and the poster into the interactive
leaming going on in the community group discussion

+ is able to restate information from the radio and in the poster in ways that enable
everybody to understand

is able to restate opinion offered by members of the group in ways that honor their
contribution but make it better understood at the same time

+ is able to steer the group away from confrontation by honoring the contribution of
each member without committing to any.

© Is able to effectively manage the administrative aspects of leading a community
group discussion, including the use of the project's contribution, the development
and presentation of the community’s matching contribution, and the development
of mini-reports that capture on paper the opinion that was generated in the group
 Additional strategies, techniques and characteristic of effective facilitators that will be
included in community group facilitator training include:

4) Knows about and draws upon participants, culture, past experiences and interests
as a point of reference when presenting new information;

2) Designs group activities that allow participants to discover answers on their own
or with the support of the facilitator /or other participants;

3) Allows participants to participant interaction to occur;
4) Encourages participants to think and work independently;

5) Encourages participants to pose questions and to initiate interactions on their
own;

6) Creates new and interesting experiences for participants in the group (e.g. does
not use the same strategy over and over again with no variation);

7) Adapts instruction to the individual learning styles and needs of participants;
8) Explains his or her thinking process aloud in simple terms;

9) Allows participants to guess, to develop theories and explanations about a topic or
problem, even if their theories and explanations are not necessarily correct;

10) Prompts the participants to explain how they reached their conclusion (if a good
one) or helps reason through the questions or problems to a good conclusion;

41) Asks the participants to explain his or her reasoning and guides the participant in
order to achieve greater understanding;

42) Gently acknowledges and corrects participants when they are wrong, using
phrases such as “That is a good try, but it is not correct. Let’s see if we can correct

it together”;

4. Biodiversity Survey
Q. What is biodiversity survey?

Ans: This name is short for Biological Diversity Survey. It is the study of life and
structure of living things. It includes plants, animals, insects (butterfly), amphibians
(frog), reptiles (snake) etc.

Q. Who will be involved in the biodiversity survey?

Ans: Scientists from University of Papua New Guinea, Other International NGOs
like World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS),
Forestry Department and Forest Research Institute.

Q. Will the local people be involved?

Ans: Yes. It is very important that local people are involved in the survey. Local
people are needed to identify species of plants and animals native to their area.
They will also tell the scientists about their local names and how they use these
species of plants and animals.

1 2 3 4 5

Q. How will the survey be done?

Ans: There are 7 types (taxa group) of surveys:
Reptile/Snakes

2. Mammals

3. Plants

4. Amphibians/Frogs
 5. Freshwater Fish & Crustaceans
6. Entomological/Insects/Moths (including aquatic insects)
7. Ornithological/Bird

Q. Will these seven types of surveys be done all at once?

A: No. It will cost a lot of money to do all the surveys at once. Depending on how
much money PWM currently has for this survey, PWM is going to do only one
survey which is the Entomological/Insects/Moths (including aquatic insects). The
others will follow later once funding becomes available.

Q. How will the survey benefit the people now and in future?

Ans: The survey will benefit the people in:
Giving information to the local people on the types of plants and animals
they have on their land, in the forest and in the rivers.

= Telling the local people the population/figures/inumbers of the plants and
animals they have on their land, in the forests and in the rivers; and their
survival on whether or not these species are threatened to die out.

= Telling what humans are doing to the habitat of these plants and animals
and what the local people can do to protect them.

= Telling the local people other knowledge that they do not know about their
native plants and animals and inform the people on ways to protect these
species.

= Elementary children will be able to leam the scientific names of the native
species along side their local names.

= When other areas in PNG no longer have the plants and animals, the
Managalas people can be proud and show the rest of PNG what you still
have on your land.

= The medicinal value of the plants will be so much that the Managalas area
will be the source of many drugs not known to medical scientist.

= The Managalas people will still have for their grandchildren the forest and its
animals. The children will be proud of their fore fathers of what they have
done to their environment and its habitat.

* The Managalas people will still have its cultural identity when many areas in
PNG will have lost theirs.

achieved by the organization, does the board interfere with the day to day activities
of the organization?

3. Liklik Dinau Moni
Q. What is liklik dinau moni?

Ans: It is a system of allowing people to borrow small amount of money from a
seed source (seed money) to start small businesses, make profit, and repay the
amount borrowed from the seed money with very small interest.

Q. Why liklik dinau moni?

Ans: Liklik dinau moni is easy and flexible with no administrative procedure like the
commercial banks (ANZ, BSP, Westpac) where one is required to have capital
assets or counterpart money in order to get a loan.

1 2 3 4 5

Q. Why is a survey needed before implementing this ‘liklik dinau moni’?

Ans: Before PWM begins this liklik dinau moni, a survey will be carried out to find
out that the money will not be wasted on an activity that will not bring in a good
profit. The survey will also find out other useful information that will determine
whether or not it is worth implementing a ‘liklik dinau moni’ on the plateau.

1 2 3 4 5

Q. Who will be involved in the liklik dinau moni on the Plateau?

‘Ans: Depending on the results of the survey, the “liklik dinau moni” will be
implemented on the Plateau. PWM is planning to allow ONLY women’s groups who
meet the eligible criteria to borrow the “liklik dinau moni”. This is because examples
from around the world in other big countries overseas have proven records of
women as being the best managers in managing ‘“liklik dinau moni’ so we would
 like to give the Plateau women a chance to show their management skills in
managing this ‘tiklik dinau moni’.

1 2 3 4 5

= The rate of repayment of the principle seed money plus the interest has to
be flexible and also affordable.

= The principle seed money borrowed by each group has to be repaid within

‘Strategic Direction — Faciltated by Barefoot
 Namiai Community Development Association Inc.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY.

‘The Namiai Community Development Association (NACODA) Strategic Planning was
very new to most of the participants. After the workshop they all felt that it is a very
useful tool to guide the work of NACODA. The strategic planning workshop looked at
the focus areas and plan for NACODA, through identifying critical issues, tensions and
needs of the organization. The strategic plan also helped NACODA to come up with a
proposal budget for their program activities identified from the strategic planning
workshop.

The Strategic Planning Workshop looked at the New Strategic Direction for
NACODA and help members to self-appraise themselves. The participants were
facilitated using participatory approaches, tools and methods and processes

to identify and decide on the following ;

NACODA’’s shared Vision and Mission Statements.
Core Values and Beliefs

Goals

Culture of the organization.

The participants in smaller groups shared experiences and learned from each
other as they go through cultural experiences on how to strategize and plan a

traditional marriage situation and feast for the dead. After the group presentations a brief
summary was done on what is Strategic and what is Planning,, its effect on an individual
and organization and what are the consequences if they failed to plan or if the plan did
eventuate.

The participants were briefly introduced to PNG Pre- history Timeline and the
Changing Societies that PNG is going through. Participatory participation was
explained through an “House Building” exercise. The participants were then
taken to look at what is not Development and what is Development. Introducing
the participants to CARGO DEVELOPMENT and the true development, the
INTEGRAL HUMAN DEVELOPMENT.

‘The participants used SWOT (Strength, Weakness, Opportunities & Threats) analysis to
identify the Strengths and Weaknesses of the NACODA and then they went on to doa
scan of the trends (SWOT- Opportunities and Threats) that are coming from the outside
and affecting NACODA as an organization and upon its individual membership. By
looking at the challenges obstacles and/or issues faced by NACODA and the Managalas
communities internally as an organization and individual membership, family, clan and
the plateau overall. These exercises led the participants to identify and discuss fully the
NACODA Needs. The Trends Scan and the Community Need Analysis helped the
participants identify issues that created tensions within themselves as individuals, the
community at large, NACODA as an organization and it’s relationship with PWM.

3
Strategic Direction ~ Facilitated by Barefoot

Namiai Community Development Association inc.

Furthermore, the participants together discussed in smaller groups what is currently
happening and what needs to happen to address these trends and community
needs/issues/challenges/obstacles. The Internal scan, the Trend scan and the NACODA
Community Need Analysis including the comments and discussions raised during recap
and group presentations helped the participants to come up with organizational program
‘components/strategies- the actual Focus areas. Using SMART (being Specific,
Measurable Achievable, Relevant and Time bound) tools the participants in smaller
‘groups formulated objectives , identified major activities, then minor activities and
performance indicators to achieve relevant to these objectives. NACODA will at a later
date develop tasks and estimated cost/budget for a possible proposal for its programs to
be forwarded to it’s donors.

Finally the group defined and have in place a new Strategic Direction and plan. This plan
be implemented once funding is available. This executive summary must be read
together with the whole strategic plan if one is not familiar with the concept and
approaches in Participatory Strategic Planning tool.

Background

‘The socio- economic impact of the Okari nut project on the Managalas plateau became
apparent that communities became organized around it. The establishment of Partners
with Melanesia tasked to organized the Managalas communities around their cultural and
natural resources and further carry out research into Okari nut as a viable non forest
product. There were already threats of large scale logging moving into the plateau. PWM
facilitated communities to be organized into zones created structures like the Combined
Forum Steering Committee Meetings zone boards, clan committees, zone office and
admin support staff and program staff. There are ten zones established on the plateau.
‘There were few zones that were suspended along the way, while the most organized
zones got incorporated as recognized Legal Entities of their own with IPA. The most
notable ones are zone 1, zone 2- NACODA and the umbrella body on the plateau, the
Managalas Development Foundation.

In 2001 seven years afier the overall Managalas Conservation Area Support Project
(MCASP) , PWM held its first Strategic Planning Workshop at Naukanane. The focus
areas identified were, Consensus Building, Training, Gender and Eco- enterprising
became the main focus components of all the programs carried out on the plateau. As
identified in the strategic plan where there were low interest in eco- enterprising
consensus building stopped. The literacy program in the non formal sector was
established prior to the MCASP and strengthened through the formation and
incorporation of the Barai Non-formal Education Association (BNEA). There were many
activities that were not implemented in Gender and the Training components.

The new Strategic direction for NACODA identified the need to further up skill staff
program officers and volunteers and provide gender equality in MCASP on the plateau.

4

Namiai Community Development Association Inc,

THE NEW DIRECTION FOR NACODA

Introduction

This is the report of the New Strategic Direction for NACODA Inc. It is written and
submitted to the Board of NACODA , MDF, PWM and Donors and the Stakeholders of
Managalas plateau. It will outline what strategies and plan the one week Strategic
Planning workshop identified. This will enable board members of NACODA to improve
its governance within it’s organizational and program implementations. Most importantly
this report contains the Vision/ Mission Statement Core Values and Beliefs, Goals and
Culture of NACODA.

The objectives of this workshop are;

1. Kisim save long mekim kamapim stretigik plen

2. Long dispela woksop bai yumi mas kamapim stretigik plen bilong NACODA
(youth, women, church, WDC, health na education etc..)

3. Husat yumi kamap nau bai yumi serim expiriens long wok bilong yumi long ples
yumi stap long en

4, Long kamapim stretigik plen bilong NACODA long wok halivim olgeta komuniti
long zone 2.

5. Bai gat plan (activities) wantaim rot olsem wanem bai yumi lukautim moni

Then outline in general the issues as identified when the strengths and weaknesses of
NACODA, through a SWOT analyses exercises as carried out during the workshop.

As results of the participatory exercises, prioritized strategies were artived at for
NACODA. The focus areas and key activities were identified together with their
Performance Indicators. The issues affecting the Board and Management relationship,
Policies at the board level were highlighted and critiqued in the participatory group
exercises.

A Plan of Action was documented as an end result of this participatory strategic planning
workshop.

Finally some recommendations for the NACODA board and PWM to consider urgently.

Vision

The Namiai Community Development Association was set up in 1992 as a Community
Based Organization in zone two.

NACODA is committed to co coordinating and supporting the work of its members in
zone 2 towards a fuller realization of a community that is rich in resources, fresh clean
water and abundance in forest, life, land and people, where it’s people respect each other,
and live harmoniously now and in the future.

“THE VOICE OF NAMIAI WHO LIVE TOGETHER EQUALLY IN A COMMUNAL
SOCIETY IN HARMONY WITH THEIR ENVIRONMENT”

This vision is echoed through this version of the participant’s dream,
“A voice in the forest is calling the children of the Tattoo tribe of Namiai to the feast of
initiation, a society of people who work together in a spirit of respect and love”

‘THE NACODA MISSION STATEMENT:
‘THE MISSION
The Namiai Community Development Association strive ;

To build consensus amongst the Namiai Community in order for them to make
collective decisions and to cope with the changes taking place whilst protecting and
conserving their culture and natural resources for now and the future generation.

This mission will be achieved through:

* promoting appropriate opportunities for all members of NACODA through community
development processes and community participatory approaches.

* building, linking and supporting a series of community based income generating
enterprises and home grown team of volunteers, CBOs and other stakeholders in all
levels of government, NGOs, CBOs, Churches, Women, Youth and their Developmental
Partners.

* the creation of learning opportunities for the children of Namiai and the surrounding
villages through programs that provide awareness, consensus building, build knowledge
and skills transfer trainings and critical literacy and learning how to read and write in
their local dialects and sponsorship.

* through Gender Equality promoting a sustainable way of life that is culturally and
spiritually appropriate.

*Promoting the co-operation with other CBOs from the plateau, MDF, PWM, NGOs,
Churches, Women, Government agencies, donors, partner NGOs, the private sector and
the whole communities of Afore District, Oro Province and PNG as a whole through
Networking.

NACODA CORE VALUES.

CORE VALUES SUMMARY
The workshop participants NACODA core values are summarized as follows:

+ HOLISTIC and INTEGRATED
NACODA believes that for the whole community to benefit , the developmental process
must take into account the Physical, Mental, Emotional and Spiritual development
aspects of an individual, the family, the community and the country.

+ PEOPLE PARTICIPATION
NACODA believes that stakeholders and all people must be active participants in any
transformation processes or programs intended to develop their resources and in order to
improve their lives, through what they have within in order to live and upon which their
well being depends.

= EQUALITY AND SOCIAL JUSTICE

NACODA believes in the equal participation of all stakeholders within the whole
population of community elders, adults (women and men), youths and children of all
back grounds and abilities, allow equal distribution of resources and access to services,
The Managalas plateau has its own ethnic groups with indigenous cultures in addition to
ethnic groups that have migrated and settled in the area permanently. As there are
differing cultures, there are different religious groups that are to participate equally and
should not be over looked.

PROGRAMME GOALS, OBJECTIVES AND ACTIVITIES

The Strategic Planning Workshop emphasized a need for a strategic plan and areas of
focus in program implementations. The main emphasis of this direction will be the
interrelationships between the NACODA and MDF and PWM, the decentralization of
which programme activities to the NACODA to be implemented at community levels
through strengthening of the community based organizations (CBOs) and a closer and
clearer coordinated working relationship with NACODA. and other agencies including
the government through trainings. awareness gender. income generating and networking
through publications and information.

8
Strategic Direction ~ Facilitated by Barefoot

Namiai Community Development Association Inc.

For the NACODA programmed activities to be implemented successfully. NACODA
and stakeholders of zone 2 will have to go through a process of consensus building,
community organizing and participation that enables them not only to work with each
other but also be able to work with the other zones, MDF, CBOs partners and agencies
that are carrying out similar activities on the plateau.

CREATIVE TENSIO!

This is the first time a Strategic Plan has been drawn up for NACODA. As such a lot of
critical issues that have plagued the organization since it was established have been
discussed openly. The Strategic Planning workshop re-visited the organization’s
Structure. Constitution, and Stakeholders. These have shaped the organization as such,

However, there are still many that need to be continually addressed and discussed at
televant forums and levels. These issues will continually shape the organization because
they will always be there. These are the Creative Tensions that are unique to NACODA
because of the programs and activities it is involved in as well as the culture of the
organization- how NACODA do things.

The most important tensions are as follows:~

1, Working relationship with MDF
It has been realized that there is a great need for the MDF to implement planned activities
with NACODA.

2. Relationship between PWM and NACODA

There are people who have negative views about the work of NACODA. This will
remain a continuous tension as long as Roles and Responsibilities are not clearly defined.
This tension can only be addressed on a case-by-case basis and will remain for as long as
there is an absent of organization and program plan in operational.

3. Equal distribution of Funds.
Another tension that remains to be addressed continuously is the equal distribution of
funds to the Managalas plateau and especially NACODA for project implementation.

4. Clarity of roles, responsibilities and Functions of NACODA by MDF and PWM.
There has been need to clarify the roles, responsibilities and functions. This tensions can
be said to have started from the fact that a ot of the existing stakeholders have had no
say in the establishment of NACODA and what its primary functions are.

5. Legitimacy of the NACODA

The NACODA was incorporated in however the Organisations governance requirements
needed to be in place.

‘There is a great need to carry out awareness on NACODA to the communities in zone

2 Introduction

Conservation programme is one of the core activities coordinated by PwM for the Managalas
Conservation Area Support Project in the Plateau. Under this conservation programme,
biodiversity survey is the main activity programmed to support the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area Support Project. The PY the Biodiversity Survey Reports as the
main ingredients for writing proposals to don ig agencies.

Partners with Melanesians has been working with the Managalas people for more than a
decade to promote biodiversity conservation and sustainable natural resources development
and management. Eco-enterprise, rainforest literacy and other minor projects initiated and
promoted by PwM in the Managalas Plateau is to sustain the local communities’ livelihoods
and encourage them te develop economic and social or environmental activ would
maintain their living standards

However, development projects that are destructive to the natural environment, and have
implications on the social well-being or the development is unsustainable, the project should
not be encouraged or allowed in the Proposed Conservation Area Support Project. On the
contrary, sustainable livelihoods does not comes easy, it requires environmental destruction,
and that is, part and partial of the natural environment has to be destroyed or at least part of an
ecosystem containing biodiversity has to be disturbed.

3. The Biodiversity Survey

The biological diversity or ‘biodiversity’ of the Managalas Plateau is rich and diverse and
most of its plant and animal species are near extinction, and are confined to the Managalas
Plateau alone. The scope of the field survey on biodiversity of Managalas Plateau was to find
out about different species of flora and fauna at different locations at different altitudes of the
Proposed Conservation Area.

R
 ‘The main area undertaken during the survey was basically on fauna, especially on vertebrate
species (birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians/frogs) and flora (plants species). Thus, the field
survey was carried out to quantify the number of flora and fauna species at certain habitats
and ecosystems and the biodiversity they contain.

The Biodiversity Survey is a follow up of last year’s Rapid Biodiversity Assessment. This
year’s survey was much longer than last year’s and covered a cross section of the Managalas
Plateau and the results were very good.

The survey took three weeks and it took place at three different localities unlike the previous
survey that took only two (2) weeks, and only one site was selected for the survey. The
Survey was very in-depth and detailed and covers most of the areas of biological fauna and
flora species and knowledge of their presence in the Managalas Plateau.

4. Selected Sites for the Biodiversity Survey

The Biodiversity Survey was conducted from 07 — 27 November 2005. The Survey was
carried out at three different sites at different altitudes at the Managalas Plateau. The Survey
took place at the following localities/places. The Survey was conducted for a total of 20 days.

a. Locality 1
Murayane, Kriemi Mountain Ranges. Anatua Village (Zone 2). The Elevation at
Murayane was over 1240 meters above sea level. Duration: 08 - 13 November, 2005
(6 days).

b. Locality 2
Putei/Firin, (Near Barige River). Tahama Village (Zone 2). The Elevation at Putei was
over 600 meters above sea level. Duration: 15 - 19 November, 2005 (5 days).

c. Locality 3 :
Pongani Bridge, Kawara. Pongani Village (Zone 8). The Elevation at Pongani Bridge
was appox.100 meters above sea level. Duration: 21-25 November, 2005 (5 days).

A total of 16 days was allocated for the survey from 20 days survey. The remaining four (4)
days were used for traveling, especially for the movement of survey equipment and food items
from one area to another. The Survey ended on Friday 25 of November 2005. The
scientists/students overnight in Popondetta and returned to Port Moresby on Saturday 26" of
November 2005.

Amount allocated for consultants fee was K19 500 (57.5%). From this amount K300 was paid
to the consultants as incidental allowance, K2000 was for students allowance (K400/student to
3 students), and K7500 for the scientists (K25GU/scientist to 3 scientists). The remaining
K9500 will be paid to the consultants when they produce the final field survey report in Port
Moresby at the PWM office.

Amount allocated for cheque and cash expenses in Port Moresby was K7300 (21.5%). From
this amount, K4500 was spent for aircraft charter, K1300 for equipment and medical supplies,
K1400 for store goods and K100 for fuel in Port Moresby. However, K100 for fuel was never
used, so it was included in the K400 taken to the project site for emergency.
