 6.

Constraints/ Difficulties

Though the Survey was completed as planned, we still encountered so many problems not
expected. The following are some of the problems encountered.

Lt

2 Number of carriers at the plateau surpassed the planned number of carriers because the
size of the survey equipment, food items and personal belongings were so many, and
each equipment/item is too big for one person to carry. Therefore, I had to arrange for
additional carriers to complete carrying the materials from one end to another. That
where I had to pay additional funds to continue carry the Survey team’s stuff.

2 Garden foods brought into the campsites by local villagers to sell were very expensive,
and that they demanded that price of garden food be decided by themselves. This is
one of the observations I made from this field trip — that is, local communities at the
Plateau are not really helping PWM to help them to alleviate poverty and improve
their living standards or developing their natural resources sustainably. From what T
saw, people want cash for any simple activity that they did for the survey.

a Additional number of cooks, field assistants and camp guards had to make their own
way into the survey sites without me choosing them. In this case, I only paid the
selected individuals for the survey. However, some of them demanded that they still be
paid. I never paid them, anyway.

Community Response

So far response from the local communities regarding the survey had been very good, but not
to my expectation. As mentioned earlier, people want payment for whatever activity they did,
wether it be simple or difficult.

People should be more responsive and responsible, however, this did not occur. They should
regard the survey as the community's environmental development project. Indirectly, their
social and economic conditions will improve through such biological/environmental surveys.

8.

Recommendations

‘The following are some of the suggestions for next year’s programme for biodiversity survey.

@ Number of carriers should be at least twenty (20) or more. This may reduce
inconveniences and workshops or other activities carried out in the Plateau by PWM
will be more efficient and effective.

@ PWM should let the local communities to be more generous and supportive in any
activities in the Plateau. This has to be done through MDF field coordinators, CBO
managers and activity coordinators, so that the people will be more willing to help
without payments or returns.

2 MDF field coordinators (east/west) should let the responsible communities aware in
advance of the activities/workshops to avoid inconveniences, and that people will be
able to respond positively and able to understand the scope of the activity being
carried in their boundaries or zones.

1S
 y is 10 be considered. Because the last two surveys were conducted at the same
vear (N ‘December), and the results may have been similar.
Therefore. change of time for next biodiversity surveys would very good. I suggest
June/July for a Biorap Survey, and a major survey at the end of the year
(November/December).

a Carry out awareness about the biodiversity survey because most local people do not
really understand the nature of the survey as experienced from last year's Biorap and
the recent biodiversity survey. As I noted the reactions by people at Pongani, people in
those areas or zones do not understand the conservation work carried out by PWM that
is going in the Managalas Plateau. I recommend that more conservation awareness
should reach those areas.

9. Comments/ Conclusion

1 am relieved that the survey has completed. The final field reports by scientists and students
will be delivered in due course. Hopefully their reports will be of help to the PWM efforts in
securing fimds for next year's biediversity survey from donor agencies and organisations.

 1.0 Introduction

‘The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area covers a land area of over 360,000 hectares.
The Managalas Plateau itself is situated within and around the Owen Stanley Range to the
South and West, the Sibuim Ranges to the South-east and Mount Lamington to the North and
East. The Managalas Plateau encompasses a wide variety of vegetation types from alpine
forests at altitudes of 3,800m, to tropical rainforests in the mountains and hills, as well as
savanna grassland and anthropogenic garden areas. The Managalas Plateau is isolated from
most of the urban centers within the Oro Province as a result of poor road conditions, which
are poorly, if at all maintained.

Anthropogenic activity is restricted to mid-altitude valleys as in most parts of Papua New
Guinea, leaving the surrounding mountains virtually uninhabited. More than 15,000 people
from about 150 clans live in more than 70 villages within the Managelas Plateau. Most if not
all of these people enjoy a subsistent livelihood, with much dependence being placed on the
surrounding environment.

Through conservation awareness programs initiated and conducted by Partners With
Melanesians (PwM), the people within the Managalas Plateau have decided to conserve their
forests. Hence, a core group was formed, the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF),
which has worked in close partnership with PwM to develop sound development strategies
for the area. Following on from a preliminary biodiversity survey conducted by a team of
scientists from the University of Papua New Guinea and the Department of Environment and
Conservation, a further study was conducted from the 7" ~ 26" November 2005, in selected
sites of varying altitude within the Afore District of Oro Province. The survey conducted was
similar to that of the previous year in that it involved surveys on plants, birds, mammals and
herpetofauna,

The objective of the survey was to provide baseline information on the flora and fauna
within the selected sites and to make comparisons of their distribution and diversity at
various altitudes. The information collected and compiled on the flora and fauna will be used
toward the establishment of the Wildlife Conservation Area status for the Managalas Plateau.
In conjunction with this, PwM in its drive to promote capacity building among young Papua
New Guineans has taken on the initiative to facilitate for the training of university students in
field techniques and skills required for biodiversity surveys.

2.0 Methods

There were three sites surveyed, all of which were located within the Afore district of the
Oro Province. The first site surveyed was called Murayane, located at 1240m above sea level
(asl) along the Krerim Ranges, a few kilometers outside of Anatua Village. The second site,
called Putei was 660m (asl) and was located about 5 kilometers outside of Tahama Village.
The third site was a village at Pongani, positioned at 70m (asl). At all the sites surveyed a
total of about 4-5 days were spent in conducting the survey. The day prior to the actual
sampling a general observation of the site vegetation and the landscape was done basically to

wo
 identify the appropriate spot to place the traps, mist nets and transects for the flora and fauna
surveys

Flora survey
2.1 Plant sampling

The main objective of the flora sampling was to identify the species diversity and the
structure of the forest within the selected sites of the Managalas Plateau. The main sampling
method used, consisted of the use of a 50m x 50m plot being placed within each of the three
selected sites. Within each of these plots five quadrats of 10m x 10m were drawn and
sampled. This enabled every 10m interval within the 50m x 50m plot to be sampled.

Within each of the five quadrats, the different tree species encounted with a diameter at
breast height (DBH) greater than 5 were recorded together with their estimated heights
Within the Som x Om plot, ten random plots measuring Sm x Sm were also selected and
marked out. From these random plots all the trees and shrubs found were identified and
tallied. This was done to estimate the abundance of tree species within the forest. Thus, apart
from sampling, plants specimens were collected, pressed in paper and taken back to the
UPNG Herbarium for storage and preservation as a record of the species of plants found
within the area surveyed.

Fauna survey
2.2. Bird sampling

Due to time constraints and other difficilties faced with the land geomorphology, the method
used for bird sampling was ‘random mist netting’ rather than the standard line transect
method. Within the random placement method, mist nets consisting of 5 layers were attached
to poles of 2 metres in length and placed at selected positions. The selection of sites for the
placement of the mist nets are done so as to maximize the catch rate in as little time as
possible since we were only allowed to stay in a particular site for about 5 days. In the
random placement method, the sites selected were 10-20m apart. The mist nets were placed
up to 2 metres above the ground. Generally, in instances where it is perceived that more birds
can be caught closer or lower to the ground, the nets are placed closer to the ground, at about
0.5m above the ground. In other instances where it is deemed that the catch can be increased
by placing the nets higher above the ground, then the nets are placed at distances of 1-2m off
the ground. In this case the nets were placed 1-2m above the ground with the mist nets
stretching up to Sm above the ground.

The mist nets as stated, consist of 5 layers of netting with an overlapping pocket between
each layer where the trapped birds are supposed to drop into and remain until they are
removed from the net. The netting material is soft so as no to damage the birds whilst they
are held within the net.

The nets were checked at regular intervals in the momiing, during the day, in the aftemoon
and during the night. This was done so as to minimize the amount or the period of time that
the birds are left in the nets or held in captivity. The birds trapped were then collected and

 weighed initially. After the weighing, those birds that were collected as specimens on the
previous trip were released if they were still alive but if they were not, then they were
disposed of appropriately. For any new specimens that were collected, the weights along with
various other measurements of the birds’ features were taken and the details recorded on bird
specimen data sheets provided by Mr. Kulmoi from the Department of Environment and
Conservation (DEC). These data sheets were to be filed at the DEC as a representation of the
bird species that are to be found within the area surveyed. Other methods also employed in
the data collection for the bird species found in the area included; general observations and
biological resource utilization surveys where the local people were interviewed on their
knowledge of what bird species they knew to be present within the area.

The specimens themselves were skinned and stuffed by Ms. R. Singadan to be kept at the
UPNG- NSRC Animal collection also as a representation of the bitds’ species to be found
within the area surveyed.

2.3 Mammal sampling.

For the mammals, there were basically two types of methods used to catch them. For the bats
we used the mist nets that were used for the birds also and as for the rodents and other small
marsupials we used trapping system. The mist nets were basically set to catch lower canopy,
fruit birds and bats.

The traps used were of two types, the Tomahawk and the Elliot traps. At times lizards and
snakes are caught in these traps. In the process of trapping, baiting was very important and
necessary to get a good catch. The baits we used were wheat bix, peanut butter, cooked
coconut and at times ripe banana.

‘The traps were set in quadrats of 50 by 50 m and within this quadrat they were placed along
transect lines positioned at every 10m intervals. A total of 36 traps were set in the marked out
quadrat.

After the mammals were collected, the desired species were then dissected, skinned, dried
and packed for the UPNG mammal collection. Ms. Rose Singadan did all these and at times
we were allowed to perform these tasks under her supervision.

2.4 Herpetofauna sampling.

The herpetofauna sampling was based on mainly the frogs. However, we came across other
specimens such as snakes and lizards. These specimens were collected, photographed and
preserved also in alcohol and brought to the UPNG museum

In the frog sampling at each of the three camps, the sites we selected were located near
creeks, rivers, ponds, whilst on the land we looked under dead and fallen leaves, beneath the
ground, under dead logs and rotten wood, near roots and old tree barks, Others were found
lying on the leaves and branches of trees ranging from about a few centimeters to more than
 three meters above the ground. These areas were located within walking distances ranging
from about ten minutes to an hours walk from the camp.

Some of the frogs were found during the day. However the best catch time was found to be
during the night or from dusk till dawn. It was during these times that all the different
sounds made by the different species of frogs were heard, easily distinguished and recorded
accordingly using a specialized tape recorder.

During the day, the frog specimens collected during the previous night were identified,
photographed and preserved in alcohol. The heart from each frog species collected was
removed and placed into a labeled vial that would be sent overseas for DNA sequencing. The
specimens collected would then be stored in the UPNG Animal collection.

Further information on the species of reptiles to be found within each of the sites were
obtained from the local people via their ethnographic knowledge. Thus, we were able to get a
‘feel’ of what was actually within the area despite our insufficient catch rate.

3.0. Result

3.1. Brief evaluation of the Species found.

‘The Appendix provides a listing of all the flora and fauna species that were confirmed to be
found within the Managalas Plateau. This conveys the magnitude of animal and plant species
that were found within the site surveyed; yet the Plateau encompasses a vast area and these
species may be doubled or even tripled with further research, bearing in mind that this is only
a preliminary study of the area.

Firstly for the flora sampling in general we discovered that the vegetation at each of the sites
varies according to the different aititude and climate. In that as altitude decreases the plant
numbers and height varies. Hence the Managalas Plateau is observed to have a rich diversity
of plants and from this survey it was site 2, Putei that had the highest diversity of trees.

The bird sampling results showed that there is a vast number of bird species to be found
within the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area. Some of the birds found there include the
Raggiana Bird of Paradise as well as other species of Bird of Paradise such as the Rifle Bird
of Paradise and several species of the Kingfisher Bird of Paradise. These birds are protected
by law and thus add to the conservation status of the area surveyed. There was observed to be
a general trend of increase in species diversity with decrease in altitude and the Bird of
Paradise species were observed to be rather common in the sites surveyed.

As for the mammals the most common species found were mostly of bats and rats. Bats
being the Synconycteris australis (Common Blossom bat) from the Chiroptera family while
the rats being the Paramelomys mollis and Rattus exullants both from the family of Muridae
Cuscuses were also observed in two of the sites (I and 2), which we surveyed. Southern
brown cuscus and Dorias tree kangaroo from the family of Phalangeridae and Macropodidae
respectively were the common cuscuses sighted.
 As shown in the appendix, we collected a total of twenty-five different species of frogs and
listed them into their families. The Hylidae family had eight species; the Microhylidae family
had thirteen species thus becoming the family with the largest number of species collected.
The Myobatrachidae family had only one specimen collected (Lechriodus melanopyga)
thereby being the family with he least number of species collected, while the Ranidae family
had three specimens collected. The highest numbers of species found were of the Litoria sp.
with six different species found in the Hylidae family, three different Hylophorbus sp. in the
Microhylidae family while the rest had two and one species.

4.0 Discussio!

4.1. Experiences:

It was a great opportunity to have been part of this biodiversity survey team. We learnt so
much during this training. Not only did we put the theoretical skills we learnt in school into
practice, but the general expectations of what is required in order to carry out biodiversity
surveys.

4.1.1 Flora sampling encounters and experiences

Through observations from all three sites, distinct differences could be seen in the types of
vegetation. Each site was located at various altitudes and so each was exposed to different
environmental factors such as temperature and soil type. In site 1, Murayane, mosses and
ferns were more abundantly distributed. This was seen to be typical of areas of high
altitudes. With site 2, Putei, the common vegetation features included buttress roots and
cauliflorous plants. These features are found mostly in lowland rainforests. As for site 3,
Pongani, the area was identified to be that of flood plain.

In terms of the skitls acquired from the flora survey, it was learnt that one of the most
important tools in conducting a survey is selecting an appropriate sampling technique. Plants
unlike animals are immobile however it is impossible to count every single species in an area
so using the right method, such as the line transect, can give a more realistic account of the
whole forest vegetation. In collecting the required data, we learnt to use a dbh tape to find the
diameter of trees at breast height. We also learnt to estimate tree heights during the sampling.
The identification of trees was another vital skill required for the field and as beginners we
learnt to distinguish a few trees species. But apart from the above, simple observations were
learnt to be another important feature especially in trying to understand the distribution of
certain species. Hence, the overall experience from the flora survey was very worthwhile
and it taught us just how much diversity there are in the number of tree species in Managalas.
This experience also helped us all to enhance much of what leamt from our various Plant
Biology courses.
 4.1.2 Bird sampling encounters and experiences

On general observations alone, it can be stated that there was a general trend of increase in
the diversity of bird species with decrease in altitude. That is, the bird species diversity
increased as we moved form the higher altitude site down to the other two sites of lower
altitude. The bird species diversity at the first site was minimal with only a few species being
able to adapt to the conditions at such high altitude. The second site showed an increase in
the bird species diversity in that some of the same birds from the first site were caught along
with several other new species. In the second site we were able to catch two different species
of Kingfisher Bird of Paradise, and they were observed to be rather common within the area
surveyed. At the third site, we also caught a different species of Kingfisher Bird of Paradise
along side this we had the opportunity to see a female Raggiana Bird of Paradise. It was an
exhilarating experience to be able to feel and have a ‘hands-on’ encounter with these
magnificent birds.

Skills leamt in the bird surveys and mist netting includes general observations and listening
for birdcalls that were used for identification of species not caught but observed to be within
the area surveyed. We were also taught how to put up the nets and also how to select the sites
in order to obtain a maximal catch. We also learnt how to remove the birds from the nets
efficiently so as not to cause too much harm and discomfort to the trapped birds. We also
acquired skills on how to take proper measurements of the birds’ identifying features and
characteristics and on how to fill out the proper forms as required by the Department of
Environment and Conservation. In addition to all these, we were also shown techniques on
how to preserve the specimens for future reference.

4.1.3 Mammals sampling encounters and experiences

‘Mammals are only a small part of the whole living kingdom. To have a better understanding
of mammals it is very important to study their environmental lifestyle and morphological
structures. For species identification one has to carefully study the morphological differences
that lie between species of rats or bats or any mammals in general. It is of significant
importance that our diverse mammals’ species must be conserved not only for scientific
research purposes but also for our future generation to appreciate the various mammal
species the Managalas Plateau has in abundance.

In carrying out this mammal sampling during these three weeks, we had the privilege to learn
so many things. We were mostly putting into practice what we have leamt in school (biology
courses) while other skills learnt were

INTRODUCTION

‘The Island of New Guinea fauna consists largely of frogs. According to Richards (2002), the 250
frog. species were documented from New Guinea, more diverse compare to other countries. This
is because New Guinea has a constant warm and wet environment that provides humid habitats
‘and cool temperature at widely different elevations (0-3600m asl) (Richards 2002).

Frogs and other amphibian make up the important component of New Guinea ecosystem and
‘occur at high densities. They provide important source of food to other organisms and for many

local people (Allison, Bickford et al. 1998).

One aspect of identifying diversity of plants and animals species is to understand and make
broader ecological assessment of biodiversity (Richards 2003). For example Orsak, Easen et al.
(2001), illustrated Lepidoptera, especially moths were chosen because it was used as a general
biodiversity indicators.

This study was intended to document frogs of Managalas Plateau, within approx. 3600 hectares
of virgin forest. Papua New Guinea has difficult mountain terrain which is inadequate to conduct
studies in many interior areas.

Frogs collected at Managalas will contribute to our knowledge of frog fauna in Papua New
Guinea.

The main objectives of Herpetofauna biological survey were to:
1. Document the number of frog species found at 3 elevations at each sites.
2. Identify species abundance and diversity, enable proper management and promote
conservation in sustainable way.

METHODS

A month biological survey was conducted at Managalas plateau, Oro Province from 8" — 24"
November. I conducted frog survey at night by search and visual encounter survey. I detected
frogs by their advertisement calls and recorded their calls using a tape recorder. I also did
thorough search on the forest floors, turning over logs and going along streams and search
rugged mountain and steep hill slopes.

At daytime I took photographed of all new frog species in life. I took several body measurements
of frogs and fixed the specimens in 10% formalin and later store them in 70% ethanol. I also
took tissues for future DNA study.

For the purpose of this report, I identify and named frog species according to their morphological
characters. Proper identification of specimens will be given with scientific names and the
specimens will be stored at Natural Science Resource Centre (NSRC) at University of Papua
New Guinea.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

‘Species Diversity and Abundance

A total of 110 individual frog specimens was collected of which 27 species was documented
during the survey from 4 families (Table 2).

Managalas has a promising high diversity of frog fauna. The frog assemblage at Managalas is
comprised of common frogs and few rare frog species especially smaller frog species from
family Microhylidae. It is true Managalas has wide selection of habitats that is good for frogs.

Compare number of species collected at 3 elevations. More species was collected at site 2,
followed by site 1 and site 3. This does not mean there are less number of species at sitel and
site 3. High diversity of frog call was heard at site 1 and site 2 but were scattered in camp 3. Few
of the species were widespread and abundant at all 3 sites. The reason some of the species were
not collected because of some nights had continuous heavy rain (Figure2).

Frog family and species in brief

Hylidae: Common name Tree Frog. Several species collected were very abundant, calling early
hours of the evening during and after the rain, two Litoria species were collected down hill on
small trees about 1.5m-<3m above ground along the stream at Site 1, (1200m). Other 3 Litoria
species were collected during the rain. Litoria sp3. was collected at stilled old pooled water, ~
2m-5m on the tree. Litoria sp2 and Litoria sp4 both collected on the forest floor next to the
stream. Nyctimystes species is the only species in different genus, distinguished by large eyes
and a membrane when close. A specimen was collected in the day along a fast flowing river
upstream, Site 1, (1200m) and other specimen collected at camp 2, (660m) on forest floor, closed
canopy. Litoria thesaurensis and Litoria infrefranata are lowland species live in open pooled
and swampy area; the call of L. infrefranata was heard adjacent to the main road next to the
village Site 3 (~S0-70m).

Microhylidae: Most frogs in this family dwell on the forest floor and above ground on tree leaves
about <Im-15m or more. Microhylids were abundant, several calls heard were very difficult to
capture. Albericus sp was the only specimen collected at montane forest, Site 1, down hill on
leaves of small shrub trees about >Im adjacent to the stream. 3 Austrochaperina species were
abundant, captured on the forest floor at the lower montane forest, Site 1, (1200m) and some
frogs were brought during day time by local assistances. In addition, Hylophorbus species were
found abundant on the forest floor at Site 1 and Site 2. The Oreophryne (arboreal sp.) abundant
at Site 1 calling above ground about 1.5m-2.5m on tree leaves, it was also collected at Site 2 but
only one individual specimen was collected in Site 3. On the other hand Oreophryne (nr
hypsiops sp.) were abundant at Site 2 but was absent in Site 3, only one specimen was collected
near Anatua village 3m on the coconut palm (~800m). Cophixalus species was abundant at Site 1
and Site 2 including Site 3 (~1200m-70m). The species is small compared to other species and
often hard to locate on forest floor. Sphenophryne sp. and Xenorhina sp. are two species
captured in Site 1 and Site 2. Sphenophryne sp. is not so abundant in Site 1, (1200m) 2
specimens were collected in the day on the ground under the tent during the rain. It was different

CONCLUSION
Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) has extremely high diversity of frog fauna.

There was a significance differences in frog species collected at 3 sites. Some species of frogs
collected live and are found only at certain elevation and habitats, (e.g. A/bericus sp) was found
in montane forest, other species do well in high and low elevation, e.g. Oreophryne (arboreal sp).
Some species lived only in low elevation (¢.g. Platymantis papuensis).

‘The data showed high species diversity in family Microhylidae at site 1 and site 2. The other
family Hylidae, Ranidae may likely show increase diversity. In addition different frog species
forage different habitats. For example, Hylidae are tree frogs and are common along streams,
rivers and live above ground on trees.

SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATION

1) Actively carry out awareness program to educate resource owners the importance of
research and conservation.

2) Clearing large areas for gardening increase temperature within surrounding environment,
this practice in future provide good habitat for other introduce animals, e.g. Bufo marinus
(introduced toad), easily finds its way in hot temperature. Many frog species become
disadvantage when their habitats and environment change and will from the heat.

3) Develop long term monitoring and research into special plants and animal species. Such
long term monitoring guide good forest management and promote sustainable
development and is vital for decision makers in future.

Your wise decision in protecting the forest and wildlife will support you TODAY and for your

4.0 INTRODUCTION

‘The Managalas Plateau Proposed Conservation are is situated in the south eastern part of the
Souther Papuan region in the ljivitari District - Oro Province. The Proposed Conservation
Area constitutes an area of approximately 300.000 hectares and is located on a Plateau now
known as the Managalas Plateau.

‘The area is predominantly wet tropical rainforest and surrounded by the Owen Stanley
Mountains to the west, lowland rainforest extending to the coastal areas to the west.

Composition and diversity of animals are relatively unknown in any literature in the Managalas
proposed Conservation Area although there have been studies (unpublished reports) done by
individual researchers in other parts of Oro Province and in neighboring Provinces (Milne Bay
and Morobe Province), that this Province share Provincial boundaries with.

Introduction:

Iwas tasked by Partners With Melanesians Inc. and Managalas Development Foundation
to conduct a research and provide to the two (2) organizations some Non Timber Forest
Products (NTFP) that are found on the Managalas plateau in order for the organizations
to utilize them to serve the people of the Managalas plateau who have given their land for
the purpose of conservation and have opted against destructive logging, mining and large
scale agricultural plantations and farms.

‘The main purpose of this survey was to identify the commercial potential of Non-Timber
Forest Products of the Managalas Plateau.

This rapid assessment included seven days of field visits and interview with locals form
the area in identifying the species and documenting them. Each species was assessed for
its commercial potential and recommendations were given for development and further
work. A further 14 days was taken in compiling this report using data collected from the
field.

Despite being assigned to note down only five NTFPs that are economically viable for
the Plateau, I have produced ten priority NTFPs because some NTFPs were not found to
occur in some areas which left other areas having their own priority NTFP.A total of 44
NTFPs are also listed for PWM to consider.

It is recommended that further detailed information, botanical and NTFP specimen and
plant species including quantitative and qualitative work be carried out on these as a
matter of priority.

‘Although economic overheads in the Managalas plateau are considerable (in particular
the lack of and cost of transport and poor communications), it may still be profitable to
commercially develop some NTFPs with careful species and product selection and a
marketing strategy that emphasises the links between their production and biodiversity
conservation in the area.
 Paul Konial NTFP! Managoasl survey 200907

Geographical Location:

Managalas Plateau is located at approximately 9 degrees longitude north and
approximately 148. 2 degrees latitude south of the equator. The district head quarter is
called Afore District and it is administered at the township of Popendetta. The province
was formally called Northern Province but was later changed to Oro province where
Managalas Plateau is located.

The total population of Oro province is about 120,000 people according to the 2000
census of which the Managalas people makes up 5% of the total population which is
almost 16000 (15,000 accordingly to the National Census in 2000).

Managalas Plateau is located at the most remote part of the Oro Province and almost
isolated from the rest of Papua New Guinea. The total land area is approximately 360,000
heetares. Thus life at Managalas Plateau for an outsider can be very challenging due to
the fact that walking is difficult on the rugged terrain while basic and essential
government services are very minimum or non existent at very isolated locations through
out the plateau.

Access to the Managalas Plateau is either by foot, a four-wheel-drive to Afore or a twin-
Otto aeroplane serviced by the third level airline, Airlines PNG. There are five (5)
airstrips on the Plateau which are at Afore, Itokama, Sakarina, Sila and Gora, However,
Ttokama airstrip is the only one commercially serviced by Airlines PNG while the others
have been closed because people were not using it regularly or they have not met the
requirements of the Civil Aviation Authority in one way or another.
 Paul Konia/ NTFP/ Menagulat- sarvey 2005107

Paul Konia! NTFP/Managalas- survey 2005/07

By: Paul P Konia.

Recommendations & Assumptions:
Common Name: Kopi/Kofi (Tok Pisin)

English: Coffee

Local Dialect: Kofuke

ScientificName: Coffea Arabica- Family: Rubiaceae

Ba Is

Around the birth of Jesus Christ, coffee was reportedly first discovered growing in
Ethiopia by a sheepherder named Khaldi. Whenever he moved his sheep into one
particular pasture, the sheep would start acting extremely lively and erratic after
eating the “red cherries” on a particular bush found in that pasture. Tentatively,
Khaldi tried eating a few of the beans himself and experienced the same reaction.
‘The local area monks heard about Khaldi and this “devil’s fruit” but soon they too
were eagerly sampling it so they could stay awake for their prayers. Arab traders,
during a trading expedition, decided to bring back some beans to their homeland
and began to plant and grow their own beans. Soon they began to boil the beans and
produced a drink called “qahwa” (meaning “unable to sleep”). The drink gained
popularity until around 1453 when the Ottoman Turks introduced the beans to
Constantinople and in 1475 the world’s first coffee shop; “Kiva Han” was opened in
the city. The “coffee craze” developed to a point where women could even divorce
their husbands if they failed to provide the women with a daily ration of coffee. The
mere existence of the plant was a closely guarded secret in the Moslem countries
 when an Arab named Baba Budan started the actual spread of this delicacy to the
outside world illegally. Baba Budan smuggled some beans to Mysore, India where
descendants of these first smuggled plants can be found to this day.

In 1600, Italian traders brought some of the beans to Pope Clement VIII who was
urged to ban the drink as “unholy” because it came from Moslems that were “Non
Christians” but he surprised them by “baptizing” it instead, Now “coffee” was an
acceptable beverage for Christians. A few years later, Dutch traders smuggled out
cofiee plant from the port of Espresso to the island of Ceylon and to their East
Indian colony of Java, source of cofiee’s nickname today. In 1713, the Dutch
unwittingly gave a coffee bush to Louis XIV of France that, from which, in 1723, a
French naval officer, Gabriel Mathieu do Clieu, stole a seedling and took it to
Martinique. Eventually, 90 percent of the world’s coffee spread from this one plant.

Jamaican Blue Mountain Coffee:

In 1728 Sir Nicholas Lawes, then Governor of Jamaica and owner of Temple Hall
Estate, brought the first coffee plants to Jamaica. First, cultivation started in the
foothilis of St. Andrew but soon plantations extended deeper into the fertile Blue
Mountains. The coffee industry has experienced many ups and downs from those
early days until today.

From 1800 to 1840, Jamaica produced 70,000 tons per year making her the largest
producer in the world. Then, in 1838, came the abolition of slavery. This spelled the
end to many coffee plantations, as newly freed farmers began planting and clearing
all the available hillsides to earn a living and to have land to live on. By 1891, the
coffee industry was in general disarray so legislation was passed to provide
“instruction in the art of cultivation and curing by sending certain districts,
‘competent instructors.”

‘The effort to increase quality was largely unsuccessful as the largest buyer in those
days was the Canadian market and they resisted it as being unacceptable. Finally, in
1944 the Jamaican government established a Central Coffee Clearing House where
all cofiee for export had to be processed. This cleaning and grading process was a
giant step in the improvement in the quality of the Jamaican coffee being exported.

Following the devastating hurricane of 1951, there were only three Coffee
Processing Plants (called “pulperies”) remaining in operation in the Blue
Mountains. In an attempt to regulate the growth that was sure to follow, the Coffee
Industry Board was formed to establish guidelines in quality, cultivation and
processing. The Coffee Industry Board is still an active force today and garners
some of the credit for the resurgence of Jamaican coffee. In 1973, the three coffee
processing plants at Mavis Bank, Silver Hill and Moy Hall along with a new comer,
Wallenford, registered the name “Blue Mountain Coffee”.

A few years ago, the Twyman family’s Old Tavern Estate Coffee won the legal right
through the Jamaican courts to also sell its superior product under the “Blue
Mountain” name.
 Jamaica is famous for producing some of the finest coffee found anywhere in the
world. What makes this little island such a prime spot for growing a world-class
coffee? As in real estate, it's “Location, Location, Location” and in this case, that
location is the Blue Mountains. Cofiee plants need to be well watered, well drained
and experience periodic coolness dusing some stages of development. To be called
“Blue Mountain Coffee”, it must be grown at altitudes between 2,000 and 5,000 feet
in the Parishes of Portland, St. Andrew and St. Thomas and, most importantly, be
grown on the estates of; Mavis Bank, Silver Hill, Moy Hall or Wallenford. Coffee
grown elsewhere in the Blue Mountains or anywhere else in Jamaica cannot be
called “Blue Mountain Coffee. Blue Mountain coffee is exclusively made from the
‘Arabica Bean. The Arabica bean is more fragile to grow but is considered more
flavorful and has less caffeine than the Robusta Bean grown in many parts of the
world.

Small growers like James Dennis in the District of Section are finding success in
selling their production directly to discriminating tourists as most of the “official”
Blue Mountain Coffee is currently exported to Japan. First they must harvest their
beans and then sun dry them on bamboo racks before roasting them over a smoky
wood fire. They weigh and package the beans in plastic bags for sale to passing
tourists and locals. Want your cofive ground? They will pour the roasted beans into
an old hollowed-out log and have someone pound and pulverize the beans using a
stout, tapered hardwood branch with a flat surface on the end.

More small growers, like James Dennis, along with the officially recognized and
established “Blue Mountain Coffee” growers known as JABLUM (Jamaica Blue
Mountain) are growing and producing what is regarded as the “Best Coffee in the
Caribbean” and quite possibly the “Best Coffee in the World”.

Coffee was introduced to Papua New Guinea in the late 1940s thus in the late 1960s
it was taken up to Afore and the Managalas plateau by the colonel administration to
be grown as a cash crop.

The Managalas plateau has almost over 700 farmers who grow more than 800 000
cofiee trees that can produce about 8000 bags annually at an average weight of 360
000 (45kg per bag) kilograms. In monetary terms, the current coffee buying price at
the plateau is K2.00 which means that the revenue going in annually will be about
K720 000.00. Moreover, if cofiee is sold at factory door price in Goroka which
stands at K4.50 per kilogram, then farmers of Managalas plateau would have
collected K1, 62000.00 annually.

Plant Description: The cofive plant is a woody perennial evergreen dicotyledon that
belongs to the Rubiaceae family. It has a main vertical trunk (orthotropic) and
primary, secondary, and tertiary horizontal branches (plagiotropic). Two main
species of cofive are cultivated today. Coffea arabica known as Arabica coffee
accounts for 75-80% of the world's production. Coffea canephora, known as
Robusta coffee, is more robust than the Arabica plants, but produces an inferior
tasting beverage with a higher caffeine content. The coffee plant can grow to
 heights of 10 meters if not pruned, but producing countries will maintain the coffee
at a height reasonable for easy harvesting.

A.common tended, planted or cultivated medium-large tree with distinctive lateral
branches, deciduous green to red leaves and fruits with hard corky pink/ purple
shell that is cut open in to equal halves.

Plant Development: Three to four years after the coffee is planted, sweet smelling
flowers grow in clusters in the axils of the leaves. Fruit is produced only in the new
tissue. The Arabica species is self-pollinating, whereas the Robusta species depends
on cross pollination. About 6-8 weeks after the flowers are fertilized, cell division
occurs and the fruit remains as a pin head for a period that is dependent upon the
climate. The ovaries will then develop into drupes in a rapid growth period that
takes about 15 weeks after flowering. During this time the integument takes on the
shape of the final bean. After the rapid growth period the integument and
parchment are fully grown and will not increase in size. The endosperm remains
small until about 12 weeks after flowering. At this time it will suppress, consume,
and replace the integument. The remnants of the integument are what make up the
silverskin. The endosperm will have completely filled the cavity made by the
integument nineteen weeks after flowing. The endosperm is now white and moist,
but will gain dry matter during the next several months, During this time the
endosperm attracts more than seventy percent of the total photosynthesis produced
by the tree. The mesocarps will expand to form the sweet pulp that surrounds the
bean. The cherry will change color from green to red about thirty to thirty-five
weeks after flowing.

Root System: The root system can extend 20-25 km in total length and the absorbing
surface of a tree ranges from 400 to 500 m*. There are main vertical roots, tap
roots, and lateral roots which grow parallel to the ground. The tap roots extend no
further than 30-45 cm below the soil surface. Four to eight axial roots may be
encountered which often originate horizontally but point downward. The lateral
roots can extend 2 m from the trunk. About 80-90% of the feeder root is in the first
20 em of soil and is 60-90 cm away from the trunk of the tree (Mavolta, 195-196).
However, the greatest root concentration is in the 30 to 60 cm depth. The roots
systems are heavily affected by the type of soil and the mineral content of the soil.
To be thick and strong the root system needs an extensive supply of nitrogen,
calcium and magnesium. During planting the main vertical roots are often clipped
to promote growth of the horizontal roots, which then have better access to water
and added nutrients in the top soil.

Leaves: The elliptical leaves of the coffee tree are shiny, dark green, and waxy. The
leaf area index is between 7 and 8 for a high-yielding coffee. The coffee plant has
become a major source of oxygen in much of the world. Each hectare of coffee
produces 86 Ibs of oxygen per day, which is about half the production of the same
area in a rain forest (source: Anacafe).

Harvesting: Each year coffee is harvested during the dry season when the coffee
cherries are bright red, glossy, and firm. Ripe cherries are either picked by hand,
 stripped from the tree with both unripe and overripe beans, or all the beans are
collected using a harvesting machine. These processes are called selective picking,
stripping, and mechanical harvesting, respectively.
To maximize the amount of ripe cofive harvested it is necessary to selectively pick
the ripe beans from the tree by hand and leave behind unripe, green beans to be
harvested at a later time. In Brazil, harvesting the same tree several times is more
cost prohibitive than separating and discarding the unripe ot overripe cherries.
‘Therefore, Brazil typically harvests using the stripping method when 75% of the
crop is perfectly ripe. Stripping is feasible and cost effective in Brazil due to the
uniform maturation of Brazilian coffees. In stripping the beans are pulled from the
tree and fall to the ground where they are caught by sheets. The beans are removed
from tree debris by tossing the coffee in the air allowing the wind to carry away
sticks and leaves. The coffee is then put in 60 L green baskets, which is the
measuring tool used by coffee producers to determine wages. Some estates, such as
Fazenda Monte Alegre in Sul de Minas Brazil, have a computerized system to
determine wages, which accounts for the amount of coffee collected from each
person, the difficulty of the harvesting conditions, and the production of the region
being harvested. About 12-20 kg of export ready cofite will be produced from every
100 kg of coffee cherries harvested.

Processing: Irrespective of the harvesting method, green coffee beans and overripe
coffee cherries inevitably end up mixed with the perfectly ripe cherries and must be
separated. Over ripe cofive cherries, undeveloped cofiee cherries, sticks and leaves
float in water. Ripe coffee beans and green coffee cherries are dense and sink.
Therefore, the first separation step takes place by separating the floaters from the
sinkers. The floaters are usually sent directly to the patio to be dried and are then
slated for internal consumption. The ripe and green cherries can be sent to the
patios to be dried using the natural (dry) process or can be sent to the pulping
machines.

The first stage of pulping is used to remove the green cherries from the ripe
cherries. In the pulping machine the internal pressure is monitored to push the
coffee against a screen with holes only large enough for a coffee bean (not cherry) to
pass through. Since the ripe cherries are soft they break and the seed is released
Mirogetethelserties.are hard and cannot be pulped. Instead of passing through the
screen, the green beans pass to the end of the barrel system and are separated from
the ripe beans. The pressure inside the barrel controls how many cherries will be
pulped. A very high pressure will cause all of the cherries including the green beans
to be pulped. It is necessary to continuously monitor the pressure so that about 3%
of ripe cherries are not pulped and are removed with the green cherties. This
margin of error ensures that no green cherries are mistakenly pulped. The pulp
and beans are then separated by centrifugal force and a barrel screen system.

The beans covered in the slippery mucilage can be sent to the patios to dry as
pulped natural coffees or can be sent to fermentation tanks. The fermenting tanks
are used to remove the mucilage before drying. The pulped beans are put into
cement tanks with water and are allowed to ferment for 16-36 hours. On the way to
 the fermentation tanks another density separation can occur. The highest quality
coffees are the most dense and should be separated and fermented in a different tank.

The fermentation time depends on a number of factors including the amount of
coffee fermenting, water temperature, and humidity. The mucilage is made up of
pectin materials including protopectin (33%), reducing sugars including glucose
and fructose (30%), non-reducing sugars such as sucrose (20%), and cellulose and
ash (17%) Protopectin is not water soluble and will hydrolyze to pectinic acid in the
fermentation tanks. Hydrolysis of the protopectin and degradation of the pectin by
enzymes is the process that occurs to remove the mucilage during fermentation
(Wrigley, 455). Currently, the best way of determining the end of fermentation is to
feel the beans to determine if the beans are still encased in mucilage. If the beans
are fermented for 36-72 hours stinker beans develop. Lactic, acetic, and propionic
acids are produced in this process and are believed to prevent the traditional
fermentation taste by inhibiting mold growth that regularly occurs during drying on
Srmtiatin fxrmizheatiditianks the beans are moved to drying patios and dried to I1-
12% moisture content. A small portion of the lot is hulled and milled by a mini-
huller. Three hundred grams of cofiee is classified for defects (100 grams is often
used), and the percentage of each screen size is determined. Then, 200-300 grams of
coffee is roasted in a sample roaster and cupped to determine quality. Ideally no
lots will be mixed until the coffee has been classified and cupped. The coffee
remains in pergamino until shipment time to help protect the flavor and aroma of
the coffee.

Before shipment coffee must be dried from approximately 60% moisture content to
11-12% moisture content. Coffee is typically dried on large patios made of asphalt
or cement and then transferred to mechanical dryers. The coffee on the drying
patios is shifted every 30-40 minutes and is shaped into long rows of no more than 5
cm in height. Next to each row is open ground, which is warmed and dried by the
sun, The coftee is then shifted onto the dry portion of the patio, and the section
where it was previously is now allowed to dry in the sun. This helps accelerate the
drying process and prevents fermentation and moldy beans from developing. This
method is widely used in Brazil, but less widely used in Guatemala or Costa Rica
where the coffee is more often piled perpendicularly to the old piles. To dry coflee
solely by patio drying it takes 6-7 days for washed coftees, 8-9 days for pulped
naturals (semi-washed), and 12-14 days for natural (dry-processed) coffees. This is
why coffees are typically dried on a patio until they reach a moisture content of 15%
and are then transferred to mechanical dryers. Once the coffee reaches 25%
moisture or less it can be piled at night and covered with cotton cloths to allow the
coffee to breath. If it rains these piles can also be covered with plastic. Coffee should
not be covered with burlap sacks since this will impart a distinct burlap flavor and
aroma to the cofiee.

In a study done in Kenya, the report highlights that there are six stages to drying
¢)Bkin drying. Moisture 55-45%.

2) White Stage drying. Moisture 44-33%.

3) Soft Black stage, Moisture 32-22%.

4) Medium Black Stage. Moisture 21-16%

 5) Hard Black Stage. Moisture 15-12%
6) Fully dry coffee and conditioning. 11-10%.

In this study it was discovered that sun drying for stage three is mandatory for
coffee quality. It also reported that as long as the temperature was between 40-
50°C--which means a bean temp of 35°C--then the coffee quality will not be
seriously compromised during the other stages.

‘The final two stages (15-11% moisture) in just six hours at 40°C in a mechanical
dryer. There are several dryer systems available. Many older dryers are converted
grain dryers that are not as efficient as the new horizontal barrel dryers. The new
dryers are designed to mix the coffee evenly to ensure uniform drying. Drying by
using mechanical dryers accelerates the slowest part of the drying process (15-11%)
and helps prevent fermentation. In some environments that have a high humidity
the entire drying process must take place in mechanical dryers. Mechanical dryers
should never be set higher than 40-45°C and this question should be asked before
buying any coffees that have been mechanically dried. At higher temperatures the
germ is killed and the flavor potential of the coffee is ruined. At extreme
temperature the bean crystallizes and when smashed with a hammer will break like
glass.

The best, but least utilized method of drying coffee is by using drying tables. In this
method the pulped and fermented cofive is spread thinly on raised beds, which
allows the air to pass on all sides of the coffee. The coffee is mixed by hand and the
drying that takes place is more uniform and fermentation is less likely. Most coffee
from the Managalas Plateau is dried in this manner and it is the commonly used
drying method used widely in Papua New Guinea. It is sometimes known as Solar
Drying. Solar Dryer is good during rains and at nights. A drying bed is built with a
shelter over it with plastic sheet. The sides and ends of the bed are properly covered
and coffee parchments are spread on the bed to dry. Parchments are turn regularly
for sun to dry all sides. It takes about 3-4 weeks for the parchment to dry properly.

Introduction

‘The proposed Managalas Conservation Arca encompasses about 360 000 hectares of pristine
rainforest in the Managalas Plateau, Ijivitari District, Oro Province. The area is bordered by the
Owen Stanley Range to the southwest and the Sibium Range to the southeast. Popondetta town
and the famous Kokoda Trail are situated north of the proposed conservation area.

Like most areas of NG, the Managalas Plateau harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora, but at
the moment is poorly documented. Biologists from the University of PNG have carried out two
previous surveys but the true biodiversity of the plateau is far from complete. This is evident
from the diverse frog fauna sampled during this survey, because frogs are a good indicator of a
rich and a vibrant environment.

There are about 250 frogs recognised from NG. This number increases at a fast rate because new
species are discovered and described every year, some remain undescribed in museum
collections throughout the world (e.g. American Museum of Natural History, British Museum of
Natural History, Bishop Museum, South Australian Museum), More than 50% of NG frogs
comprising the one family Microhylidae reproduce out of the water. Therefore the wet and
humid environmental condition of the whole Managalas Plateau provides an abundance of habits
for these frogs. However, no previous attempts have been made to quantitatively document this,
rich component of the plateau before the previous two surveys by members of this team.

This report summarises the results of the herpetological survey conducted during Phase III of the
Managalas Plateau from 20" May 2006 to S* June 2006.

Methods

Frogs were detected at night by locating calling males and by visual encounters. Efforts were
equally distributed along rivers and streams for aquatic frogs, and away from water bodies for

non-aquatic frogs.

‘Some frogs were identified in the field, and voucher specimens were also collected for further
confirmation and storage at the UPNG Natural Science Resource Centre.

Snakes and lizards encountered were also captured and specimens collected for preservation.
Three snakes Furina ists, Stegonotus modestus and Tropidonophis statisticus were brought to us by
local people.

Survey sites
Numbumare, Aiare village along Musa River.
Altitudinal range: 547-600m.

GPS location: 09° 19° 50” S, 148° 13° 50” E

Dakara, Umwate village
Altitudinal range: 778-800m_
GPS location: 9° 16” 27” S, 148° 14° 50" E

‘The vegetation of both sites are typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs are well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp. palms
and Calamus spp.

Results

A total of 15 species of frogs from three families were recorded. Of these 47% of the species are
of the family Microhylidae, a normal observation for other parts of NG where microhylid frogs
usually dominate. The other families, Ranidae and Hylidae constitute 26.5% of the total species
cach. Six species of snakes and three species of lizards were also documented during the survey,
although less time was diverted for snakes and lizards (Table 1).

Local information mentions the presence of Green Tree Python (Morelia viridis), Death Adder
(Acanthophis sp) or probably NG Ground Boa (Candoia) because the later two snakes
superficially resemble each other. Local informant also mentions the presence of large green
frog, which could be Litoria infrafrenata. These animals were not encountered so are not
included in the species accounts.

Discussion

Frogs are secretive animals and hide during the day but come out during the night to feed, mate
and carryout their other essential biological functions. Daytime encounters are usually
accidental, or when one actively looks for them in likely hiding places. Therefore sampling has
to be done during their active periods so that maximum encounters can be made. Heavy rains

also trigger higher frog activity but some species of the subfamily Asterophryninae may call
during the day.

Diversity Patterns

Diversity at generic and specific levels is high for microhylid frogs in the Managalas Plateau
(Figure 1). This is expected because elsewhere in NG, microhylid frogs usually dominate the
Anuran fauna. For example, Richards (2002) recorded 30 microhylid frogs, 19 hylid frogs and 5
ranid frogs from the Kikori Basin. Richard’s survey was conducted for three years covering
  a RI SL SL I SUE OS, Oa I

altitudinal range of 40-1300m. It is expected that the number of frog species in the Managalas
Plateau will increase as more surveys are conducted covering all altitudinal ranges of the plateau.

‘Some species documented at Nabumare were not recorded from Dakara and vice versa, but this
is an artefact of environmental conditions and sampling period. Dakara was much dryer than
Nabumare, so the number of species encountered at Nabumare was higher than for Dakara
(Table 1). At the moment this comparison does not mean anything at all, because a long term
sampling with a lot of rainy periods will reveal the true diversity of frogs from the two sites. But,
there is some similarity between the two sites, with the presence of four ranid species,
Hylophorbus sp and Mantophryne lateralis at both sites. The three Nyctymystes species collected
along the Musa River were not encountered along smaller creeks, suggesting these species
preferred larger fast flowing rivers compared to smaller creeks.

‘The six snakes and the skink lizards documented during this survey should be indicative of a
more diverse component of the Managalas fauna. Additional efforts directed towards these
components of the fauna should be prioritised during future surveys.

New Species

A sizable frog fauna (47%) of the surveyed sites are undescribed, including a small skink lizard,
suggestive of many new species yet to be documented. As the survey moves higher to over
1000m new species, especially hylid frogs that prefer fast flowing mountain streams would
undoubtly be discovered. The three Nyctymystes frogs, a genus endemic to NG appears to be new
to science, but further analysis will be done to confirm this.

Environment and Conservation Considerations

Frogs are sensitive to environmental change and are a good indicator of the status of an
environment. In a pristine environment free of pollution, the diversity of frogs at the family,
generic and species levels are usually high. Most of the environment of NG is still under pristine
conditions, except probably around the vicinity of large mining/industrial areas and cities. By
comparing past frog diversity to future diversity should large scale environmental degradation
activities occur, the status of the environment could be determined by assessing the decline in
diversity of frogs.

‘The environment in the Managalas Plateau still remains intact providing numerous microhabitats
for many animals to utilize. The consequences of clearing forests for large scale agricultural
activities, logging or mining operations would be loss of habitat for many of the rich biota. These
include the Bird-wing Butterfly, Tree Kangaroos, Cuscus, Bandicoots, and a host of many new
species of frogs yet unknown to science.

All these rich biota are the traditional rights and heritage of the Managalas people. Everywhere
in PNG, people are close to their forests and depend on it more than 90% of the time and would
not sustain a good living should the forests go, especially in rural areas where government
services are lacking. A comprehensive list of forest products depended upon by the Managalas
people is out of the scope of this report, but suffice is to say that, wood, food, building material,
Okari nut, bamboo, rattan, Pandanus are some of the things that come to mind. If NEC approves
the Managalas conservation area, the forest will continue to provide for the current generation
and those to come in the future.
  Recommendations

‘The following recommendations are drawn afier sampling at lower altitudes (547 — 785m) in the
Proposed Managalas Conservation Project Area, Afore District, Oro Province from 20" May to
5® June 2006.

a) Several more surveys should be carried out at 2 or 3 higher altitude localities, Uwolome
Range (2800m) and Sibium Range (180m). I suggest one survey each close to or at the
summit of these ranges, and a further down at around 1200 — 150m. These will provide
a comprehensive preliminary fauna and flora checklist covering all altitudes for decision

making.

b) Frog survey should be prioritised for higher altitudes to document species in these areas
so that future environmental decisions can be made by comparing present results with
future results. As mentioned above, frogs respond to environmental change quicker than

other animals, and the changes in diversity can be utilized to determine the status of the
Managalas environment in the future.

©) On future surveys, include people exclusively for the survey of snakes, lizards, insects
(and other arthropods) and fresh water fauna. These are also an integral component of the
environment and play their role in the Managalas ecosystems.

d) Two to three times as much coffee, sugar, tea, etc must be bought for the field so that a
general hot water pot for every body on-site be strategically placed in the middle. This
action from PWM and the survey team will:

© Cut down “barriers” between the local people and the PWM / survey team.

© Local people “feel included” in the survey, not to stay at their own end, while the
survey team stay at their own end.

© Local information, an integral part of a survey, can easily and freely be obtained
while sharing a cup of coffee.

1. INTRODUCTION

The second and the follow-up training on Rice cultivation was again conducted by Keosai Damboro
from the Village Development Trust (VDT)- Lae.

The original Plan of the training was scheduled on the 2st. 29" September 2006, However due to the
very late change of the boat Scehule (Lae- Orobay) and Poor attendance of Participants: the training
was postponed and held on the following week from the 2™- 6" of October 2006,

Even though we had the some problem with poor attendance we went ahead and conducted the training
with participants from four (4) zones (Zone |, 2, 3 and 9) and farmers from the hosting community
(Tahama).

 Rice Survey Report
Date of Survey: 23-27 August 2006
Location: East of Managalas

Survey Done by: Mack Kumoro- PwM Project Officer

Introduction:

As part of PwM’s attempt to alleviate poverty and to improve local livelihood in the
Managalas Conservation Area, under the [UCN funding, this survey was carried out.

Survey location:
The rice survey was carried out in almost all parts of the Managalas Plateau. The survey area

as was divided into two parts. The Eastern part which covers villages and zones starting from
zone 5, at Siribu, Ugunomo, through the zone 6 (Dea, Tabuane, koino, Numba, Kaira, Sila,
Kavoki and Afore was carried out by myself.

‘
Starting from Koruvo (Zone 4) up to Kaitavna, Tahamo thepagh to Serepuna, Kokoro,
Buamfu, Anatua, koe, Itokama and Nokunane Villages was carried out by PwM’s Eco-
Enterprise Coordinator (Doradora Sogaye)..

Farmer Information:
Managalas people have not yet gone seriously into rice forming. The survey indi
only few farmers have actually tried out planting, but on a very small scale.

During the course of this survey, the list of interested farmers names was collected.

We also noticed there was lack of knowledge on farming methods. From few rite plots
observed, it became obvious that we found the following:

a) None of the farmers had attended any formal training on rice farming

b) Harvested rice (from few farmers) had not been properly consumed- no proper
milling equipment and all harvested grains got spoilt

©) Current farmers admitted they got their rice seeds from friends and trukai rice
Industries at Popondetta.

Sub- topics for the workshop. The four topics have their own aims and objectives
for the participants.

2.0: PRINCIPLES OF BOOKKEEPING

‘The main aims and objectives of this topic are:
+> To apply the basic book keeping rules
+ Identify the responsible of Treasure & book keeper & Committees
 2.1; BASIC PRINCIPLES OF BOOK KEEPING

2.1.1. What is book keeping?

1, Financial records correct (accurate recording)
2. Total amount of money received
= membership
- grants
office rents
Bookkeeping is a process of accurately recording income, all money received or going
in and accurately recording expenses (all money paid out) of a group. Simple book
keeping is a CASH BOOK.

2.2.2. Why is Bookkeeping Important?

(a: Group money belong to the member of the groups, the moni
the group has does not belong to the treasurer or committee.
belongs to all members together.

():  -Know what happen to the money
Know how much money the group has and how it is used.

Help to use money according to plan
Know how much money is left to spent or already spend
Know how much to spend on other things

(@): Show that a group can take care of money (keep good record)
2.2.3. PARTS OF BOOK KEEPING (8 important parts)

(a) Treasurer/bookkeeper — looks after money
(b) Finance Committee:

a group that help the bookkeeper /treasurer look after the money.
(©) Cash book ~ safe
(@) Bank account ~ Bank keeps money
{e} Cash book ~ Booic where you record Incomes & Expense
() Receipts - Book showing money moved from one person to another.
(g) Monthly Report - Income and Expense record for one month.

(h) Procedure ~ good way to do book keeping.

2.2.4. ‘TREASURERS & FINANCE COMMITTEE

A Treasurer and Finance Committee are people who look after group's money.

‘The Treasure or Finance Officer (Roles & Responsibility)

(@) A treasure is an Individual man or woman who looks after money.

(b) He or she should know how to read, write and work with numbers (add,
subtract, multiply and divide)

(¢) Treasurer keeps the Cash box, cash book, receipt and receipt book, he/she holds
the bank documents (if they have a bank account.

(a) He/She records down Income & Expenses

{e) Only treasurer takes money out or puts money in the Cash box.

{Treasurer has the power to take money out of this account.

(@) Finance Committee gives permission to the treasurers to buy some items (they
set limit).

(h) Treasurer submits monthly report.

() Treasurer teachers one or two people to do book keeping.
 2.2.5. FINANCE COMMITTEE

(a) Small group of people who helps the treasure look after the money.
(b) They decide what the treasurer can do and can not do.
(©) They decide how much can be used within the budget.
(d) They ask the treasurer to report to them

Record keeping are,
+ Records of financial transaction (receipts & invoice)
+ Records of financial for goods & equipment (stocks)
+ Records of financial of important documents (contact, agreement)

Financial records means to write down organisations money received and paid out.

(2) Control Cash

¢) Invoice
Is a business document that shows quantity, description, unit price and total

at anytime,

PARTNERS WITH MELANESIANS’ RAINFOREST LITERACY PROGRAM

Scriptwriters’ Series II Design Workshop

(15 ~ 19 March 2004 and follow-up planning 22-25 March)

Summary:

The overriding objective of the Series II Workshop was to provide the Senior Scriptwriter
with a simpler, more streamlined plan for executing the second series of radio
broadcasts and interactive community group discussions. With that in mind, back-up
strategies were developed for keeping progress on target, whether or not difficulties
‘emerged in terms of getting people to and from the Plateau or in terms of people
‘communication over the radio as planned. The production, distribution, and use of the
newsletter (to be completed by the CLCs) was separated from the production,
distribution, and use of the remaining materials (radio programs, flip charts, and
booklets) which will be completed according to schedule in Port Moresby with the help of
Managalas families in POM even if timely checking on the Plateau becomes a problem.
In another move to make things simpler, instructions for helping the facilitators will be
printed on the back of the flip charts.

Finally, the cascade system for training facilitators which called for training events in
each zone following the East/West training of Activity Coordinators has also been
simplified. This year the Activity Coordinators will attend the Master Training Workshop
along with Simon Savaiko, PWM and MDF staff involved in rainforest literacy activities
Then, all the participating group facilitators will attend either the East or West facilitator
training workshops that follow. Zone level activity coordinators will offer additional
coaching to weak facilitators during the four weeks of broadcast but no zone level
trainings as such will be held.

These changes plus technical changes arising from the formative evaluation feedback
are expected to keep the production and implementation of the Series Il broadcasts on
target in terms of meeting broadcast goals and help make the overall program easier for
the limited staff at PWM to manage.

What follows here is a day to day outline of accomplishments over the week of the
workshop and the first part of the following week where follow-up activity was carried out
by Micael and Ruth at the PWM office.

1.0: INTRODUCTION:

‘The Sewing workshop was conducted from the 19" ~ 23° of April 2004. This workshop was to
help the mothers to know the basics of sewing and how to sew various type of clothing so they
don't have to spent money on buying expensive cloths. Also to help the women on the plateau
to generate income to help improve their living standard. The sewing workshop was conducted
in Itokama village, Zone one (1) which lasted for five days (one week}.

‘There were 24 women participants participated in the workshop. Six participants each from
zones 1, 2, & 3 and two and four from zones 4 & 10 from the Westerns side of Managalas
attended the workshop. Ten (10) groups of women were formed of three participants each and
were allocated a machine in each group. The participants represent their zones to attend the
workshop so they can go back to their respective zones and teach the mothers. Some
participants came with their husbands who were willing to observe what the mothers were
doing and help get some notes for them. They stayed all through out the workshop till it was
closed on Friday

Generally the workshop was conducted well, not much inconvenience was caused but the
mothers were really happy for such a workshop to be conducted in the plateau because that
was what the mothers were desperately in need to know. This workshop was first of its kind to
be conducted up in the Western side of the plateau.

1.1: AIMS:

‘The main aim of the sewing workshop was to teach the women basic sewing skills so that they
can sew their own clothes and to know how to use the machine. Also to get to know each and
share what they have in common.

1.2: OBJECTIVE:

The main objective of the workshop

+ Teach the women the basic skills of sewing,

+ Teach them how to handle and fix the machines.

+ Participants to go back and transfer the knowledge /ideas/skills to the women in their
respective zones.

1.3: PARTICIPANTS EXPECTATIONS:

Learn how to show various patterns
Generate income from sewing and selling
Learn how to fix machine parts

Know basic skills on sewing
Transferring of skills.

2.0: BACKGROUND INFORMATIO!

‘This sewing workshop was first of its kind to be conducted up in the Western side of the
Managalas Plateau. The participants and the observers were overwhelmed about what we did

during the workshop.

‘The women participants came from far and near by villages to learn, This was a new thing to
them especially the different types of pattern being thought and demonstrated to them. Every
participant took part and was given changes to try out practically and no one was left out. This
workshop was also an opportunity for the participant to come together to know each other and
share ideas and experiences to help cach other in the long run.

3.0: CONTENT OR DISCUSSION:

We held open discussion or teaching. I did the explanation of how to sew the patterns and
demonstrate it at the same time to the participants. The participants all came around formed a
circle to watch and listen to me and what I was doing. After the demonstration, the participants
went back to their groups to sew practically. During the session, they asked questions to get
more information of how to go about sewing the particular pattern. | taught them five different

Main parts discussed and elaborated on were as follows:
1, Handi Turns the wheel

2. Wheel: Raise’s and lowers the needle
Spool pin: Holds the reel of the thread

Take up lever: ‘Take up thread from the reel after each stitch is made

Tension nob: Controls the upper thread tightness

Pressure foot: Holds the fabric firmly during stitching

Needle clamp: Holds the needle firmly in position

Needle: ‘Takes the thread and out of the fabric

Teeth: Moves the fabric along after each stitch is made

Bobbin case: Holds the bobbin and controls the tightness of the lower stitching
thread

Bobbin: Holds the thread for lower stitching

Teeth control: Raises and lowers the teeth

Stitch regulator: Controls the length and direction of the stitch

Bobbin winder: Winds the thread on to the bobbin.

5.1: EVALUATION - QUESTIONS & ANSWERS:
QI: What was best about the workshop?

The new skills and ideas they've learnt from sewing and how to sew various types of clothes.

1. Need more sewing machines, three participants to a machine is not good
enough.

Il, Length of time to be extended when ever such Workshop is conducted.

Yes we need to know more skills on sewing and other various patterns of clothing apart from

5.2: OTHER OBSERVATION & COM!

‘There were complaints by the participants on the first and second day of the workshop which
the observers caused inconvenience for the trainer and the participants. The observers took
over the participants in handling the machines which they were not supposed to do because
they were only there to observe and not to part take. However, this problem was announced on
Tuesday 20/04/04, which saw some observers were unhappy and left while the others accepted
it and stayed back to observe and gain some basic knowledge. The observers who left, turn to
discourage the other women who were trying to learn and they were the one’s who have
knowledge of sewing but refuse to share their skills and knowledge to others. Generally the
participants were really happy to have such workshop conducted and they learnt a lot
especially the different type of patterns being thought to them. They did practical sewing and
the end results prove that they did understood what they were learning cach day. During
practical sessions they asked questions to get more information showing that they were knee
and interested. This was a new world and an eye opener to them. The participants were happy
and wanted another sewing workshop to be conducted again.

‘The main purpose of the workshop was to help train the women to learn the basic skills on how

standard of living.

explained through an “House Building” exercise. The participants were then
taken to look at what is not Development and what is Development. Introducing
the participants 0 CARGO DEVELOPMENT and the true development, the

The participants used SWOT (Strength, Weakness, Opportunities & Threats) analysis
to identify the Strengths and Weaknesses from within the MDF and then they went
‘on to do a scan of the trends (SWOT- Opportunities and Threats) that are coming
from the outside and affecting MDF as an organization and upon its individual
membership. By looking at the challenges obstacles and/or issues faced by the

Furthermore, the participants together discussed in smaller groups what is currently
happening and what needs to happen to address these trends and community
needs/issues/challenges/obstacle. The Internal scan, the Trend scan and the MDF
community need analysis including the comments and discussions raised during recap
and group presentations helped the participants to come up with organizational
program components/strategies. Using SMART (being Specific, Measurable
Achievable, Relevant and Time bound) exercise the participants in smaller groups

Finally the group defined and have in place a new Strategic Direction and plan, This

whole strategic plan if one is not familiar with the concept and approaches in
Participatory Strategic Planning

Background

The socio- economic impact of the Okari nut project on the Managalas plateau
became apparent that communities became organized around it. The establishment of
Partners with Melanesia tasked to organized the Managalas communities around their
cultural and natural resources and further carry out research into Okari nut as a viable
non forest product. There were already threats of large scale logging moving into the
plateau. PWM facilitated communities to be organized into zones created structures
like the Combined Forum Steering Committee Meetings zone boards, clan
committees, zone office and admin support staff and program staff. There are ten
zones established on the plateau. There were few zones that were suspended along the
way, while the most organized zones got incorporated as recognized Legal entity with
IPA. The most notable ones are zone 1, zone 2, and the umbrella body on the plateau,
Managalas Development Foundation.

In 2001, seven after the overall Managalas Conservation Area Support Project
(MCASP) PWM held its first Strategic Planning Workshop at Naukanane. The focus
areas identified were, Consensus Building, Training, Gender and Eco- enterprising
became the main focus component of all the programs carried out on the plateau. As
identified in the strategic plan where there were low interest in eco- enterprising
consensus building stopped. The literacy program in the non formal sector was
established prior to the MCASP and strengthened through the formation and
incorporation of the Barai Non-formal Education Association (BNEA). There were
many activities that were not implemented in Gender and the Training component.

‘The new Strategic direction for MDF identified the need to further up skill staff
program officers and volunteers and provide gender equality in MCASP on the
plateau.

‘This report is written and submitted to the Bourd of MDF, PWM and Donor and the

the one week Strategic Planning workshop identified to enable board members of
MDF to improve its governance within it’s organizational and program
implementations. Most importantly this report contains the Vision/ Mission Statement
Core Values and Beliefs, Goals and Culture of MDE.
